title: Yucktober: Morning team tries Bangor Fire Department’s Strombi dish
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The WABI Morning Show tried Strombi Friday morning, a dish that has been a Bangor Fire Department staple for decades.
WABI General Manager Kim Petry, whose father, Larry Sherman, was a firefighter, prepared the dish for the crew Friday morning.
The Bangor Fire Department started making the dish in the 1960s. It was a meal firefighters cooked frequently, but it eventually became too expensive and became something only cooked for special occasions.
The dish was originally served like a sloppy joe sandwich. It has since evolved, and other ingredients can be added as well, like Tabasco sauce.
Recipe
- 1 pound of hamburger
- 1 onion
- 2 green peppers
- 1 block Velveeta cheese
- Garlic powder, salt and pepper

title: Breezy and bright with a dry weekend on deck
text:
Hard freeze tonight with the weekend warming up
Winds ease and skies remain clear ...for awhile!
Hard freeze tonight with the weekend warming up
Winds ease and skies remain clear ...for awhile!
We’ll finish the workweek with sunshine and a cool breeze in Maine. Friday’s highs reach the lower 50s, with north winds of 10 to 15 mph gusting to 25 to 30 mph. The wind eases tonight as temperatures fall into the lower to mid-20s under clear skies.
Our weekend brings lighter winds and a gradual warmup. Saturday’s temperatures climb into the mid- to upper 50s, followed by upper 50s to lower 60s Sunday. Both days look sunny, though overnight readings dip into the mid- to upper 20s Saturday night before holding near freezing Sunday night.
Monday delivers the warmest afternoon of this stretch, with highs in the mid-60s and plenty of sun. Clouds begin to increase that night as temperatures settle into the mid-30s.
The milder air won’t last. We drop back into the lower 50s Tuesday and hover around 50 Wednesday, with sunshine both days. Overnight lows return to the 20s before Thursday brings a mix of clouds and sun and afternoon readings in the mid-50s.

title: Justice Department sues over Dan Sullivan
text:
Justice Department sues over Dan Sullivan
Justice Department sues over Dan Sullivan
The Justice Department under President Trump is suing to block Alaska from certifying its election, citing concerns over voter confusion caused by two candidates with the same name.
The dispute involves Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is running for reelection against Democrat Mary Peltola, and another candidate named Dan Sullivan, an independent, who is also on the ballot.
Republicans argue that the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan could confuse voters and cost Sen. Dan Sullivan votes.
The Justice Department is seeking to prevent Alaska from certifying the election if Democrats and the independent Dan Sullivan remain on the ballot.
The case will now be taken up by a federal court. Alaska's Supreme Court has already rejected an effort to remove the independent Dan Sullivan from the ballot. The case will now be taken up by a federal court.

title: InvestigateTV+ Weekend: Billion Dollar Blitz
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Fans pack the stands and coaches cash in. Chris Nakamoto found an increasing part of the bill is landing on students and universities.
Plus, accountability disappears online when a company vanishes the second something goes wrong.
Billion Dollar Blitz
Here’s a number that might make your jaw drop: $12.8 billion. That’s what 109 public universities are spending on college athletics, and each year it’s taking a bigger bite out of public universities’ coffers and students’ pockets.
At the same time, football coaches’ salaries are skyrocketing, and it’s not just head coaches. Our team looked at contracts across America and found 31 assistant coaches are making more than $1 million.
National Investigative Reporter Chris Nakamoto went to Auburn, where fans reacted to one fired coach after another walk out the door. A sports economist with decades of experience said this system is not sustainable.
Meanwhile, Congress is looking to pump the brakes on this runaway spending - particularly in football.
Sports fan questions merchandise
When your team wins big, it’s natural to want to celebrate – maybe even grab some gear to mark the moment. But online shoppers are finding out that not every website selling that gear is what it claims to be – especially the moment a popular product sells out everywhere else.
One Michigan fan found that out after trying to buy his team’s championship gear online.
Reporter Tammy Elliott shows us what showed up at his door – and why getting his money back wasn’t easy.
Injuries take mental toll on athletes
For athletes, an injury doesn’t just sideline the body – it can take a toll on the mind, too. Doctors say stress, fear and even depression are common during recovery – but often go unspoken in a sport built on toughness.
At Clemson, football players and sports psychologists are opening up about what really happens when an athlete can’t play. Reporter Kari Beal in South Carolina takes us inside their journey back – mentally and physically.
Lunch options for your student
Sending kids to school with lunch means thinking about the budget, too. The average packed lunch now runs about $6 a day, according to Deloitte.
But Susan Campbell found families have more options than they might think – whether they’re packing or buying. She breaks down the real numbers, and some ways to bring that cost down.

title: Crucial products for Maine's agricultural industries will be exempt from tariffs, Sen. Collins says
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Crucial products for Maine's agricultural industries will be exempt from tariffs, Sen. Susan Collins says
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, announced Friday that nine categories of products, which she said are crucial for Maine's agricultural industries, will be exempted from U.S. tariffs on Canada amid the ongoing trade war between the neighboring countries.
The categories of products receiving tariff exemptions include plastic boxes and crates; plastic packing bags; refrigeration and freezing equipment; packing and wrapping machinery; paperboard cartons and boxes; seaweed and algae products for human consumption; non-adhesive plates, sheets, film, foil and strip; agricultural machinery for cleaning, sorting and grading; and machinery for filling, sealing, closing and labeling.
Collins said the exemptions will benefit Maine businesses and farms that produce blueberries, potatoes, apples and seaweed.
“These producers are a vital part of our state's economy and support our rural and coastal communities. Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," Collins said in a statement.
The latest round of exemptions followed continued conversations between Collins and Trump administration officials, including U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
“In my repeated conversations with Ambassador Greer, Secretary Lutnick, and other senior administration officials, I have asked for tariff relief for these important products and stressed the burdens additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families," Collins said.
Last month, Collins worked to get the Trump administration to exempt road salt, cement and pulp from the list of tariffed items from Canada.
Collins is running for her sixth term in the U.S. Senate and her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, has been critical of the senator throughout his campaign, claiming Collins is not doing enough as chair of appropriations to stop tariffs.
“I would just think that someone that is the most powerful senator in the United States Senate would be able to do more than get us road salt back,” Jackson said last month.
On Friday, Jackson said Collins begs for relief from chaos she helped create.
"Trump’s trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire," Jackson said in a statement to Maine's Total Coverage. "Mainers needed help long before Susan Collins needed saving. But apparently, families struggling to pay their bills wasn’t enough of an emergency. Her losing her job is."
Collins said she will continue working directly with the Trump administration to seek additional relief from tariffs.

title: Why walking is a step toward healthy aging
text:
(Aging Untold) — Walking is one of the simplest tools we have for healthy aging, and the benefits add up even in short bursts.
The Aging Untold hosts break down how to make every step count, why muscle loss happens faster than most people realize, and why using a walker or cane is nothing to be embarrassed about.
Start small, stay consistent
“Steps count by just doing it. You’ve just got to jump in and do it. You don’t have to go out and run a marathon. You just start small and just start moving,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Rogers said walking reflects the health of the entire body — it draws on muscle strength, balance, heart health and oxygenation.
“So how many times you see people — how far can they walk, that distance when they start gasping for breath? That’s oxygenation. That’s heart health,” Rogers said. “What about these people with chronic lung diseases like COPD and all that? They need that oxygenation. That’s one of the first signs you see in them — their ability to walk.”
Rogers said gait, or the way someone walks, can also be a clue to neurological issues.
“That can be a clue that something else is going on in your body,” she said. “It’s your body’s report card.”
Rogers cited a randomized trial showing that people who did aerobic exercise three times a week for 40 minutes increased their hippocampal volume, the brain’s memory center.
“So walking, all that, is more than just an exercise — that’s a ‘brain-cize,’” she said.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said the idea of hitting 10,000 steps a day can feel overwhelming, but it doesn’t have to be the goal.
“I like to tell people consistency beats intensity,” O’Rourke said. “If you can’t walk or have difficulty walking, try just lifting your knees up from the chair, maybe walking to the front door and back, maybe walking for five minutes, 10 minutes and just extending the amount of time.”
O’Rourke suggested turning walking into a friendly challenge.
“Maybe it is that you set up a competition with somebody to say, let’s take a walk and see how far we can walk, and then keep track of how many miles you’re building up,” she said. “But don’t start too big, because you’ll set yourself up for failure.”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck also advised pacing walks so there’s enough energy to get back.
“When you’re going out and you’re going to see how far you can walk, make sure that you can walk back,” Cradduck said.
Muscles weaken faster than people expect
Cradduck said muscle loss can happen quickly, even in healthy older adults.
“I don’t think people realize just how quickly muscles atrophy,” Cradduck said. “You take somebody that’s a little older and they go into the hospital and they’re bedbound for a week in the hospital for a urinary tract [infection], and then all of a sudden they’re not able to walk.”
Cradduck said people who are unable to walk should still try to keep their legs moving, such as with foot or leg pumps.
She added that walking also supports cognition because it requires multiple coordinated steps in the brain.
“There’s a lot of brain steps in taking a step,” she said. “The foot has to move a certain way, and the leg has to move a certain way. The balance has to happen.”
For people who are immobile, Rogers said placing their legs on a vibrating plate can help.
“Really it’s about circulation,” she said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said mobility is tied to independence.
“Just think of mobility as freedom,” she said. “It gives you your independence, your ability to move.”
Don’t let pride stand in the way of using a walker
Ths hosts said strength and fitness training help maintain walking ability over time, and that avoiding long periods of sitting matters too.
“Every hour, get up,” O’Rourke said. “If you’re working, get up, take a walk. Even standing up, sitting down — just start somewhere.”
Cradduck said fear of falling, including concerns about hip fractures, often causes people to stop walking altogether — which can do more harm.
“I will tell anyone: use a walker, use a support system,” Cradduck said. “It is no different than me having glasses on my face right now so I can see. This is something that I need as an aide. A walker, if that keeps you moving and keeps you going, and it keeps your brain healthy, keeps your heart healthy, and it keeps you from falling, don’t be embarrassed by it.”
Cradduck said people are more likely to draw sympathy from inactivity than from using mobility aids.
“People are going to feel sorry for you when you’re lying in the bed, unable to move — not when you’re walking around using a walker for safety,” she said.
Ambrose said the stigma around walkers is often self-imposed. Her 12-year-old grandson had his birthday party at a roller-skating rink in Chicago and kids used PVC pipe skating aids that resembled walkers.
“So they’re using it as tools,” Ambrose said. “I like to say we’re an evolved species. We’re supposed to use tools. We wear eyeglasses when we need them. We wear hearing aids when we need them, and we use walkers, wheelchairs, walking sticks — whatever we need, when we need them.”
O’Rourke said pride and ego often get in the way.
“I think pride gets in the way, ego gets in the way, and you can see it when someone’s not using a walker and they’re afraid of falling,” she said. “They’re almost putting themselves at risk for falling more. They do more harm.”
Ambrose also said home environment matters for staying active, especially during bad weather.
“Think about your environment,” she said. “What can I do so I can walk inside my home? Or if you moved to independent living, you can walk hallways. So think about where you live — that’s going to matter too.”
Key takeaways
- Strength training protects your walking gait.
- Mobility aids are tools, not weaknesses. Walkers, canes and wheelchairs support independence and safety, similar to glasses or hearing aids.
- Consistency beats intensity. Keep moving by turning chores into exercise.
- Stand up hourly and park farther away to prevent rapid muscle atrophy.

title: At Acadia, a missing Wabanaki marker and the fight over what national parks should tell
text:
In the soft light of dawn, an Ohio tourist studied the interpretive sign at the summit of Cadillac Mountain in Acadia National Park, reading about how magma formed the ground under her feet.
There is one sign she and the other 4 million-plus tourists who visit Acadia annually can no longer see at the summit: a marker explaining the mountain’s sacred significance to the Wabanaki people in the region. “Today, visitors from everywhere find meaning on the mountain,” it said.
It was among 30 markers removed from Acadia under a Trump administration campaign to strip national parks of materials deemed disparaging to American history, according to the National Parks Conservation Association.
But when park staff took down the summit sign at the orders of Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, they also unraveled some of the trust that took decades to build between Acadia National Park and the Wabanaki people. The Wabanaki Confederacy, also known as “the people of the dawnland,” has inhabited the northern seaboard for over 10,000 years and was the first known stewards of land that includes much of the national park. It was a gathering place to trade, hunt, fish and pick sweetgrass.
Some of the signs removed from Acadia were developed over years of partnerships with organizations including Friends of Acadia, the Schoodic Institute and the Native Plant Trust — with consultation from citizens of the Wabanaki Nations. They know the mountain in Maine as Wapuwoc — “white mountain of the first light.” From October to March, it’s the first place to see the sunrise in the continental United States.
“Getting to a place where our language is in these parks and it is educational … erasing that or setting that back has big implications for how far we’ve come,” said Maulian Bryant, the Wabanaki Alliance’s executive director.
Bryant says the removed signs reflected “the good stuff.”
“These signs don’t say 96% of Wabanaki people died from smallpox, or there were 26 nations and now there’s four,” she said. “If we really want to get into the real history, that’s a whole other slice of cake.”
Other signs removed from Cadillac’s summit addressed issues of climate change, informing visitors that “Acadia’s future will be warmer and wetter” and that “In the last century, average annual precipitation has increased by six inches.”
During their tenure under the Biden administration, former National Park Service director Chuck Sams and former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland — the first Native Americans to hold these positions — aimed to reflect the experiences of all Americans throughout the national parks. Before leaving his post in February 2025, Sams saw parts of his work unraveled by the current administration.
This “attempt to rewrite history into a single narrative … is also counter to our democracy. And counter to the idea that we are a plural nation,” said Sams.
Lawsuit against national park removals advances
Now, a coalition of conservation, history and science organizations are fighting in court to get the Acadia signs and hundreds of other items put back. Under Burgum’s 2025 campaign, signs, books, films and exhibits covering topics such as slavery, climate change and the massacre of Native Americans were flagged and removed from national parks and monuments nationwide.
“Some of it’s been put back, and then some of it has been removed again,” said the Center for American Progress’ Angelo Villagomez. He was part of the progressive policy group’s team that examined a database leaked earlier this year and found that a third of national parks had flagged exhibits featuring history or science. Of those, Black and Indigenous history were most targeted.
Portions of all flagged material have since been reviewed and cataloged by a committee led by Joy Beasley, a National Park Service associate director. However, in a June affidavit, she writes that the spreadsheet is “unlikely to capture every removal, revision, or replacement.”
The Interior Department did not respond to The Associated Press’ questions about the current status of sign and exhibit removal or the ongoing lawsuit filed by the nonprofit coalition in February against the federal government.
The parks “are America’s storytellers,” said Todd Martin of the National Parks Conservation Association, a plaintiff in the lawsuit. “It’s their duty to preserve and interpret American history, the good, the bad, and the ugly.”
Jenny McBurney, a government publications librarian at the University of Minnesota who co-founded the project Save Our Signs, feels it’s more important than ever for park visitors to document revised signs.
“People are going to go to the parks and think that they will get to learn history there when in fact they will be learning an incomplete history,” said McBurney.
Wabanaki culture — past and present — shared in Acadia
Despite the job cuts, threats of land reduction, talks of privatization and even demolition within some parks, Indigenous groups and park partners have persevered.
In Maine, members of the Wabanaki Confederacy — comprised of the Maliseet, Mi’kmaq, Passamaquoddy, Penobscot and Abenaki principal nations — carry on the cultural traditions and spiritual practices that helped them maintain sovereignty and connection to their ancestral land after settlers arrived. That includes sharing their culture with tourists.
Penobscot Nation citizen Jennifer Neptune had mixed emotions about the attempted erasure of her people from Acadia and their ancestral homeland.
“It’s hard to get good signage in national monuments, in national parks,” said Neptune. “It’s a real gut punch when it (removal) happens, not just for Indigenous people, but for Black people, for the people whose stories don’t get shared.”
Over the past decade, she’s seen real change from the National Park Service, playing an integral part in bringing Wabanaki voices to the table to create Indigenous-designed spaces.
In partnership with Acadia, the privately owned Abbe Museum, which is largely overseen by Wabanaki people, hosts a program that brings Native voices into the park through music, arts and culture.
Nick Bear and members of a Wabanaki drum circle perform on Cadillac Mountain annually as part of this collaboration. “That’s just like bringing those ceremonies right back to the original sites,” he said.
In July, Passamaquoddy basket maker Lydia Soctomah demonstrated traditional Wabanaki basketry using pounded ash bark and sweetgrass outside the Sieur de Monts Nature Center. Both the ash tree and sweetgrass are part of the Wabanaki creation story, she said.
“Making a basket is worth 1,000 memories for me,” said Soctomah, whose grandmother was a well-known basket maker. “I was always told it holds a part of your spirit.”
Sweetgrass access an example of shared stewardship
Access to sweetgrass has long been difficult for Wabanaki people as they were pushed from coastal lands onto reservations. In Acadia, it’s been nearly nonexistent since the park’s creation in 1916. But over the past decade, park staff and Wabanaki members have collaborated to change that.
In 2017, scientist Suzanne Greenlaw, a citizen of the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, partnered with the U.S. Forest Service, Acadia’s Schoodic Institute and 14 traditional gatherers to conduct a Wabanaki-led sweetgrass study in hopes of allowing tribal access.
“It was really impactful because we had never had those kinds of co-stewardship relationships,” said Greenlaw, adding that those relationships, built over time, have not changed.
By the end of the Biden administration, there were over 400 co-stewardship or co-management agreements with tribes, 159 within the National Park Service alone, says Sams. Programs in Acadia were among them.
These programs, he says, allow tribes to fulfill their obligation to protect, preserve and enhance natural resources, and the federal government to fulfill its obligation to allow tribal access for hunting, fishing, and gathering foods and medicines.
Sams cautiously hopes there will be a rebuilding period for the park service under the next administration.
“There are always ebbs and flows with every administration,” he said. “Nobody has seen that more than American Indian tribes.”

title: Mom who survived school shooting comforts son during school shooting in Oregon
text:
BEND, Ore. (CNN) - Parents in Bend are comforting their children after last week’s deadly shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School. One mother said she understands what her son experienced because she survived a school shooting herself.
Michelle, whose last name was withheld, said she found out about Thursday’s shooting when her fifth-grade son called and texted her from his Apple Watch, saying there was a shooter.
In the text message, Michelle told her son everything would be OK. She also told him about her own history of surviving a school shooting.
Michelle was a freshman at Granite Hills High School in El Cajon, California, when a gunman opened fire in 2001. Two teachers and three students were wounded.
Michelle said she was always nervous when she dropped her sons off at school, even before last Thursday’s shooting.

title: Obituary: Cleora Mae “Perk” (Perkins) Vaillancourt Ramsay
text:
BRUNSWICK – Cleora Mae “Perk” (Perkins) Vaillancourt Ramsay, 92, of Bath, died Oct. 14, 2026, at HillHouse. Born March 4, 1934, in Dresden, daughter of George Winship Perkins and Alice O. (Lilly) Perkins, she was raised by her aunt and uncle, Mary and Milton Carlton.
A 1953 Morse High graduate, she married James J. “Chick” Vaillancourt in 1954; they had three children, Jim, Leon, and Ann. After Chick’s death in 1974 she married Robert W. “Bob” Ramsay in 1982.
For many years she ran “Perk’s Place” at C.W. Rogers, selling crafts and donated items to benefit Big Brothers Big Sisters of Bath/Brunswick. In recognition of her service the organization named its Perk Ramsay Acts of Service Award after her.
She was predeceased by her parents; her aunt and uncle, Mary and Milton Carlton; her sister, Marjorie Label; her brother, Robert Perkins; and her husbands, Chick Vaillancourt and Bob Ramsay.
She is survived by children, James J. Vaillancourt Jr. (Patricia), Leon J. Vaillancourt (Kelly), Ann Marie London (Eric); stepchildren, Robert T. Ramsay (Cheryl), Randy E. Ramsay, and Lori E. Rines (Mark); and several grandchildren and great-grandchildren.
Visiting hours are 9–10:30 a.m., Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026, at Desmond Funeral Home, Bath, followed by a celebration of life at 10:30 a.m. and burial at Oak Grove Cemetery at 11:30 a.m. Family and friends are invited to gather afterward at the Londons’ home, 250 Centre Street, Bath, at 12:30 p.m. for a light lunch.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to Big Brothers Big Sisters of Bath/Brunswick,
85 Maine Street,
Brunswick, ME 04011,
in honor of Perk’s long support of their youth mentoring programs.

title: Bangor’s public transit bus garage is about to get a nearly $10M upgrade
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bangor is gearing up to start construction on a nearly $10 million renovation project to its Community Connector bus storage facility, which will include the addition of a driver training center.
City officials hope the upgrade will make the outdated facility more functional and help with driver retention, which has been a persistent issue in Bangor and across the country. Until the transit system can get more drivers, it won’t be able to restore Saturday bus service.
The Planning Board approved a land development permit for the project earlier this month, but the renovation has been in the works for years.
Parts of the site at 511 Maine Ave. haven’t been renovated since it was built in the 1960s, according to Laurie Linscott, the city’s transit administrator. The building needs significant electrical work, and parts of the ceiling are falling down. An addition that was built in 2004 doesn’t need quite as much work, but it will get a new roof and other fixes to replace items that have reached the end of their useful life.
The city determined that it would be cheaper to repair the storage building than to tear it down and build a new one, Linscott said. She secured a nearly $8 million federal grant for the project in 2023, which covers most of the project costs. The city is also contributing about $1 million, and another $1 million comes from the Maine Department of Transportation.
The storage facility, which is more than 35,000 square feet, has had various uses over the years and once operated as a recycling center. Community Connector previously shared the space with the public works department, but took over both sides of the building for bus storage as the city’s public transit fleet has grown, Linscott said.
The renovation will help the transit agency clean buses more efficiently and add a new drive-through vehicle wash that can be used for city vehicles from across departments, Linscott said. That will have space for vehicles up to 16 feet tall, Peasley added.
The project will also set up the infrastructure for electric vehicle charging, Linscott said, as part of broader plans to transition to hybrid and electric buses.
The city plans to break ground on the renovation this winter and wrap up by late spring or early summer 2028, according to Hannah Peasley, a civil engineer for the city who’s working on the project. During the construction, buses will be stored in a nearby space owned by the airport.
That work will include building a more than 6,000 square foot addition on the side of the building to house a new training center with a 40-student classroom, a break room, bathrooms, bus dispatch, offices and lockers for the city’s bus drivers, Peasley said. Those are all amenities that the current bus storage facility lacks.
The addition is intended to help with driver retention and increase training capacity, according to Linscott. The new facility will have dedicated space for ongoing annual driver training that is usually held elsewhere, in space borrowed from other city departments. It also gives the city the option to hold commercial driver’s license training in house.
Bangor, like many cities nationwide, has struggled with a driver shortage for years. A 2023 report by the American Public Transportation Association found that 96% of surveyed transit agencies were experiencing a workforce shortage.
The training for a commercial driver’s license is a lengthy process, and drivers often leave public transit jobs for higher-paying work in the private sector. Transit agencies also have an aging workforce, with a significantly higher average age than U.S. workers more broadly, according to data from the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics.
“If we need to, we will,” Linscott said of the possibility that the city would offer commercial driver’s license training in the new facility, but she added that she also recently got a state grant to offer that training through a partnership with Eastern Maine Community College.
That partnership could be “a way of getting us over the hump to get some more drivers and get Saturday service back,” Linscott said. She hopes to fill that class by January, which could produce more drivers by July.
Bangor City Council also approved more than $100,000 in this year’s budget to transition some bus drivers to full-time status, which could also help address staffing challenges. That transition will likely be implemented in January, Linscott said.

title: DSA’s rise puts left flank at center of Democrats’ 2026 fight
text:
NEW YORK (Gray Media) - As Democrats hope to secure a majority in one, potentially both chambers of Congress, the rise of their left flank is in focus.
Democratic Socialists of America say they’re fighting for a democracy powered by everyday people, not capitalists. DSA members are now some of the most prominent voices in the Democratic Party, occupying roles from the Halls of Congress to the mayor’s mansion in New York City.
“For a long time, they were completely irrelevant,” said Lincoln Mitchell, a political expert at Columbia University. Mitchell says the organization’s roots trace back to the 1960s, but it only recently became a major player on the national stage.
“What DSA has done powerfully is to center working people and to center poor people in the story of urban America,” Mitchell said.
Sen. Bernie Sanders is often credited with igniting democratic socialism over the last decade. Mitchell says Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani brought the DSA into the mainstream by defeating established Democratic politicians.
“Among people today who are under 40 years old, socialism isn’t a bad word,” Mitchell said.
The duo uncovered an appetite for youthful energy combined with policies catering to American workers. The DSA and adjacent candidates are having a strong 2026. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed hopes to become the first Muslim U.S. Senator. A handful of House candidates are primed to win and grow the movement’s numbers in Washington. And figures like AOC and Mamdani rank as two of the most powerful endorsements in the election cycle.
“The energy is on the DSA left, and that is for certain,” Mitchell said.
The election on November 3rd will tell us a lot about not just the next two years, but potentially the next decade. The Democratic Socialists of America are a big part of the evolving political landscape, and they hope to be for a long time.

title: Patriots battle through injuries, but time runs out against Bears
text:
The Patriots’ three-game winning streak is over after they ran out of time and luck in their 30-24 loss to the Chicago Bears on Thursday night.
However, with New England dealing with multiple injuries, including two starters on the offensive line, coach Mike Vrabel left Soldier Field feeling disappointed in the outcome, but not about the resolve of his team going forward.
“We fought. I would say that we need to (force opponents to) turn the ball over and tackle better and those are fundamental skills. But I like the way they competed and we certainly gave ourselves a chance,” Vrabel said.
With left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) joining right guard Mike Onwenu (ankle) on injured reserve this week, the Patriots went with recent addition Matt Pryor and Walter Rouse in their place. Quarterback Drake Maye was sacked twice, but the 10th different offensive line combination the Patriots have used this season held up well.
Maye completed 24 of 31 passes for 321 yards and two TDs and a rushing score. After the loss he put the onus on himself to make better decisions, namely his costly second-quarter interception in the end zone when he was trying to complete a pass to tight end Eli Raridon. The Bears scored on their ensuing drive to take a 20-7 lead.
“I thought we battled the environment well,” Maye said. “And I thought we did some good things but didn’t execute at a high enough level to win.”
What’s working
Despite the loss, New England’s offense didn’t show much regression. Maye had the one interception, but it was on a pass in the red zone.
What needs help
The running game took a step back. The Patriots entering the game averaging 130.7 rushing yards per game, but gained just 70 on the ground Thursday. Though they were playing catch-up for most of the night, it made the offense a lot more predictable in the second half, allowing the Bears to drop more players into coverage.
Stock up
Running back Rhamondre Stevenson. He finished with five catches for 93 yards, including pulling in a short pass from Maye and rumbling 48 yards for a touchdown on the final play of the first half to cut Chicago’s lead to 20-14. It was his fifth career career TD reception.
Stock down
Rookie edge rusher Gabe Jacas. New England trailed 13-7 in the second quarter when Bears quarterback Caleb Williams connected on a pass with Luther Burden for a 22-yard gain. Jacas was called for roughing the passer for an extremely late hit on Williams. It added an additional 15 yards to give Chicago the ball on the New England 33. The Bears scored five plays later on a 24-yard TD pass from Williams to Burden.
Injuries
Safety Kevin Byard departed after he was checked out by trainers with 9:44 left in the second quarter before returning. Defensive tackle Christian Barmore departed late in the game with an undisclosed ailment.
Key number
Minus-7 — That’s the Patriots turnover differential through seven games. Only Indianapolis (minus-8 through six games) is worse.
Next steps
The Thursday night game gives the Patriots a little extra time to rest and prepare before visiting Miami on Nov. 1.

title: Everest Recovery Centers expands access to recovery services in Hancock County
text:
ELLSWORTH — Everest Recovery Centers in Ellsworth is now open and treating new patients. The clinic provides outpatient treatment for opioid use disorder.
Everest Recovery Centers new facility is located at 190 Bangor Road. They look forward to improving access to opioid addiction treatment services in Hancock County. This is Everest Recovery’s fourth clinic in Maine and fifth overall.
“People in Hancock County deserve access to high-quality opioid-use disorder treatment without having to travel long distances,” Heather Camara, CEO of Everest Recovery, said. “The opening of our clinic in Ellsworth helps ensure that residents in Downeast Maine can access life-saving treatment where they live, work and raise their families.”
The opening of an opioid treatment center in Ellsworth addresses a well-documented need for accessible substance use disorder treatment in Downeast Maine. More than 8% of residents in the Downeast Maine region are estimated to be living with a substance use disorder. For many individuals in Hancock County and surrounding communities, accessing treatment has historically required lengthy travel to larger population centers. By bringing evidence-based medication-assisted treatment, counseling and recovery support services directly to Ellsworth, patients can receive care closer to home, reducing barriers that often delay or prevent treatment.
Research shows that medication-assisted treatment reduces illicit opioid-use, decreases overdose risk, improves employment and family stability, and helps individuals remain engaged in long-term recovery. Expanding access to these services supports not only individual recovery, but also healthier families, a stronger workforce, and a safer community.
Everest Recovery Centers is a company led by seasoned veterans with over 25 years of experience in the opioid treatment industry. Everest Recovery provides proven treatment for adults struggling with opioid addiction. Services include medication-assisted treatment, diagnostic assessment, recurrence prevention and support groups, addiction education, counseling and more.

title: Some Maine farm supplies now exempt from U.S. tariffs on Canada
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MAINE (WABI) - Nine categories of of products used in Maine agricultural industries are now exempt from U.S. tariffs on Canada.
Senator Susan’s Collins’ office announced Friday that seaweed and algae products as well as numerous materials commonly used to harvest and ship Maine-grown products like like blueberries, potatoes, and apples will now be exempt.
Agricultural cleaning, sorting, and grading machinery is included among the exemptions as well as numerous materials and equipment used for packing and shipping items long distances.
Collins credits the change to her continued conversations with trade and commerce officials within the Trump administration.
The Maine Democratic Party is critical of the change, citing a Wall Street Journal article before the official announcement saying President Trump was planning the exemptions to help Collins in her re-election bid.

title: Central Maine Ghost Hunters take on historically haunted Vassalboro mill
text:
VASSALBORO, Maine (WABI) - What’s Halloween without a haunting?
Searching for the unseen is the specialty of Central Maine Ghost Hunters, a team of about 10 that has ventured into places others would run from for over a decade.
“I’ve had experiences growing up and I watched the shows,” explained Dustin Marcia, founder and lead investigator. “I said, ‘I can probably do this.’ So I said, ‘Let’s try it,’ talked to a buddy of mine, let’s try it, see what we can do. And sure enough, it’s come here.”
Along with house calls, the crew visits supposedly haunted locations. WABI joined them on their investigation into the old American Woolen Company Mill in Vassalboro.
Local man Ray Breton bought the property for $35,500 in 2010.
“Late 1700s, the wooden building burned, and then, so they started with putting brick buildings up. So, the wings are all different. They’re dated almost for every war there was,” Breton described. “The building you walk through, the wing here is 1850. This wing here, once you walk through the brick causeway, this is 1917, First World War.”
He says as the mill was considered the largest on the Eastern Seaboard, employment peaked at about 500 people. With that, many accidents had been logged over the years, including 33 drownings over 100 years, electrocutions, and someone allegedly being pushed down the elevator shaft.
Over the years, Breton says one spirit has made himself especially noticeable. Called “The Captain,” an old man wearing what looks to be a captain’s hat can be seen in the back of photographs and first-hand accounts.
To speak with spirits, Central Maine Ghost Hunters use electromagnetic sensors, lights, radio waves and bells to reach the other side.
Despite the name, they say they’re more in the business of helping ghosts rather than hunting them.
“People need help and we try to help people. Even if they don’t have anything at their homes, at least give them a peace of mind,” Marcia said. “And we try to, if we can, try to help the spirits move on.“
On Saturday, you can get an inside look at a hunt yourself!
Saturday from 6 p.m. to 11 p.m., Central Maine Ghost Hunters are inviting the public to the Giberson Funeral Home in Bingham for a meet and greet before a 4-hour investigation of the building.

title: Melania Trump helps forge a ceasefire deal in Russian-occupied Oleshky
text:
Melania Trump helps forge a ceasefire deal in a Russian-occupied Ukrainian city, White House says
First lady Melania Trump has brokered an upcoming ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the war-ravaged Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid and the evacuation of civilians, the White House announced on Friday.
The localized ceasefire is set to begin on Oct. 29, with the American first lady saying in a news release that the situation there is “on the brink of disaster.”
The White House said Melania Trump had initiated the discussions and that she and a representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the ceasefire.
Related video: Melania Trump on new women's health NIH division
Ukraine’s lead negotiator for the agreement thanked Melania Trump for her involvement and said the deal would be “extremely challenging to implement.”
“Under our agreement: first a ceasefire will be put in place; second, humanitarian aid will be delivered to Oleshky; and third, civilians will be allowed to move freely out of Oleshky,” Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, said in a video message posted online. “The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement. I will therefore keep Ukrainian society informed and share the results of the operation.”
Russia’s chief of the general staff, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, said Russian forces “will cease fire on the Kherson axis” starting at 4 a.m. Tuesday Moscow time “in connection with the humanitarian operation near Oleshky.” The Russian forces will also carry out “engineering reconnaissance” and ensure “safe movement of the humanitarian convoy” into the city, Gerasimov said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov also said Moscow was grateful to the first lady and that effort was discussed during the latest call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and President Donald Trump, he said.
Peskov said "those who want to leave it would be able to do so.” He would not say whether those who evacuate will be taken to Russia- or Ukraine-held territory. He also demurred when asked how long the evacuation will last, saying only it would likely take several days.
Melania Trump has made helping children in conflict one of her signature issues and hosted a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year. She has written Putin to work on efforts to reunite families with children who have been displaced by the war.
“What she wants to do is save children, and that’s her focus,” the president said of the first lady during a question-and-answer exchange with journalists in Washington.
Tensions between Washington, Kyiv are rising
The development comes as tensions have increased to new highs between the Trump administration and Ukraine’s government. Kyiv has faced restrictions on the satellite internet system that it relies on to knock down Russian attacks, with Trump and other top U.S. officials sending mixed messages about who was responsible for throttling the Elon Musk-made Starshield system.
Trump also has recently waived new Russian sanctions, reached an agreement with Russia to import diesel and pushed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make a deal to end the war that began in February 2022. In renewed efforts to revive the peace process, Trump envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Norway this week for talks with Zelenskyy before meeting with Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Zelenskyy did not mention the ceasefire in Oleshky during a remote appearance at the Hudson Institute, a Washington think tank. He did note that American Patriot missile interceptors were still on hold and Starshield and Starlink speed limits were still in place.
He also spoke of the importance of the United States to renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war, including a possible joint meeting with Trump and Putin.
Dire situation in Oleshky
Food and medical supplies have been scarce for months in Oleshky, which sits on the Dnipro River that separates Ukrainian forces from the city’s Russian occupiers. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Roads leading from town are mined and dotted with burned-out cars. Drones buzz overhead.
Once a city of about 24,000 residents, Oleshky was captured by Moscow’s forces on the first day of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned, and its infrastructure damaged. In June 2023, floodwaters inundated the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed from an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed.
Those left in the city along Ukraine’s southeastern front face death from hunger or disease as another harsh winter looms. Ukraine has appealed repeatedly for a local ceasefire to organize evacuations. Russia, as the occupying power, is obligated by international law to ensure civilians under its control have what they need to survive.
Melania Trump details the mission
Melania Trump said in the White House news release that civilian leaders from Ukraine and Russia will visit Oleshky residents to determine the level of assistance they require.
“Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination,” she said. “I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine.”
Melania Trump also said “an impartial American media organization” will accompany and document Russian and Ukrainian teams on the ground throughout the process.
"This will play a significant role in ensuring that the wishes of each family are faithfully respected,” she said.
The statement did not identify the media organization.

title: Devils acquire US Olympic goalie Connor Hellebuyck in a trade
text:
New Jersey Devils acquire US Olympic goalie Connor Hellebuyck in a trade with the Winnipeg Jets
A deal with the Devils ended the lingering saga of Connor Hellebuyck in Winnipeg.
Hellebuyck finally has a new home with New Jersey after the Jets granted the three-time Vezina Trophy winning goaltender's trade request on Friday.
The Devils sent forward Dawson Mercer, goalie Nico Daws, prospect Alexander Command, a 2029 second-round pick, a 2027 seventh-rounder and long-term injured forward Nick Bjugstad to Winnipeg for Hellebuyck.
"It really does come down to what teams are willing to do and willing to pay," Jets general manager Kevin Cheveldayoff said at a news conference in Winnipeg. "It's not necessarily what I got. It was more like what other teams were willing to pay."
The long-awaited, blockbuster trade ends months of speculation, a failed bid to move the U.S. Olympic gold medal winner and 2024-25 NHL MVP in June, and the Jets' suspension of Hellebuyck for failing to report to training camp in a standoff that required the involvement of the league and the Players' Association.
"It certainly hasn't been fun," Cheveldayoff said. "Connor made his choice to do how he chose to do it. And, as an organization, we had to act accordingly and we did. He asked for a trade. We told him we would do our best to make it happen. And if it happens whatever months ago when he first asked, we would have done it then. Unfortunately it took to this time now."
The 33-year-old Hellebuyck, who backstopped the U.S. to Olympic gold at the Milan-Cortina Games in February, leaves Winnipeg after spending his entire 11-year career there. Hellebuyck joins Jack Hughes, who scored in overtime of the final to defeat Canada, with the Devils and immediately puts them closer to being a Stanley Cup contender.
When training camp opened, new Devils general manager Sunny Mehta said he was very comfortable with the team's goaltending situation. Since then, Daws and Jake Allen combined for an .880 save percentage, which ranks 23rd among 32 teams.
"When Sunny got serious, he got serious real quick," Cheveldayoff said. "There was no beating around the bush with each other. We kind of laid our cards on the table and said this is what it's going to take."
It was not immediately clear how soon Hellebuyck might be ready to play for his new team. He has been skating in his home state of Michigan while trade talks were ongoing.
Hellebuyck has five seasons left on a seven-year contact with an annual salary cap hit of $8.5 million. He leaves the Central Division for the Metropolitan, much to the delight of rivals who will see him less often moving forward.
"I don't mind," Colorado coach Jared Bednar said. "You knew he was getting traded at some point. You just didn't know where. To see him go to Jersey doesn't hurt my feelings."
He becomes the latest high-profile American to depart Canada for the United States. In June, Ottawa dealt captain Brady Tkachuk to Florida, where he joined his brother Matthew. In December, Vancouver traded star defenseman Quinn Hughes, a brother of Jake and teammate Luke, to Minnesota.
The process to trade Hellebuyck became messy, especially after the goalie went public with his request to leave Winnipeg in September. The Jets suspended the goalie for failing to report for camp in a disciplinary move that extended into the season with Hellebuyck not getting paid.
The length of suspension became an issue with the league and union determining Hellebuyck would be allowed to rejoin the Jets on Friday. Instead, a move to New Jersey materialized ahead of Winnipeg hosting the outdoor Heritage Classic this weekend.
"Certainly wish I could have done it five or four months ago — whatever when the opportunity first started," Cheveldayoff said. "We were looking, but here we are."
The post-Hellebuyck plans went into motion over the summer, signing Stuart Skinner in free agency. The Jets claimed Clay Stevenson off waivers before the season began, and their combined .907 save percentage is seventh-best in the NHL.
Cheveldayoff said the plan is to carry three goaltenders for now.
The Jets were second-guessed for not dealing Hellebuyck in June, when teams had more options to prioritize salary cap space to make room to acquire the goalie. The Sabres were among the teams expressing interest in Hellebuyck, and were preparing to package a deal that included swapping first-round draft picks — Buffalo had the No. 4 selection, and Winnipeg had the eighth.
The challenge for Winnipeg became finding a willing trade partner to acquire a goalie with a high price tag and a lengthy contract well after most teams had set their rosters and had little salary cap space to work with.
"A goalie market is a little bit of a different market," Cheveldayoff said. "You find out who has legitimate interests. You find out who has legitimate needs. You go through the process of what assets they have within their organization, and more importantly, what assets they are willing to move."
Another question mark involved Hellebuyck's age and track record of following regular-season success with a spotty playoff record.
After Hellebuyck went 9-8 in leading the Jets to the Western Conference finals in his playoff debut in 2018, he has gone 15-26 since since, with the Jets advancing to the second round just twice in their next six playoff appearances. In four first-round exits, Hellebuyck had a combined 5-15 record.
The disparity of regular season vs. postseason success was evident in 2024-25. Leading Winnipeg to the Presidents' Trophy and winning the Hart Trophy as MVP, Hellebuyck recorded a career-best 47 wins, then went 6-7 in the playoffs as the Jets were eliminated in Dallas in the second round.
With a 345-208-55 regular-season record, Hellebuyck ranks 27th in career wins on the NHL list, and fifth among U.S.-born players. Among U.S.-born goalies with 300 or more career starts, his .916 save percentage ranks fourth and 2.58 goals-against average ranks sixth.
___
AP Sports Writer Pat Graham in Denver contributed to this report.

title: Daycare operator arrested after viral video seemingly shows kids fighting in her home
text:
SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WNDU/Gray News) - A daycare operator is facing charges after a viral video allegedly showed kids fighting inside her home in Indiana.
Tysharae Jones, 29, faces charges of battery with injury to a person under 14, neglect of a dependent resulting in bodily injury and contributing to the delinquency of a minor.
Police said the fight happened in June 2026. The special victims unit with the prosecutor’s office has been handling the case.
Even though the fight happened at Jones’ personal home and not at her South Bend daycare, prosecutors said she still has a duty to report what happened. This is because Indiana is a universal reporting state.
Indiana state code says every adult -- not just teachers, doctors, or police -- who suspects child abuse must report it to authorities. Failure to report is against the law and could lead to charges.
We are choosing to not share the viral video due to the nature of the contents.

title: With Gorham farm for sale, owner, employees reflect on 5 years
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
GORHAM — Erica Gottshalk sat clutching a steaming cup of coffee at a picnic table in Thursday morning’s crisp air. A lone chicken circled the Orchard Ridge Farm owner as customers stopped in the store behind her for breakfast sandwiches. A sprawl of pumpkins and a sign for apple picking enticed visitors to explore. She faced the patch of land where her home used to be.
Gottshalk and her husband, Will, announced Sunday that they will sell the 38-acre farm about nine months after a fire destroyed their family’s 1858 house on the property, prompting an outpouring of community support. They have put it on the market for nearly $1.7 million after five years of ownership.
Losing her home was not the primary reason she decided to move on, Gottshalk said. She said she has accomplished what she set out to do when she took over in 2021 — transforming the farm into a community space —but it has become too challenging to manage alone. She called the change bittersweet.
“As hard as it is to put that down and walk away, I realize that the amount of time and energy that it takes to do it all yourself is a little bit more than I have left in me, especially after the fire,” Gottshalk said.
Gottshalk has two children — a 3-year-old and 13-year-old — that she said she wants to spend more time with. They have rented houses in Gorham since the fire and intend to relocate to the Midcoast region to be closer to Will’s parents as Gottshalk contemplates her next career move.
A three-bedroom, chalet-style home is under construction at the back of the property for the new owner.
Buying the farm from Steve and Amy Bibula, the couple that added the orchard to the property, was a shared vision between Gottshalk, her sister, Kristen Walker, and their mother, Mary Walker. Kristen had a background in farming and Gottshalk came from the restaurant and hospitality industries. When Kristen decided to step away in 2023 and Mary reached retirement age, Gottshalk wasn’t ready to give up.
Starting a bagel and breakfast business, selling beer and wine, hosting events such as birthday parties and bridal showers, scheduling regular live music, adding picnic tables and a playground, bringing in more animals and diversifying the orchard’s fruit trees are on the list of what Gottshalk has done.
“It’s a place where people can kind of just come and enjoy, no matter what their background is, or socioeconomic situation, families can just come and not spend a dime,” Gottshalk said.
She said business has quadrupled in the past five years. Starting with no employees other than family members, the farm now has about 15 seasonal and eight year-round workers.
Beth Jourdan, an employee of four years who wears multiple hats at the farm, from bagel making to farming to building animal pens, said the staff has become like another family for her — one she will be sad to no longer see every day. She found the job when her then 8-year-old daughter became friends with Gottshalk’s son at school.
“My daughter came home from school and said, ‘My new best friend lives at Orchard Ridge,'” she said. “Erica and Orchard Ridge, in general, have been a great source of support and friendship.”
Becky Curtis has been a seasonal cook at the farm for four years, too.
“I love the regulars that come in,” Curtis said. “That’s probably my favorite part. And making sandwiches — I think when I die, they’re gonna put on my gravestone, ‘Here lies Becky, she made sandwiches.'”
Jourdan and Curtis said they are open to staying under new ownership, depending on the new owner’s plans. They said Gottshalk’s departure gives them an opportunity to reflect on their own next steps in life, too.
Gottshalk said she will miss the visitors she has seen pass through various life stages. Supportive messages flooded the farm’s social media pages after the announcement.
“Not only have you changed a farm into something special, you have transformed people,” one patron wrote on Facebook.
“We visited the farm before you owned it, but you really brought it to life. Thank you for cherished memories with our children,” another said.
“I am a little worried because I don’t know how much I’ll miss it,” Gottshalk said. “I’m worried about walking away and being like, ‘Oh my gosh, that was a really big part of my everyday.'”
She said she thinks there is still room for growth under a future owner, including adding spaces for weddings and larger events. Or, she said, someone could simply make it their new home.
The farm will stay open through the holidays if it is not sold before then.

title: Friday’s high school football: Cheverus routs Biddeford, earns playoff berth
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Nick Deschambault threw two touchdown passes in the first quarter, Colton Jewett rushed for two scores, and Cheverus secured a Class B South playoff berth with a 44-8 win over Biddeford on Friday night at Waterhouse Field in Biddeford.
Cheverus improved to 3-5 with its second straight win. Biddeford fell to 5-3 and missed out on a chance to secure a first-round bye.
A 66-yard yard run by Jackson Holmes set up an 8-yard touchdown pass from Deschambault to Sam Minervino on the Stags’ first drive. Deschambault then hit Holmes for a 35-yard touchdown pass just over two minutes later.
Will Baker scored on a 3-yard run and Jewett on a 31-yard run in the second quarter, before Ernie Dore got Biddeford on the board with a 2-yard run after throwing a 61-yard pass to Cameron Rowe.
Kevin True scored on a 6-yard run for Cheverus in the third quarter, Holmes kicked a 36-yard field goal, and Jewett scored on a 2-yard run in the fourth.
Jackson Holmes and Isaiah Hounchell each had an interception for Cheverus.
WESTBROOK 21, GORHAM 17: Cole Tanner rushed for more than 200 yards and three touchdowns in the first half, and the Blue Blazes (3-5) survived a late comeback by the visiting Rams (2-6) as they clinched a spot in the Class B South playoffs and eliminated Gorham.
Tanner raced 76 yards on the first play from scrimmage, then added a 1-yard TD run later in the first quarter and a 43-yard touchdown in the second as Westbrook built a 21-0.
Gorham’s Caleb Yaeger kicked a 30-yard field goal in the third quarter. Midway through the fourth, the Rams struck for two quick touchdowns. Wyatt Walker made it 21-11 with a 1-yard run and a 2-point conversion, and after Gorham recovered an onside kick, Isaac Vail scored on a 12-yard run around right end.
The Rams got the ball back at midfield with 3:36 left after a Westbrook punt, but the Blue Blazes eventually held on downs and ran out the clock.
GREELY 21, FALMOUTH 20: Jackson Justice scored the go-ahead touchdown in the third quarter, and a missed extra point in the fourth quarter proved costly for Falmouth (3-5) in a loss to visiting Greely (7-1).
Justice broke a 14-14 tie when he dove to catch a 5-yard pass from Luke Piper. Jack Carthy’s extra point gave Greely a 21-14 lead.
Falmouth had a chance to pull even midway through the fourth quarter when Harper Drosdik threw a 13-yard touchdown pass to Alex Hau on fourth-and-8, but a bad snap enabled Greely to block Theo Roediger extra-point kick.
Greely, ranked 10th in the Varsity Maine poll, did all of its scoring through the air as it twice rallied from deficits in the first half.
Falmouth’s Owen Ross opened the scoring with an 8-yard run, set up by a 47-yard pass from Micah Derrig to Dane Langelier.
The Rangers answered in the second quarter with a 20-yard halfback option pass from Justice to Rocky Axelsen. Derrig then threw a 12-yard TD pass to Hau, but Greely converted a fourth-and-15 gamble near midfield, then tied the game again on a 40-yard pass from Piper to Thomas Brown.
PORTLAND 33, DEERING 18: Alex Martin rushed for three touchdown, leading the Bulldogs (6-2) to a hard-fought win over the host Rams (1-7).
Martin scored on a 28-yard run in the first quarter and a 1-yard plunge from the Wildcat formation in the second. He made it 21-0 with a 4-yard run in the third quarter.
Deering fought back with three touchdowns in the second half including two TD pass by Anthony Profenno, who connected with Matt Ciampi (33 yards) and Nathan Foley (38 yards). Ciampi added a 1-yard scoring run.
Portland stayed in control, however, with the help of a 36-yard strike from Reece Wildes to Maddox Meas, and a 7-yard TD run by David Gomes.
FRYEBURG ACADEMY 48, SKOWHEGAN 32: Marcus Sutton ran 56 yards for a touchdown 19 seconds into the third quarter to give the Raiders (4-4) the lead, and they pulled away from the River Hawks (5-3) in a Class B North regular-season finale in Fryeburg.
Fryeburg earned its second straight win and will be the No. 4 seed in the upcoming playoffs. Skowhegan, which had a four-game winning streak snapped, is the No. 3 seed. Both teams will be at home in the quarterfinals next week.
Sutton threw a 22-yard pass to his brother, Darryl, with 25.2 seconds left in the second quarter to pull the Raiders within 24-20.
In the third quarter, Lars Bruhn returned an interception 45 yards for a score and Buk Awe ran 21 yards for a touchdown. Bruhn scored on a 33-yard run after an interception by Riley Hodges in the fourth quarter.
Austin Lancaster threw touchdown passes to Blake Kenyon (61 yards) and Matthew Keister (15 yards) and scored on a 14-yard run in the first half as Skowhegan built a 24-14 lead. Mike Stantze scored twice for Fryeburg in the first half on runs on 1 and 3 yards.
Lancaster threw a 20-yard touchdown pass to Kaden Pelletier in the fourth quarter.
OXFORD HILLS 34, NOBLE 14: The Vikings (6-1) used big plays to spark their offense in a Class A matchup against the Knights (3-5) in Paris.
Carter Davis had a 33-yard catch in the first quarter that set up the only touchdown in the first half — an 11-yard screen pass from Toby Oufiero to Mason Ridley.
Davis then opened the second half with a 95-yard kickoff return that made it 13-0. On the ensuing Noble drive, Tucker Hilden returned an interception 36 yards for a TD, extending the lead to 20-0.
Tristan Miniutti put Noble on the board when he reversed field on a 43-yard touchdown run.
Oufiero, though, found Davis for a 30-yard reception and scored on a 3-yard keeper on the next play for a 27-7 advantage.
Noble’s Mark LaPointe connected with Bryson McCormack for a 36-yard touchdown pass in the fourth quarter.
Ridley answered with a 34-yard TD reception from Oufiero.
MOUNTAIN VALLEY 26, POLAND 21: Colton Gallant ran for two scores as the Falcons (2-6) secured a postseason berth with a victory over the Knights (1-7) in a back-and-forth Class D South contest in Poland.
Mountain Valley moves into the sixth and final playoff spot in Class D South, while Poland’s season comes to an end.
Gallant scored the first touchdown on an 8-yard run in the opening quarter. Poland went ahead 14-6 on pair of second-quarter TDs on screen passes from Lucas Gayton — a 17-yarder to Christian Benson and an 8-yarder to Lucas Verrill. On both plays, the receivers weaved their way through traffic and into the end zone.
Early in the third quarter, Mountain Valley pass rusher Josh Pollis got into the backfield so quickly that he was able to tip Gayton’s pitch away just as it left the quarterback’s hand. Pollis picked up the fumble and ran 43 yards to the end zone, and Gallant’s 2-point conversion run tied the game.
An interception by Jimmy Arsenault set up Mountain Valley’s next score, a 24-yard TD run by Gallant. Benson answered for Poland with a 23-yard TD run, and Verrill’s kick gave Poland a 21-20 advantage.
Cole Curtis put the Falcons ahead for good with a 72-yard scamper late in the third quarter. Curtis also had an interception in the fourth.
A Falcons punt with 1:19 left gave the Knights the ball at their own 45. Big plays by Shawn West and Benson moved them near the red zone, but Mountain Valley’s Keygan Boucher knocked down a fourth-down pass to preserve the victory.

title: Fans camp out for first foldable iPhone
text:
(WSVN) - Customers waited outside the Apple store in Miami Beach as a line formed Wednesday morning for Apple’s new iPhone Duo, released Friday.
The iPhone Duo is the first foldable iPhone. The new design folds down to approximately the size of a passport.
When unfolded, the Duo becomes the largest iPhone display Apple has ever made.
The larger inner screen lets users run two apps side by side.
The departure from the iPhone’s standard design is what has so many eager to pick up the Duo.
Apple said it will have limited numbers for walk-in customers when it launches.
It also said online orders sold out in minutes, even pushing delivery times for some customers until January.
However, that did not stop anyone from camping out to get an early grab on the new phone.
The iPhone Duo costs $1,999, and it was released at 7 a.m. Friday.

title: Former teen idol Michael Gray has died at 75
text:
Michael Gray, a teenage heartthrob from the 1970s, has died
Actor Michael Gray, best known as Billy Batson in the 1970s Saturday morning television series "Shazam!" has died at the age of 75.
His publicist confirmed that Gray died of natural causes on Oct. 16 in Palm Desert, California. He is survived by his wife, Stacy Bennon Gray, and his two stepchildren.
Video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
Gray was a teenage heartthrob who appeared in a dozen TV shows throughout the 70s. He made his television debut as a background actor in "Room 222," and rose to prominence in "The Brady Bunch" when he dated Marcia Brady while she was working in an ice cream shop.
He spent three seasons on "Shazam!" as Batson, who would turn into superhero Captain Marvel.
“I remember when we were experimenting with the change from Billy to Captain Marvel, using a sort of flash device, and poof — the smoke would clear and I was a little singed,” Gray said in an interview with Comic Book Resources. “They changed that real quick. That definitely didn’t work.”
He was born in Chicago on Sept. 2, 1951, and was raised in Miami Beach before he headed to Hollywood, where he studied acting at the Pasadena Playhouse.
Later in life, Gray made a cameo appearance in the 2023 DC movie "Shazam! Fury of the Gods" and provided the voice for a fictionalized version of himself in "Archer."

title: White House announces Melania Trump secured ceasefire in Russian-occupied Ukrainian city
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Ukraine’s top negotiator involved in a humanitarian mission led by U.S. first lady Melania Trump told The Associated Press late Friday that a local ceasefire with Russia will start Oct. 27 — two days before the mission begins — and last several days.
Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators reached a deal Friday to provide humanitarian assistance in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine.
Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian ombudsman and his country’s chief negotiator in the talks, said the ceasefire would take effect across the Kherson region and neighboring areas essential to the operation. He added that the initiative could act as a model for future humanitarian missions.
THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below.
First lady Melania Trump has brokered a coming ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid and the evacuation of civilians, the White House announced on Friday.
The localized ceasefire is set to begin Thursday, with the American first lady saying in a written statement that the situation there is “on the brink of disaster.”
The White House said Melania Trump had initiated discussions after learning about the situation during an event she held during the U.N. General Assembly session last month. It said she and a representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the ceasefire.
Ukraine’s lead negotiator for the agreement thanked Melania Trump for her involvement and said the deal would be tough to accomplish.
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, said the agreement calls for a ceasefire, followed by the delivery of much-needed humanitarian aid. Lastly, civilians will be allowed to leave Oleshky, he said in a video message posted online.
“The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement,” Lubinets said.
Russia’s chief of the general staff, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, said Russian forces “will cease fire on the Kherson axis” starting at 4 a.m. Tuesday Moscow time “in connection with the humanitarian operation near Oleshky.” Russian forces will also carry out “engineering reconnaissance” and ensure “safe movement of the humanitarian convoy” into the city, Gerasimov said.
Russia’s human rights ombudswoman, Yana Lantratova, confirmed Friday that Melania Trump had brokered an agreement on “organizing a humanitarian mission” in Oleshky. Lantratova, who said she participated in negotiations, said providing such assistance is Russia’s priority.
The first step will be to clarify what people need and organize the delivery of food, medicine, hygiene products and other essentials, Lantratova said in an online statement. Safe passage will be guaranteed for anyone who wants to leave the combat zone, she said, adding that it will require abiding by the ceasefire and creating safe conditions for humanitarian vehicles.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow was grateful to the first lady and that Russian President Vladimir Putin and President Donald Trump had recently discussed the effort.
Peskov said “those who want to leave it would be able to do so.” He would not say whether those who evacuate will be taken to Russia- or Ukraine-held territory. He also demurred when asked how long the evacuation will last, saying only it would most likely take several days.
Saving children is the first lady’s focus, president says
Melania Trump has made helping children in conflict zones one of her signature issues in her husband’s second term. She hosted a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year, and last year wrote Putin about efforts to reunite families with children who have been displaced by the war. She has helped reunite nearly three dozen children, according to her senior adviser, Marc Beckman.
“What she wants to do is save children, and that’s her focus,” the president said about his wife during a question-and-answer exchange with journalists at the White House.
Marc Beckman, senior adviser to the first lady, portrayed her work on the ceasefire as an extension of the effort she has been putting in to help reunite Russian and Ukrainian children with their families after they were separated by Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Tensions between Washington and Kyiv are rising
The development comes as tensions have increased to new highs between the Trump administration and Ukraine’s government. Kyiv has faced restrictions on the satellite internet system it relies on to knock down Russian attacks, with Trump and other top U.S. officials sending mixed messages about who was responsible for throttling the Elon Musk-made Starshield system.
Trump also recently waived new Russia sanctions, reached an agreement with Russia to import diesel fuel and pushed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make a deal to end the war that Russia began in February 2022. In renewed efforts to revive the peace process, Trump envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Norway this week for talks with Zelenskyy before meeting Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Zelenskyy did not mention the ceasefire in Oleshky during a remote appearance at the Hudson Institute, a Washington think tank. He did note that American Patriot missile interceptors were still on hold and Starshield and Starlink speed limits were still in place.
He also spoke of the importance of the United States to renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war, including a possible joint meeting with Trump and Putin.
The situation in Oleshky is dire
Food and medical supplies have been scarce for months in Oleshky, which sits on the Dnipro River that separates Ukrainian forces from the city’s Russian occupiers. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Roads leading from town are mined and dotted with burned-out cars. Drones buzz overhead.
Once a city of about 24,000 residents, Oleshky was captured by Moscow’s forces on the first day of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned, and its infrastructure damaged. In June 2023, floodwaters inundated the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed from an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed.
Those left in the city along Ukraine’s southeastern front face death from hunger or disease as another harsh winter looms. Ukraine has appealed repeatedly for a local ceasefire to organize evacuations. Russia, as the occupying power, is obligated by international law to ensure civilians under its control have what they need to survive.
Melania Trump details the mission
Melania Trump said in the statement that civilian leaders from both countries will visit Oleshky residents to determine what level of assistance they require.
She said residents who want to leave will receive “coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination,” adding that she anticipated that some will want to go to either country.
The first lady also said “an impartial American media organization” will accompany and document Russian and Ukrainian teams on the ground throughout the process. The presence of journalists will help ensure everyone’s wishes are “faithfully respected,” she said.
The chosen news organization is Newsmax, a conservative outlet founded by Christopher Ruddy, a longtime friend of President Trump.
___
Associated Press writers Konstantin Toropin and Darlene Superville in Washington, Volodymyr Yurchuk in Kyiv, Ukraine, and Dasha Litvinova in Tallinn, Estonia, contributed to this report.
__
Associated Press writers Derek Gatopoulos and Susie Blann in Kyiv contributed.
