title: Maine men’s hockey shuts out Colgate
text:
The Maine men’s hockey team scored in each period and Petter Wickstrom Stumer earned the shutout in a 3-0 win over Colgate on Friday night in Orono.
Maine got its second straight win and improved to 3-2. Colgate fell to 0-5.
Tanner Klimpke scored a power-play goal in the first period to give the Black Bears the lead. Owen Bowler and Sully Scholle each had an assist. Loic Usereau scored from Isa Parekh and Klimpke in the second, and Lee Parks scored from William Gerrior and Max Scott in the third.
Wickstrom Stumer, a junior from Sweden who transferred from Canisius, stopped 24 shots in his first win for the Black Bears.
Maine will try to make it a sweep at 7 p.m. Saturday.

title: Maine’s working waters are not dumping grounds for foreign corporations
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rock Alley is a Jonesport lobsterman and president of Protect Maine’s Fishing Heritage Foundation. Jason Faulkingham is a lobsterman from Beals.
We’ve spent our lives learning Maine’s waters.
If you work on the water, you learn to pay attention. You learn the tides, the bottom, the weather, how your gear moves. Families pass down their trade and their best spots from generation to generation.
For lobstermen and women, fishermen, clammers, wormers, shellfish growers and the businesses that depend on us, Maine’s bays are our workplaces. Clean water is not an abstract idea or slogan. It is the difference between making a living or losing one, and between a thriving community or a collapsing one.
That is why lawmakers and regulators should be paying close attention to the Conservation Law Foundation’s (CLF) lawsuit against Cooke Aquaculture.
A federal court in Maine recently allowed most of CLF’s Clean Water Act claims against Cooke to move forward. The court has not decided whether Cooke violated the law, but it has allowed allegations involving pollution, monitoring and reporting at Cooke’s open-net salmon farms to proceed.
CLF alleges that Cooke’s operations have discharged waste, uneaten feed, dead fish and other pollutants into surrounding waters and onto the seafloor. That matters to anyone whose livelihood depends on a healthy marine ecosystem. If pollution harms the bottom, it can affect the habitat and food sources that lobster and other fisheries depend on.
Outside the courtroom, this case raises a basic question for Maine: Who should carry the risk when a private corporation is given access to a public resource?
Industrial salmon farming is often sold as progress. We are told it means more seafood production, more efficiency and more jobs. I understand why those promises can sound appealing, especially in rural coastal communities like ours where every economic opportunity feels precious. Nobody who works on the water is against jobs. And Cooke employees are not the opposition.
Cooke is a multinational company operating in Maine’s communal waters, and the communities, not Cooke, pay the cost of any harms. A state lease may give a company permission to operate in a particular place, but that should not equate to Maine communities accepting pollution, escaped farm fish, weak monitoring or limited transparency as the cost of doing business.
The corporation may be headquartered elsewhere, but the environmental and economic consequences stay here. Mainers deserve that private industrial infrastructure have meaningful accountability to the people already working there.
We have seen this pattern before in other parts of the food system. Industrial production gets promoted as efficient and inevitable. Then operations consolidate, decision-making moves farther away from local communities and the costs are pushed onto the people who live nearby. Farmers, workers, rural towns and ecosystems are left to absorb the consequences while corporations keep expanding.
Lawmakers and regulators have an opportunity to keep that exact pattern from playing out on Maine’s coast.
Before leases are renewed or industrial salmon farming expands, we call on the commissioner of the Department of Marine Resources and the next governor and Maine Legislature to enforce stronger accountability, transparency and public input.
The burden should not fall on coastal residents to prove harm after the fact. Companies operating in public waters should face strong monitoring, clear reporting and real enforcement from the start, with that information easily accessible so communities can see what is being discharged, what regulators are tracking and how they are responding.
Accountability is not anti-business. It is the basic expectation that any company profiting from Maine’s waters should protect the resources and communities that make that business possible.
Protections for our waters only matter if they are enforced. Public hearings only matter if the voices of people most affected carry real weight. Oversight only matters if it is strong enough to prevent harm before it is too late.
The court’s decision to allow most of CLF’s claims to move forward should be a wake-up call. Our waters should not be treated like dumping grounds. Nor should permission to operate there be mistaken for ownership of a resource that belongs to all of us.
If a corporation wants access to Maine’s working waters, it should meet the highest standard, not the lowest one. That’s why CLF’s lawsuit matters. That’s why lawmakers must act now.
Maine’s working waters have sustained families for generations. Now is the time for our decisions to ensure they can support generations to come.

title: Woman dies after falling from horse-drawn wagon, family says
text:
MOORESVILLE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A woman who was critically injured after falling off a horse-drawn wagon in North Carolina has died, according to her son.
Eddie Quesenberry said that on Oct. 17, his mom and aunt were seriously injured after a tree branch fell and hit a wagon at Lazy 5 Ranch in Mooresville.
Lazy 5 Ranch said the horses jumped after the wagon hit the branch, causing three people to fall and be hospitalized. Following the incident, Quesenberry told WBTV’s Michael Warrick that his mother had serious head trauma and was likely going to spend several months in the hospital.
He posted an update on Facebook on Thursday that his mother had died from her injuries.
He said his mother was an organ donor and that it made him happy knowing that, even in their darkest moment, her love and generosity could bring hope to others.
Quesenberry did not say what condition his aunt was in.
WBTV has reached out to Lazy 5 Ranch for a statement, but has not heard back. According to its website, Lazy 5 Ranch is privately owned and offers a drive-thru safari experience, wagon rides and a petting zoo with animals from all over the world.
Quesenberry launched a GoFundMe to help his mother and aunt with medical expenses.

title: New vaccine shown to cut melanoma risk
text:
(CNN) - An experimental mRNA vaccine has been found to cut the risk of melanoma recurrence.
The vaccine is combined with the approved drug Keytruda.
Officials said it reduced the risk of cancer coming back after surgery compared with Keytruda alone.
It also reduced the risk of death.
The results are set to be presented during a European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid on Saturday.

title: Controlled burn in Standish delayed until spring
text:
A controlled burn scheduled for Saturday in Steep Falls Village Preserve in Standish has been postponed until spring due to unfavorable wind conditions.
Planned by the Presumpscot Regional Land Trust and Standish Fire-EMS, the burn was intended to help manage the preserve’s vegetation, mitigating chances of future wildfires. It would have taken place on 5 acres of the 25-acre preserve and closed the preserve for up to a few weeks while crews cleaned up.
However, Abigail Edenfield, an environmental steward with the land trust, announced Friday that wind conditions appeared problematic ahead of the burn, meaning it would have to be delayed.
Edenfield explained that winds from the northwest would push too much smoke from the fire toward Standish residents and Route 113. She also said the wind speed will be low, and therefore smoke would not disperse quickly enough.

title: See which children’s products have toxic chemicals
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Despite a longstanding Maine law that requires manufacturers to disclose certain toxic additives before selling a product in the state, some companies have not done so, according to a recent review of public records. 
Defend Our Health, a Portland-based advocacy group, analyzed filings for children’s toys and art supplies that were submitted to a chemical reporting system shared by Vermont, Washington and Oregon. The Maine Department of Environmental Protection confirmed that some manufacturers, including Crayola and Build-A-Bear Workshop, did not file reports in Maine before offering the same products here. The comapnies did not respond to requests for comment. 
The DEP said it is working on a way to make Maine’s chemical disclosures accessible to residents. But if you’re wondering which items could be hazardous, here are the children’s products reported in Vermont, Washington and Oregon from October 2024 through March 2026.

title: Netanyahu's office orders closure of West Bank after soldiers kill 2 men behind an alleged attack
text:
Netanyahu's office orders closure of West Bank after soldiers kill 2 men behind an alleged attack
Israeli soldiers shot and killed two men who the military said had launched an attack near the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank on Friday morning. At least five people were injured, including some critically.
The army said it prevented a “terror attack against Israeli civilians” and that the gunmen carried an M16 rifle and a handgun. It did not elaborate on the target of the alleged attack. There was also no word on the identities of the two dead and those injured.
A few hours later, Israel ordered the army to prepare for a full closure of the West Bank. The office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said it instructed security forces to immediately cordon off the city of Hebron and prepare to fully close all of the West Bank, starting Friday.
The deadly shooting comes as Israeli voters will decide next Tuesday whether to grant Netanyahu yet another term as prime minister — or usher in a new era of Israeli politics. The election comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza.
Israel’s government has warned of potential attacks by the country’s “enemies” in the lead-up to the election.
Netanyahu holds an emergency meeting
Following the shooting, Netanyahu held an emergency meeting of his Security Cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies. He blamed Hamas, saying the militant group was “planning a major attack aimed at murdering innocent civilians.”
“Our brave soldiers thwarted this attack with courage and determination," he said, without elaborating on what the planned attack entailed.
"I commend them for their actions and wish our wounded a speedy recovery,” he added but did not say if the wounded were soldiers or civilians.
Earlier Friday Israel’s far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for extremist views, said that the attack shows that Israel needs to restrict the Palestinians’ freedom of movement in the West Bank.
“The lives of the residents of Judea and Samaria, of the settlers, the lives of the soldiers, the lives of the police officers, the lives of our fighters are a million times more important than freedom of movement,” he said, using an Israeli reference to the West Bank.
Ahead of the anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack that triggered the war, Netanyahu said the Palestinian militant group could attack Israel in a bid to influence the outcome of the elections. He did not provide evidence to back up the claim.
The injured are evacuated to a hospital, medics say
Emergency responders said five people were injured, some critically, and were being evacuated to hospitals in Israel. A statement from the responders said gunfire was still ongoing as they arrived at the scene of the attack near the Yehuda Junction in the morning.
Two men in their 20s had gunshot wounds to their lower limbs, one was unconscious and seriously injured, the responders said.
“We arrived at a difficult scene while shooting was still taking place in the area," said Tzuriel Edri with the response team.
An investigation was underway, authorities said.
Also Friday, the army said soldiers and Israeli security and intelligence agencies conducted dozens of operations in the West Bank and apprehended dozens of people, including those affiliated with Hamas and Islamic Jihad militant groups. It also said it had located weapons, including M16 rifles and submachine guns.
Closures of the West Bank, such as the one ordered Friday, are growing more common in the territory. It’s the fourth time in the past month that Israel has imposed restrictions across the area, shutting gates and checkpoints connecting Palestinian villages to major roads.
Meanwhile, Israeli roads in the territory remain open to Israeli drivers, including settlers, who can still travel through the area but may face delays.

title: Houlton gears up for Halloween events as holiday falls on a Saturday
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
HOULTON, Maine (WAGM) - Halloween is a little over a week away, and the town of Houlton is preparing for a full day of events.
According to Jane Torres, executive director of the Houlton Chamber of Commerce, Houlton has become a popular Halloween destination, especially with the holiday falling on a Saturday this year.
“It’s almost like we’ve become the place to be for Halloween,” Torres said. “You know, we have the early visitors who can bring the little kids and then they can go home and then we have something for the older kids and even the adults. We have a family category for the costume thing and sometimes we had one last year that they came as the Adams Family.”
Schedule of events
Several events are planned throughout the day, beginning with the Monster Dash 5K at 11 a.m. at Market Square.
Other events include:
- Spooktacular, noon to 2 p.m.
- A free movie at 1 p.m.
- Carnival games, 2 to 3 p.m.
- A haunted house, noon to 5 p.m.
- Downtown All Shires Eve Truck or Treat and Halloween Celebration, 3 to 8 p.m.
Trick-or-treating
Torres said many people still go out for trick-or-treating following the organized events.
“Everybody just seems to spread out and go to all the streets around Houlton,” Torres said. “Park Street’s a big one, there is usually a traffic jam on Park Street because it’s just traditional that everyone goes there, but there’s a lot of candy given out that day. Spooktacular alone we are expecting 1,200 kids.”
More information can be found on the Houlton Chamber of Commerce Facebook page.

title: Presque Isle council candidate for economic development and transparency
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A former Presque Isle Recreation and Parks director is seeking a City Council seat because he wants to see the city expand its commercial base and gain better property tax control.
Eugene Cronin, 46, is one of three candidates vying for two open City Council positions on Nov. 3.
The other candidates, incumbent and Council Chair Jeffery Willette and Jeremiah Harris, declined interviews with the Bangor Daily News.
“I’m not running because I think one person has all the answers,” Cronin said. “I’m running to bring a working knowledge of city operations, a willingness to listen and a focus on making decisions that are responsible and transparent to our taxpayers and residents.”
A graduate of Alaska Pacific University, Cronin has served on the board of directors for the Presque Isle Utilities District and Recreation and Parks Advisory Board, along with several winter recreation organizations.
Presque Isle needs a stronger and more diverse commercial tax base to help relieve the high burden residents face, Cronin said. The city has faced challenges with the loss of its economic development director, a position that remains unfilled, and with what he called “runaway” property taxes.
“We’ve also recently lost the exceptional director of our industrial council, who was a driving force in local development,” he said, referring to Tom Powers, who died in March. “That leaves us in a different economic development climate, and I believe the city needs to give this area renewed attention.”
Cronin would start by listening to local businesses, property owners, the industrial council and community partners about what’s working, any roadblocks and where the city can grow, he said. He would urge officials to engage with prospective businesses and learn their workforce and infrastructure needs.
His other top priorities include responsible budgeting and transparent property assessments.
Residents should clearly understand how their property is assessed and how taxes are distributed, he said. He favors learning about assessment methods and how Presque Isle compares with other communities, and keeping residents in the loop about any changes.
His time managing a city department taught him that putting off maintenance work can make things more expensive down the road, he said. He learned about budgets, employees, facilities and capital projects, and believes departments should look at both immediate costs and future needs.
“Good decisions start with asking questions, understanding the facts and listening to the people affected,” he said.
The council could keep improving how it communicates with residents, and needs to prioritize the community’s interests, he said. Councilors should share information, encourage public input and be willing to explain decisions they make.
Cronin, a small-business owner, has spent much of his career building relationships and solving practical problems, he said. He has 20 years of experience in the recreational vehicle manufacturing industry, including sales and dealer development.
He has volunteered with many local organizations, and received the Presque Isle Rotary Club’s Rotary Community Service Hero Award in 2022.
“I’m proud of the community connections I’ve made through that work, and I believe Presque Isle benefits when people bring different experience to public service,” he said. “I want Presque Isle to remain a strong place to live, work and do business. Maintaining reliable city services and public assets, supporting local businesses and making the city welcoming to families all contribute to that.”

title: Portland could revert winter warming shelter to off-peninsula industrial park location
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After previously having secured a downtown location, Portland officials will soon consider funding a warming shelter in the Riverside Industrial Park — at the same location as the city’s often-criticized shelter operation last winter.
The last-minute change comes with increased costs.
The City Council will be asked during a special meeting Monday to approve appropriating $900,000 in opioid settlement funds toward the shelter proposal after officials reached an impasse over the initial plan to host a nightly operation at the Elena’s Way facility downtown.
The new proposal for 166 Riverside Industrial Park, which requires a lease agreement and transportation plan for shuttling people on and off the peninsula, is estimated to cost $1.2 million — a $500,000 increase from the downtown option.
The meeting Monday comes roughly three weeks before a shelter is supposed to be up and running, with the Biddeford-based Seeds of Hope slated to host between 45-50 individuals per night in the basement of Preble Street’s building on Portland Street.
However, earlier this month, staff said zoning requirements in place on the building — as well as ongoing neighborhood concerns over the existing shelter — complicated the planning and forced officials to consider alternatives.
The conditional use standards for Elena’s Way stipulate that the sleeping area be limited to the upper level, and that a maximum of 40 shelter guests would be allowed at one time.
City staff previously said that while the planning director has the authority to approve a temporary use, doing so at Preble Street’s building would contradict zoning requirements already in place there, and it’s not something staff can override.
Further complicating the issue was a recent city inspection of Preble Street’s operation, which found that the organization is not following parts of its management plan, including its responsibility to monitor safety in the area.
According to a council memo, Seeds of Hope informed staff that it is no longer willing to operate an emergency shelter at Elena’s Way “due to community resistance and regulatory challenges,” and Preble Street also declined to operate it.
Faced with few options, staff began looking elsewhere. It reviewed city-owned buildings (including the Homeless Services Center on Riverside Street) and contacted the St. Vincent de Paul and First Parish churches, which have previously been involved in city warming shelters. It also looked at last year’s location.
A council memo said staff began real estate negotiations on the building in Riverside Industrial Park in response to guidance from officials during an Oct. 13 executive session. While it wasn’t considered the ideal choice, it soon became one of the only options.
The memo states there is another option available that will need to be discussed in executive session.
Last winter, faced with few options and no social service agency taking the lead, the city operated a warming shelter at 166 Riverside Industrial Park, the site of a former shelter for asylum seekers. The operation received $400,000 in state funding and opened based on temperature and precipitation thresholds that were often criticized. The location was also panned as being too far for many of the city’s most vulnerable residents to reach easily, especially during inclement weather.
Councilor Anna Bullett, chair of the health and human services and public safety committee, said she’s frustrated by the process. She said officials relayed to staff that finding a better solution was a priority early this year, in hopes of avoiding the setup of last winter’s operation.
“I feel like I’m in a time loop, because this is what happened last year,” she said Friday.
The $361,000 MaineHousing recently awarded to Portland’s initial shelter plan at Elena’s Way has been built into the budget for the Riverside proposal. The city would also need to update its contract with Seeds of Hope to operate it.
According to the memo, the item must be read on two separate days, but staff is requesting that the second reading be waived, which requires seven affirmative votes from the nine member council. Staff is also requesting that it be passed as an emergency, which also requires seven affirmative votes.

title: Collins touts Trump decision to remove some farm products from Canada tariffs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Nine categories of agricultural products will soon be exempted from the Trump administration’s 50% tariffs on Canada, Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, announced Friday.
The soon-to-be exempted products, which range from corrugated cardboard to agricultural machinery used in Maine’s blueberry and potato farms, have been subject to the steep import duties as part of President Donald Trump’s ongoing trade war with Canada.
But the tariffs that were implemented this summer have been deeply unpopular in Maine; two-way trade between the state and Canada, pretariffs, was worth $6 billion per year. Collins, a Republican fighting against political headwinds and Democrat Troy Jackson to win a sixth term in the Senate, had broken from her party’s leader and called for the tariffs to be rescinded.
The Wall Street Journal reported Friday just minutes before Collins’ news release that the Trump administration was rescinding the tariffs to help Collins in her reelection bid, citing people familiar with the situation.
Collins’ office publicized the changes before the White House, via a news release just after 2 p.m.
In that release, Collins touted her connections in the Trump administration and said she secured the exemptions after “repeated conversations” with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
The product groups exempted under the forthcoming order include cardboard boxes; plastic boxes and crates; plastic packing bags; cooling equipment; cleaning, sorting and grading agricultural machinery; packaging machinery; non-adhesive plates, foil and strip; and seaweed and algae products, Collins’ office said.
“Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” Collins said in the release.
The original value of the 50% tariffs on Canada was about $20 billion; Collins’ office did not note the value of these new exemptions. The White House said the changes will take effect Oct. 30.
The senator said that she had “asked for tariff relief for these important products and stressed the burdens that additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families.”
“I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally and largest trading partner,” Collins said.
Collins has also claimed credit for the exemption of several other goods from tariffs in recent months, including Canada’s removal of American seafood products from its own list.
Collins’ claim that she secured the exemption of road salt from Canadian tariffs produced a memorable moment in her second debate with Jackson earlier this month, when Jackson told Collins that Mainers “can’t eat road salt.” Both candidates oppose the duties.
Tariffs have caused significant uncertainty for Maine businesses, experts and industry leaders said this summer.
That uncertainty has been amplified by the volatility of the trade war, with its rounds of rescissions and add-ons. Trump implemented the taxes over the summer with a never-before-used provision of a Great Depression-era law that allows the president to issue retaliatory tariffs. Court challenges are ongoing.
The tariff exemption is the latest of several recent preelection announcements from Collins’ office attempting to portray the five-term senator as a well-connected leader who secures funding for Maine as chair of the appropriations committee.
Collins’ office also recently touted her efforts to secure the early release of heating assistance funds amid price surges driven by the ongoing war in Iran. And Collins claimed credit for the release of emergency heating oil following a letter she co-wrote with Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, to Trump administration officials.

title: At Acadia, a missing Wabanaki marker and the fight over what national parks should tell
text:
In the soft light of dawn, an Ohio tourist studied the interpretive sign at the summit of Cadillac Mountain in Acadia National Park, reading about how magma formed the ground under her feet.
There is one sign she and the other 4 million-plus tourists who visit Acadia annually can no longer see at the summit: a marker explaining the mountain’s sacred significance to the Wabanaki people in the region. “Today, visitors from everywhere find meaning on the mountain,” it said.
It was among 30 markers removed from Acadia under a Trump administration campaign to strip national parks of materials deemed disparaging to American history, according to the National Parks Conservation Association.
But when park staff took down the summit sign at the orders of Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, they also unraveled some of the trust that took decades to build between Acadia National Park and the Wabanaki people. The Wabanaki Confederacy, also known as “the people of the dawnland,” has inhabited the northern seaboard for over 10,000 years and was the first known stewards of land that includes much of the national park. It was a gathering place to trade, hunt, fish and pick sweetgrass.
Some of the signs removed from Acadia were developed over years of partnerships with organizations including Friends of Acadia, the Schoodic Institute and the Native Plant Trust — with consultation from citizens of the Wabanaki Nations. They know the mountain in Maine as Wapuwoc — “white mountain of the first light.” From October to March, it’s the first place to see the sunrise in the continental United States.
“Getting to a place where our language is in these parks and it is educational … erasing that or setting that back has big implications for how far we’ve come,” said Maulian Bryant, the Wabanaki Alliance’s executive director.
Bryant says the removed signs reflected “the good stuff.”
“These signs don’t say 96% of Wabanaki people died from smallpox, or there were 26 nations and now there’s four,” she said. “If we really want to get into the real history, that’s a whole other slice of cake.”
Other signs removed from Cadillac’s summit addressed issues of climate change, informing visitors that “Acadia’s future will be warmer and wetter” and that “In the last century, average annual precipitation has increased by six inches.”
During their tenure under the Biden administration, former National Park Service director Chuck Sams and former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland — the first Native Americans to hold these positions — aimed to reflect the experiences of all Americans throughout the national parks. Before leaving his post in February 2025, Sams saw parts of his work unraveled by the current administration.
This “attempt to rewrite history into a single narrative … is also counter to our democracy. And counter to the idea that we are a plural nation,” said Sams.
Lawsuit against national park removals advances
Now, a coalition of conservation, history and science organizations are fighting in court to get the Acadia signs and hundreds of other items put back. Under Burgum’s 2025 campaign, signs, books, films and exhibits covering topics such as slavery, climate change and the massacre of Native Americans were flagged and removed from national parks and monuments nationwide.
“Some of it’s been put back, and then some of it has been removed again,” said the Center for American Progress’ Angelo Villagomez. He was part of the progressive policy group’s team that examined a database leaked earlier this year and found that a third of national parks had flagged exhibits featuring history or science. Of those, Black and Indigenous history were most targeted.
Portions of all flagged material have since been reviewed and cataloged by a committee led by Joy Beasley, a National Park Service associate director. However, in a June affidavit, she writes that the spreadsheet is “unlikely to capture every removal, revision, or replacement.”
The Interior Department did not respond to The Associated Press’ questions about the current status of sign and exhibit removal or the ongoing lawsuit filed by the nonprofit coalition in February against the federal government.
The parks “are America’s storytellers,” said Todd Martin of the National Parks Conservation Association, a plaintiff in the lawsuit. “It’s their duty to preserve and interpret American history, the good, the bad, and the ugly.”
Jenny McBurney, a government publications librarian at the University of Minnesota who co-founded the project Save Our Signs, feels it’s more important than ever for park visitors to document revised signs.
“People are going to go to the parks and think that they will get to learn history there when in fact they will be learning an incomplete history,” said McBurney.
Wabanaki culture — past and present — shared in Acadia
Despite the job cuts, threats of land reduction, talks of privatization and even demolition within some parks, Indigenous groups and park partners have persevered.
In Maine, members of the Wabanaki Confederacy — comprised of the Maliseet, Mi’kmaq, Passamaquoddy, Penobscot and Abenaki principal nations — carry on the cultural traditions and spiritual practices that helped them maintain sovereignty and connection to their ancestral land after settlers arrived. That includes sharing their culture with tourists.
Penobscot Nation citizen Jennifer Neptune had mixed emotions about the attempted erasure of her people from Acadia and their ancestral homeland.
“It’s hard to get good signage in national monuments, in national parks,” said Neptune. “It’s a real gut punch when it (removal) happens, not just for Indigenous people, but for Black people, for the people whose stories don’t get shared.”
Over the past decade, she’s seen real change from the National Park Service, playing an integral part in bringing Wabanaki voices to the table to create Indigenous-designed spaces.
In partnership with Acadia, the privately owned Abbe Museum, which is largely overseen by Wabanaki people, hosts a program that brings Native voices into the park through music, arts and culture.
Nick Bear and members of a Wabanaki drum circle perform on Cadillac Mountain annually as part of this collaboration. “That’s just like bringing those ceremonies right back to the original sites,” he said.
In July, Passamaquoddy basket maker Lydia Soctomah demonstrated traditional Wabanaki basketry using pounded ash bark and sweetgrass outside the Sieur de Monts Nature Center. Both the ash tree and sweetgrass are part of the Wabanaki creation story, she said.
“Making a basket is worth 1,000 memories for me,” said Soctomah, whose grandmother was a well-known basket maker. “I was always told it holds a part of your spirit.”
Sweetgrass access an example of shared stewardship
Access to sweetgrass has long been difficult for Wabanaki people as they were pushed from coastal lands onto reservations. In Acadia, it’s been nearly nonexistent since the park’s creation in 1916. But over the past decade, park staff and Wabanaki members have collaborated to change that.
In 2017, scientist Suzanne Greenlaw, a citizen of the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, partnered with the U.S. Forest Service, Acadia’s Schoodic Institute and 14 traditional gatherers to conduct a Wabanaki-led sweetgrass study in hopes of allowing tribal access.
“It was really impactful because we had never had those kinds of co-stewardship relationships,” said Greenlaw, adding that those relationships, built over time, have not changed.
By the end of the Biden administration, there were over 400 co-stewardship or co-management agreements with tribes, 159 within the National Park Service alone, says Sams. Programs in Acadia were among them.
These programs, he says, allow tribes to fulfill their obligation to protect, preserve and enhance natural resources, and the federal government to fulfill its obligation to allow tribal access for hunting, fishing, and gathering foods and medicines.
Sams cautiously hopes there will be a rebuilding period for the park service under the next administration.
“There are always ebbs and flows with every administration,” he said. “Nobody has seen that more than American Indian tribes.”

title: First tanker of Russian diesel sets sail for the US despite Ukraine's protests, Kremlin says
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
First tanker of Russian diesel sets sail for the US despite Ukraine's protests, Kremlin says
A first tanker carrying Russian diesel to the United States under a new import agreement has set sail, the Kremlin said Friday, two weeks after President Donald Trump said he struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin despite Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.
“The first oil tanker has sailed off to customers, and regular supplies will continue,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said without elaborating.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said earlier this week that the first shipment would amount to 40,000 tons of diesel, according to Russia’s Interfax news agency.
Marine intelligence firm Kpler said the vessel was signaling it was headed to New York to arrive Nov. 7 and would be the first Russian diesel delivery to the United States since July 2023.
The abrupt reversal of U.S. sanctions policy on Russia over its invasion of its neighbor was seen as an attempt by Trump to address high fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections.
The diesel shipment of 40,000 tons amounts to around 300,000 barrels, or about 7% of the roughly 4 million barrels of diesel the U.S. economy consumes in a single day.
The import agreement, which Trump says foresees millions more tons of Russian diesel reaching the U.S. in coming months, is unlikely to make a dent in painfully high prices at the pump or elsewhere, energy policy experts say.
Russia’s diesel production has come under strain from repeated Ukrainian long-range drone strikes on its oil refineries. The attacks caused fuel shortages, which now have eased. Trump last month asked Kyiv to stop the attacks.
The U.S. diesel decision caused alarm and dismay in Ukraine, which has pleaded with foreign countries to tighten sanctions on Moscow and deny it revenue for its invasion launched in February 2022.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called Trump’s decision “a weak decision by strong partners.”
The diesel agreement was a sudden policy reversal, coming just weeks after Trump signed into law a sweeping sanctions package that directed him to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas. He later put the measures on hold.
The development is the latest twist in the at times volatile relationship between Trump and Zelenskyy, which in recent weeks has reached a new low.
Starlink still isn't back to normal despite U.S. promises, Zelenskyy says
Zelenskyy said he spoke Friday with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, after they consulted with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg. They also spoke with the Ukrainian leader earlier this week in Norway.
Kyiv is keen to add momentum to peace efforts in a planned three-way meeting between Ukraine, Russia and the United States that may take place next month at a venue to be decided, Zelenskyy said in comments via video link to the Hudson Institute research organization in Washington.
"We need diplomacy to move forward,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine's pressing issues are protecting its power grid from Russian attacks ahead of winter, getting more U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors to counter Russia's ballistic missiles, and finding more financial support from foreign countries, Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine is still experiencing Starlink and Starshield speed limits that are choking its drone operations, Zelenskyy said. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said earlier this week that the service would be fully restored within 72 hours, according to the Ukrainian leader.
Moscow airports temporarily close, and other developments
Meanwhile, Russia’s civil aviation authority, Rosaviatsia, said Friday afternoon that all four Moscow airports — Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo, Domodedovo and Zhukovsky — stopped flights arriving and departing for security reasons.
At Sheremetyevo airport, passengers were told to take shelter, Russian news agency Interfax reported. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that air defenses downed 21 Ukrainian drones targeting the Russian capital in the afternoon.
The restrictions in Moscow's airports were lifted three hours later.
Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine exchanged hundreds of prisoners of war for the first time since August.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said each side released 270 prisoners. Ukraine said 270 of its soldiers and civilians were freed, most of them held in captivity since 2022.
Also Friday, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said a Russian embassy staff member has been declared persona non grata after a Russian drone violated its airspace and crashed near residential homes.
Police said a local resident discovered a drone in the village of Chistelnita in Telenesti District, less than 100 meters (330 feet) from a home. Specialists were sent to investigate. No casualties were reported.
“Russia’s war keeps putting Moldovan lives at risk," Sandu wrote on X. "Today, a Russian Geran attack drone violated our airspace and fell near family homes and an energy facility.”
“We condemn this latest dangerous act. In response, we have declared a Russian embassy staff member persona non grata.”

title: Man accused of killing girlfriend as she visited him in hospital, police say
text:
INDEPENDENCE, Mo. (KCTV/Gray News) - A man in Missouri is accused of killing his girlfriend while she visited him in the hospital, according to authorities.
James F. Lawson was charged with second-degree murder in the death of Jessica Cyrus.
The shooting happened as Cyrus visited Lawson at Centerpoint Medical Center on Oct. 22.
According to court records, Independence police responded to the hospital Thursday and found the victim dead with a gunshot wound to her chest.
Investigators say hospital surveillance showed Lawson in a wheelchair facing the victim as she struggled to breathe and bent forward, while Lawson appeared to reach at his pants and hip area with a dark object in his right hand.
When officers arrested him, he had a holster on his hip and ammunition in his wheelchair.
A Jackson County judge set bond at $250,000 cash.

title: Classes canceled in Rockland after ‘unexpected death’ of staff member
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine (WABI) - Oceanside High School in Rockland has canceled classes for Friday after the death of world language teacher, according to school district leaders.
They say Megan Thill passed away unexpectedly
In a notice to the school community on Facebook, officials said that counselors will be available at the school from noon to 2 p.m. for students who might need emotional support.
According to officials, students attending Maine Career and Technical Education programs may still go if they arrange their own transportation.
School officials didn’t share more information but are working through their “crisis plan” and said they would share more when they “are able to do so.”

title: Hospice doesn’t have to happen at home
text:
(Aging Untold) — Hospice care is often misunderstood as “giving up,” but it’s really about comfort, dignity and quality of life.
For some families, that care doesn’t have to happen inside the family home — and knowing the alternatives can take the pressure off an already difficult decision.
“There’s no right or wrong”
“I like to take all judgment out of it. There’s no right or wrong. There’s no one way,” Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “People have very strong feelings about dying and how it should look.”
O’Rourke shared the story of a young client who wanted to die in a facility rather than at home, despite his sister’s wishes.
“What it was is he felt safe in a facility, community where there were nurses around, machines around,” O’Rourke said. “He felt less anxiety in that setting, and that was really what drove that.”
She said families should weigh care, safety and cost, but also check their own assumptions.
“Really take the heat out of the conversation by knowing what are your values and are you imposing that on your loved one?” O’Rourke said.
Hospice can follow you anywhere
“I’ve seen a lot of cultural issues where having someone pass in your home isn’t what the family wants,” “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “Going through that final sunset doesn’t have to be in your house. It can be in a community. It can be in independent living.”
She said she’s even seen families rent apartments in independent living communities specifically to set up hospice care outside the home.
“For me, it’s whatever brings comfort to the family,” Cradduck said. “At this point, we’ve got to make sure that the person’s comfortable, that they’re being provided the care and the dignity they deserve.”
She said the decision often comes down to whether a family can live in a space afterward.
“It really comes down to, am I going to be able to walk into my living room if that’s where I lost my spouse?” Cradduck said. “Or is it easier for me to remove that setting from the place I’m going to continue? And what if I have small children in the home or my grandkids are there frequently?”
Hospice means support, not a location
“One of the biggest things is people have to define and make sure that they understand what hospice is, and it doesn’t mean the end, doesn’t mean you’re giving up,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. “It’s just to provide additional services when people need it. And it’s the philosophy of comfort.”
Hospice can be delivered in a hospital, in independent or assisted living, or in a private home — it isn’t tied to one setting, the Aging Untold experts said.
“It doesn’t define the location,” Rogers said. “We all make these choices about what we want, what we’re living. We should be given the same choice about how we want to die.”
Katherine Ambrose, an aging-well coach, also addressed concerns about a death affecting a home’s value.
“I’m very used to people calling and asking if anyone’s ever died in that home. I wouldn’t want people to worry that it would affect your real estate value,” Ambrose said. “The only time I feel like it really makes a difference is if there was a traumatic death where the home is psychologically impacted or stigmatized.”
Plans can change — and that’s OK
“Many people want to die peacefully at home. That’s their wish, but sometimes there has to be a change of course,” Ambrose said. “Just like a childbirth plan — you might have a plan, but then you might have to change your plan. Because if you can’t control the pain or something changes, then you might make another decision.”
Morphine eases breathing
Cradduck said medications commonly used in hospice are frequently misunderstood.
“Morphine is used for many good reasons,” Cradduck said. “One, to open up airways, to help you breathe easier. So when you’re passing, the struggle to breathe as your body is shutting down — a lot of people don’t realize that the medications that are used are to prevent those struggles.”
“Morphine is not just a pain medication,” Cradduck said. “Oftentimes it is used to allow you to breathe easier because it relaxes and dilates.”
She added that other medications serve specific comfort purposes as well.
Key takeaways
- Deciding on end-of-life care is a deeply personal decision — there’s no single right answer.
- It’s OK if home does not feel like the right setting for hospice care.
- Hospice can be delivered in clinics, specialized communities, independent or assisted living, hospitals or inpatient units — it is not limited to one location.
- Focus on comfort and where you and your loved one feel safest.

title: Frances Perkins Center visitor numbers perk up 50% in 2026
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine homestead of Frances Perkins, one of the architects of the New Deal social welfare programs in the 1930s, tallied a 50% increase in visitors in its second season as a national monument. More than 6,200 people visited the Newcastle site in 2026.
Located along the Damariscotta River in Newcastle, the 57-acre estate includes the historic Perkins family Brick House, a barn housing a self-guided exhibit and scenic walking trails.
Exhibits and educational programs highlight Perkins’ contributions to American history, including her key role in establishing Social Security, unemployment insurance and other landmark labor protections. There’s also a store that sells books and other merchandise, and a cardboard cutout of Perkins in one of her signature tricorn hats for photo ops.
“We are thrilled to see continued growth in visitation and interest in Frances Perkins’ remarkable story,” said Amanda Hatch, executive director of the Frances Perkins Center.
“Welcoming visitors from across Maine and the country, and seeing them leave with a deeper appreciation for her contributions to American life, is incredibly rewarding,” she added. “We are grateful for our partnership with the National Park Service and for everyone who helped make this season a success.”
Perkins, the first woman to be appointed to a Cabinet position, served as Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s secretary of labor from 1933 to 1945.
The Welcome Center and self-guided exhibit are closed until next spring, but the monument’s trails remain open to visitors daily.

title: The prison-based American Legion post helping incarcerated veterans rebuild lives
text:
ST. GABRIEL, La. (InvestigateTV) - American Legion Veterans Memorial Post 432 at Elayn Hunt Correctional Center was the first prison-based American Legion post in Louisiana, helping incarcerated veterans heal and rebuild their lives.
The program is recognized for a zero percent recidivism rate. No one from the post comes back to prison.
The members of the American Legion Veterans Memorial Post 432 maintain their connection to the military and find camaraderie among other inmates who are veterans.
Veterans reconnect with service identity
These organized meetings at Elayn Hunt started in 2018 and give veterans who are serving time a chance to reconnect to the part of themselves that chose to serve their country.
“I ended up going to Germany, to where I was transferred from Germany to Iraq. And so, I spent time in Desert Storm for about a year, a little over a year,” said Daren Kitchen, a Hunt inmate and veteran.
Kitchen has now been at Elayn Hunt for nine years; an experience he said has saved his life that was once consumed by drugs and crime.
“PTSD was never explained to me. So, it wasn’t until I was incarcerated here at Hunt that I went through my first PTSD class. And for all of those years, nobody...I didn’t think anybody understood... or I didn’t have anybody to relate to,” Kitchen said.
It’s a story Elayn Hunt program manager Dr. Lawton Searcy has heard time and time again on the prison grounds.
“I was astounded that we had some 60 to 70 incarcerated veterans here at Hunt. There were 3,500 within the state of Louisiana that were either incarcerated or on active parole,” Searcy said.
Veterans mentor younger inmates
Hunt inmate Frederick Reed joined the Army National Guard at 18 to pay for college. He’s now 55 and behind bars.
“I made a mistake and I ended up coming to prison. Things happened. But I’ve been able to transfer those skills that I learned through the military,” Reed said.
As part of its veteran’s program, Hunt has created a veteran’s dorm where former service members help to mentor young inmates trying to turn their lives around. Their art covers the walls, and military structure is on display.
“Incarcerated veterans are just, in a lot of ways, very different than what you may call a typical inmate. Because they do understand discipline. They do understand respect. But in suffering with PTSD, most... they’re trying to self-medicate,” Searcy said.
“I was trained for war, but I wasn’t trained for life after war. So, when I exited the military, I bounced all around. The drugs, the alcohol, the addictions,” Kitchen said.
Kitchen has found stability, partly due to the other veterans and Post 432.
American Legion supports incarcerated veterans
“We stand for the veterans that are still incarcerated. Because no veteran will ever be left behind again for any reason in the United States,” said Byron Comeaux, who is on the American Legion national executive committee.
His goal is to make sure that when veterans leave prison, they don’t come back.
“The minute you get out. The door lets you out and you’re right back in. This program has stopped that door from opening back up for the individuals because they have a sense of pride,” Comeaux said.
Warden Travis Day, who took over the facility plagued with problems earlier this year, sees the veterans as a valuable resource.
“I go home every night. These mentors are here 24 hours a day, seven days a week. They are in the dormitories. They are on the wall. They’re in the cafeteria,” Day said.
“We pretty much are doing what we... continuing the service that we have already started with our military service. We have just branched that over into helping those who are in our community,” Reed said.
“We know who’s being released from prison. And we can have an impact on who returns to our society, into our communities, around our families. So, I look forward to finding what’s the next thing that we can do to make this place better,” Kitchen said.
According to the American Legion, more than 107,000 veterans are currently incarcerated in the U.S. There are now more than 30 American Legion posts in correctional facilities.

title: Irving Focuses on Expanding Restorative Practices in Third-Term Bid
text:
District Attorney Natasha C. Irving, D-Rockland, is running for a third term to lead Prosecutorial District 6, driven by her desire to seek justice.
Prosecutorial District 6 covers Lincoln, Knox, Sagadahoc, and Waldo counties. Irving is running unopposed for a third term in the position. She faced Barbara Ann Cray, D-Westport Island, in the June primary and won 16,043-9,883.
Irving grew up in Waldoboro and attended Loyola University, where she attained a bachelor’s degree in philosophy in 2005. After graduating, she worked as an AmeriCorps volunteer before attending University of Maine Law School and graduating in 2009.
Irving worked as a labor organizer and political organizer, then as an attorney at her general practice, Natasha C. Irving Attorney at Law. She was elected to the position of district attorney in 2018, defeating incumbent Jonathan Liberman, R-West Bath, and becoming the district’s first woman and first Democrat elected to the position.
Irving is a member of the Maine Accidental Drug Overdose Death Review Panel, which recommends accidental drug overdose death prevention methods, and from 2021-2022 she served on Maine’s Commission to Examine Reestablishing Parole, which researched parole law and compared Maine law to other states.
Irving leads a team consisting of two assistant district attorneys, two legal assistants, a victim witness advocate, and a prosecutor’s assistant who doubles as the office manager. Her team typically has 2,400 active cases they are pursuing, and are overwhelmed by the amount, Irving said.
It is a difficult time for hiring prosecutors in Maine, due to the noncompetitive salaries and the public perception of law enforcement, as well as the view that the justice process is “punitive,” Irving said, a notion she wants to change.
“From what I see, there’s been a huge amount of progress,” Irving said. “And if you’re somebody that cares about justice in the community, one of the places you can have the greatest impact would be a prosecutor’s office as an attorney.”
Irving’s team makes recommendations or charges based on its evaluation of a case. Evaluating cases begins with reviewing all available evidence, Irving said. The team then identifies the necessary witnesses and looks to see if any evidence could compromise the case. Every trial is a risk, and the justice system would “grind to a halt” if every case made it there, she said.
The team weighs the strength of the case and asks the likelihood of losing versus the chance of winning, Irving said.
“The other part of the balance is going to be, if I lose and there’s no conviction, is that acceptable, or am I going to be having felt extremely irresponsible for not having agreed to a felony conviction, which this person can never use or possess a firearm again, and they’ll go to prison, and they’ll be on probation,” Irving said.
One of the team’s goals is to parse out which defendants can be diverted into community help programs without facing criminal charges. Putting low risk individuals in jail tends to turn them into individuals at a high risk of committing future crimes, Irving said.
With domestic violence cases, Irving said her goal is to ensure the entire case does not rest on a victim’s testimony. Her first priority is securing the safety of the victim and their family members.
Irving’s philosophy of victim-centered and trauma informed work plays into her approach to domestic violence cases, she said. Her first step is to listen to what the survivor is saying they need and have that inform how they proceed.
“Just because they’re victims of domestic violence doesn’t mean they’re not intelligent, doesn’t mean they know their lives better than we know their lives,” Irving said. “And on top of it is that if maybe we respect victims and give them some agency and make sure they know that we are trustworthy, and that we will take their wishes into account, and we do see them as a whole person and not just as a victim, that if it happens again, that they will be more likely to work with us and be able to work with us.”
When examining a case, Irving said she seeks to understand how each consequence from a charge, such as firearm access or deportation, could impact a person over the course of a lifetime.
“Bureaucracy should not get in the way of justice, in my opinion,” Irving said. “We have to hold people accountable, yes, but we don’t need to destroy people’s futures.”
Pursuing cases requires communication with law enforcement, with transparency as a priority Irving said.
“We have to make an independent assessment of whether there’s probable cause in the case and of other considerations of whether we charge and what the ultimate result of the charges, if there are charges, would be,” Irving said. “So sometimes that causes some conflict, but it’s our role.”
Irving also maintains relationships with the four counties she covers, which she said can be difficult as they may not agree on funding for districtwide positions.
In November, the Lincoln County Budget Advisory Committee recommended allocating $1 to Irving’s office. Irving said this stemmed from a misunderstanding over the role her office played in the stay of execution a man received – her office had argued against it, she said. According to previous reporting, Nobleboro Select Board member Richard Powell, a member of the budget advisory committee, cited unhappiness with Irving’s administration as reasoning for the recommendation.
Irving said that she has a “really good working relationship” with most of the commissioners in her district and she is working to improve them.
“Part of that is the fact that I am just not willing to sacrifice the work, the legal work in this office on my cases that are extremely serious to go and grovel in front of a group of people who are statutorily obligated to fund my office,” Irving said.
One of Irving’s future goals is establishing more “problem-solving courts,” such as the existing adult treatment and recovery court, a specialty court for people whose alleged crime was driven by a substance disorder, she said. The adult treatment and recovery court for Lincoln, Knox, Sagadahoc, and Waldo residents operates out of Knox County Superior Court in Rockland.
Irving said she is advocating for a veterans’ court, a mental health court, and a court for people charged with operating under the influence. These courts would seek to address the roots of criminal behavior, she said. She is also lobbying for a dedicated domestic violence prosecutor.
Continuing public service is why Irving said she is running for a third term.
“This isn’t like, you get crowned as district attorney and you have this position forever because you’re the incumbent and you should have it forever,” Irving said. “It’s a position that you’re elected. You need to earn it every day that you’re doing it.”
When she is not working, Irving said she enjoys spending time with her two daughters and husband, working her garden, or reading.
For more information, email [email protected].
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

title: Woman dies after falling from horse-drawn wagon at a ranch, family says
text:
MOORESVILLE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A woman who was critically injured after falling off a horse-drawn wagon in North Carolina has died, according to her son.
Eddie Quesenberry said that on Oct. 17, his mom and aunt were seriously injured after a tree branch fell and hit a wagon at Lazy 5 Ranch in Mooresville.
Lazy 5 Ranch said the horses jumped after the wagon hit the branch, causing three people to fall and be hospitalized. Following the incident, Quesenberry told WBTV’s Michael Warrick that his mother had serious head trauma and was likely going to spend several months in the hospital.
He posted an update on Facebook on Thursday that his mother had died from her injuries.
He said his mother was an organ donor and that it made him happy knowing that, even in their darkest moment, her love and generosity could bring hope to others.
Quesenberry did not say what condition his aunt was in.
WBTV has reached out to Lazy 5 Ranch for a statement, but has not heard back. According to its website, Lazy 5 Ranch is privately owned and offers a drive-thru safari experience, wagon rides and a petting zoo with animals from all over the world.
Quesenberry launched a GoFundMe to help his mother and aunt with medical expenses.

title: 3-year-old dies after accidentally shooting himself with father’s gun outside Burger King
text:
BARTOW, Fla. (Gray News) — Florida authorities say a young child died following a shooting outside a Burger King Thursday evening.
According to the Polk County Sheriff’s Office, the shooting occurred at a Burger King on East Van Fleet Drive when a father and his 3-year-old son went to the drive-thru to get food.
However, while attempting to pay, Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said that the father was having trouble with his credit card.
Judd continued, saying the father then parked the car to check why the card wasn’t working. During this time, he was bending over, and he removed a gun that was in his waistband because it began to cause him discomfort.
According to Judd, the child, who was in the backseat of the vehicle, got hold of the gun while the father was distracted by dealing with the credit card.
The child was playing with the firearm before accidentally shooting himself in the face, Judd said.
The 3-year-old was rushed to an area hospital, but he did not survive.
Judd described what happened as a “horrible tragedy.” He stated that no arrests were immediately made nor were any charges filed.
The sheriff noted that Florida has a statute regarding culpable negligence when leaving a loaded firearm within reach of a minor results in injury or death. This would be a third-degree felony.
The Polk County State Attorney’s Office is also said to be reviewing the case to determine whether criminal charges would be filed.

title: ‘I have to go in’: Father who killed Oregon school shooter recounts deadly attack
text:
‘I have to go in’: Father who killed Oregon school shooter recounts deadly attack
A 36-year-old father shot and killed a gunman who took the lives of three students and a teacher at an Oregon elementary school. Now, Kaylub Giamanco is breaking his silence.
“I’ve always wanted to change the world, but I’ve felt small. I’m just a carpenter from Bend, Oregon. I was a nobody other than to my friends and family,” Giamanco said in an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting.
A week ago, Giamanco, a military veteran, shot and killed a 16-year-old shooter who forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon.
Above video: Kaylub Giamanco speaks to Oregon Public Broadcasting, via CNN Newsource
The gunman killed four people: Three students, aged 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher.
Authorities say the death toll would be higher, if not for Giamanco.
Giamanco said Oct. 15 started like any other day. He dropped off his two daughters at Silver Rail Elementary School, then headed off to a job site for the day. Just before 1 p.m. that afternoon, Giamanco said he decided to go home for lunch to eat leftover tacos with his wife. He passed his daughters’ school on the way home.
Giamanco told OPB that he saw a “man in black” holding a long gun near the school grounds. He watched curiously at first, thinking it must be a prank, until that man fired twice at a pickup truck and once more at a woman mowing the school’s lawn.
Then the shooter hopped over the school fence and headed toward the school.
“That’s when panic fled into my brain, and that’s when I opened my center console,” he said.
Inside his truck console was a gun that had just been “collecting dust,” Giamanco told OPB. He clutched it, and called 911.
“I just was in full panic, like, ‘No, there’s children, there’s babies in there,’” Giamanco told OPB. “I told my Siri to call 911.”
He told the dispatcher what he saw, but didn’t stay on the call long.
“I said, ‘I’m sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,’” he said.
Giamanco recounted the details. Clutching his gun, he hopped over the fence and followed the gunman into the school.
“That’s when I started hearing children pleading for their lives and then I started hearing gunfire and I just started army crawling faster and faster and I told myself this is probably the last thing that I’m ever going to do,” Giamanco told Oregon Public Broadcasting.
Giamanco said he peeked into the classroom where the gunman was. He saw a teacher struggling with the shooter.
“I knew that he did not know that I was there,” Giamanco said. “And I fired.”
The teacher and shooter fell to the floor. The shooter then scrambled for his weapon, and the teacher ran from the room.
“I looked at (the shooter) and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn’t move because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else,” Giamanco said.
In the aftermath of the tragedy, news of Giamanco's actions made national headlines, with many people calling him a hero.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz praised his actions and the actions of the teacher who grappled with the shooter, saying “I don’t think we can underestimate or under-appreciate that courage.”
President Donald Trump even weighed in, saying Giamanco was “a great hero that went in and did the business.”
But Giamanco said he does not see himself as a hero. He think about the victims, and wishes he could do more.
“I want to apologize for not saving their babies,” he said of the victims' families. “The gratitude for saving people’s children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn’t save.”

title: Volunteer fire department chief says new study will help in fight for more funding
text:
Chief of Maine volunteer fire department says new study will help in fight for more funding
A new study about staffing at Maine fire departments had some stark findings, but also offered some solutions about how to turn staffing issues around.
The joint study between the University of Maine and the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office surveyed 219 fire departments, more than half of the nearly 400 across the state, and interviewed 25 fire chiefs.
The survey found that 47% of the fire departments that responded reported being too short-staffed to respond to some calls in the last three years.
Liberty Fire Chief Bill Gillespie, who is also the president of the Maine Fire Chiefs' Association, said none of what was found in the study comes as a big surprise. Gillespie also noted, however, that the survey and its findings provide the proof firefighters need to fight for more money from the state.
"Now, we have that data that we can go back to the Legislature with and say, 'We actually have the facts that show we are in a very difficult position,'" Gillespie said.
Gillespie said the staffing problem is going to get worse with more than 30% of firefighters who are over the age of 50 retiring over the next 10 years.
Gillespie's wife is the assistant chief of the Liberty Fire Department and one of his sons is a firefighter. The department has a staff of 12 volunteers, and with increased calls, Gillespie said he could use 12 more.
Unlike some other studies, this study offered recommendations to address the staffing issues.
"You can have dozens of volunteers, but if none of them are available 9 to 5 to respond to calls or to attend trainings, then it's less a numbers problem and more an availability problem," said Dominic Piacentini, a co-author of the study and a research associate at UMaine's Margaret Chase Smith Policy Center.
The study's recommendations include putting more training facilities in areas that do not have them and working with employers so volunteer firefighters can leave work to fight fires, as well as a call for a culture change.
"The civil commitments and the civic commitments aren't there," Gillespie said. "If you look at the Shriners or any of those organizations, their numbers are not flourishing and we're no different. We are relying on people to give up their spare time to help us."
The researchers behind the study said what is even more troubling is some of the Maine fire departments that are struggling the most did not have the time to participate in the survey.

title: Maine Finally Has a Standalone Toys 'R' Us Store Again, and It's Now Open
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s First New Standalone Toys ‘R’ Us Opens at the Auburn Mall
The time has come for the return of a standalone Toys 'R' Us to Maine.
Inside the Auburn Mall is a new, smaller version of the once-popular toy store, and it's now open.
Hopefully, it sticks around for more than just the holidays!
Where Is Toys 'R' Us in Maine?
South Portland and Bangor were the last of Maine's Toys "R" Us stores before they closed in 2018.
Toys "R" Us technically returned to South Portland in 2022, but in a different form, as its own little section inside Macy's.
But the first new standalone Toys "R" Us in Maine moved into the Auburn Mall at 550 Center Street in Auburn in October 2026.
Is Toys "R" Us Making a Comeback?
I thought Toys "R" Us was just a fond memory of the past, but it seems to be making a comeback.
Just a few years after the company went bankrupt and liquidated, it was acquired by WHP Global and then later partnered with Go! Retail Group to push for store expansion, according to Forbes.
Now, for this year, USA Today reported that Toys "R" Us is opening 120 new stores. That's a pretty big turnaround from before, right?
Is the Toys "R" Us in Auburn, Maine, Just for the Holidays?
A big question many probably have involves the staying power of Toys "R" Us and whether it can be a staple spot even after the holiday shopping season is over.
While there's not a definitive answer regarding the Auburn Mall location, it will likely depend on whether there's enough demand for it year-round.
In a Facebook post announcing the new store in Auburn, the mall noted that the decision "depends on the community. If people shop it, they will stay. So it really is in the hands of the public."
READ MORE: Here Are 4 New Businesses Coming to the Auburn, Maine, Mall
Are you excited for the return of Toys "R" Us?
Sure, it's not going to be like when kids got to browse the tons of aisles inside a massive space back in the day. And maybe the nostalgia for that is so strong it makes you brush off a reboot that isn't the exact same as the one from the past.
But I don't think you should.
It's nice seeing a little piece of childhood coming back to life, seeing Geoferry the Giraffe once again, and knowing that nearly 70 years after the first Toys "R" Us opened, it hasn't been erased for good.
Even in 2026, you can still be a Toys "R" Us kid.

title: How AI technology is giving ALS patients their voice back
text:
LEICESTER, Vt. (InvestigateTV) - ALS, often called Lou Gehrig’s disease, is a cruel illness. There is no cure, it’s always fatal, and Vermont has the highest rate per capita in the country with around 27 people living with it now in the state.
To help those losing independence and their, a nonprofit is working to restore the ability to communicate with loved ones and doctors.
Paul Francoeur’s days didn’t always start like this, but when they did, it was difficult. The cough-assist machine helped the 67-year-old clear his lungs when he couldn’t do it himself. His ALS weakened his muscles and motor skills too much.
“I think soon after diagnosis you realize how this road ends,” said Kris Francoeur, Paul’s wife.
That diagnosis came in 2019.
Kris turned into a caregiver, allowing her husband to remain at home. They get help from their son Ben. But it’s getting more challenging, especially as Francoeur loses his ability to communicate.
During a tele-medicine appointment with his doctor, the couple learned that with no better medicine or treatments, he would have to stay the course.
“Hardest part...” Francoeur said. “...Is worrying about other people,” Kris said, finishing his thought.
She helped him communicate. He was also good at eye-gaze technology, where eye movements control mouse clicks to spell out words. The software then generates synthesized speech.
“It is very flat and robotic,” Kris said.
But new technology by the company ElevenLabs uses AI to clone voices, replacing the robot sound. It even creates emotion in each word. The trouble is that Francoeur needed enough clear audio from before he started losing his voice, and they couldn’t find any old recordings.
But WCAX did.
The Channel 3 News featured the couple in a “Made in Vermont” story 14 years ago. At the time, Francoeur made spinning wheels, seven years before ALS stole his voice.
The footage takes the couple back to another time. “I think more than anything, it’s just to see Paul walking and talking... using tools. It’s amazing to see. I miss all that. He misses all that,” Kris said.
For Paul, it was hard to remember that level of physical freedom.
But in a couple of months, that WCAX story would give Francoeur back the voice he thought he’d lost.
Richard Cave with ElevenLabs said they were able to use 16 seconds of sound from Paul in that 2012 story to mirror his voice.
“What we’ve done here is use AI for good, to enable people to recreate their natural voice,” Cave said.
“The voice that will come out of the computer will sound like him,” Kris said.
“Like me,” added Francoeur.
“This disease robs people of so much of their lives,” said Dr. Mark Garret, who runs the ALS clinic at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center and is also Francoeur’s doctor. “When speech really becomes affected by ALS, it’s one of the things that most profoundly impacts quality of life.”
Garret calls the couple inspirational for making the most of the time Francoeur has left, and is touched by their advocacy for others living with ALS.
“I think Paul, the way he confronted a terrible prognosis and a terrible disease and made the best of life throughout all of that has been extraordinary,” Garret said. And, he said, it may be part of the reason that he has survived so long after the diagnosis. Typically, ALS patients live two to five years.
Francoeur made it to year eight.
His first words through the new technology were a thank you message and raising awareness about ALS.
“Vermont has the highest rate per capita than any state in the country,” he said, the cloned voice a perfect match.
“That does sound just like you,” Fuller said.
“Made me feel more human,” Francoeur said.
“It’s been a long time since I’ve heard Paul’s voice,” Kris said.
His next big speech was for his grandkids, who’ve never heard his real voice. “The next time I see the grandkids, I can tell them I love them with actual emotion.”
ElevenLabs offers the voice cloning technology to ALS patients for free. The organization Bridging Voices helps families connect with the company.
Seven months after reporter Darren Perron talked to the couple, Paul would pass away. He is remembered by his wife and family.

title: How today’s buyers can make an offer that opens doors
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
While prices, interest rates and trends are in flux, today’s real estate market remains highly competitive. Even when higher interest rates lead sellers to lower their asking prices, buyers still face competition for available homes. When inventory is limited, prospective buyers must be ready to pounce and make an offer before the competition kicks up and the home is off the market.
Here are some steps to improve your chances of standing out in a competitive market.
Use recent sales data to inform your offer
Though there are places with nondisclosure laws that do not mandate property sales prices be made public, such data is readily available in many areas. That information can be invaluable to homebuyers in competitive real estate markets because it gives them a strong idea of how much homes have been going for in towns and even specific neighborhoods they’re targeting with their search. That data also tends to be relied upon when sellers list their homes. Sellers may see how much a neighbor’s home sold for and use that to set the price of their own homes. With that knowledge in hand, buyers can tailor their offers to reflect recent sales figures.
Obtain a mortgage preapproval
Bank of America notes that a mortgage prequalification estimates what buyers might be able to borrow based on a credit check and information they provide, such as income data. Once that information is provided, prospective buyers may obtain a preapproval if a lender deems them creditworthy. A preapproval is important because it shows sellers that a buyer has the credit and financial backing necessary to follow through on an offer. Many sellers ask if bidders are preapproved because the preapproval facilitates a quicker sale.
Increase your earnest money offer if you’re truly committed to buying a particular home
Fulton Bank advises buyers to offer more earnest money, which is akin to a good-faith deposit toward the purchase of a home. A typical earnest money deposit may be somewhere between 1% and 3% of the purchase price, but an earnest money offer of 5% may indicate to sellers that you’re a committed buyer. But Fulton Bank notes that buyers who rescind their offers may or may not have their earnest money refunded.
Speak to your real estate agent about including an escalation clause
When you find a property that interests you in a competitive market, discuss with your real estate representative whether an escalation clause might boost the chances that your offer is accepted. Rocket Mortgage notes that an escalation clause is part of a real estate contract that indicates a buyer is willing to automatically raise their offer on a home if the seller receives a higher offer. The escalation clause indicates the most a buyer is willing to offer. The inclusion of an escalation clause is a big decision, which is why it can be so helpful to speak with your representative before deciding for or against including one in your offer.
