Portland committee unanimously advances Franklin Street redesign plan
The proposal would narrow the roadway, improve pedestrian safety and create opportunities for new housing
Portland committee unanimously advances Franklin Street redesign plan
The proposal would narrow the roadway, improve pedestrian safety and create opportunities for new housing
A proposal to transform one of Portland's major downtown roadways is moving forward after a city committee voted unanimously Wednesday to send the plan to the full City Council.
The Sustainability and Transportation Committee voted to advance the Reimagining Franklin Street design concept, which aims to transform the corridor connecting I-295 to downtown Portland.
The proposal calls for narrowing Franklin Street, reducing travel lanes and removing the wide grassy median to create more space for pedestrians, cyclists and potential housing development.
According to a presentation during Wednesday's meeting, the revised design would create more developable land than previous versions of the proposal and expand Lincoln Park.
The plan also includes environmental improvements, such as additional trees, green infrastructure and sewer separation.
The proposal is expected to go before the full Portland City Council on Nov. 16 for consideration, according to the presentation.
If the project moves forward, officials plan to begin the preliminary design phase in 2027.

title: Obituary: Edward A. McGuire
text:
WOOLWICH – Edward A. McGuire, 76, passed away at his home on Oct. 2, 2026. He was born on Sept. 7, 1950, in Boston, Massachusetts, to John and Patricia McGuire. He graduated from Morse High School in 1968. He served in the United States Navy, earned two degrees from UNH, spent time with the Sheriff’s Department, and worked many years at the Bath Iron Works.
One of Eddie’s biggest moments was when he hitchhiked to Woodstock in 1969. Eddie coached Little League for 25 years and also served as its president. He coached soccer and enjoyed many special family trips to Lobster Lake over the years. An avid sports fan, especially of the Patriots and Red Sox, Eddie made sure everyone knew not to interrupt him during a game. He never let his mother forget the time she came in during one and, according to him, caused the Patriots to lose. He also enjoyed ice fishing with the many friends who stopped by his home on Nequasset Lake. He also was proud of his boasting rites to the Biggest Buck in Maine Club in 1982.
He received a double lung transplant in July 2015 and often reminded people that he had done so well, he considered himself “the poster child” for lung transplants. Even after his surgery you could find him at the Bath Country Club, enjoying long days of golf.
Eddie is survived by his wife, Donna, who was by his side through his transplant, many trips to Cleveland Clinic and his care at the end of his life. He is also survived by his sons, Michael Scott (Nikki), Christopher (April), and Shawn (Stephanie); stepsons, Donnie and Jacob, his grandchildren, Maya, Micah, Delaney, Georgia, Finn, Eli, Emma, and Sophia; his siblings, Brian (Debbie); Michael (Mary); Mary (Paul); and many nieces and nephews. He was predeceased by his parents; his siblings, David, John, and Patricia and his sister-in-law, Martha.
Eddie was a lifelong member of St. Mary’s Catholic Church.
There will be a Mass of Christian Burial held at St. Mary’s Catholic Church on Nov. 16, 2026, at 11 a.m. In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to the Trenton 8th Grade Class Trip, C/o Chris McGuire,

title: UMF students can earn credits toward biotechnology master’s
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FARMINGTON — University of Maine at Farmington biology students can now begin working toward a master’s degree in biotechnology before finishing their undergraduate studies through a new partnership with Northeastern University.
The program, launched this fall, allows eligible UMF biology majors to take three graduate-level science courses that count toward their bachelor’s degrees and up to seven credits toward a master’s degree at Northeastern University’s Roux Institute in Portland.
The partnership is supported by a $400,000, three-year National Science Foundation grant awarded to UMF in 2023 to help smaller colleges develop partnerships, expand innovation and strengthen workforce opportunities.
“The life sciences sector is a growing industry in Maine that offers meaningful career opportunities to academically strong and motivated students throughout the state,” UMF President Joseph McDonnell said in an Oct. 6 news release.
“This new pathway between UMF and the Roux Institute provides our students a head start toward earning their master’s degree in biotechnology and developing the skills that will advance their careers and help support the state’s workforce needs,” he said.
The three courses, Theory and Methods of Scientific Inquiry, Biotechnology Laboratory and Biostatistics, will be taught by full-time, tenured UMF science faculty. They are the university’s first graduate-level science courses and have been approved to count toward degree requirements at both institutions.
Timothy Breton, UMF associate professor of biology and principal investigator for the federal grant, said the courses are intended to create opportunities for students while supporting the biotechnology industry in Maine and beyond.
“Life science and biotechnology industries are among the fastest growing sectors in New England, especially in Maine, and this pathway will help our students advance their careers in this expanding profession,” Breton said.
Students must maintain a grade point average of at least 3.0 through completion of their UMF bachelor’s degree and earn a B or better in each graduate course for the credits to count toward Northeastern’s master’s program. They must also meet Northeastern’s admission requirements.
The pathway does not automatically grant students a master’s degree. Those admitted to Northeastern must complete the university’s remaining graduate degree requirements.
The Roux Institute, Northeastern’s graduate campus and research center in Portland, focuses on technology, data science, life sciences and entrepreneurship, connecting academic programs with research and industry partnerships.
“We are excited to establish a clear pathway between UMF and the Roux Institute for UMF students interested in an advanced degree in the life sciences,” said Aileen Huang-Saad, director of life sciences, health and engineering programs at the Roux Institute.
“This partnership exemplifies how academic institutions can work together to offer students a diversity of choices for career advancement,” she said.
UMF students interested in the program can contact Breton at [email protected] or 207-778-7364.

title: See which children’s products have toxic chemicals
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Despite a longstanding Maine law that requires manufacturers to disclose certain toxic additives before selling a product in the state, some companies have not done so, according to a recent review of public records. 
Defend Our Health, a Portland-based advocacy group, analyzed filings for children’s toys and art supplies that were submitted to a chemical reporting system shared by Vermont, Washington and Oregon. The Maine Department of Environmental Protection confirmed that some manufacturers, including Crayola and Build-A-Bear Workshop, did not file reports in Maine before offering the same products here. The comapnies did not respond to requests for comment. 
The DEP said it is working on a way to make Maine’s chemical disclosures accessible to residents. But if you’re wondering which items could be hazardous, here are the children’s products reported in Vermont, Washington and Oregon from October 2024 through March 2026.

title: Man hit and killed by Tesla in self-driving mode on California interstate, authorities say
text:
Man hit and killed by Tesla in self-driving mode on California interstate, authorities say
A 71-year-old man was killed after being hit by a Tesla on Interstate 80 early Thursday after the driver told investigators the car was operating in its full self-driving mode, the California Highway Patrol said.
Video above: Are self-driving cars safe? Experts explain the challenges
The crash happened around 2:30 a.m. on I-80 in Solano County, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.
The Tesla’s dash camera showed the man entering the interstate from the right shoulder as the car traveled about 70 mph, CHP said.
The Tesla braked, veered left and struck the man with the right front portion of the car, according to CHP.
At least one other vehicle later struck the man as he lay on the highway. First responders determined he had died from his injuries, per the SF Chronicle.
The 26-year-old driver from San Francisco stopped, cooperated with investigators and provided the dash camera footage, CHP said. No other drivers stopped at the scene.
The Tesla driver was not cited. CHP Officer Scott Heitman told the Chronicle that charges could be filed through the district attorney’s office if the investigation finds the driver was negligent in a way that caused the crash.
The San Francisco Chronicle contributed to this article.

title: Video: Second-grader surprised by military mom, and all it took was one wish
text:
Video: Second-grader surprised by military mom, and all it took was one wish
A little girl got the surprise of a lifetime, and all it took was one wish.
Meet Isabella Myers, a second-grade student at David J. Jones Elementary School in Greensboro, North Carolina.
Isabella received a special gift from her mom, Quiana Quiros, who is currently in the military – a genie lamp.
“My mom said she'd give me this,” said Isabella. “So I miss my mom really, really much.”
Isabella explained to the others in the school’s office that if she rubbed a genie lamp, her mom said her biggest wish would come true.
After Isabella rubbed the lamp, service member Quiros appeared in the office.
That one wish created a moment the two will cherish forever. You can watch the heartwarming video in the player above.

title: A split vote could save the Maine sheriff that Janet Mills wouldn’t remove
text:
Two years after Gov. Janet Mills declined to remove him from office and said Oxford County voters should decide his fate, Sheriff Christopher Wainwright is asking for a third term.
The Republican sheriff, whose tenure has drawn multiple Bangor Daily News investigations since his high-profile role in blowing the whistle on his former boss, may face an easier path because he has two challengers on Nov. 3: Deputy Justin Brown, an independent who lost to him by 344 votes in 2022, and Democrat Timothy Holland, a 45-year police veteran.
The race is the first time voters get to weigh in on Wainwright since he survived Maine’s most serious attempt to remove a sheriff in nearly a century. The general election for sheriff isn’t decided by ranked-choice voting. That means Brown and Holland could split the vote against Wainwright in a county he carried narrowly four years ago.
Both challengers know that split could hand Wainwright a win. Holland said his campaign is going well but that he’s “highly concerned” that votes against Wainwright will be divided between him and Brown.
“Obviously that’s going to split votes,” Brown said of Holland’s presence in the race. “Either way, I do hope that the citizens of Oxford County are fortunate enough to get a new sheriff because it’s long overdue. It’s desperately needed.”
Wainwright, of Dixfield, joined the sheriff’s office at 19 and has spent 36 years there. He rose to the top out of the office’s biggest scandal. In 2017, when he led its criminal investigation division, he was involved in an FBI investigation into then-Sheriff Wayne Gallant, who was accused of sexually harassing several people.
Wainwright later testified about what investigators found, and he emerged as a leader in the office after Gallant resigned that year. Gallant quit before then-Gov. Paul LePage could act on the commissioners’ request to remove him. Wainwright won the open seat in 2018.
Within four years, his own conduct was under scrutiny. In 2022, he pressured a deputy to dismiss a traffic ticket for a woman he’d grown up with. When that deputy and another reported it up the chain of command, Wainwright berated them in a recorded phone call.
More revelations followed in 2023. The BDN found that Wainwright had sent uncertified officers into schools with guns and badges. It also found he had traded guns and gun parts from evidence to a gun shop for credit without notifying owners or the county, and with almost no paperwork.
A county investigator concluded that the trade broke state law and that Wainwright may have committed theft, though he was never charged. In February 2024, the all-Republican county commission unanimously asked Mills to remove him. After a hearing run by a retired judge, Mills, a Democrat, called his conduct unprofessional but said it didn’t meet the constitutional standard for removal.
Wainwright called the decision a vindication. Two months after Mills ruled, commissioners refused to pay his legal bills from the removal fight. The county also settled a sex-discrimination lawsuit in 2024 from a former clerk who said Wainwright tried to fire her for criticizing him.
Mills’ decision left Wainwright in charge of the deputies who had cooperated with the investigation against him. Brown was one of them.
In August, he and two colleagues filed complaints with the Maine Human Rights Commission. They allege that Wainwright escalated discipline against them after he kept his job, and that the county didn’t protect them. The sheriff has called the complaints a political attack.
Brown was demoted from lieutenant to deputy in 2025 over his role in a police shooting and hasn’t worked since last October, when he was put on leave over a weapons allegation. A state panel dismissed a related challenge to his truthfulness in July, but Wainwright suspended him for 90 days without pay in August.
Brown is running as a change candidate. His recent campaign materials focus on lowering costs, cutting unnecessary overtime and maintaining professionalism. In a recent Facebook video, he said “employees don’t quit bad jobs, they quit bad leadership or bad bosses.” Holland says he’s also running for change. His campaign has garnered many endorsements, including some from beyond his party, which he shares on Facebook.
Wainwright’s campaign has focused on his work, sharing statistics about high call volumes and partnerships with local police. He’s confident he’ll win, acknowledging the split field may help him, and he also said the headline-grabbing parts of his record are not coming up on the campaign trail.
He criticized Brown for running a more negative campaign than his own and Holland’s, although he noted his deputy’s role in the shooting unprompted during an interview.
“I’ve kept it clean and positive, and that’s what I’m going to continue to do,” he said.
Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between the Bangor Daily News and The Maine Monitor, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

title: 'We felt betrayed': Trump's gains with Arab Americans may be at risk in battleground state
text:
'We felt betrayed': Trump's gains with Arab Americans may be at risk in battleground state
In the nation's largest Arab American community, some voters who backed President Donald Trump in 2024 told us that his war with Iran was a turning point for their support.
'We felt betrayed': Trump's gains with Arab Americans may be at risk in battleground state
In the nation's largest Arab American community, some voters who backed President Donald Trump in 2024 told us that his war with Iran was a turning point for their support.
President Donald Trump's inroads with the Arab American community helped him secure the swing state of Michigan and a second term in office, but at least some of that support appears to be slipping because of his war with Iran.
Some voters who backed Trump in 2024 described feeling disappointed or even betrayed ahead of the midterm elections. That could affect a key Senate race that will help determine control of Congress.
In the last presidential election, backlash to the Biden-Harris administration's handling of the Israel-Hamas war caused many longtime Democrats to shun the party in Dearborn, Michigan — which hosts the nation's largest Arab American community. Many voted third party in protest, while others supported Trump, who became the first Republican candidate to win the city in more than two decades.
"So our uncommitted movement, I think, was a first warning shot to the Democratic Party," said Nasser Beydoun, chairman of the Arab American Civil Rights League.
Beydoun said many in Dearborn had family members under fire as the human cost of the conflict mounted. It's laid bare in a 100-foot mural called the "Wall of Tears," memorializing thousands of children killed in Gaza.
"You either support genocide, or you don't," Beydoun said. "If you support that, you have no humanity. I'm not going to support you."
Israel, a longtime U.S. ally, has denied genocide accusations and described its military campaign in Gaza as self-defense following Hamas' deadly surprise attack Oct. 7, 2023.
Trump announced a ceasefire deal that aimed to end the war last year, but Israel has continued launching strikes, and progress on parts of the agreement has stalled, including the disarmament of Hamas.
"That was not the breaking point because it was better than what Biden had done," said Sam Luqman, who voted and campaigned for Trump in 2024, when asked about the shaky ceasefire in Gaza.
Luqman said the turning point for her was when the U.S. and Israel launched a war against Iran.
"Certainly, the people that led the effort to vote him into office, we felt dumb. Like, we felt betrayed," Luqman said.
Describing Trump's 2024 campaign stop in Dearborn, Luqman added, "We actually threw up peace signs with our fingers and took a selfie and said, 'Peace in the Middle East' instead of 'cheese.' So the message was that there will be no new wars."
Asked to respond to Arab American voters who feel Trump broke his campaign promises, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly defended the success of his military operation and reiterated that the Iranian regime cannot be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon. She said only Trump "possessed the courage to take this national security threat head-on."
The war with Iran was also a turning point for Faye Nemer, founder and CEO of the MENA American Chamber of Commerce, who backed Trump in 2024.
"That was completely shortsighted on the part of the administration. It is not in American interests to be fighting that war," Nemer said.
Despite her disappointment, Nemer is undecided in Michigan's high-stakes Senate race, in which both candidates have called for ending the war with Iran. She said she sides with conservatives on prioritizing small government and fiscal responsibility, but some of Republican Mike Rogers' rhetoric has given her pause.
 Rogers has accused his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, of accepting support from groups with ties to Islamic extremists, comments El-Sayed has dismissed as attacks on his Muslim faith. 
"His very first campaign message was Abdul's ethnic background and his faith, and I found that to be very disingenuous," Nemer said.
Rogers says his criticism has nothing to do with religion.
RNC spokesman Hunter Lovell said that Republicans like Rogers are earning support from voters of all faiths and backgrounds by focusing on expanding employment opportunities, rather than dividing people. Lovell accused El-Sayed of alienating Black and Jewish voters in previous remarks, including his initial response to an attack on a Michigan synagogue, which El-Sayed later apologized for.
Luqman, who still identifies as a Republican, is planning to support El-Sayed, in part due to his calls to spend taxpayer dollars in America rather than buying weapons for other countries, like Israel.
"Those are 'America First' policies. That is the definition of MAGA," Luqman said. "He's essentially saying what Republicans should be saying at this time." 
It's an issue dividing both parties on Capitol Hill, where most Republicans and some Democrats shot down an effort to slash military aid to Israel in a test vote ahead of midterm elections. Those opposed to cutting aid argued that it would hurt America's ability to confront Iranian proxies in the region, like Hamas and Hezbollah.
Rogers has said that he supports Israel's right to defend itself.
The debate is personal in Dearborn. Beydoun says his family home was destroyed in southern Lebanon, where Israel is fighting Hezbollah.
"Obviously, we're upset knowing that our government provided the bombs that destroyed American property, and I'm not the only one," Beydoun said.

title: Justice Department sues Alaska over Senate candidate names
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (Gray DC) - The U.S. Department of Justice is suing Alaska over the handling of the state’s U.S. Senate election, according to a lawsuit filed by the Trump administration.
The lawsuit seeks to prevent certification of the election results in the race for Alaska’s Senate seat.
The lawsuit centers on two candidates in the race who share similar names: incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican, and a candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan.
According to the filing, the Justice Department is suing because it said it is in the interest of the federal government to protect the integrity of elections.
The lawsuit describes Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy as frivolous and intended to confuse voters with incumbent Dan S. Sullivan, which it says could hand the Senate seat to Democrat Mary Peltola.
The lawsuit includes the two candidates’ campaign logos as examples.
A sample ballot included as evidence in the lawsuit lists candidates alphabetically. Dan S. Sullivan’s entry is listed with the terms “registered Republican” and “incumbent.” Daniel J. Sullivan’s entry has no modifiers, according to the lawsuit.
President Donald Trump traveled to Wasilla for a rally in support of incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan Oct. 13.
“Well, I’m the one who said do it. They have two guys, run, named Dan Sullivan,” Trump said.
Election experts said lawsuits like this one are rare. They said they could not recall a previous example of one, and said the lawsuit relies on a novel reading of the National Voter Registration Act.
Alaska asks voters to rank their choices on the ballots.

title: Father who killed Oregon school shooter describes deadly attack, taking down armed teen
text:
BEND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - In an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting, Kaylub Giamanco, 36, the man who took down the elementary shooter last week, described what he saw that day as he confronted the armed teen.
Giamanco explained in the interview about crawling through a damaged school building, hearing children crying for help and encountering the 16-year-old shooter at Silver Rail Elementary School.
The Oregon father, whose two daughters were at the school at the time of the shooting, said panic set in after seeing the gunman throwing a rifle over a fence at his daughters’ school.
He said he opened his center console, where his gun was, repeating “no, no, no, no, no.”
Giamanco said he then moved toward the school building after hearing children pleading for help and hearing gunfire. He said he army-crawled faster, thinking it could be the last thing he ever did.
The father said he moved low past a recycling bin and into a corridor toward the doors, then crawled through the bottom of a broken-out window onto a rug in a small entryway with stairs. He said the special-needs classroom was to his left.
Giamanco said he got to his hands and knees, checked his weapon to confirm a live round was chambered, then looked through a window into the classroom.
He noted seeing a teacher on the left struggling with the gunman holding a rifle on the right. He said both were turned sideways to him, with the shooter not knowing he was there.
Giamanco said he then pushed the door open, stepped in and fired.
The 36-year-old called his mother after what occurred.
“I just had to take the life of what I think might be a child because he went into my daughters’ school with a gun,” he recalled telling her.
Giamanco said she told him to calm down, that he did the right thing and saved lives.
Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher were killed in the school shooting last Thursday. The teen shooter was identified as a former student of the school, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II.
Police said John blasted his way through locked doors with a shotgun and attacked a special-needs classroom.
Another student was critically injured and a teacher was injured and hospitalized.
Police have said Giamanco was carrying his gun legally in his truck and have credited him and the unarmed teacher who confronted the gunman with saving lives.

title: Your Choice, Your Voice: How rising costs are impacting Mainers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Your Choice, Your Voice: How rising costs are impacting Mainers
Leah Bolden is a stay-at-home mom, raising her three kids in Farmington alone. Her oldest has autism and her younger two have other disabilities.
"It's hard. Some days I really want to give up," Bolden said.
She's a Maine State Parent Ambassador and is a part of the Equal Justice Partners' Circle.
"We have to put a lot of dedication into repetition and just keeping a very consistent schedule," Bolden said. "Not to mention, like dealing with behavioral issues or calls from the school because they need support."
Between child support, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits and other services, Bolden says she's bringing in about $1,400 a month. However, with rising costs at the gas station and the grocery store, she's just scraping by.
"We're just down to the bare bones right now," Bolden said.
She said she's thought about leaving the state, looking for somewhere more affordable.
"If we can't survive, if we can't have a quality life, we can't stay," Bolden said.
Bolden isn't the only one pinching pennies. The U.S. Congress Joint Economic Committee says inflation is up roughly 3.74% compared to last September.
At the pump, AAA said the national average for gas as of Friday, Oct. 23, is roughly $4.29 per gallon. Here at home, Maine sits just above that at $4.30 per gallon.
Bolden said she's spending more than $600 on gas each month, including school drop-offs.
"They can't ride the bus just because of their disabilities, so I'm responsible for making sure they're there on time every day, and that adds up," Bolden said. "I'm doing four school runs a day because my kids go to two different schools."
Her biggest worry is keeping food on the table. Bolden said she's been paying double at the checkout line. She said her children's safe foods, which are low-stress meals, are more expensive.
"If that's what they eat, then I have to give it to them," Bolden said.
Bolden said she wants lawmakers to look at the realities families like hers face every day. She says she wants to be able to afford her bills, but there's no room to make that happen.
"I need them to consider that we aren't just statistics," Bolden said. "We are real people who want better, but there's just not the possibility to be able to do better."
For now, Bolden wants her kids to know that she did everything she could to give them the best life.
"I hope that they know that even if things are hard, they can still have a future.
"They can still achieve everything and that opportunities are still in their hands," Bolden said. "Just because things are difficult now doesn't mean that they have to stay that way."
Election Day is on Nov. 3.

title: What to know about the AI-detected security bug impacting wide swaths of the internet
text:
What to know about the AI-detected security bug impacting wide swaths of the internet
The language that's known as the backbone of the internet is now subject to what experts describe as one of the most notable vulnerabilities in recent memory.
PHP is a widely used general-purpose scripting language that is geared toward web development, and thus, it powers the majority of websites around the world. When the organization behind the language and the FBI’s cyber division warned Wednesday of significant vulnerabilities in the language, government agencies, corporations and other organizations were sent into a flurry.
The episode also highlights how artificial intelligence is changing the game when it comes to web security.
Here's what to make of the discovery of the vulnerabilities and the fallout.
The vulnerabilities opened sites to a host of potential security concerns
The official website for PHP and several other organizations and agencies released security advisories Wednesday urging PHP users to patch two critical vulnerabilities or shut down their sites if they couldn’t update them immediately.
The PHP Foundation, which works to provide transparency and accountability with the language, said the vulnerabilities could be exploited and allow bad actors to get unauthenticated access to sites running PHP.
This would mean attackers could control a web server remotely without needing a password, said James Sullivan, director of cyber and tech at the Royal United Services Institute in London. That could allow a hacker to steal data, alter data or use the system as a platform from which to launch other attacks, he said.
Exposure is vast, and some sites are still down
PHP powers about 70% of websites globally, so the possible exposure to vulnerability was immense.
The language is free and open-source, which contributes to its prevalence online. PHP is behind the content management systems WordPress and Drupal, which are commonly used by governments for their sites, and MediaWiki, the software that runs Wikipedia.
In accordance with the security advisories issued this week, several websites were taken offline to prevent exposure while they fixed the problem. There has been disruption to some government services and websites, including in the United Kingdom, Finland and Japan.
Some websites may still be down because there are multiple patches available for different types of software, and some organizations may still be waiting to receive them. They also need to be tested to make sure they work.
Charl van der Walt, the head of security research at Orange Cyberdefense, said he believes the reaction to the vulnerabilities is just the “early tremors” of the disruption they could cause in the weeks and months ahead. He said there likely will be further service disruptions as bad actors scan the internet for vulnerable systems.
The issues may have been lying dormant
The vulnerabilities have been known about since at least 2024, according to the PHP Foundation. A security team developed several competing approaches to solutions, but each had downsides. It seemed there wasn't a practical or concrete way attackers could exploit the vulnerabilities, so progress on a fix stalled, the foundation said.
The group took responsibility for not coming up with a fix sooner, saying: “We won’t pretend otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the security team’s decision process and its lack of resources.”
Some experts say the discovery of the vulnerability could have been even earlier than 2024.
The AI cat-and-mouse game between attackers and defenders persists
Although humans first discovered the vulnerabilities, artificial intelligence agents helped to identify how they could be exploited, and also supported the process of testing and validating the fixes. In a blog post, OpenAI said it had led a coalition of researchers, security providers and others to address vulnerabilities in PHP over the past two months. Researchers at Wiz, a cloud security platform, also said they independently used AI to identify the vulnerabilities.
The accessibility of AI means that many organizations big and small now have more advanced ways to proactively and reactively respond to security threats. But it also means bad actors have more advanced ways to exploit digital weak points, and at great scale and speed.
“It’s not quite as easy for defenders as it is for attackers,” van der Walt said. “You find the vulnerability in something. You replace it. But with what? Is there an alternative that is patched and robust and tested and approved?”
Sullivan, of the Royal United Services Institute in London, said while the push-and-pull can be worrisome, he's focused on the positive side.
“We’ve actually seen quite a decent use case here where AI can discover some critical vulnerabilities and then the community can come together to remediate them,” he said.

title: Trump administration files lawsuit to block possible Democratic win in Alaska Senate race
text:
Trump administration sues to block possible Democratic win in Alaska Senate race
The Trump administration has filed a lawsuit to block certification of the Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses the contest while another candidate with the same name is on the ballot, kicking off what many have feared could become a lengthy battle between the U.S. government and states over certifying an election where the president's party is struggling.
Many in both parties believe the fight over control of the Senate could come down to Alaska, where Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman. Also on the Alaska ballot is a Daniel J. Sullivan from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg. He has said he decided to run on his own, but Republicans have contended he is a Democratic plant to siphon votes away from their candidate.
The lawsuit Thursday by Republican President Donald Trump's Department of Justice in federal court in Alaska demands that the state be blocked from certifying a Peltola win if Daniel J. remains on the ballot. “The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska,” the lawsuit says, contending that federal law requires states to protect the integrity of federal elections.
The legal challenge came 11 days before the Nov. 3 election and months after the final ballot was set.
The Alaska Supreme Court rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, and the state's Republican officials made the decisions about how to list him on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent. Alaska's ranked choice voting system also will allow voters to select both of the men if confused.
Peltola and Sen. Sullivan were top vote-getters in nonpartisan primary
The senator received more than 68,000 votes in the August primary, while the challenging Sullivan got 4,107, about 2% of the total vote. Peltola, who had previously served one term in the House, was the top vote-getter in the nonpartisan primary. Both parties expect that whoever wins in November will do so by a tight margin in a state of 738,000 people.
The senator's campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment nor did Daniel J. Sullivan, whose presence on the ballot is at issue in the lawsuit.
“Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses,” said Devan Barber, executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.
The Department of Justice has increasingly been used to bolster the president's political operation, targeting his enemies and suing Democratic-controlled states before the election. Democrats and many voting rights advocates have long feared that the administration will try to block certification of elections that Trump's party loses, much as he unsuccessfully tried to do when he lost the White House race to Democrat Joe Biden.
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that was unlikely outside of extreme circumstances. “It is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process," he told reporters Thursday in Virginia before the lawsuit was filed.
The lawsuit was signed by Associate U.S. Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who represented Trump allies and Jan. 6 defendants before becoming one of the top appointees at the department.
Constitution gives states the power to run elections
Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the lawsuit would likely only kick in if Republicans narrowly lost the Alaska Senate race and that it probably would not survive long. “The statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification,” Muller said. “The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month.”
The U.S. Constitution grants states the power to run their own elections. Elections for federal office like the Senate must comply with standards set by Congress. That division of power has frustrated Trump, who repeatedly has tried to seize control of election procedures through executive orders that courts have blocked.
The final step for a state election is formally certifying the winner, the act that the administration's lawsuit seeks to prevent, it requests, “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for. Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
The process in Alaska is complicated by the state's ranked choice voting system, which Trump opposes, and many expect it to take weeks before a winner is known. Also on the state's ballot is an initiative to repeal that system.
Trump has stepped up complaints about a ballot with dueling Sullivans
Trump has complained about Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot, making reference to it during a rally in Alaska this month and in repeated social media posts, including one this week where he called it “CHEATING.”
“We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness,” the president wrote on Wednesday.
Clogging a ballot with third party candidates to siphon off votes from the other major party is a long-standing tactic in the country's two-party system. Republicans have been linked to an effort to persuade Ohio voters to support a socialist in that state's Senate race, which could help Republican Sen. Jon Husted fend off a challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown.

title: 'Brave, strong and confident': Viral moment reveals family's hardship
text:
Family finds strength beyond the gym after cancer diagnosis
A viral father-son moment carries a deeper meaning as the family faces a life-changing diagnosis.
Family finds strength beyond the gym after cancer diagnosis
A viral father-son moment carries a deeper meaning as the family faces a life-changing diagnosis.
Azariah Townsend can barely reach the pull-up bar in his family’s home gym in Iowa, but he already knows strength is not measured by height.
The kindergartner and his father, James, have worked out together almost every day. Their time together is about more than building muscle; it's about believing in yourself.
“I’m going to show you how to be brave, how to be strong, how to be confident,” James said.
The father’s encouragement to his young son created an emotional moment that has inspired viewers online.
In the video posted to Instagram, James Townsend and his 5-year-old son, Azariah, were stacking weight plates for a jumping challenge. His son had already cleared five plates. But when the stack reached six, the nerves set in. Instead of pushing him, Townsend reminded his son of what he had already accomplished.
“You just did five,” Townsend told him. “You can do it.”
The kindergartner took a deep breath, counted down and jumped. He landed on top of the stack — then burst into tears. The emotional reaction caught both by surprise.
“I was about to cry,” he said, smiling. “But I wanted to be put together and strong for him so he could understand what he was feeling and what he did. That moment was him being brave."
A lesson in courage was viewed millions of times online.
For James and his wife, Amy, the moment reflects what they have taught their three children: bravery, confidence and strength.
Video below: Dad's encouragement lifts son to new heights
That lesson carries greater meaning; Amy has been diagnosed with stage 4 cancer and is undergoing chemotherapy treatment.
“I do believe that God has made me strong enough to handle this,” Amy said. “I’m going to make the most out of every day that I have left, and I’m going to be present, and I’m going to fight.”
When treatment feels overwhelming, Amy thinks about her children’s courage, including Azariah’s leap.
“When I’m having my — you know, just really struggling with, ‘I can’t do this anymore. I’m not strong enough’ — it’s like, you know, my kids have believed in themselves,” Amy said. “I need to be a good example and show them strength, grace and asking for help when you need it.”
For James Townsend, the viral exercise was never just about athletic ability. It was an opportunity to teach his son how to understand fear and move through it with confidence.
“It’s not just about the physical, but also your mental and emotional state,” he said. “You can be brave in school. You can be brave with your friends. You can be brave on your schoolwork.”
Thousands online resonated with the tenderness between father and son. Townsend hopes the video encourages other parents to become more present and supportive in their children’s lives.
“People saw the connection,” he said. “For people to be able to see that, it’s magical.”
Townsend also hopes the moment creates a ripple effect, inspiring parents to offer their children the same patience, care and encouragement.

title: When health changes your sex life, intimacy doesn’t have to disappear
text:
(Aging Untold) — Health changes don’t just affect the body — they can reshape confidence, connection and communication between partners.
The Aging Untold experts tackle the questions many couples are afraid to ask out loud: When is it safe to resume sex? What if it isn’t? And what should you ask your doctor?
Start with what’s changing — and why
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first step is figuring out what’s behind the change.
“What’s changing it and why is it changing?” Cradduck said.
Cradduck noted that competency and consent are the first things to consider.
“Is it a matter of competency and consent? And if it is, then it’s off the table,” Cradduck said. “I’m not talking about lucidity. I’m saying if somebody cannot consent, then sex is off the table at that point. It’s not consensual.”
Cradduck added that for physical issues, like erectile dysfunction, a doctor can often help.
“Seeing a doctor can absolutely take care of it, and take care of things that are before, that are coming after,” Cradduck said. “There’s a lot of reasons to change, and there’s a lot of things that happen. We know with women, we have our own issues as we’re post-menopausal.”
Cradduck encouraged couples not to let embarrassment stop the conversation.
“Don’t be embarrassed by it, and say, ‘Hey, this isn’t working,’ or ‘This is hurting,’ or ‘This is something I want to participate in, but I’m not in the mood to,’” Cradduck said.
Intimacy and sexuality aren’t the same thing
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said one of the biggest misconceptions couples carry is treating intimacy and sexuality as interchangeable.
“I think one of the biggest misconceptions is that intimacy and sexuality are the same — and they’re not,” Rogers said. “Intimacy is that connection, and sexuality is an expression of that connection.”
Rogers said the best time to talk about these changes is before a health crisis hits.
“I think the best time for people to have these kinds of discussions is before a crisis,” Rogers said. “These are things we need to be talking about when we’re younger, because we know we’re going to age. We know there’s going to be a trajectory for different chronic conditions that may interfere. Perhaps if we start to take the time to discuss it early, we have a better understanding, the communication.”
When you’re exhausted from caregiving, intimacy can look different
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said intimacy is ultimately about feeling seen.
“To me, intimacy is feeling seen and understood and loved,” she said. “So when I think about that, I think talking is so important, and really honest conversations.”
O’Rourke acknowledged that caregiving fatigue can get in the way of a partner’s desire for sex.
“If you’re the caregiver and you’re taking care of somebody, you’re going to be tired a lot,” she said. “Maybe the other person wants to have sex, and maybe you’re just so exhausted you just can’t do it.”
Her suggestion: bring back date night.
“Go back to that,” O’Rourke said. “Set aside some time, just the two of you, no caregiving job in front of you, and talk. And maybe intimacy for you guys is just going to be holding hands. Maybe it’s going to be watching a TV show with your arms wrapped around each other. Maybe it’s going to be just a little bit of cuddling at night. So you can replace a few things until maybe you get back to possibly having sex again.”
A husband’s question: dementia, desire and what’s OK
Cradduck shared a story from a husband who called her with what he described as an awkward question. His wife had dementia, and he said she wanted to have sex.
“He said, ‘This is going to be an awkward conversation,’” Cradduck said. “I said, ‘Shoot it, I’m good.’”
Cradduck said the couple had a decades-long love story — high school sweethearts who found each other again later in life, only for her to later be diagnosed with dementia.
“He said, ‘She wants to have sex,’” Cradduck said. “And I said, ‘Do you want to have sex with her?’ And he said, ‘Well, of course I do. But is it OK?’ And I’m like, ‘Absolutely, it’s OK. She wants to.’”
Cradduck said the husband handled all of his wife’s care tasks — bathing her, helping her use the toilet — and she offered him a practical way to separate his roles.
“I did tell him, if you want that separation between your caregiving and your intimate life, wear gloves when you’re caregiving so that touch is clinical, and then touch her with your bare hand when you’re her husband,” Cradduck said. “That helped him, because he was having trouble himself moving from ‘I’m the caregiver’ to ‘I’m the husband.’ It gave him that separation.”
Understanding consent when cognitive decline is involved
Rogers said cognitive decline adds complexity to questions of consent.
“Do you guys see a difference when you bring cognitive decline into it for the person? That can be a whole different avenue to explore, because now you’re looking at that consent. When do they know, and how do you even broach that?” Rogers said.
Cradduck explained that consent and lucidity are not the same thing.
“If she’s not able to consent, if she’s not able to agree to what’s happening, or if she’s uncomfortable in those actions, then that’s not consent,” Cradduck said. “If she is not a willing participant, that’s not consent. And lucidity and consent are not the same thing. You can have moments of cognitive impairment and still be consensual in this relationship.”
Cradduck added that cognitive impairment can also lower inhibitions, which can change how a person expresses desire.
“Sometimes cognitive impairment also takes away some inhibitions,” Cradduck said. “So some people become more amorous.”
Rogers noted that consent for someone with dementia can shift moment to moment.
“I’ve seen people with dementia, and they change. They might outburst, ‘Don’t touch me,’ and then everything is fine,” Rogers said. “You have to be consenting at the time of whatever that emotion is.”
Cradduck added that you have to respect it if the consent gets removed in the midst of things.
O’Rourke also recalled a moment from working as a nursing home administrator, when a caregiver ran down the hall to report that a couple living together was about to be intimate.
“They’re about to do it. What do we do?” O’Rourke recalled the caregiver asking. “And I said, ‘You shut the door.’”

title: Trump is dead wrong about Russia and Ukraine

“Disgrace,” that’s what President Trump said of Ukraine’s decision to resume bombing Russian oil refineries. He got it wrong. The “disgrace” is Trump’s willingness to subvert the sanctions on Russian fuel — a deal that he himself signed purely for political reasons, with the midterms coming up.

Arundel

title: Kenduskeag Haunted House returns for spooky season
text:
KENDUSKEAG, Maine (WABI) — The Kenduskeag Haunted House is back for another season, a couple years after celebrating its 40th anniversary.
The community-run attraction offers elaborate sets, special effects and themed scares, with proceeds benefiting town sports and field maintenance.
Organizers say it’s thrilling but family-friendly, as most of the ghouls are local students earning community service hours. The attraction is not recommended for children under 12.
This week, performers are getting ready for the weekend.
“We are close and up personal. We like our rooms tiny. We like our hallways narrow. We like you to have that feeling from the smells and from the dangles that might be grazing against your face as you walk through. Unlike many other houses, we may touch you. You may get grabbed. We want to freak you out. It’s the unexpected. And we have a lot of unexpected,” said Wendy Cousins, head of the Haunted House Committee in the Kenduskeag Rec Department.
The house will be open Friday and Saturday from 7 p.m. to midnight, or possibly later depending on attendance.
Tickets are $15 per person. The house is located at Cole Memorial Field on Kenduskeag Levant Road.

title: Throwback Thursday
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Halloween is just around the corner, and whether you carve them, paint them, or turn them into pie, pumpkins have long been a big part of the season. It’s the focus of this week’s Throwback Thursday with Brian Bouchard.
For a lot of people, picking out the right pumpkin is part of the fun of Halloween. Then comes the bigger question... what are you going to do with it? In this week’s Throwback Thursday, we dial the time machine back to 1985, when WAGM Reporter Laurie Quinlivan looked at everything from carving and painting pumpkins, to picking out the perfect one.
The signs are everywhere. Halloween is coming. And it’s time to start thinking about preparing your pumpkin. WAGM’s graphic artist shares a few carving tips.
“Usually I just draw the picture of some idea of what I want for a face down on a piece of paper. Then I take a magic marker and I lay it down on the pumpkin. And usually I use a thin, stiff knife, which allows me to go around corners really easy.”
Of course, if you can’t stomach the thought of gutting your pumpkin, take a few hints from these artists at work.
“It’s gonna be a boy. He has a tongue that’s white, and he has a whole bunch of red hair.”
“Well, I’m painting this stem and I painted it green, and now I’m painting it white, and it’s going to look good.”
“I like to make it like hair and stuff because it looks like a real pumpkin sometimes.”
“What do you want him to look like?”
“My brother.”
One of the wildest pumpkins in the class was John Fisher’s Indian pumpkin.
“That’s supposed to be its mouth in some place in there. That’s their war marks. Back here, that’s describing what type of Indian it is. Up here it’s a blonde one. And those are supposed to be its fleas.”
“Fleas?”
“Yeah.”
“What do you think of this guy’s pumpkin over here?”
“I think it’s weird.”
“How come?”
“It’s not realistic.”
“What kind of pumpkin do you have?”
“A smiling pumpkin.”
“You think that’s realistic?”
“Not really.”
“Why?”
“Because usually pumpkins look mean.”
“They do?”
“Like Adams”
The beauty of the pumpkin is you can make it look like anything you want to. Give it stripes, change the color, make it patriotic, or even give it a hat. But there’s nothing you can do to make your pumpkin look as good as the Great Pumpkin.
“What do you think the Great Pumpkin really looks like?”
“I don’t know......A big pumpkin.”
“It’s orange and it’s painted like a jack-o’-lantern.”
“Well, it’s really big and it’s got a great big face. It’s magic”
“Where do you think he can be found?”
“In a patch”
Linus tells us every year the great pumpkin rises from the best-kept pumpkin patch...Chances are it won’t be this one.
“It’s been about a thousand rotting pumpkins that would have been a good crop if we hadn’t had a frost early in the spring, which set back the pumpkin so much that it wasn’t worth keeping up the patch.”
Meibaum says people are picky when it comes to pumpkins.
“We buy pumpkins like buying a car. They look it over. They want the perfect round pumpkin. And no one seems to realize that they all grow on their sides and they have a flat spot. They look it over and they go from one to the other. And I think that’s the best part of growing pumpkins is selling them and watching people pick them out.”
To some people, pumpkin means something totally different and delicious.
“Rene, wow’s the pumpkin pie?”
“Good, man.”
Seems like these guys know good pumpkin when they taste it. You can eat it, you can paint it, or you can carve it. But any way you slice it, Halloween just wouldn’t be the same without pumpkins.

title: The top 3 finalists to be the next James Bond have been revealed
text:
The finalists to be the next James Bond have been revealed
The search for the next actor to get the "Licence to Kill" may soon be coming to a close.
Reports from Deadline and The Hollywood Reporter suggest Amazon MGM is on the cusp of determining who will be the next actor to fill the role of the iconic British spy, James Bond.
Related video above: Sylvester Stallone digs into painful memories and the making of 'Rocky'
Both outlets say Amazon MGM — the new owner of the Bond franchise since the Broccoli family sold the rights in 2024 — is screen-testing three or four finalists for the role this week, with a final decision expected to be made as soon as this weekend.
Multiple inside sources say the top three finalists are Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor, and Jack Lowden. Turner most recently starred in the romantic comedy "One Night Only," which hit theaters this past August.
O'Connor is best known for his role as the young Prince Charles in Netflix's hit series "The Crown," playing the future monarch for two seasons. O'Connor also starred in 2025's "Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery," alongside former 007 actor Daniel Craig.
Lowden has a slew of credits to his name, including as a Spitfire pilot in Christopher Nolan's "Dunkirk" as well as a disgraced MI5 agent in Apple TV's "Slow Horses."
A fourth finalist is also believed to be screen-testing this week, but their identity is not known at this time. "Sinners" actor Jack O'Connell and "Euphoria" star Jacob Elordi were also in contention at one point, but both actors are considered to be out of the running.
It is unknown when the identity of the next actor to portray the legendary MI6 agent will be officially revealed, but history can give us some clues.
Daniel Craig was revealed to be taking over the role from Pierce Brosnan on Oct. 14, 2005, not long after his final screen test for the role in late September 2005, so an official reveal for the next actor could come as soon as early next week.
The next James Bond movie will come with some baggage. It will likely mark the longest time between releases of Bond movies since the six-year gap between 1989's "Licence to Kill" and 1995's "GoldenEye." It will also have to be a soft reboot for the series, given Craig's last turn in the role, 2021's "No Time to Die," ended on a definitive and somewhat controversial note for the character.
The next entry in the long-running franchise will be helmed by "Blade Runner 2049" and "Sicario" director Denis Villeneuve, who will be wrapping up his sci-fi epic "Dune" trilogy in December with the release of "Dune: Part Three."

title: ‘Total disgrace’: Trump blasts LeBron James for not standing still during national anthem
text:
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday accused LeBron James of disrespecting the United States after the NBA star appeared to continue his warmups while the national anthem was performed before Philadelphia’s season opener on Tuesday.
“I said right from the beginning that he’s no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE,” Trump said of James in a social media post sharing the video. “LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!”
James appeared to practice a golf swing and jump shot as “The Star-Spangled Banner” was performed Tuesday at New York’s Madison Square Garden. James, starting his first season with Philadelphia, was lined up alongside teammates who mostly stood still during the anthem.
Trump and James have been critical of each other for years, occasionally trading public swipes.
“It must be a slow news day at the office,” James said. “Slow news day at the office.”
The 41-year-old James, in his record 24th NBA season, had 17 points and 10 rebounds in the biggest comeback win of his career, 114-106 over the Cavaliers in Philadelphia’s home opener on Thursday night. The Sixers rallied from a 29-point deficit.
James put his arms behind his back and bowed his head while Boyz II Men sang the anthem ahead of the game. James was introduced to a roaring ovation from the crowd of roughly 20,000.
Coach Nick Nurse had talked at length since training camp opened about the Sixers’ need to tune out outside distractions. Hours before their home opener, the Sixers had to deal with one from the president.
“I think that goes right in with other outside noise we’ve already had,” Nurse said before the game. “I keep saying the same thing. All I really care about is getting to the practice floor, getting them in the film room, getting them to the game floor. The focus that they’ve had and the intent and all the stuff like that has been outstanding.”
Trump, speaking Thursday night at a campaign rally in Sioux City, Iowa, reiterated his complaint.
“And what about LeBron James? Did you see that deal?” Trump said. ‘No, he’s doing, during the national anthem he’s practicing his golf swing. I said what the hell is that. It’s a big scandal kind of a story. I don’t understand it.”
Here are some of the more notable times James became entangled with the president or politics:
LeBron wears 1 black shoe, 1 white shoe
James was with Cleveland in 2017 when he made a statement with his shoes — one black, one white, with the word “equality” in capital gold letters on the back of each.
Then, after the game, James made a statement about Trump, saying: “This is a beautiful country and we’re never going to let one person dictate how beautiful and how powerful we are.”
James had called Trump “ a bum ” on Twitter and also said earlier that season of the president: “He doesn’t understand how many kids, no matter the race, look up to the president of the United States for guidance, for leadership, for words of encouragement. He doesn’t understand that, and that’s what makes me more sick than anything.”
Shut up and dribble
James showed determination to speak out on social issues and the nation’s political climate after Fox News host Laura Ingraham criticized the four-time NBA champion for his 2018 comments about social issues.
“We will definitely not shut up and dribble,” James said. “I will definitely not do that. I mean too much to society. I mean too much to the youth. I mean too much to so many kids that feel like they don’t have a way out and they need someone to help lead them out of the situation they’re in.”
James referenced Muhammad Ali, Jim Brown, Bill Russell and Jackie Robinson as athletes who previously spoke up for equality and change with no concerns about the consequences or any rewards.
“We know it’s bigger than us,” James said.
Response to Morey’s tweet about Hong Kong
James said in 2019 that former Houston Rockets general manager Daryl Morey “was either misinformed or not really educated on the situation” regarding the potential consequences of his actions when he tweeted in support of Hong Kong’s pro-democracy protests.
“Yes, we do have freedom of speech,” James said. “But at times, there are ramifications for the negative that can happen when you’re not thinking about others, when you only think about yourself. I don’t want to get into a word or sentence feud with Daryl Morey, but I believe he wasn’t educated on the situation at hand, and he spoke.”
Morey deleted the tweet, but it nonetheless sparked a rift with the Chinese government, which severed ties with the NBA for several years.
Getting people to the polls
James was named The Associated Press’ Male Athlete of the Year in 2020 in large part for leading the Los Angeles Lakers to a championship and helping to persuade many people who had never voted — at the peak of the Black Lives Matter movement — to head to the polls.
“I still know what I do on the floor and obviously, I give everything to the game,” James said. “But I can make a greater impact off the floor right now, more than I can on the floor. And I want to continue to inspire people with the way I play the game of basketball. But there’s so many more things that I can do off the floor to help cultivate people, inspire people, bring people together, empower them.”
James rejects Ibrahimovic’s criticism of activist athletes
AC Milan striker and former LA Galaxy star Zlatan Ibrahimovic blasted socially conscious athletes in a 2021 interview. Ibrahimovic called it “a mistake” for James and other athletes to get involved in political causes, saying they should “just do what you do best, because it doesn’t look good.”
James, naturally, rejected the criticism.
“I would never shut up about things that are wrong,” James said.
___
Associated Press writers Collin Binkley in Washington and Darlene Superville in Sioux City, Iowa, contributed to this report.

title: Collins touts Trump decision to remove some farm products from Canada tariffs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Nine categories of agricultural products will soon be exempted from the Trump administration’s 50% tariffs on Canada, Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, announced Friday.
The soon-to-be exempted products, which range from corrugated cardboard to agricultural machinery used in Maine’s blueberry and potato farms, have been subject to the steep import duties as part of President Donald Trump’s ongoing trade war with Canada.
But the tariffs that were implemented this summer have been deeply unpopular in Maine; two-way trade between the state and Canada, pretariffs, was worth $6 billion per year. Collins, a Republican fighting against political headwinds and Democrat Troy Jackson to win a sixth term in the Senate, had broken from her party’s leader and called for the tariffs to be rescinded.
The Wall Street Journal reported Friday just minutes before Collins’ news release that the Trump administration was rescinding the tariffs to help Collins in her reelection bid, citing people familiar with the situation.
Collins’ office publicized the changes before the White House, via a news release just after 2 p.m.
In that release, Collins touted her connections in the Trump administration and said she secured the exemptions after “repeated conversations” with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
The product groups exempted under the forthcoming order include cardboard boxes; plastic boxes and crates; plastic packing bags; cooling equipment; cleaning, sorting and grading agricultural machinery; packaging machinery; non-adhesive plates, foil and strip; and seaweed and algae products, Collins’ office said.
“Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” Collins said in the release.
The original value of the 50% tariffs on Canada was about $20 billion; Collins’ office did not note the value of these new exemptions. The White House said the changes will take effect Oct. 30.
The senator said that she had “asked for tariff relief for these important products and stressed the burdens that additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families.”
“I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally and largest trading partner,” Collins said.
Collins has also claimed credit for the exemption of several other goods from tariffs in recent months, including Canada’s removal of American seafood products from its own list.
Collins’ claim that she secured the exemption of road salt from Canadian tariffs produced a memorable moment in her second debate with Jackson earlier this month, when Jackson told Collins that Mainers “can’t eat road salt.” Both candidates oppose the duties.
Tariffs have caused significant uncertainty for Maine businesses, experts and industry leaders said this summer.
That uncertainty has been amplified by the volatility of the trade war, with its rounds of rescissions and add-ons. Trump implemented the taxes over the summer with a never-before-used provision of a Great Depression-era law that allows the president to issue retaliatory tariffs. Court challenges are ongoing.
The tariff exemption is the latest of several recent preelection announcements from Collins’ office attempting to portray the five-term senator as a well-connected leader who secures funding for Maine as chair of the appropriations committee.
Collins’ office also recently touted her efforts to secure the early release of heating assistance funds amid price surges driven by the ongoing war in Iran. And Collins claimed credit for the release of emergency heating oil following a letter she co-wrote with Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, to Trump administration officials.

title: White House announces Melania Trump secured ceasefire in Russian-occupied Ukrainian city
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Ukraine’s top negotiator involved in a humanitarian mission led by U.S. first lady Melania Trump told The Associated Press late Friday that a local ceasefire with Russia will start Oct. 27 — two days before the mission begins — and last several days.
Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators reached a deal Friday to provide humanitarian assistance in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine.
Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian ombudsman and his country’s chief negotiator in the talks, said the ceasefire would take effect across the Kherson region and neighboring areas essential to the operation. He added that the initiative could act as a model for future humanitarian missions.
THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below.
First lady Melania Trump has brokered a coming ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid and the evacuation of civilians, the White House announced on Friday.
The localized ceasefire is set to begin Thursday, with the American first lady saying in a written statement that the situation there is “on the brink of disaster.”
The White House said Melania Trump had initiated discussions after learning about the situation during an event she held during the U.N. General Assembly session last month. It said she and a representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the ceasefire.
Ukraine’s lead negotiator for the agreement thanked Melania Trump for her involvement and said the deal would be tough to accomplish.
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, said the agreement calls for a ceasefire, followed by the delivery of much-needed humanitarian aid. Lastly, civilians will be allowed to leave Oleshky, he said in a video message posted online.
“The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement,” Lubinets said.
Russia’s chief of the general staff, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, said Russian forces “will cease fire on the Kherson axis” starting at 4 a.m. Tuesday Moscow time “in connection with the humanitarian operation near Oleshky.” Russian forces will also carry out “engineering reconnaissance” and ensure “safe movement of the humanitarian convoy” into the city, Gerasimov said.
Russia’s human rights ombudswoman, Yana Lantratova, confirmed Friday that Melania Trump had brokered an agreement on “organizing a humanitarian mission” in Oleshky. Lantratova, who said she participated in negotiations, said providing such assistance is Russia’s priority.
The first step will be to clarify what people need and organize the delivery of food, medicine, hygiene products and other essentials, Lantratova said in an online statement. Safe passage will be guaranteed for anyone who wants to leave the combat zone, she said, adding that it will require abiding by the ceasefire and creating safe conditions for humanitarian vehicles.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow was grateful to the first lady and that Russian President Vladimir Putin and President Donald Trump had recently discussed the effort.
Peskov said “those who want to leave it would be able to do so.” He would not say whether those who evacuate will be taken to Russia- or Ukraine-held territory. He also demurred when asked how long the evacuation will last, saying only it would most likely take several days.
Saving children is the first lady’s focus, president says
Melania Trump has made helping children in conflict zones one of her signature issues in her husband’s second term. She hosted a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year, and last year wrote Putin about efforts to reunite families with children who have been displaced by the war. She has helped reunite nearly three dozen children, according to her senior adviser, Marc Beckman.
“What she wants to do is save children, and that’s her focus,” the president said about his wife during a question-and-answer exchange with journalists at the White House.
Marc Beckman, senior adviser to the first lady, portrayed her work on the ceasefire as an extension of the effort she has been putting in to help reunite Russian and Ukrainian children with their families after they were separated by Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Tensions between Washington and Kyiv are rising
The development comes as tensions have increased to new highs between the Trump administration and Ukraine’s government. Kyiv has faced restrictions on the satellite internet system it relies on to knock down Russian attacks, with Trump and other top U.S. officials sending mixed messages about who was responsible for throttling the Elon Musk-made Starshield system.
Trump also recently waived new Russia sanctions, reached an agreement with Russia to import diesel fuel and pushed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make a deal to end the war that Russia began in February 2022. In renewed efforts to revive the peace process, Trump envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Norway this week for talks with Zelenskyy before meeting Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Zelenskyy did not mention the ceasefire in Oleshky during a remote appearance at the Hudson Institute, a Washington think tank. He did note that American Patriot missile interceptors were still on hold and Starshield and Starlink speed limits were still in place.
He also spoke of the importance of the United States to renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war, including a possible joint meeting with Trump and Putin.
The situation in Oleshky is dire
Food and medical supplies have been scarce for months in Oleshky, which sits on the Dnipro River that separates Ukrainian forces from the city’s Russian occupiers. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Roads leading from town are mined and dotted with burned-out cars. Drones buzz overhead.
Once a city of about 24,000 residents, Oleshky was captured by Moscow’s forces on the first day of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned, and its infrastructure damaged. In June 2023, floodwaters inundated the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed from an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed.
Those left in the city along Ukraine’s southeastern front face death from hunger or disease as another harsh winter looms. Ukraine has appealed repeatedly for a local ceasefire to organize evacuations. Russia, as the occupying power, is obligated by international law to ensure civilians under its control have what they need to survive.
Melania Trump details the mission
Melania Trump said in the statement that civilian leaders from both countries will visit Oleshky residents to determine what level of assistance they require.
She said residents who want to leave will receive “coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination,” adding that she anticipated that some will want to go to either country.
The first lady also said “an impartial American media organization” will accompany and document Russian and Ukrainian teams on the ground throughout the process. The presence of journalists will help ensure everyone’s wishes are “faithfully respected,” she said.
The chosen news organization is Newsmax, a conservative outlet founded by Christopher Ruddy, a longtime friend of President Trump.
___
Associated Press writers Konstantin Toropin and Darlene Superville in Washington, Volodymyr Yurchuk in Kyiv, Ukraine, and Dasha Litvinova in Tallinn, Estonia, contributed to this report.
__
Associated Press writers Derek Gatopoulos and Susie Blann in Kyiv contributed.

title: 'Press 3' option restored for 988 Lifeline after 14-month absence
text:
'Press 3' option restored for 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline after 14-month absence
October is LGBTQ History Month, a time to honor the people and progress that have shaped the LGBTQ+ community.
The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline recently brought back its "Press 3" option for LGBTQ+ young people, more than 14 months after it was shut down.
Sweetser spokesperson Justin Chenette said Press 3 connects young people under the age of 25 with a crisis counselor who is specially trained to support LGBTQ+ youth.
When the 988 Lifeline was launched in July 2022, LGBTQ+ youth could call and press 3, text "PRIDE" or chat online. The Trevor Project ran the original pilot and the network later grew to seven crisis centers.
In June 2025, federal officials announced that they would "no longer silo" these services and Press 3 went dark on July 17, 2025. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services said the program had run out of its congressionally directed funding.
Lawmakers from both political parties, mental health advocates and families pushed to bring Press 3 back, and in February, Congress passed legislation requiring the services be restored with $33.1 million in funding. Press 3 came back on Sept. 30, the last day of Suicide Prevention Month.
Chenette said advocates are still watching closely to ensure every LGBTQ+ young person, including transgender and nonbinary youth, gets the care they deserve.
According to the Trevor Project, restoring Press 3 will be critical in addressing the public health crisis of suicide among LGBTQ+ youth. Data shows that contacts from LGBTQ+ youth made up about 10% of all 988 contacts nationwide, and that Press 3 answered more than a million calls, texts and chats, approximately 2,100 per day.
Chenette said that when a young person in crisis reaches a counselor who understands them and does not judge them, they do not have to explain or defend who they are, and they can just get the help they need. The Trevor Project's latest national survey found that 36% of LGBTQ+ young people seriously considered suicide in the past year, including 40% of transgender and nonbinary young people. The survey also found that one in 10 LGBTQ+ young people attempted suicide in the past year, and that 44% of LGBTQ+ young people who wanted mental health care in the past year could not get it.
The Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is available at 988 by call or text, and young people under 25 can press 3 to reach the LGBTQ+ line. People can also contact the Trevor Project by calling 1-866-488-7386, texting "START" to 678-678 or chat at TheTrevorProject.org.

title: $5,000 reward offered for missing Gulf of Maine research vessel
text:
HANCOCK COUNTY, Maine (WMTW) - Researchers are offering a $5,000 reward for information leading to the recovery of an unmanned research vessel that was last seen monitoring a harmful algal bloom in the Gulf of Maine.
According to a notice from the Northeastern Regional Association of Coastal Ocean Observing Systems, researchers lost communication with a SeaTrac unmanned vessel on the night of Oct. 12.
The vessel was last reported 30 nautical miles southeast of Frenchman Bay, where it had been holding position to recharge.
A boat dispatched to the area a week later was unable to locate the vessel.
The yellow research vessel measures approximately 16 feet long and bears the markings “SeaTrac” on its bow and “Uncrewed Surface Vehicle” on the stern.
Reward eligibility will be determined by the vessel’s operator team at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and the Northeastern Regional Association of Coastal Ocean Observing Systems.
Anyone with information is asked to contact Mike Brosnahan at mbrosnahan@whoi.edu or 508-289-5633.
