title: Teacher accused of selling pills to student in classroom, police say
text:
MONTGOMERY, Ala. (WSFA/Gray News) - An Alabama teacher is accused of selling pills to a student in a classroom, according to authorities.
Langston Carter, 30, was taken into custody Thursday after Montgomery police were called to L.E.A.D. Academy.
Court records say a student was found with two pills containing 5 milligrams of oxycodone hydrochloride and 325 milligrams of acetaminophen. The student told officers he got the pills from Carter, his teacher.
The student said he paid $10 for the pills after Carter allegedly offered to sell them to him on multiple occasions. He was told to send the money via Cash App to Carter’s girlfriend, but he had to ask another student to send it because he didn’t have an account. Investigators later verified the transaction, court filings state.
After the money was sent, Carter gave the student the pills in the classroom, according to court documents.
L.E.A.D. Academy confirmed Thursday that students were placed on lockdown that afternoon at the direction of the Montgomery Police Department “to ensure integrity of the investigation.”
Court filings say after hearing the accusations, a K-9 officer conducted an open-air sniff outside Carter’s vehicle. The K-9 indicated an odor, and police opened the trunk where they reported finding a sling-style bag containing:
- 6.9 grams of marijuana
- a digital scale
- empty plastic bags
- 18.9 grams of mushroom-infused gummies
- nineteen 5-milligram oxycodone hydrochloride and 325-milligram acetaminophen pills
- a loaded Beretta 9 mm handgun
- other narcotics-related items
In a statement posted Friday morning, the school confirmed the teacher, now identified in court records as Carter, has been fired.
Montgomery police said Carter faces multiple felony charges, including possession of a firearm on school property, two counts of unlawful distribution of a controlled substance and first-degree possession of marijuana.
He is being held in the Montgomery County Detention Facility on $300,000 bond.

title: Aroostook Paints Purple Pinkies for Polio
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - This week schools across the county are doing their part to help fund polio vaccines across the globe. The Purple Pinkie Project is an initiative that paints students’ pinkies purple and collects donations to help eradicate polio worldwide.
Since 1985, volunteers have administered polio vaccines to over 3.1 billion children worldwide in an effort to eradicate polio. This week the Presque Isle Rotary has been visiting county schools to help with the cause. This Saturday, Oct. 24th, is World Polio Day and throughout the week rotary members set up tables at different schools and colored pinkies purple for polio awareness.
“For every purple pinkie that is donated there’s a dollar that goes towards a vaccination to hopefully end polio. Elise here has her pinkie painted purple. The little kids absolutely love it. Even the older kids love it as well,” said Presque Isle Rotary member, Chantal Farnham.
“Yes, we paint their pinkies purple because in other countries, say we don’t speak the language, or even if we did, we might not be sure a kid is telling us the truth as to whether they’ve received the vaccine or not. So, then when they have their pinkie painted, we know they have received a dose,” added Elise Browning, another rotary member.
Thomas King, an Easton high schooler, says he’s been participating in the project since kindergarten. “It’s a tradition now but as I’ve gotten older, I get to understanding it more and really, it’s just important that we get rid of it because you want to make the world a better, safer place for people and get rid of diseases like this that I mean ruin people’s lives.”
Each year, with the help of local schools, businesses, and county residents, the world gets a little closer to eradicating polio.

title: Letter to the Editor: Support for Trevor Doiron
NEH Library launches zine, hosts Maine Lit Fest event
text:
NORTHEAST HARBOR — Artists and writers gathered at the Northeast Harbor Library for a night of reading and conversation.
The event, held on Oct. 7, was part of the 2026 Maine Lit Fest, a statewide celebration of books, stories, and community organized by the Maine Writers & Publishers Alliance. This year’s festival theme was “responding to the moment.”
Zachary Taibi, circulation librarian and programs coordinator, saw a call for event proposals and came up with the idea to pair writers and artists to respond to the Lit Fest theme and create a zine. He worked alongside local writer Martha Dudman to bring the project to fruition. Once the event was approved to be included in the 2026 Lit Fest lineup, they started reaching out to writers.
Three poets were selected and given three months to create a piece to submit based on the festival theme “responding to the moment.” Once the writers finished their pieces, Taibi carefully matched artists with each poem to create a piece of art in conversation with it. Taibi and Dudman brought the art and writing together into a zine that was published and handed out at the main event.
A zine is a self-published booklet, sometimes handmade, usually containing art and writing related to a particular theme or topic.
The result came in the shape of reWorks Volume 1, a collaborative literary art project that culminated in the early October event.
The night opened with an introduction from Dudman, who served as moderator for the event. The first reading came from Samaa Abdurraqib, a Maine poet who currently serves as executive director of the Maine Humanities Council. Abdurraqib’s piece, “Pomegranate Place,” follows a mirror composition, meaning the second stanza reflects the first stanza by repeating it line by line in reverse order. Together the stanzas create a poem that feels like the two sides are talking to each other, almost like a call and response, reflecting themes of home, connection and taking care of our neighbors.
Artist Jennifer Judd-McGee was paired with Abdurraqib to create a piece of artwork in conversation with the poem. Judd-McGee owns Swallowfield on Main Street in Northeast Harbor, and works across mediums but is best known for her hand-rendered paper cuttings. For this zine, she created an illustration utilizing the distinct shape of a pomegranate and monochrome ruby-red color. Instead of clusters of pips and flesh within the pomegranate, houses and nature motifs appear across the fruit.
Abdurraqib remarked how well she felt Judd-McGee’s piece reflected her poem and captured what she aimed to express.
Gary Rainford took the stage next to read his short poems to the group. Rainford lives on Swan’s Island year round, and explained that much of the inspiration for these poems came from his time there.
Thematically, Rainford’s “Congregation of Moments” focused on the natural world as he described distinct scenes from winter on the island. Ice, snow and wind appeared in the poems, harkening back to the time of year when the area is shrouded in cold.
In response, Katelyn Miller, a multimedia artist, created a painting incorporating imagery used in the poems. She utilized different shades of blue from pale powder blue to nearly black navy to conjure a wintry nighttime scene in her painting, “A Resilience of Faith.” The focal point, positioned in the very center of the canvas, is a rosa rugosa bloom, a stark contrast to the otherwise cool-toned piece which appears in one of Rainford’s accompanying poems.
Josie Sibara took a different approach to the theme and referenced the “moment” outright throughout their poem, making it a character throughout. It also followed a different structure with one long stanza in justified alignment, meaning the block of text stretched flush to the edge of the margin on every line making straight margins on either side. One of the most common uses of justified alignment is in newspapers to densely fill a compact area with a still clean looking block of text.
The poem, titled “Responding to the Moment” follows a prose style and plays with what a moment is. Using imagery, Sibara’s poem calls distinct moments to view, pulling the reader into each scene and further into the poem.
Local photographer Katherine Emery sat with Sibara’s poem this summer, reading it repeatedly and snapping photos on film to capture the right moment. Her final piece came in the form of a multiple exposure photograph titled “The Aegis.”
The photo is rich with orange and red tones, with a wooden deck stark along the bottom left corner of the composition. The familiar glitter of sunlight dancing on water glints in the background. A window can be seen in the right side of the photo with another sliver of a body of water on the other side of the pane of glass.
Dudman guided the writers and artists through questions to better understand their process and how each final product was reached. Much like their writing styles, each writer took a different approach once they heard the prompt.
Abdurraqib saw the prompt as the first piece of the puzzle for creating her final piece, allowing it to guide her to a moment she wanted to respond to, while Rainford wrestled a little more with feeling boxed in by it. Sibara took the opportunity to more broadly explore what a moment is, and what its implications can be.
The conversation broadened to include each artist’s perspective, and they all shared their gratitude to the writers for sharing their work.
Members of the audience were allowed to ask questions at the end of the event, and one of the writers actually turned the Q&A around and asked the audience what made them attend the event. The question shifted the event from a panel discussion to a group conversation as numerous attendees stood up to share why they had come. Many cited their interest in supporting local artists and others shared they came seeking a chance to see the world from a different perspective through the art and poetry.
Emery closed the event by thanking the library for bringing these artists, writers and community members together for a night of sharing.
“I would like to say thank you too for the library and as part of my consideration for participating, I thought about what libraries do for us,” said Emery. “Libraries remind us that we belong to something much bigger than ourselves and they’re safe places where we can feel and be different and disagree.”

title: Defense attorneys in Charlie Kirk's killing say they need years to prepare for trial
text:
Defense attorneys in Charlie Kirk's killing say they need years to prepare for trial
Defense attorneys for the man accused of assassinating conservative activist Charlie Kirk are suggesting a 2029 trial date because they say it could take them that long to prepare their case.
Attorneys for Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, said Thursday that the defense's proposed schedule was “absurd” and defendant Tyler Robinson was simply trying to delay.
Utah District Court Judge Tony Graf has scheduled a Friday hearing to set a trial date.
Related video: Charlie Kirk statue vandalized
Robinson pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in last year's killing of Kirk while the ally of President Donald Trump spoke to a crowd of several thousand people at Utah Valley University. The 23-year-old defendant turned himself in a day after the shooting, and his lawyers have not offered alternative theories for Kirk’s death. He could be eligible for the death penalty if convicted.
Utah County prosecutors allege Robinson targeted Kirk for his political beliefs. They say a bullet found in the rifle used to kill Kirk was engraved with “Hey Facist! CATCH!” and that Robinson wrote in a text message about Kirk: “I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can’t be negotiated out.”
Trump weighed in on the trial date in a social media post prior to the hearing. He said the case should be tried “within a month” and accused the judge of “taking forever to ask questions that people already know the answer to.”
Prosecutors said in court filings they anticipated a 17-week trial and said they would be ready by October 2027. But rather than hold the proceedings during the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays, they proposed the trial begin Jan. 31, 2028.
Erika Kirk’s attorney, Jeffrey Neiman, said the trial should start next October, the earliest date identified by prosecutors.
“Under the Defendants’ proposed schedule, Mr. Kirk’s two children, who were one and three at the time he was murdered, will be six and eight years old by the time the trial concludes,” Neiman wrote. “They will face the uncertainty of this criminal proceeding longer than they had their father in their lives.”
But Robinson's attorneys said in court filings this week that they must sift through tens of thousands of files turned over by prosecutors.
They said they'll have to conduct extensive investigations into Robinson's life in search of mitigating factors that could influence his sentence if convicted, and must devote “substantial time” to issues such as jury selection.
The defense lawyers said they respected the court's attempt to set a “realistic trial date.” Yet because it's a complex death penalty case, trying to predict when it will be ready for trial “is an exercise that, at this time, will necessarily be infected with false precision,” they wrote in a document filed Wednesday.

title: Cooper Flagg hurt in Mavericks’ win over Pacers
text:
INDIANAPOLIS — A jarring flagrant foul knocked Cooper Flagg awkwardly to the floor and eventually out of the game Friday night.
Now it’s unclear whether the Dallas star will miss any more time.
Last season’s NBA Rookie of the Year did not play in the second half of Dallas’ 121-105 victory Friday night over the Indiana Pacers after landing hard on his left shoulder after Aaron Nesmith tried to block his shot from behind to prevent a breakaway dunk.
Instead, Flagg landed hard on his shoulder.
“Cooper has left shoulder soreness, he’ll be evaluated in the next couple of days,” Mavericks coach Dusty May said before addressing whether Flagg needed an MRI. “I really don’t know. I saw him in the locker room, he’s in good spirits. We’ll know in the next couple days what’s next.”
Flagg, of Newport, did not speak to reporters following the game.
He was off to a fast start in his second pro season. Two days after scoring 32 points to become the highest scoring teenager in a season opener in league history, Flagg was on pace for his first triple double of the season. He finished with 14 points, five rebounds and six assists in 17 minutes.
But it was how he left that had everyone talking and scuffling as Mavericks players came to the defense of their hurting teammate.
Forward Naji Marshall confronted Nesmith under the basket, drawing players from both teams into a brief fray. After a replay review, the refs assessed double technical fouls to Nesmith and Marshall. Flagg then made 1 of 2 free throws and continued to rub his shoulder as he walked toward the locker room.
Two Mavericks players also appeared to leave the bench though May said he thought both went to check on Flagg, perhaps avoiding any disciplinary action from the league.
“Look, Nesmith is a great guy, a heck of a player. I’ve known him since he was in high school,” said May, who reached two NCAA Final Fours and won last year’s national championship just a few blocks away from Gainbridge Fieldhouse. “Obviously, an unfortunate play. Hopefully, Coop’s fine.”
Another brief scuffle broke out between the teams near midcourt in the second half though it led to technicals or flagrant fouls. Pacers coach Rick Carlisle noted that Indiana has now played two games that have resulted in multiple scuffles.

title: Maine man pleads guilty to VA fraud after claiming to be paralyzed
text:
A Maine man who claimed to be paralyzed for more than a decade and then faked his death pleaded guilty to making false statements.
Gregory Heimann Jr. of Princeton, who had claimed to be paralyzed since 2004, walked into U.S. District Court of Maine in Bangor on Friday morning. He stood without assistance while speaking to the judge. He pleaded guilty to making a false statement to the government and admitted he knowingly lied to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.
The plea comes more than two decades after he first claimed to be paralyzed. Federal agents knew Heimann could walk since May 2023 but did not issue an arrest warrant until after he faked his death in April 2024.
The VA has paid approximately $244,075 in disability benefits to Heimann since January 2016, according to court documents. He was receiving about $5,000 a month, records said.
Heimann served in the U.S. Army from 1993 to 1997, before serving in the U.S. Army National Guard until 2005. He started submitting disability claims to the VA in 1996, according to court records.
In 2008 he was found to be 100% disabled and paraplegic by the VA. During an examination medical staff had to transfer Heimann from a wheelchair to an exam table because Heimann said he could not support himself with his legs.
A 2023 exam again found him to be wheelchair bound and said he could not lift his legs. But, federal agents followed Heimann to a Danforth hardware store where he walked in without an assistive device, according to court records.
Security camera footage from various businesses show Heimann walking in 2023 and 2024, court records said.
During a Feb. 22, 2024, interview with federal agents Heimann used a wheelchair. He said he’d used one since 2006, records said.
However, during the interview Heimann said his condition began to improve around 2015 but that he was afraid of losing his lifestyle and didn’t want his benefits to change.
About a month and a half after that interview, Heimann gathered his belongings in a canoe and traveled to a river near the Canadian border on April 19, 2024, and disappeared. A large search ensued until Maine game wardens found out Heimann was not dead and ruled his disappearance suspicious.
Heimann remains in the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service. He is scheduled to be sentenced at a later date. The charge carries a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a fine up to $250,000.

title: Obituary: Cliff Shea
text:
AUGUSTA – Cliff Shea, 60, of Augusta, Maine, passed away peacefully on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026, with his loving wife of 40 years, Jean, by his side.
Born in Waterville, Maine, Cliff worked as a woodsman and laborer, forming many lasting friendships throughout the years, including his special friend, George Gray.

title: Vance intensifies rapidly and could become a major Category 3 hurricane
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Hurricane Vance rapidly strengthened into a Category 2 storm Friday as it neared Mexico’s Pacific Coast, the National Hurricane Center said.
Vance had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (170 kph) as it churned about 425 miles (685 kilometers) south-southwest of Acapulco, according to an advisory from the Miami-based hurricane center.
It could become a major Category 3 hurricane before the end of Friday, the center said.
It was moving northwest at about 5 mph (8 kph), and this motion is expected to continue through the weekend, approaching the Puerto Vallarta area by Monday. The hurricane’s outer bands were already funneling gale-force winds and rough seas into Mexico’s Gulf of Tehuantepec, the center said.
It’s been an intense hurricane season in the Pacific Ocean, with storms spawning in assembly-line fashion near Hawaii and Mexico as El Niño conditions worsened by global warming create unusual weather, like this week’s severe flooding and tornadoes hitting the southwestern United States and the prolonged drought in Central America’s Dry Corridor.
Vance would be the seventh major hurricane in a row this year in the Pacific, following Nolo, Odalys, Polo, Rachel, Simon and Trudy. The World Meteorological Organization’s Hurricane Committee doesn’t use less common names beginning with Q and U.

title: 3-year-old dies after accidentally shooting himself with father’s gun outside Burger King
text:
BARTOW, Fla. (Gray News) — Florida authorities say a young child died following a shooting outside a Burger King Thursday evening.
According to the Polk County Sheriff’s Office, the shooting occurred at a Burger King on East Van Fleet Drive when a father and his 3-year-old son went to the drive-thru to get food.
However, while attempting to pay, Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said that the father was having trouble with his credit card.
Judd continued, saying the father then parked the car to check why the card wasn’t working. During this time, he was bending over, and he removed a gun that was in his waistband because it began to cause him discomfort.
According to Judd, the child, who was in the backseat of the vehicle, got hold of the gun while the father was distracted by dealing with the credit card.
The child was playing with the firearm before accidentally shooting himself in the face, Judd said.
The 3-year-old was rushed to an area hospital, but he did not survive.
Judd described what happened as a “horrible tragedy.” He stated that no arrests were immediately made nor were any charges filed.
The sheriff noted that Florida has a statute regarding culpable negligence when leaving a loaded firearm within reach of a minor results in injury or death. This would be a third-degree felony.
The Polk County State Attorney’s Office is also said to be reviewing the case to determine whether criminal charges would be filed.

title: Beloved Bangor gift shop changes hands after 40 years
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A Bangor gift shop known for its European imports is changing hands after 40 years.
Ingrid’s and Sunnyside Greenhouse officially sold Oct. 22, but the new owners say all its charm is staying the same.
Historic greenhouse, 40 years of ownership
Ingrid’s on Buck Street in Bangor — known for European imports, especially German goods — has been run for 40 years by Ingrid Perkins and Rick Gilbert.
Attached is the historic Sunnyside Greenhouse.
“My aunt and uncle started it in 1927. So it’s almost 100 years old. And it survived the Great Depression, World War II,” Gilbert said. “And it’s a good strong old-fashioned greenhouse. Probably one of the last left in a city because they’re all condos now.”
Perkins said her lasting memories are the customers.
“Meeting all the people that we met. A lot of them are good friends now for a long time. And it was fun to build up the business from scratch,” Perkins said. “But now we have wonderful new owners. We waited long enough to get them.”
New owners are longtime customers
The new owners are sisters Serine and Kari Steinnes.
Serine was a longtime customer who first joked about buying it three years ago when Ingrid first mentioned retiring.
“I said, just kind of offhandedly, it’s too bad you’re doing it this year. If you waited a couple of years, we might even be able to buy it, my sister and I. And she looked at me and she said, ‘that’s okay. I’ll wait for you,’” Serine Steinnes said.
The sisters say they want to keep the shop essentially the same, while adding a few touches — like Scandinavian products and more community outreach in the greenhouse.
“It’s like a little piece of magic, right? It’s unique. To have that go away would be so sad. And everyone who’s been coming into the store says, ‘oh, please keep it the same,’” Kari Steinnes said.
The former owners say they’ll miss their customers most — but are looking forward to spending their first Christmas in Germany in 40 years, since the holiday season is the shop’s busiest time.
“We want to take the opportunity to thank all our customers for all this support. We made many friends over the years and certainly we will miss them,” Perkins said.
“Christmas merchandise is in. It’s all going up now,” Serine Steinnes said. “If you’re looking for holiday stuff, come on in. We are here and we are ready.”
Bangor’s European Market inside Sunnyside Greenhouse will keep going under the new owners. It runs Saturdays from 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. They’re expecting a big crowd on Oct. 24 as customers see Ingrid and Rick off into retirement.

title: Parkinson’s doesn’t always start with a tremor — here’s what to watch for
text:
(Aging Untold) — When most people picture Parkinson’s disease, they picture a tremor. But the disease often begins long before that, with subtle changes that are easy to miss — and easy to dismiss.
The early signs most people miss
“Most people think that when they think of Parkinson’s, you think of tremors. But signs really do, in fact, occur much earlier, very subtle signs like the loss of smell is a big one. And constipation or the changes in the handwriting,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Rogers explained what’s happening inside the brain during those early stages.
“What’s going on is there is a misfolding of these abnormal proteins that they start to form these things called Lewy bodies,” she said. “And they accumulate and they damage the dopamine-producing neurons in a part of the brain called the substantia nigra.”
By the time tremors appear, Rogers said, significant damage has often already been done.
“The problem is, by the time you see tremors, you’ve probably damaged 50% to 70% of those dopamine secreting neurons,” she said.
Real-life examples of early warning signs
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said she’s seen those early signs play out with people she’s worked with — sometimes missed, and sometimes caught in time.
“I remember a client of mine was telling me that her husband’s writing started to get smaller and smaller and smaller, and then his arm — like when he walked, one arm moved and the other one didn’t,” O’Rourke said. “Two very common symptoms that if she had brought him to the doctor, something could have been done.”
O’Rourke also recalled a different kind of story — one of long-term resilience.
“I was watching this university professor teach a class, and in the middle of the class he said, ‘You know, I have Parkinson’s and I’ve had it for 15 years,’” she said. “He began to tell us about the life that he built and all the support network that he used to continue living his life with Parkinson’s.”
Rogers pointed to another early sign that’s often overlooked.
“I think the one sign that people miss is that acting out dreams during the middle of REM sleep,” she said. “That can be an early sign as well too.”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck also drew a distinction between a typical tremor and one that could signal something more serious.
She said essential tremors, which can happen if you’re active, writing or you’re doing something for a long time, are not out-of-the-ordinary things.
“It’s when you’re at rest and you see that tremor, especially early on. If you see anything, then there’s something neurological going on that you need to have checked out,” Cradduck said.
She added that tremors aren’t a guarantee, even in advanced cases.
“Not every presentation of Parkinson’s, even in an advanced stage, has tremors,” she said.
Movement and community make a difference
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said staying active is one of the most powerful tools available to people living with Parkinson’s.
“There are really great examples out there of people that have just thrown themselves into boxing, dance, water exercise, rock climbing, urban pole walking — all kinds of really great exercise sets promoted within the Parkinson’s community,” Ambrose said. “It really makes a huge difference for those that are able to and choose to do that.”
O’Rourke also praised the support systems available nationwide.
“I think the Parkinson’s community has done a phenomenal job with all the support and care that they offer all across the country — the Parkinson’s Movement Disorder Alliance, the Michael J. Fox Foundation, the Parkinson’s Voice Project,” she said. “I’ve spoken at a lot of the Parkinson’s groups, and they bring in education ranging from housing to finances to legal. They really give both the caregiver, the family and the person with Parkinson’s a lot of support.”
Rogers pointed to Michael J. Fox’s role in raising awareness of the disease.
“Michael J. Fox really brought awareness to Parkinson’s,” she said.
Cradduck agreed, calling Fox a pioneer.
“I believe that he has been a pioneer in showing the resilience of the human body and what you can go through and what you can still do and what you can still accomplish,” she said.
Resources
Key takeaways for Parkinson’s patients and families
- It’s a diverse spectrum. Parkinson’s looks different in everyone and can start years before tremors show, with early signs like sleep issues or loss of smell.
- Movement is medicine. Consistent exercise like boxing, dance or balance training protects brain function and helps preserve independence.
- Never walk alone. Isolation makes Parkinson’s harder. Joining a support community is just as important as medical treatment.

title: USPS raises some shipping rates ahead of holiday season
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — The U.S. Postal Service is temporarily raising prices on some package deliveries ahead of the holiday season. A shipping industry expert says the cost could eventually land on consumers’ receipts.
USPS said in a press release the temporary rates apply to some Priority Mail, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select shipments starting Oct. 4 and will stay in place through mid-January.
In its announcement, the Postal Service said the adjustment is “to help cover extra handling costs to ensure a successful peak season.”
Joseph DiSorbo, founder and CEO of SHIP.com, said the rate increase is tied to several factors.
“It’s probably tied to some diesel costs, but I also think it’s just tied to the USPS not really making money and they’re trying to get their financials correct,” DiSorbo said.
Impact on retailers
DiSorbo said small retailers under pressure from larger retailers may have to absorb some of the added costs, which would affect their margins in the short term.
“I would say on the small retailers, that are under pressure from the larger retailers, they might have to absorb some of those costs, which will put pressure on their margins, at least in the short term. I think ultimately it gets passed on to the end user consumer,” DiSorbo said.
DiSorbo said smaller retailers in particular may feel the squeeze.
“So I don’t think we’re going to see anytime soon, free shipping will disappear. But I think, it’s gonna over time have to be passed along to the consumer in some way, shape or form,” DiSorbo said.
What retailers and shoppers can do
DiSorbo said retailers should start planning now.
“I would be calling my shipper, whether it’s USPS or UPS or FedEx, and ask them, what are the plans for holiday season? What can I expect? So you can get out ahead of that. So then you can plan properly,” DiSorbo said.
For consumers, DiSorbo recommends waiting to shop.
“I would shop a little bit after Thanksgiving and see if I can get a great deal on something,” DiSorbo said.

title: Horses were a hit, part II
text:
For the second time this year, residents of St. Andrews Village Retirement Community got up close and personal with horses, this time on Friday, Oct. 23.
Back in mid-August, Ella Watts of Burke’s Island Farm in Boothbay, along with her father, Robbie, brought two horses to the Village where about 50 residents got to greet, brush and feed the Wattses’ horses, Jimmy and Marley. Ella also works at the Village and she and Resident Services Coordinator Sarah Hackler set up the visit.
On Friday, 11 residents took a field trip to Burke’s, located on Route 27, where Ella and Burke’s owner Amy Reny gave them a grand tour of the 12-year-old facility and the 16 horses being boarded there.
The hour-long visit under sunny but breezy conditions saw the residents view the paddocks, petting those horses who came to the fencing, and asking questions about the various horses on display. Ella and Amy then brought two horses – 26-year-old Ruby and Memphis – into the barn where the Village visitors got to meet them face-to-face.
The farm offers lessons for children and adults who compete at horse shows in the spring and summer. Ella also showed the visitors the riding facility – where it was decorated for the next day’s Halloween event. Ella, who works with mostly adults, explained that Amy, who works mainly with kids, has provided a safe and affordable place.
Many of the visitors related their experiences with horses when they were at a younger age to Ella, Amy and the newspaper.
As one of the three farm cats roamed around the barn, the visitors then walked down to the lower paddocks to meet Jimmy and Marley again. Amy also brought out for viewing the lone pony being boarded.
The nine women and two men from the Village, as well as their bus driver and Resident Services employee Kim Baxley, took many photos of the horses to relive their visit.

title: Orland campground owner fined $8K over substandard waste piping
text:
The owners of an Orland campground have been ordered this month to pay $8,000 in fines over 20 campsites that violated town development ordinances.
The owners of Wanderin’ Moose Campground, which sits on the shore of Toddy Pond in Hancock County, have been in a multi-year dispute with the town of Orland after adding 20 unsanctioned campsites that were not part of their original approved site plan, according to court documents. The town alleged that the campground violated local laws about cutting down shoreland-adjacent trees and installing professionally-graded sanitary waste piping and electrical hook ups.
The Orland campground — which offers an unspecified number of tent sites, 10 full hookup RV units and 12 water and electrical sites — is owned by Norman Jacques Jr., Michael Jacques and Aline Jacques, each of whom are listed as defendants in the case.
“You don’t own the land, you rent it,” Norman Jacques Jr. said Friday. “We’ve worked our whole lives for this and this is what the town comes in and does.”
Although the owner technically does own the land, he said the town’s overreach over how many trees he should plant and the way he installs sanitary waste piping and electrical systems has left him with little authority over his property.
A Hancock County judge found the family in contempt of court on Oct. 7 after they failed to meet conditions agreed upon in a 2025 consent order with the town. Norman Jacques Jr., who is representing himself in the matter, said he wasn’t aware he was acceding to a consent agreement at the time of his signing.
Since the judge’s latest order, Norman Jacques Jr., who has owned the Leisure Way land since 1986 but opened the campground in 2005, said he is left with no choice but to satisfy the terms of the agreement by June 2027, as stipulated by the court. The owners risk being charged $137,000 if they fail to do so, according to the contempt order.
Patrick Lyons, an attorney for the town, said Friday the owners had failed to comply with two consent agreements over the last three years.
Lyons, on behalf of the town, asked the court to order the owners to pay $113,000 in fines — which is in line with state statutes for land use enforcement actions — though the judge refused to do so, saying such “crippling fees” would guarantee the owners would not be able to satisfy the agreement.
“The town never wanted it to come to this: the town’s goal all alone is just to protect the resources and bring it into compliance,” Lyons said. “Had the property owner done so initially, this all could have been avoided.”
The case, filed in Ellsworth District Court, dates back to September 2023 when the town’s code enforcement officer learned the campground had violated two local ordinances, according to court documents. Though the owners failed to correct the violations, they did pay $5,000 to the town.
But since then, the Jacques’ only completed some of the stipulations outlined in that consent agreement. The owners were required to hire a licensed forester, electrician and sanitary waste professional to meet the agreements’ conditions.
“I’m trying to run a family business — we work our butts off — and they’re mad because I do all the work myself,” Norman Jacques Jr. said. “We can’t afford to hire people to do work: we’re Mainers, we do stuff ourselves. But, because it’s commercial, you can’t do that.”
The owners hired a forester to design a reforestation plan, but it has not been fully implemented, according to the contempt order. The family did not have enough money to complete the plan, which would have cost roughly $71,000, Norman Jacques Jr. said. The Jacques’ planted 76 of the 142 trees that were required by the plan.
“Similarly, the defendants have not hired a licensed professional to design or document the underground sanitary waste piping and hook ups for the 20 campsites that were on the premises, illegally,” the order says. “Rather, they put in pipes on their own and covered them with dirt to protect the pipes without the input of a licensed professional or a plan.”
The owners said they were unable to afford to hire a licensed professional to install an underground sanitary waste piping system for the 20 sites.
The family did hire a licensed master electrician, though they are waiting to meet with the state’s electrical inspector for final certification.
“This is a situation of their own creation,” Judge Terrence Harrigan wrote in the order. “Their actions in installing the 20 sites falls under the heading of ‘it is better to beg for forgiveness, then to ask for permission.’ The credible testimony demonstrates that they ignored the approved plan and put the 20 sites in an unapproved location.”

title: Florida officer took possession of man’s home after finding him dead 4 years ago, police say
text:
(AP) - A Florida police officer who found a man dead during a welfare check in 2022 is accused of taking possession of the man’s home and impersonating him for years while fixing up the place, authorities said.
The officer said he took possession of the property weeks after discovering the homeowner’s body to “prevent squatters from taking control of it,” according to a court document he filed.
Investigators in South Florida have accused Lauderhill police officer Brian Sguros of carrying out a “complex scheme” to take control of the $400,000 home. They say he made it appear the man was still alive by using his identification to pay taxes on the property and obtain permits to make repairs.
Sguros was arrested this week and charged with five felonies, including official misconduct and criminal use of deceased personal identification. He appeared in court at a brief hearing on Wednesday and then dashed away from reporters outside.
Messages seeking comment were left Thursday with one of his attorneys and Sguros, who has been suspended from his job.
Court documents in a related civil case show that the officer’s attempt to take possession of the two-story house in a tidy neighborhood just outside Fort Lauderdale became known after a real estate group bought the house from the man’s relatives in 2025.
Sguros said in an affidavit that in August 2022 — less than a month after he found Dennis West dead inside the Lauderhill home — he took possession of the property and spent the next 2 1/2 years making repairs, spending more than $200,000 of his own money.
He said the house had been filled with trash, that its roof was partially collapsed and that the structure was unstable.
Sguros said in another court document that he took over the property “believing that by cleaning, securing, and restoring a dangerous and abandoned residence he was acting lawfully and responsibly to protect the surrounding community.”
He argued that he made no attempts to hide what he was doing.
But investigators with Broward County Sheriff’s Office said the deception began when the officer told the county medical examiner that he was friends with West, who had died of natural causes, and that the man had no family, which was not true.
Sguros paid taxes and utilities at the home in West’s name, and forged his signature to get permits for work at the home, the sheriff’s office said. Investigators said Sguros also used his access to law enforcement databases to find information about West.
The officer in February 2025 filed paperwork with the county appraiser stating his possession of the home. But after the real estate group later acquired deeds to the property, he filed a civil case against the company seeking to be reimbursed for the money he spent on repairs.

title: Justice Department sues Alaska over Senate candidate names
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (Gray DC) - The U.S. Department of Justice is suing Alaska over the handling of the state’s U.S. Senate election, according to a lawsuit filed by the Trump administration.
The lawsuit seeks to prevent certification of the election results in the race for Alaska’s Senate seat.
The lawsuit centers on two candidates in the race who share similar names: incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican, and a candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan.
According to the filing, the Justice Department is suing because it said it is in the interest of the federal government to protect the integrity of elections.
The lawsuit describes Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy as frivolous and intended to confuse voters with incumbent Dan S. Sullivan, which it says could hand the Senate seat to Democrat Mary Peltola.
The lawsuit includes the two candidates’ campaign logos as examples.
A sample ballot included as evidence in the lawsuit lists candidates alphabetically. Dan S. Sullivan’s entry is listed with the terms “registered Republican” and “incumbent.” Daniel J. Sullivan’s entry has no modifiers, according to the lawsuit.
President Donald Trump traveled to Wasilla for a rally in support of incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan Oct. 13.
“Well, I’m the one who said do it. They have two guys, run, named Dan Sullivan,” Trump said.
Election experts said lawsuits like this one are rare. They said they could not recall a previous example of one, and said the lawsuit relies on a novel reading of the National Voter Registration Act.
Alaska asks voters to rank their choices on the ballots.

title: Eastport health center to be renovated; new building nixed
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A planned new health center will not be built in Eastport after all, since bids for the project, first announced in early 2024, were much higher than expected. However, the expansion of services in Eastport will still occur, but at the current facility on Boynton St.
Michael Farrell, chief executive officer of Eastport Health Care and St. Croix Regional Family Health Center, which are now merged as a single nonprofit, says five bids for the new building were received, ranging from $18 million to $23 million, with the bidding process having closed last week. "It would have cost about $6 million to just put up the walls" for the building, he says. With only a little over $5 million available in funding, the health center's board decided instead to use the monies to remodel the existing building.
"We can do this with the funding we have with no additional debt," Farrell says. "All of the services planned for the new building will be put in the current building." An architectural firm, Foresight Engineering of Lincoln, has begun redesigning the building, and the project will be placed out to bid "as soon as possible," Farrell says. It should be completed by September 2027.
The administrative offices in the back of the building, with much of that space no longer occupied, will be remodeled, and the dental offices will move out there. The medical area will then be refurbished, with exam rooms added where the dental offices were.
The new building would have been on outer Key St., next to the former R&M IGA building, with work scheduled to have begun this month. The health center still owns the land, and Farrell says they will look for grants to carry out a project there that will align with the health center's mission in the community.
"We were disappointed" about the new building, Farrell says. "We were excited about what that project would do. But there is now a new opportunity to bring top-quality care to the area, and that will still be our goal with this project."
"I think our new project will allow the flexibility to bring more for both our patients and our team," he says. By not incurring any new debt, the health center will be able to undertake projects in the future, including a pharmacy at its Eastport location. "We can tackle that more quickly than we could have," Farrell says. He notes that there is higher demand than available access for pharmacy services not only in Eastport but in Calais, Princeton and Machias.
Work to begin at Calais site
Foresight Engineering also is working on renovating the new building that St. Croix Regional Family Health Center has purchased in downtown Calais. A bidder for the work is expected to be selected this week, with the renovation scheduled to begin this year. Work will start on the Lowell St. side so that the health center's services that are offered in its current Calais offices, also on Lowell St., can move there. The second phase of the project will be to renovate the side of the building facing Main St., with a pharmacy and dental services to be provided in that portion of the building.
Changes in services, staffing
In other changes, Farrell reports that St. Croix Regional Family Health Center will be switching over to Athenahealth Inc. for electronic medical records. Eastport Health Care uses Athena, and he says it will help to have both using the same company. More information will be released in the coming weeks.
Also, the organization was recently awarded $1 million over a four-year period from the federal Health Resources and Services Administration to enhance remote patient monitoring. Farrell says the funding will allow health center providers to work on chronic conditions that patients may have, such as diabetes or high blood pressure, without them having to come to the medical office. Since travel can be a barrier to accessing medical services in the area, this service will prove beneficial. The grant was written by Delia Yates, the director of grants and community development for the organization, and Farrell notes that the health center was one of only 20 organizations selected throughout the country for the funding. "It was a very competitive grant," he says. Speaking of Yates, he says, "We're proud of her work for us."
As for changes in services and staffing, Farrell reports that chiropractic and podiatry services are now offered at the health center's locations in Princeton, Calais, Eastport and Machias. At the beginning of the year optometry services will be offered in Machias.
The Eastport clinic is now offering walk-in care hours for anyone, whether or not they are registered as a patient at the health center. Farrell says if a person is sick with a cold or the flu or has a sprain, they can now walk in for care Monday through Thursday either between 7 and 8:30 a.m. or 3 and 4 p.m.
Eileen Snowleopard, a family nurse practitioner who specializes in diabetes care, is now working at the Eastport clinic, and Jerry Starling, a physician's assistant, will be starting in Machias in mid-November. Ann O'Brien, a psychiatric nurse practitioner who was working in Eastport, retired in September, and Jill Rockey and Jennifer Doucette, both psychiatric nurse practitioners, have begun working in Eastport. Also, Shyla Yerxa and Brandy Fredette will begin working as counselors in Eastport and Machias.

title: Kenduskeag Haunted House returns for spooky season
text:
KENDUSKEAG, Maine (WABI) — The Kenduskeag Haunted House is back for another season, a couple years after celebrating its 40th anniversary.
The community-run attraction offers elaborate sets, special effects and themed scares, with proceeds benefiting town sports and field maintenance.
Organizers say it’s thrilling but family-friendly, as most of the ghouls are local students earning community service hours. The attraction is not recommended for children under 12.
This week, performers are getting ready for the weekend.
“We are close and up personal. We like our rooms tiny. We like our hallways narrow. We like you to have that feeling from the smells and from the dangles that might be grazing against your face as you walk through. Unlike many other houses, we may touch you. You may get grabbed. We want to freak you out. It’s the unexpected. And we have a lot of unexpected,” said Wendy Cousins, head of the Haunted House Committee in the Kenduskeag Rec Department.
The house will be open Friday and Saturday from 7 p.m. to midnight, or possibly later depending on attendance.
Tickets are $15 per person. The house is located at Cole Memorial Field on Kenduskeag Levant Road.

title: 2 ex-FBI officials charged with making false statements about Hunter Biden’s laptop
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Two former FBI officials were charged Friday with lying to Congress about their involvement in investigating Hunter Biden’s laptop in the run-up to the 2020 presidential election, the latest in a series of splashy and politically charged actions the Justice Department has undertaken ahead of next month’s midterm contests.
Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, former leaders of a since-disbanded task force set up to counter foreign election interference, appeared in federal court in Washington, where their lawyers pressed for a speedy hearing to contest allegations their clients lied to lawmakers by saying that they did not participate in FBI investigations of Biden.
The prosecution, a rare Department of Justice criminal case against a former employee, revisits a tangled and peculiar saga that roiled the final weeks of the 2020 race. It also comes amid a broader, backward-looking effort by FBI Director Kash Patel, who before taking over the nation’s premier law enforcement agency was a harsh critic of it, to scrutinize high-profile episodes from the bureau’s recent past that for years have animated President Donald Trump’s conservative base.
Floris’ attorneys called her “a patriot” and said she has “served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years.”
“Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts,” her attorneys said in a statement. “It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election.”
Attorneys for Benavides accused the government of bringing “baseless criminal charges against him in a transparently political complaint.”
“This is another sad day for the Department of Justice,” his lawyers said in an emailed statement. “But now we are in court, and the truth will come out: Brad Benavides is a true patriot who devoted his career to protecting this country and its people. These charges are a disgrace.”
A criminal complaint comes just before the midterms
The case was filed less than two weeks before the Nov. 3 elections via criminal complaint, which means prosecutors have not yet presented the allegations to a grand jury for an indictment. The Justice Department has repeatedly struggled in high-profile cases to convince grand juries in the nation’s capital to return indictments.
During the former FBI employees’ court appearance, both defense attorneys and the judge noted the unusual move to charge the case through a complaint, which is more often used by prosecutors when they have an urgent need to take people into custody because, for example, they present a danger or a risk of flight.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui remarked that it is “rare that we have charges this old coming in this nature,” and over the objections of prosecutors who pushed for more time, set a preliminary hearing for next Tuesday, citing what he said was the “sword of Damocles” hanging over the defendants’ heads.
The laptop discovery created turmoil in 2020 election
The revelation of the laptop’s existence in October 2020 injected a thorny storyline in the race between Trump, the Republican incumbent, and Biden’s father, Joe Biden, Trump’s Democratic challenger who went on to win the race.
The laptop was publicized by the New York Post, which said it had obtained from Trump ally Rudy Giuliani a hard drive of a computer dropped off by Hunter Biden at a Wilmington, Delaware, repair shop about a year earlier.
The criminal complaint aims to build on longstanding congressional Republican complaints about the FBI’s handling of the laptop, including allegations that the bureau was not forthcoming to the public that the materials on it — including emails that showed discussions of the younger Biden’s foreign business dealings — were authentic and not the product of Russian disinformation.
The curious circumstances of the laptop’s discovery raised concerns among Democrats and former intelligence officials about the possibility of Russian involvement, particularly at a time when the Trump administration’s own intelligence community had assessed that Moscow that Russia was attempting to interfere in Trump’s favor in the election and as Giuliani had traveled abroad looking for dirt on the Bidens. Dozens of former U.S. intelligence officials signed a letter saying that the laptop bore the “classic earmarks of an Russian information operation.”
But Trump’s then-director of national intelligence, John Ratcliffe, said in a letter to Congress that there was no proof foreign actors had anything to do with the laptop. The FBI under then-Director Chris Wray subsequently endorsed that position.
Hunter Biden was charged with, and convicted of, gun and tax offenses during his father’s administration. Joe Biden pardoned him in his final weeks in office.
The case shines a light on an FBI task force on foreign intelligence
The complaint alleges that in their capacity as leaders of the Foreign Influence Task Force, Floris and Benavides were deeply engaged in the investigations into Hunter Biden, and that Biden was a recurring subject at FITF meetings.
Yet, the complaint says, both downplayed their firsthand knowledge of the laptop or involvement in investigations during 2023 testimony to lawmakers who were doing their own Biden investigation.
It accuses Benavides of making a false statement by saying he learned through Wikipedia that the FBI was in possession of the laptop, and says Floris falsely claimed to have had no knowledge of Hunter Biden having been the subject of discussions at FITF.
“Lying to Congress by senior FBI officials strikes at the heart of our system. No one is above the law,” Patel said.
The case brings renewed attention to the work of the task force, which was established in the first Trump administration to police influence campaigns staged by Russia and other nations aimed at sowing discord, undermining democracy and spreading disinformation. The task force became a magnet of congressional Republican criticism in part because of the Hunter Biden investigation and was disbanded in February 2025 by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi.
The Justice Department has made other splashy moves
As FBI director, Patel has presided over widespread firings of agents who were involved in investigations of Trump or who are perceived as being against the Republican administration’s agenda.
He has also focused attention on years-old investigations like the Hunter Biden one that occurred before he became director and that have been the subject of grievances and complaints by Trump allies.
The Justice Department historically looks to avoid public and overt investigative acts in the direct lead-up to an election that involve candidates or that risk influencing a political outcome. But officials in the last two weeks have made a series of bold moves in cases with political undertones, including a search of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s house in an immigration fraud investigation and a corruption indictment unsealed Thursday against powerful Democratic Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas.
Omar and Lucas are both Trump critics. Omar, who’s from Minnesota, has called the search of her Washington home an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” Lucas has said she won’t be intimidated or bullied by the federal government in its case against her and “will not back down.”

title: New York Knicks fan couple names baby 'Knickson Fyve'
text:
New York Knicks fan couple names baby 'Knickson Fyve' in honor of team's recent championship
Caught up in the moment? Justified expression of superfandom? You be the judge.
In August, New York City parents and lifelong Knicks fans Yvonne Gonzalez-Bradford and Vance Bradford named their newborn son “Knickson Fyve” in honor of the team’s recent NBA championship.
The name references how many games it took the Knicks to defeat the San Antonio Spurs in the seven-game series: Knicks in 5.
The viral rallying cry has appeared in arena chants, as a clever greeting among diehards and now on a birth certificate.
It's not just the Bradfords who have been inspired by the Knicks ending their 53-year championship drought.
The City Reporter, a local outlet, reported that data from the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene showed that babies named Jalen more than doubled between March and early October, seemingly in honor of Jalen Brunson, the team's captain and All-NBA point guard.

title: Trump says he ordered the Justice Department lawsuit over Alaska’s US Senate race
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump on Friday said he told his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, kicking off what many fear could become a lengthy battle between the government and states over certifying an election where the president’s party is struggling.
“I’m the one that said do it,” Trump told reporters as he landed for a campaign rally in Florida.
The lawsuit, filed late Thursday, centers on one of the president’s longstanding complaints in the Senate race — the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan, who Republicans fear could siphon away votes from the incumbent in what’s likely to be a photo-finish contest with Democrat Mary Peltola, the state’s former congresswoman.
The second Sullivan, who is Daniel J. Sullivan from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg, has said he decided to run on his own, but Republicans have contended he is a Democratic plant to siphon votes away from their candidate.
The lawsuit by the Republican president’s Department of Justice in federal court in Alaska demands that the state be blocked from certifying a Peltola win if Daniel J. Sullivan remains on the ballot. “The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska,” the lawsuit says.
The legal challenge came 11 days before the Nov. 3 election and months after the final ballot was set. It is the latest example of the Department of Justice bolstering Trump’s political operation, targeting his enemies and suing Democratic-controlled states before the election.
At a forum in Anchorage Friday night, Peltola called the lawsuit “just flagrant, flagrant corruption in my opinion.” She told reporters that the legal fight was “another diversion from the issue that Alaskans want to talk about, which is affordability” and an example of how her Republican opponent was “using his connections in Washington, D.C., to manipulate the situation.”
“I am very concerned about Alaskans’ voices not being heard,” Peltola said.
Democrats and many voting rights advocates have long feared that the administration will try to block certification of elections that Trump’s party loses, much as he unsuccessfully tried to do when he lost the 2020 White House race to Democrat Joe Biden.
The Alaska Supreme Court rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, and the state’s Republican officials made the decisions about how to list him on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent. Alaska’s ranked choice voting system also will allow voters to select both of the men if confused.
Alaska’s other Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski, alluded to that in a social media post criticizing the lawsuit. “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot,” wrote Murkowski, who has endorsed the incumbent Sullivan. “The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit.”
Peltola and Sen. Sullivan were top vote-getters in nonpartisan primary
The senator received more than 68,000 votes in the August primary, while the challenging Sullivan got 4,107, about 2% of the total vote. Peltola, who had previously served one term in the House, was the top vote-getter in the nonpartisan primary. Both parties expect that whoever wins in November will do so by a tight margin in a state of 738,000 people.
The campaign for Sen. Dan Sullivan did not address whether the senator supports the Department of Justice’s intervention. “We’ll let the DOJ complaint run its course,” campaign spokesman Nate Adams said in a text message. “Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan’s strong record of delivering for Alaska.”
Daniel J. Sullivan, whose presence on the ballot is at issue in the lawsuit, did not respond to a request for comment.
“Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses,” said Devan Barber, executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.
In a statement Friday, the Department of Justice noted that Alaska’s election officials, who are Republicans, determined the other Sullivan’s campaign was an attempt to “mislead” voters and wanted him removed from the ballot. Both a state court and Alaska’s Supreme Court disagreed and kept the second Sullivan on the ballot.
“The Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters,” the department’s statement said.
Concerns about the Department of Justice’s role in the election had already reached a fever pitch this month after it filed an unusual, last-minute lawsuit demanding California segregate ballots from 20,000 voters who the Trump administration believed could be noncitizens. California said that it appeared many of those identified were indeed citizens and that they had no time to carefully investigate, as the administration threatened to prosecute the state’s election workers if there was illegal voting.
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche denied the action was a prelude to challenging certification of the midterm results in that state, adding that such a move may happen under a “doomsday” scenario but was unlikely.
“It is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process,” he told reporters Thursday in Virginia before the Alaska lawsuit was filed.
The lawsuit was signed by Associate U.S. Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who represented Trump allies and Jan. 6 defendants before becoming one of the top appointees at the department.
Constitution gives states the power to run elections
Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the lawsuit would likely only kick in if Republicans narrowly lose the Alaska Senate race and that it probably would not survive long. “The statute simply doesn’t let the Department of Justice enjoin certification,” Muller said. “The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month.”
The U.S. Constitution grants states the power to run their own elections. Elections for federal office like the Senate must comply with standards set by Congress. That division of power has frustrated Trump, who repeatedly has tried to seize control of election procedures through executive orders that courts have blocked.
The final step for a state election is formally certifying the winner, the act that the administration’s lawsuit seeks to prevent, it requests, “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan.”
The process in Alaska is complicated by the state’s ranked choice voting system, which Trump opposes, and many expect it to take weeks before a winner is known. Also on the state’s ballot is an initiative to repeal that system.
Trump has stepped up complaints about a ballot with dueling Sullivans
Trump has complained about Daniel J. Sullivan’s presence on the ballot, making reference to it during a rally in Alaska this month and in repeated social media posts, including one this week where he called it “CHEATING.”
“We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness,” the president wrote on Wednesday.
Clogging a ballot with third-party candidates to siphon off votes from the other major party is a long-standing tactic in the country’s two-party system. Republicans have been linked to an effort to persuade Ohio voters to support a socialist in that state’s Senate race, which could help Republican Sen. Jon Husted fend off a challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown.
___
Associated Press writers Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, Haven Daley in Anchorage, Alaska, Ali Swenson in New York and Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Alvin Fountain Gamage
text:
Alvin Fountain Gamage, 97, of Saratoga, N.Y., died Oct. 21, 2026 after a brief illness. He was born at home in Bristol, the first son of John Carter Fountain and Martha (Grauballe) Gamage.
He attended local schools Lincoln Academy and the University of Maine in Orono. Immediately after graduation in 1951, he was drafted into the U.S. Marine Corps. He was based at Marine Barracks, 8th & I, in Washington, D.C., where he marched in parades, met General Eisenhower’s plane when he returned from Europe, and marched in his Inaugural Parade. Thanks to the GI Bill, he graduated from Columbia University with a master’s degree in library science.
He worked as a librarian in the Enoch Pratt Free Library system in Baltimore, Md., head librarian at Brooks Memorial Library in Brattleboro, Vt., reference librarian at Trinity College in Hartford, Conn., and Reference and Head Librarian at Skidmore College, in Saratoga Springs, N.Y.
While at the U of M, he was active in the Maine Masque, and later with Schuylerville Community Theater, both on stage and backstage. He loved reading, opera, genealogy, gardening, historic houses, heritage apples, and Newfoundland dogs.
He is survived by his wife, Gay (Kimball); his daughter, Evaline; his son, Rawson Nathaniel (Kristina) and their children, Pilar Grace, Petra Rose, and Wilder Kimball Gamage; his brothers, John (Cynthia), Frank (Rhoda) and their children and grandchildren, all of Maine.
Friends and neighbors are invited to visit the family at 226 County Route 67, in Saratoga Springs on Sunday afternoon, Nov. 1 between 2-6 p.m. A service and burial will be at a later date at the Harrington Cemetery in Bristol where Alvin will rest with many generations of his family.
Memorial donations to Opera Saratoga, 19 Roosevelt Dr., Ste 215, Saratoga Springs, NY 12866.

title: 6 arrested in $1.2 million Walmart fraud scheme after dozens of packages found piling up
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PEORIA, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — What began with a Walmart driver’s tip about dozens of packages piling up at a home in Arizona led investigators to a million-dollar fraud scheme that stretched to Southeast Asia.
Authorities in Arizona said a Walmart driver told them on Aug. 22 that he’d delivered 30 to 50 packages under different names to the same Peoria-area home in just a couple of days.
Days later, a customer reported that someone had hacked their Walmart account and used it to buy items.
According to court documents, those two reports sparked a two-month investigation that ended Thursday morning with six arrests.
How it happened
Investigators say the group placed about 15,500 orders on Walmart.com using hacked customer accounts and stolen credit and debit card numbers.
They reportedly altered delivery addresses to get around fraud alerts.
“Without that delivery driver, I don’t know if it would have come across our radar,” Peoria police officer William Kennedy said.
Police linked 11,364 orders worth more than $768,000 to six drop houses in Mesa, Avondale, Glendale and Peoria, according to court paperwork.
In total, investigators put the fraud at about $1.23 million.
The merchandise was reportedly funneled through two boba shops in Peoria and Tolleson, before being driven to California to be shipped to Vietnam in containers through U.S. Cargo Shipping LLC.
“Like your average shopper who gets stuff for the dogs, the kids, their house, all those types of items were coming to those houses,” Kennedy said.
So far, police say Walmart has confirmed $57,501 in chargeback losses tied to two victims, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed 203 customers with $8,821 in unauthorized purchases.
Police shared photos showing some of the $25,000 worth of Walmart merchandise recovered in the investigation. Officers also seized $35,000 in cash and $45,000 in gold bars.
Finding the ringleader
Investigators identified 30-year-old Hoài Nguyen Nguyen as the organizer of the illegal operation, which included at least nine other people.
Nguyen denied any involvement in the crimes and told police he was only an employee for U.S. Cargo Shipping LLC, the company he is believed to be the owner of.
Two other suspects reportedly told police Nguyen recruited them to accept packages under different names, track them and load them into his van and U-Haul trailer for drives to California in exchange for a cut of the shipment values.
Search warrants were served across the Valley with help from SWAT teams, Homeland Security Investigations and Walmart investigators.
Ten people were detained; four were released.
Six people were booked into Maricopa County Jail on charges including fraud, identity theft, computer tampering and trafficking in stolen property:
- Thien Tran, 42
- Uy Vu Phan, 55
- Minh Ngọc Nguyen, 57
- Hie Xuan Le, 24
- Hoài Nguyen Nguyen, 30
- Hailey Hang Nguyen, 26
All six face charges of fraudulent schemes and artifices, possession of an access device violation, computer tampering for fraud, aggravated taking of identity and trafficking in stolen property in the first degree, according to court records.
