title: 8 people hospitalized in E. coli outbreak linked to raw milk cheese
text:
8 people hospitalized in E. coli outbreak linked to raw milk cheese
8 people hospitalized in E. coli outbreak linked to raw milk cheese
A multistate E. coli outbreak linked to raw milk cheese has hospitalized eight people so far. Here’s what you should know.
Video above: Doctor debunks myths about drinking raw milk
What products are being recalled?
Sierra Nevada Cheese Company
The California-based dairy brand Graziers has recalled all of its raw milk cheeses. The impacted products include Monterey Jack, Jalapeño Jack, Medium Cheddar, and Sharp Cheddar in sizes ranging from eight-ounce squares to 40-pound blocks.
Its parent company, Sierra Nevada Cheese Company, voluntarily initiated the recall on Sept. 24 after the FDA contacted the company about its ongoing outbreak investigation and recommended a recall. The brand continues to cooperate with the investigation.
Because the FDA and CDC have not yet identified the specific lot number, production date, or source of the E. coli, Graziers has pulled all of its raw milk cheese from shelves out of an abundance of caution.
Where were the recalled products sold?
One recalled product, a 40-pound block of cheddar sold to foodservice providers, was distributed across 13 states and totaled 1,373 pounds. The broader recall, though, includes products distributed nationwide through retailers, distributors, direct customers, and online.
As of Sept. 25, federal agencies say the outbreak spans nine states: California, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Colorado, Michigan, Kentucky, Tennessee, and Georgia.
Of the 13 cases tied to the outbreak, eight resulted in hospitalizations. Three people also developed hemolytic uremic syndrome, a serious form of kidney failure. More than half of those sickened are children age five or younger.
What should I do if I have the affected product?
If you happen to have any Graziers raw milk cheese in your fridge, the FDA advises disposing of it or returning it to the place of purchase for a refund.
The products have a long shelf life, so the agency recommends checking both refrigerators and freezers.
To avoid potential cross-contamination, it also recommends cleaning and sanitizing any surfaces or containers the cheese may have touched.
If you have consumed this brand of cheese, watch for symptoms. E. coli infections can cause severe stomach cramps, diarrhea, fever, nausea and vomiting. Symptoms can begin up to nine days after consuming contaminated food. If you experience any symptoms consistent with an E. coli infection, contact your healthcare provider immediately.

title: Maine Finally Has a Standalone Toys 'R' Us Store Again, and It's Now Open
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s First New Standalone Toys ‘R’ Us Opens at the Auburn Mall
The time has come for the return of a standalone Toys 'R' Us to Maine.
Inside the Auburn Mall is a new, smaller version of the once-popular toy store, and it's now open.
Hopefully, it sticks around for more than just the holidays!
Where Is Toys 'R' Us in Maine?
South Portland and Bangor were the last of Maine's Toys "R" Us stores before they closed in 2018.
Toys "R" Us technically returned to South Portland in 2022, but in a different form, as its own little section inside Macy's.
But the first new standalone Toys "R" Us in Maine moved into the Auburn Mall at 550 Center Street in Auburn in October 2026.
Is Toys "R" Us Making a Comeback?
I thought Toys "R" Us was just a fond memory of the past, but it seems to be making a comeback.
Just a few years after the company went bankrupt and liquidated, it was acquired by WHP Global and then later partnered with Go! Retail Group to push for store expansion, according to Forbes.
Now, for this year, USA Today reported that Toys "R" Us is opening 120 new stores. That's a pretty big turnaround from before, right?
Is the Toys "R" Us in Auburn, Maine, Just for the Holidays?
A big question many probably have involves the staying power of Toys "R" Us and whether it can be a staple spot even after the holiday shopping season is over.
While there's not a definitive answer regarding the Auburn Mall location, it will likely depend on whether there's enough demand for it year-round.
In a Facebook post announcing the new store in Auburn, the mall noted that the decision "depends on the community. If people shop it, they will stay. So it really is in the hands of the public."
READ MORE: Here Are 4 New Businesses Coming to the Auburn, Maine, Mall
Are you excited for the return of Toys "R" Us?
Sure, it's not going to be like when kids got to browse the tons of aisles inside a massive space back in the day. And maybe the nostalgia for that is so strong it makes you brush off a reboot that isn't the exact same as the one from the past.
But I don't think you should.
It's nice seeing a little piece of childhood coming back to life, seeing Geoferry the Giraffe once again, and knowing that nearly 70 years after the first Toys "R" Us opened, it hasn't been erased for good.
Even in 2026, you can still be a Toys "R" Us kid.

title: Calley Means, a key MAHA advocate, resigns as a top RFK Jr. adviser
text:
Calley Means, a key MAHA advocate, resigns as a top RFK Jr. adviser
Calley Means, a top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a chief advocate for the Make America Healthy Again movement, resigned from his position with the Trump administration Thursday.
In a statement, Means did not say why he was leaving. His departure comes as leading voices in the MAHA movement have expressed discontent with what they say is the Trump administration's lack of progress on a variety of issues, including food security and regulating the weed killer glyphosate.
Means said he "leaves with tremendous respect" for President Donald Trump and Kennedy.
"The past two years have seen historic policy and cultural change to confront the chronic disease crisis and healthcare incentives that profit from us being sick," Means said. "This movement is in the first inning and just getting started."
Means was hired as a White House adviser early in the second Trump administration. He used his perch at the Health and Human Services Department to attack the nation's leading physician groups, federal agencies and government scientists, claiming they only protect their own interests.
White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration is "grateful" for Means' time and "he has done a fantastic job for the MAHA movement." A representative from Health and Human Services did not respond to a request for comment.
Health activist Kelly Ryerson, a leader of American Regeneration who is also known as Glyphosate Girl on social media, said she is "impressed that he completed over two years at HHS fighting the food battle, despite all of the obstacles presented by corporate interests."
"At the heart of MAHA is a shared belief that the nation's health must not be sacrificed to corporate profit, and that a preventable slide into chronic disease is a threat to America itself," she said.
Means is the brother of wellness influencer, author and entrepreneur Dr. Casey Means, who failed to be confirmed as surgeon general earlier this year after doubts were raised over her vaccine stance.
Means, along with his sister, came to prominence within the MAHA movement by arguing that ultraprocessed foods, additives and pesticides could be blamed for many of the chronic health conditions facing Americans.
Means brought those arguments into the Trump administration and frequently clashed with senior White House officials who worried about alienating the powerful food industry.
At the same time, Means' emphasis on food was a source of frustration for other figures within the MAHA movement who wanted to see Kennedy focus on "medical freedom" issues. For many, that meant rolling back federal recommendations and approvals for vaccines.
Despite Means' efforts, the administration's progress on food reforms has been slow going.
Kennedy had promised the release of a first-ever government definition of ultraprocessed food in April. Instead, FDA's acting commissioner, Kyle Diamantas, told a conference that month that defining the class "is really hard."
In August, Kennedy staffers again suggested a major announcement on the issue was imminent. Instead, the announcement focused on a proposal bringing greater scrutiny to food additives. It made only passing mention of ultraprocessed foods.
Zen Honeycutt, founder of Moms Across America, said Means will be missed by her organization, which operates local and national campaigns warning against pollution, water use and electricity costs associated with data center construction.
Honeycutt said Means "brought an energy and fearlessness to the Hill, fighting for our children to have healthy food in schools and for America's health."

title: Obituary: Irene M. Fenlason
text:
STARKS – Irene M. Fenlason, 77, a longtime resident of Starks, Maine, and recently of Portland, passed away peacefully on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026, at Gosnell Memorial Hospice in Scarborough. She found a place of peace after a struggle with a lingering illness, surrounded by the best wishes for her peace from her friends and family and capable assistance of her caretakers attending.
Irene was born in Waterville, Jan. 2, 1949, the daughter of Marion (Keast) and Lyle E. Fenlason. She grew up in North Anson and Skowhegan, attending public schools and graduating from Skowhegan High School in 1967. She then attended Colby College, graduating with a B.A. in English in 1971.
Shortly after graduating from college, and after a few years of itinerant waitressing, she went to work in the family business – Kennebec Auto Parts in Madison. For nearly 50 years she worked there as a clerk, manager and eventually the owner. She was extremely proud of her accomplishments and success in a “man’s” world. She also came to know many of the people and workers of Madison, Starks, and Anson and made her long term home in Starks as an independent person who had made her own way through life on her own terms.
Irene’s interests included pets – cats and dogs all her life and a horse of her own as a teenager – gardening, reading and collecting science fiction, stained glass making and participation in the affairs of her community, serving on the Starks planning board for several years. Like many of us, she also retained a strong affection for the works of Jane Austen – one of the many authors she studied in college.
Irene is survived by her brother, Bruce and his wife Judy Fenlason of Biddeford; a niece, Sara Fenlason and her wife Trisha Kirk of Minneapolis, Minn.; her special friends, neighbors and helpers Marc and Tracy Cowan of Starks; stepdaughter, Sandy Quimby Smith of Alabama; several cousins scattered over much of the eastern part of the country and memories of her successful life and career.
No services are planned at this time. Dennett, Craig & Pate Funeral Home, Saco are entrusted with her services.

title: Rockport voters to consider requiring inspections for rental housing properties
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rockport voters will consider two questions on the November ballot, including Article 3 seeking approval of a rental housing unit ordinance.
“It came about as a response to the feedback that we got on the board from town folks about regulating short-term rentals,” Planning Board Chair Jeffrey Leclair said. “Although what’s on the article right now is not a short-term rental regulation.”
He also indicated that the proposed ordinances have been in the works for a few years.
The ordinance will require that any rental or housing unit be registered every year with an initial inspection needed the first year to make sure it meets health and safety requirements.
A group of local property owners argued in the meeting that the regulations restrict property rights and are intrusive. In addition, they stress that the town has already rejected short-term regulations at the polls and questioned the transparency of the rollout of the proposed ordinances.
Clare Tully said she felt the ordinance changes were rushed onto the ballot.
“They’re so intrusive,” she said of the proposed regulations. “It tells us how often to take out the trash!”
“This is not Camden,” she said. “We don’t want to pay registration fees.”
Short-term rental owners argue these rentals are often used so that property owners can afford their high property taxes.
The often-cited victory at the polls in the effort against short-term rental regulation came in June 2021. Residents were asked in a non-binding question if they would support an ordinance to regulate short-term rentals in the community, and it was voted down by a margin of 407-194. It was noted at the meeting last week that more than 2,000 are expected to vote in Rockport in the November election.
Select Board Chair Denise Munger said Oct. 13 this was a Planning Board initiative, not the work of the Select Board, to which some present at the meeting argued that the Select Board voted to put it on the ballot.
In an opinion piece, Leclair explained the intent of the proposed changes. “We’re doing this to fill a hole in our enforcement of life safety in dwelling units. …Our current Land Use Ordinance lacks an effective enforcement mechanism for rental housing. Already all commercial lodging (such as inns, hotels and motels), all newly constructed homes or additions, and all multi-family homes are inspected before use, and this amendment augments the ordinance to ensure that every renter in town is sleeping in a unit that meets basic life safety code.”
Opponents of the measure argued there is a difference between a small in-home unit and a hotel or inn that has multiple rooms, parking lots and other amenities.
There was some debate during the meeting about whether the new ordinance would categorize all short-term rentals as commercial operations.
Munger said in an email that town attorney Phillip Saucier reviewed the proposed amendment and noted that “Short Term Rental” is already a defined use and it’s reasonable to include it in the Land Use tables of Section 917.
“Although the proposed amendment places ‘Short Term Rental’ within the Commercial Use table of Section 917.C, that placement does not change the residential nature of a dwelling unit used as a Short Term Rental. Subsequently, no other restrictions would be automatically imposed on Short Term Rentals merely because they are listed on the Commercial table in the Land Use Ordinance.”
Town officials said in the meeting the goal was actually to make short-term rentals an identified allowed use in much of the town, but this inclusion led to the concern about their being defined as commercial. If voters approve Article 2, Munger said, short-term rentals would be formally allowed in all zoning districts except industrial, which in Rockport consist of the property occupied by Midcoast Solid Waste.
Resident Ben Lance asked in the meeting when the new law would go into effect if it were approved. Munger said that was to be determined. Lance pressed, asking if the officials didn’t know when the effective date was.
“I’m not going to answer that question,” Munger said. “I’m going to let the town lawyer…”
At that point there was some laughter in the audience.
“You guys can laugh,” Munger said, “but look, we’re doing our best to listen to you and be judicious.”
Lance said, “I wasn’t trying to give you a hard time.”
“No, you are,” Munger said.
If the ordinance change is approved, property owners will have to contact the Town Office to apply for a certificate of occupancy, according to Leclair. The code enforcement officer will conduct a life safety inspection and the fee is $100. “There is no ongoing schedule for inspections required by this amendment.”
“The inspection is to ensure the adequacy of systems already in place, namely required smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, potable water, heating, wastewater and egress,” the Planning Board chair said. “Things like electrical upgrades are not required if the systems legally existed prior to code requirements (‘grandfathered’).”
One of the loudest voices speaking out against the ordinance changes is Ethan Jones of Warrenton Street, who argues the changes do categorize short-term rentals as commercial and notes that there is no set fee schedule in the proposed ordinance. In addition, Tully had noted that Camden’s rental registration fees are higher.
Jones has also been involved in a dispute with the town on another matter, as a property owner on Warrenton Street who opposes the plan to put in a multipurpose path on the street.
“Ladies and gentlemen, there is no need to pass Articles 2 & 3,” Jones wrote in a letter to the editor as rebuttal to Leclair’s piece. “Homeowners do not want or need a new, expensive town bureaucracy. But there is a need to preserve freedom and to defend property rights. As the saying goes, ‘Once they’re gone, they’re gone.’”
One of the residents speaking out against the ordinance changes at the meeting warned the Select Board, “You’re going to see a lot more ‘no’s’ from people.”
A last-minute campaign against the ordinance articles has been launched with signs posted around town urging residents to vote the measures down.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: ‘Total disgrace’: Trump blasts LeBron James for not standing still during national anthem
text:
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday accused LeBron James of disrespecting the United States after the NBA star appeared to continue his warmups while the national anthem was performed before Philadelphia’s season opener on Tuesday.
“I said right from the beginning that he’s no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE,” Trump said of James in a social media post sharing the video. “LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!”
James appeared to practice a golf swing and jump shot as “The Star-Spangled Banner” was performed Tuesday at New York’s Madison Square Garden. James, starting his first season with Philadelphia, was lined up alongside teammates who mostly stood still during the anthem.
Trump and James have been critical of each other for years, occasionally trading public swipes.
“It must be a slow news day at the office,” James said. “Slow news day at the office.”
The 41-year-old James, in his record 24th NBA season, had 17 points and 10 rebounds in the biggest comeback win of his career, 114-106 over the Cavaliers in Philadelphia’s home opener on Thursday night. The Sixers rallied from a 29-point deficit.
James put his arms behind his back and bowed his head while Boyz II Men sang the anthem ahead of the game. James was introduced to a roaring ovation from the crowd of roughly 20,000.
Coach Nick Nurse had talked at length since training camp opened about the Sixers’ need to tune out outside distractions. Hours before their home opener, the Sixers had to deal with one from the president.
“I think that goes right in with other outside noise we’ve already had,” Nurse said before the game. “I keep saying the same thing. All I really care about is getting to the practice floor, getting them in the film room, getting them to the game floor. The focus that they’ve had and the intent and all the stuff like that has been outstanding.”
Trump, speaking Thursday night at a campaign rally in Sioux City, Iowa, reiterated his complaint.
“And what about LeBron James? Did you see that deal?” Trump said. ‘No, he’s doing, during the national anthem he’s practicing his golf swing. I said what the hell is that. It’s a big scandal kind of a story. I don’t understand it.”
Here are some of the more notable times James became entangled with the president or politics:
LeBron wears 1 black shoe, 1 white shoe
James was with Cleveland in 2017 when he made a statement with his shoes — one black, one white, with the word “equality” in capital gold letters on the back of each.
Then, after the game, James made a statement about Trump, saying: “This is a beautiful country and we’re never going to let one person dictate how beautiful and how powerful we are.”
James had called Trump “ a bum ” on Twitter and also said earlier that season of the president: “He doesn’t understand how many kids, no matter the race, look up to the president of the United States for guidance, for leadership, for words of encouragement. He doesn’t understand that, and that’s what makes me more sick than anything.”
Shut up and dribble
James showed determination to speak out on social issues and the nation’s political climate after Fox News host Laura Ingraham criticized the four-time NBA champion for his 2018 comments about social issues.
“We will definitely not shut up and dribble,” James said. “I will definitely not do that. I mean too much to society. I mean too much to the youth. I mean too much to so many kids that feel like they don’t have a way out and they need someone to help lead them out of the situation they’re in.”
James referenced Muhammad Ali, Jim Brown, Bill Russell and Jackie Robinson as athletes who previously spoke up for equality and change with no concerns about the consequences or any rewards.
“We know it’s bigger than us,” James said.
Response to Morey’s tweet about Hong Kong
James said in 2019 that former Houston Rockets general manager Daryl Morey “was either misinformed or not really educated on the situation” regarding the potential consequences of his actions when he tweeted in support of Hong Kong’s pro-democracy protests.
“Yes, we do have freedom of speech,” James said. “But at times, there are ramifications for the negative that can happen when you’re not thinking about others, when you only think about yourself. I don’t want to get into a word or sentence feud with Daryl Morey, but I believe he wasn’t educated on the situation at hand, and he spoke.”
Morey deleted the tweet, but it nonetheless sparked a rift with the Chinese government, which severed ties with the NBA for several years.
Getting people to the polls
James was named The Associated Press’ Male Athlete of the Year in 2020 in large part for leading the Los Angeles Lakers to a championship and helping to persuade many people who had never voted — at the peak of the Black Lives Matter movement — to head to the polls.
“I still know what I do on the floor and obviously, I give everything to the game,” James said. “But I can make a greater impact off the floor right now, more than I can on the floor. And I want to continue to inspire people with the way I play the game of basketball. But there’s so many more things that I can do off the floor to help cultivate people, inspire people, bring people together, empower them.”
James rejects Ibrahimovic’s criticism of activist athletes
AC Milan striker and former LA Galaxy star Zlatan Ibrahimovic blasted socially conscious athletes in a 2021 interview. Ibrahimovic called it “a mistake” for James and other athletes to get involved in political causes, saying they should “just do what you do best, because it doesn’t look good.”
James, naturally, rejected the criticism.
“I would never shut up about things that are wrong,” James said.
___
Associated Press writers Collin Binkley in Washington and Darlene Superville in Sioux City, Iowa, contributed to this report.

title: InvestigateTV+ Weekend: Billion Dollar Blitz
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Fans pack the stands and coaches cash in. Chris Nakamoto found an increasing part of the bill is landing on students and universities.
Plus, accountability disappears online when a company vanishes the second something goes wrong.
Billion Dollar Blitz
Here’s a number that might make your jaw drop: $12.8 billion. That’s what 109 public universities are spending on college athletics, and each year it’s taking a bigger bite out of public universities’ coffers and students’ pockets.
At the same time, football coaches’ salaries are skyrocketing, and it’s not just head coaches. Our team looked at contracts across America and found 31 assistant coaches are making more than $1 million.
National Investigative Reporter Chris Nakamoto went to Auburn, where fans reacted to one fired coach after another walk out the door. A sports economist with decades of experience said this system is not sustainable.
Meanwhile, Congress is looking to pump the brakes on this runaway spending - particularly in football.
Sports fan questions merchandise
When your team wins big, it’s natural to want to celebrate – maybe even grab some gear to mark the moment. But online shoppers are finding out that not every website selling that gear is what it claims to be – especially the moment a popular product sells out everywhere else.
One Michigan fan found that out after trying to buy his team’s championship gear online.
Reporter Tammy Elliott shows us what showed up at his door – and why getting his money back wasn’t easy.
Injuries take mental toll on athletes
For athletes, an injury doesn’t just sideline the body – it can take a toll on the mind, too. Doctors say stress, fear and even depression are common during recovery – but often go unspoken in a sport built on toughness.
At Clemson, football players and sports psychologists are opening up about what really happens when an athlete can’t play. Reporter Kari Beal in South Carolina takes us inside their journey back – mentally and physically.
Lunch options for your student
Sending kids to school with lunch means thinking about the budget, too. The average packed lunch now runs about $6 a day, according to Deloitte.
But Susan Campbell found families have more options than they might think – whether they’re packing or buying. She breaks down the real numbers, and some ways to bring that cost down.

title: Jayson Tatum bounces back to lift Celtics past Knicks
text:
BOSTON — Jayson Tatum scored 25 of his 36 points in the second half, including seven of his team’s final eight to help the Boston Celtics hold off the New York Knicks 107-103 on Friday night.
Paul George and Neemias Queta added 15 points apiece to help fend off a late rally by the defending NBA champion Knicks.
New York fell to 0-2 after losing its season opener to the Philadelphia 76ers.
Karl-Anthony Towns had 22 points to lead five Knicks in double figures. OG Anunoby finished with 20 points, 10 rebounds and eight assists. Deuce McBride scored 20 points and Jalen Brunson added 19.
In a game that featured 12 lead changes and four ties, Boston outscored New York 33-24 in the third quarter to increase a one-point halftime lead to 10.
The Celtics’ edge grew as high as 91-79 before a 12-3 Knicks run cut it to 94-91 on a Towns putback dunk.
New York got it back to 99-96 on Josh Hart’s 3-pointer before Queta turned it over, leading to a floater by Brunson. But Tatum responded with a 19-footer on Boston’s next possession that made it 101-98 with 1:11 remaining.
It was 103-98 when Anunoby hit a pair of free throws with less than a minute left. Tatum then drained a 3 from the wing.
Mitchell Robinson finished with four points, four rebounds and a block after struggling with early foul trouble throughout his first matchup against the Knicks team that he helped win last season’s title. Robinson was the only member of New York’s regular rotation who didn’t return to the team.
It didn’t stop him from making his presence felt opposite the team with whom he spent his first eight NBA seasons. During one sequence in the fourth quarter Robinson swatted away a layup attempt by Towns. Following a miss by Mikal Bridges, Robinson then was the recipient of an alley-oop from Derrick White.
The game was scrappy on both sides, but Queta was the only Celtics player to attempt a free throw through two-plus quarters. That didn’t change until Tatum went to the line with 3:21 remaining in the third.

title: Maine State Museum to reopen Saturday after six-year closure
text:
Maine State Museum to reopen Saturday after six-year closure
After six years and $3 million in renovations, the Maine State Museum in Augusta is set to reopen Saturday with free admission and several new displays, including the skeletons of two humpback whales.
Maine State Museum to reopen Saturday after six-year closure
After six years and $3 million in renovations, the Maine State Museum in Augusta is set to reopen Saturday with free admission and several new displays, including the skeletons of two humpback whales.
The Maine State Museum in Augusta will reopen Saturday with new exhibits, interactive displays and a celebration with free admission.
The reopening is the first phase of a $3 million renovation project that began in 2020 at the Cultural Building, which also houses the Maine State Library and State Archives.
The museum says the building’s renovation required upgrades to accessibility, energy efficiency, technology and building safety. Two of the museum’s four exhibit floors will be open initially. The remaining exhibits are planned to reopen in later phases.
Visitors will find a new exhibit featuring the skeletons of a humpback whale and her calf, along with updated displays about Maine history.
New exhibits include a look at the ship St. Mary — built in Phippsburg in 1890 and wrecked on its first voyage — and a display about outdoorswoman Cornelia “Fly Rod” Crosby.
The museum also has a new education space and updated sections of its "At Home in Maine" exhibit.
Director Bernard Fishman has led the museum through the closure and its transformation.
“It’s a great source of pride for me. Certainly it’s all a legacy that we want to leave for a generation or two, and then things will change again,” Fishman said.
To celebrate the reopening, the Maine Department of Transportation shared a photo from its archives showing an aerial photo of the Capitol area in 1974, three years after the Maine Cultural building was first constructed.
The reopening celebration runs from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday at the museum at 230 State St. in Augusta. The schedule includes a ribbon-cutting ceremony, live music, refreshments and exhibit-related activities. Admission will be free for all visitors through Dec. 31.
After the reopening, the museum plans to be open Tuesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. It will be closed Mondays and on state holidays.
WABI-TV contributed to this report.

title: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez campaigns for Troy Jackson, touts shared progressive values
text:
PORTLAND, Maine - Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) traveled to Maine on Thursday to take the stage with Senate candidate Troy Jackson in Portland. The two took several questions from college students at the event hosted by “More Perfect University,” a progressive campus group, and touched on topics ranging from immigration enforcement to healthcare.
“They are sending ICE out in droves [in Maine]. Not just to intimidate the Somali community, the immigrant community, but to intimidate all of us,” Ocasio-Cortez said, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
“I hear it from people all the time who do not support Medicare for All. ‘Well, I like my private insurance.’ Fine, and I am going to do something better than your private insurance,” Jackson said.
Jackson and Ocasio-Cortez both argued that the money that is used to fund the ongoing war in Iran and ICE should be used to fund healthcare.
“How can we afford Iran? How can we afford Gaza? How can we afford these things when folks at home can’t eat, can’t go to the doctor or build a bridge to get there?” asked Cortez.
Ocasio-Cortez also spoke about higher education and called for all public colleges and universities to be tuition-free. She said higher education has become a “luxury” in 2026.
The two appeared to agree on nearly every topic discussed. From defunding ICE and ending the war in Iran. Ocasio-Cortez spent most of the evening speaking, with Jackson chiming in. The two also spent time taking jabs at Sen. Susan Collins and called her out again for her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
“Susan Collins, one of the only Republican female senators in a unique position to protect almost every woman in America, decided to declare open season on us instead,” Ocasio-Cortez said.
The two were also asked about funding rural healthcare and public transit. Jackson said he would like to see a rail system connecting Portland and Bangor eventually built using federal funds.

title: From hot dogs to gelato: Here are the major recalls announced this week
text:
From hot dogs to gelato: Here are the major recalls announced this week
Consumers faced a wide range of recalls last week, spanning food, household products, medications and vehicles.
Among the bigger recalls last week were a massive meat recall from Kayem Foods and fire-risk recalls involving Toyota and Hyundai vehicles.
Related video above | Check your fridge: Recalled foods could already be in your home
Food alerts also covered items such as gelato, smoked salmon and cheddar cheese, while several children’s products raised concerns about button batteries or safe sleep. Toothpaste, pet medications and patio heaters rounded out a varied week for recalls.
Below is a breakdown of the major recalls issued over the past two weeks.
FOOD ITEMS
- Dried beans. Natural Grocers recalled certain 2-pound bags of its organic mung beans after customers reported sharp glass fragments. The affected lots were shipped to stores in 23 states beginning in June 2026. Click here to view the full recall.
- Ready-to-eat meat and poultry. Kayem Foods recalled about 1.58 million pounds of products, including hot dogs, bacon, deli meat and bratwursts, because they may have been held at unsafe temperatures. Click here to view the full recall.
- Gelato. Lidl US recalled one lot of Gelatelli Coffee & Vanilla Gelato after routine testing found possible Listeria contamination. The affected product was sold in Lidl stores in several states, including Georgia and South Carolina. Click here to view the full recall.
- Cold-smoked salmon. Krasnyi Oktyabr recalled Starfish Seafood Premium Cold Smoked Norwegian Salmon because it may be contaminated with Listeria. The 8-ounce product was distributed in several states, including Georgia. Click here to view the full recall.
- Raw cheddar cheese. Family Farmstead Dairy recalled a specific lot of its raw mild cheddar cheese because it may be contaminated with E. coli. The affected cheese was distributed to retailers in several states, and may have reached others through downstream distributors. Click here to view the full recall.
- Hoagie rolls. WinCo Foods recalled certain hoagie rolls because their labels did not disclose sesame, which may trigger a serious or life-threatening reaction in people with a sesame allergy. The rolls were sold at WinCo stores in California, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Washington. Click here to view the full recall.
- Raw oysters. Little Wicomico Oyster Company recalled oysters harvested from Virginia’s Little Wicomico River from Sept. 18 through Oct. 8, 2026, because they may be contaminated with Salmonella. The oysters were distributed to restaurants and retailers in multiple states, including Georgia. Click here to view the full recall.
HOUSEHOLD GOODS
- Papablic infant swings. The recalled Archie baby swings pose a suffocation risk if used for infant sleep because their incline exceeds the limit allowed for infant sleep products. Click here to view the full recall.
- LED finger-light toys. BAMAMON projecting finger lights contain button batteries in compartments children can access, posing a risk of serious injury or death if a battery is swallowed. Click here to view the full recall.
- Light-up princess costumes. CIYTI costumes were recalled because children can access the button batteries, creating a serious ingestion hazard. Click here to view the full recall.
- Convertible high chairs. Costway recalled high chairs that convert into a table and chair set because they pose entrapment and fall hazards and violate the mandatory high-chair standard. Click here to view the full recall.
- Gas patio heaters. VQQQ patio heaters were recalled because they pose fire and burn hazards that could cause serious injury or death. Click here to view the full recall.
- Commercial outdoor lights. Certain Lithonia Lighting RSX luminaires may detach from their adjustable tilt arms if a mounting joint fails, creating an impact hazard. Click here to view the full recall.
MEDICATIONS
- Toothpaste products. More than 4.3 million tubes of Brush Buddies, evo and ARU toothpaste were recalled over manufacturing practice deviations. The affected products include children’s character-themed and flavored toothpastes, as well as adult products. Click here to view the full recall.
- Compounded pet medications. Wedgewood Pharmacy recalled certain compounded veterinary medications because unreliable testing data could mean some products are too weak or too strong, potentially causing ineffective treatment or overdose. Click here to view the full recall.
- Amazon-branded acetaminophen. Certain Amazon Basic Care Extra Strength acetaminophen caplets were recalled after reports that tablets had become discolored. Click here to view the full recall.
VEHICLES
- Toyota vehicles. Toyota recalled certain vehicles after a fuel tube defect was found that could cause a fuel leak and increase the risk of fire. Click here to view the full recall.
- Hyundai and Genesis vehicles. The recall covers certain Genesis and Genesis G80 vehicles whose power seat motors could overheat if a control switch sticks, creating a fire risk. Click here to view the full recall.

title: Patriots battle through injuries, but time runs out against Bears
text:
The Patriots’ three-game winning streak is over after they ran out of time and luck in their 30-24 loss to the Chicago Bears on Thursday night.
However, with New England dealing with multiple injuries, including two starters on the offensive line, coach Mike Vrabel left Soldier Field feeling disappointed in the outcome, but not about the resolve of his team going forward.
“We fought. I would say that we need to (force opponents to) turn the ball over and tackle better and those are fundamental skills. But I like the way they competed and we certainly gave ourselves a chance,” Vrabel said.
With left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) joining right guard Mike Onwenu (ankle) on injured reserve this week, the Patriots went with recent addition Matt Pryor and Walter Rouse in their place. Quarterback Drake Maye was sacked twice, but the 10th different offensive line combination the Patriots have used this season held up well.
Maye completed 24 of 31 passes for 321 yards and two TDs and a rushing score. After the loss he put the onus on himself to make better decisions, namely his costly second-quarter interception in the end zone when he was trying to complete a pass to tight end Eli Raridon. The Bears scored on their ensuing drive to take a 20-7 lead.
“I thought we battled the environment well,” Maye said. “And I thought we did some good things but didn’t execute at a high enough level to win.”
What’s working
Despite the loss, New England’s offense didn’t show much regression. Maye had the one interception, but it was on a pass in the red zone.
What needs help
The running game took a step back. The Patriots entering the game averaging 130.7 rushing yards per game, but gained just 70 on the ground Thursday. Though they were playing catch-up for most of the night, it made the offense a lot more predictable in the second half, allowing the Bears to drop more players into coverage.
Stock up
Running back Rhamondre Stevenson. He finished with five catches for 93 yards, including pulling in a short pass from Maye and rumbling 48 yards for a touchdown on the final play of the first half to cut Chicago’s lead to 20-14. It was his fifth career career TD reception.
Stock down
Rookie edge rusher Gabe Jacas. New England trailed 13-7 in the second quarter when Bears quarterback Caleb Williams connected on a pass with Luther Burden for a 22-yard gain. Jacas was called for roughing the passer for an extremely late hit on Williams. It added an additional 15 yards to give Chicago the ball on the New England 33. The Bears scored five plays later on a 24-yard TD pass from Williams to Burden.
Injuries
Safety Kevin Byard departed after he was checked out by trainers with 9:44 left in the second quarter before returning. Defensive tackle Christian Barmore departed late in the game with an undisclosed ailment.
Key number
Minus-7 — That’s the Patriots turnover differential through seven games. Only Indianapolis (minus-8 through six games) is worse.
Next steps
The Thursday night game gives the Patriots a little extra time to rest and prepare before visiting Miami on Nov. 1.

title: “All we have is each other”: Residents push forward over a year after Minnesota fire
text:
BRIMSON, Minn. (InvestigateTV) - In May 2025, about 30 miles north of Duluth, a 27-year-old man decided to have a campfire.
The weather was record warm, windy and dry with Red Flag warnings in place.
That campfire grew into the Camp House fire, torching thousands of acres of forest and more than 180 homes, cabins and outbuildings.
What they learned -- don’t rely on leaders in St. Paul and Washington, D.C. for help. Rely on each other.
As flames began ripping across the terrain, Diane Knaffla enjoyed what she thought was a beautiful day outside her home of 36 years.
“I’m sitting under the big trees here and next thing I know my brother and nephew are tearing up the driveway, ‘Diane you gotta get out of here there’s a forest fire’”, said Knaffla. “I walked out in front of the house. I didn’t smell smoke, but when I looked that way it was orange smoke.”
Fifteen minutes later, the sheriff arrived and said it’s time to go. She left with little more than the clothes on her back in disbelief.
“It’s going to be here when I get back,” Knaffla thought. “It’s going to go around me. And yet I started to cry because looking in the rear view mirror, I thought, oh boy.”
Where a century-old home and 1,500 pine trees once stood now sits a modular house and a field.
“I love the woods,” said Knaffla. “Sitting outside under my trees was perfect for me.”
Three miles down the road, the fire took just about everything on Eric Radke’s property except for his lake view, his sense of humor, and his better half of 50 years.
“All we have is each other now,” Radke said about his wife, Sue. “The house had been here for 125 years. Why now? We just looked at it and thought this is that beautiful house we bought to retire in and we planned to live out here as long as we could stay in this part of the country, and it was just gone.”
The fires were still burning nearby on May 15, when state and federal leaders visited Brimson, pledging help in front of TV cameras. That included Governor Tim Walz, Rep. Pete Stauber, and Senators Amy Klobuchar and Tina Smith.
However, as fire victims would soon learn, that funding was to rebuild public infrastructure.
When it came to their homes and properties, it was solely up to their insurance. And insurance wouldn’t cover the cost of hauling out debris and dead trees or installation of new septic mounds, which the county required most to do.
The cost of all of that was north of $60,000 out-of-pocket for many.
After the flames were out, locals we spoke with say the recovery effort wasn’t led by elected leaders, but rather neighbors helping neighbors, and one community member in particular.
“It was extremely traumatic,” said Brimson resident Mikala Schliep.
Mikala Schliep was relatively new to the Brimson area when the wildfire broke out. She nearly lost her life.
“Closed the trunk of my car and then grabbed my dog and we were out the driveway, and it was just walls of fire on both sides of us going out,” said Schliep. “I was just screaming. It was so hot inside my car and I can’t see feet in front of me.”
After making it out just in time, and her home somehow being spared, Schliep’s devastation came from seeing the struggles of those who did lose everything.
“I just saw how much the community needed help and we weren’t getting it fast enough, at least by my standards, so that’s when we kind of stepped in,” said Schliep.
She started organizing drives, with Hugo’s Bar becoming an early drop off site for food, clothes and other necessities.
When donations overwhelmed that location, Bassett Hall became a one-stop shop for fire victims.
Eric Radke said much of his current wardrobe came from Bassett Hall.
Once everyone’s immediate needs were met, Schliep’s attention turned to cleanup and recovery, finding wreckers and volunteers to help haul out debris and downed trees, doing a lot of the work herself.
“People need to replace their septic systems, people need trees removed, and that’s where we wanted to start getting those funds and that’s where we started the non-profit side of it,” said Schliep.
She launched Brimson Strong, a non-profit aimed at raising money, obtaining grants and disbursing the funds to victims who might otherwise be out of luck.
“I did the grant writing for that,” said Schliep. “And that’s like a little win for me. I am severely dyslexic, like the worst degree you can be. So writing and reading has never come easy to me, but I’ve always been a great storyteller.”
And so far so good. The non-profit has given tens of thousands back to Brimson fire victims.
“I got a check for $5,000 for that,” said Diane Knaffla. “I’m almost getting choked up because of all that she’s done.”
“I’m still pretty new to Brimson,” said Schliep. “This place is so special and the people here are so strong and that’s why I fight so hard for it.”
Schliep and other residents we spoke with say the Red cross, United Way and St. Louis County provided much appreciate help immediately after the fire, but could only do so much.
Residents tell Northern News Now they also appreciate Rep. Natalie Zeleznikar, who they say has stayed in touch with residents.
Zeleznikar tells us she’d like the state to provide incentives for timber companies to haul out and utilize partially burned timber. She said that would significantly bring down costs for fire victim cleanup.
Here is a QR code to donate directly to Brimson Strong.
As for the the man cited for starting the fire, he’s only had to pay a $175 fine.
However, at least one of the people affected by the fire we spoke with plans to take him to small claims court.
The State of Minnesota announced exactly a year after the fire that it would allocate $250,000 for victims of the Camp House fire.

title: Aging Untold: Why walking is a step toward healthy aging
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we share practical ways to walk smarter, improve stability and boost your stamina with every step.
We also discuss what it really means when an aging loved one refuses medical treatment and how families can navigate that choice with compassion and support.
Then, a survivor shares his journey with ocular melanoma, underscoring the eye exam that can catch rare conditions early.
Walking, even in short bursts, is a tool for healthy aging.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said walking reflects the health of the entire body, and it can also provide clues to neurological issues.
Walking draws on muscle strength, balance, heart health and oxygenation, she said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said mobility is tied to independence.
“Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck says that people who have difficulties with walking should still try to keep their legs moving with foot or leg pumps. Muscle loss can happen quickly, even in healthy older adults.
Hearing that an aging loved one is refusing medical treatment can be difficult.
Rather than push back, aging expert Amy O’Rourke says to slow down, take a deep breath and listen to figure out what they are afraid of, trying to avoid or fighting for.
Rogers said the person is sometimes looking at the medications along with the side effects and weighing all those different things.
The Aging Untold experts said families should make sure a loved one’s decision is based on accurate understanding, not a misconception.
Ocular melanoma affects only five or six out of every million people each year. Ryan Gibson is one of them.
When he lost his right eye to the rare cancer, the decision before him was whether to blend in with a normal-looking prosthetic or make a statement. Gibson chose to make a statement.
He uses his prosthetic eye as a conversation starter to raise awareness about ocular melanoma.
At Emma’s Torch, a cafe and culinary school in Washington, D.C., students learn food preparation skills under timed kitchen conditions. The students are refugees, exiles and survivors of human trafficking.
Kerry Brodie founded the social justice nonprofit to help the students with self-advocacy skills, English classes, resume writing, interview prep and more.
The organization is named after Emma Lazarus, who wrote the words inscribed at the base of the Statue of Liberty: “Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free.”

title: Maine apple orchards see strong harvest despite drought
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine apple orchards see strong harvest despite drought
Despite drought conditions and rising fuel prices, some Maine apple orchards are seeing a strong harvest this fall.
At Randall Orchards in Standish, the crop is on track to reach about 30,000 bushels, according to Robert Randle, who said the orchard was uncertain earlier in the growing season whether it would reach its typical production level.
“Considering the drought, it's gone pretty well,” Randle said. “We've actually got a full crop this year, so believe it or not, we're going to hit 30,000 bushels this year.”
Randle said the orchard could even exceed that total.
The strong harvest comes after a dry growing season that created challenges for farmers across Maine. Higher fuel prices have also added to the costs of operating farms.
Despite those challenges, Randall Orchards is expecting a productive season as fall brings customers to orchards across the state.
For people hoping to pick their own apples, the weekend could be one of the last good opportunities of the season, depending on conditions at individual orchards.

title: Here’s what’s on the ballot in Hallowell
text:
Election Day is now less than two weeks away, and early voting ends Oct. 29. As voters head to the polls, it’s important to know what to expect on your ballot.
Hallowell voters will weigh in on races for the Maine State Legislature, governor, U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate. On the local level, Hallowell residents will choose candidates for mayor, county commissioner, City Council and school board.
Many candidates participated in the Press Herald Voter Guide, where readers can learn more about each race.
Voting is set to take place from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 3, at Hall-Dale Elementary School, 26 Garden Lane, Hallowell. Early voting is available through Oct. 29 at Hallowell City Hall, 1 Winthrop St., .
Here’s what’s on the ballot.
MAYOR
Lauren McPherson, Chris Walters
Lauren McPherson and Chris Walters are running to replace current Mayor George Lapointe, who is not running for reelection. Lapointe was elected in 2020 and reelected again in 2023.
McPherson has served as the Ward 5 city councilor since 2025. Neither Walters nor McPherson responded to the Voter Guide survey.
CITY COUNCIL
Ward 2: Edward “Ted” Perrin
Edward “Ted” Perrin is running unopposed for the Ward 2 council seat, which is currently held by Michael Frett, who is not running again.
Perrin, a former federal employee who is also retired from the Army Reserve, said his top three priorities are responsible stewardship of the municipal budget, ensuring Hallowell is a welcoming community for all and making sure city services are responsive to community needs.
Ward 4: Rebecca Pauline Slinger
The race for the Ward 4 council seat is also unopposed, with Rebecca Pauline Slinger set to replace current councilor Danielle Obery, who is not running for reelection.
Slinger, a French teacher who previously served in the U.S. Navy, said she wants to serve as a voice for her community, including finding creative ways to get residents more involved and engaged in the community and with one another.
SCHOOL BOARD
RSU 2 Hallowell seat: Patrick Guyer
Patrick Guyer is running unopposed for the Hallowell seat on the RSU 2 School Board. Guyer would replace Chris Myers Asch, who is not running for reelection.
Guyer is the father of two students in the district and works in nonprofit management. His top three priorities are ensuring RSU 2 schools continue to provide great education to all students; secure sufficient resources for the schools and seek cost efficiencies where possible and shape district policy on issues like technology and AI in classrooms, sustainability and climate.
KENNEBEC COUNTY COMMISSIONER
District 2: Noel Madore, Joseph Pietroski Jr.
Joseph Pietroski Jr., a Republican from Winthrop, has served as the District 2 Commissioner for Kennebec County since 2022. Democrat Noel Madore, who did not respond to the Voter Guide survey, is running to unseat Pietroski. He’s from Readfield.
Pietroski said he is focused on improving coordination and communication between county and state governments to help control costs, protect taxpayers and ensure the county receives the services residents need.
OTHER RACES
In Maine Senate District 14, voters will choose between incumbent Craig Hickman, a Democrat, and Republican Steven McGee.
Voters in House District 55 will decide between Democrat Maureen “Mo” AuCoin and Republican Charles Hippler IV who are vying to replace current Rep. Daniel Shagoury, who is not running for reelection.
Read more about all of the candidates on the Press Herald Voter Guide.

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
David Edwin Jackson, 55, of Whitefield, peacefully passed in Randolph by his friend’s side, Kimberly Soohey Rodriguez.
David was born in Gardiner in 1971 to Rose and David Jackson. He attended Whitefield Elementary, Wiscasset High School, and Lincoln Academy before attending CMCC for automotive technology, then going to work for many different companies before going to Bath Iron Works for 16 years, where he was a welder.
David E. Jackson is survived by his only son, James Jackson and wife, Kaitlyn Jackson; his parents, Rose and David Jackson; and his two brothers, Christopher Jackson and wife, Amy Jackson, and Daniel Jackson and wife, Katrina Jackson; and leaving behind eight nieces and nephews who loved him dearly.
Please join us for a celebration of life on Nov. 15, 2026 at the Whitefield Lions Club from noon to 3 p.m. at 52 Main St., Coopers Mills, ME 04341.

title: 2 Maine healthcare providers accused of violations by state
text:
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services took action against two Portland behavioral health companies that receive federal funds through MaineCare, according to records from the agency’s program integrity unit.
DHHS suspended Medicaid payments to Maine Connect Care earlier this year and another company, USA Family Wellbeing, has received violation notices for alleged overbilling, according to letters sent to the providers.
Both providers were included in a confidential list of criminal division cases the Office of the Maine Attorney General accidentally sent on Oct. 8 to reporters and other recipients outside the office. Neither company appears to have been charged in state or federal court, according to a review of online records. A spokesperson for the attorney general’s office said Thursday that she had no information to share about either company.
Neither company responded to calls and emails on Thursday seeking comment.
The attorney general’s document says the office got not response to “multiple inquiries” it made to federal prosecutors about whether these two matters, “along with a group of other matters/investigations with similar allegations,” would be pursued federally. A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Maine said he could not comment under federal policy.
The U.S. Centers for Medicaid and Medicare announced this month that it was auditing the state for fraud; its administrator, Dr. Mehmet Oz, and Vice President JD Vance have both accused Maine officials of turning a blind eye to fraud.
Maine has suspended payments to at least five providers this year, according to information the state shared in August. DHHS spokesperson Lindsay Hammes said in an email Thursday that the department refers cases to law enforcement, including the attorney general’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit, any time it’s made aware of a credible allegation of MaineCare fraud.
She said the department doesn’t provide information about those referrals to protect the integrity of the investigations.
DHHS suspended Medicaid payments to Maine Connect Care on Jan. 30, according to a letter the agency sent via certified mail. The letter stated that DHHS is required to suspend payments when there’s been an allegation of fraud, and that the suspension will last either until it’s been determined there was no fraud, or until any criminal or civil prosecutions have resolved.
The letter said there have been “general allegations” of billing for services not rendered, billing for individuals who aren’t eligible for MaineCare reimbursements, and billing for services provided by unlicensed individuals.
USA Family Wellbeing, meanwhile, has appealed a notice of violation that it received from DHHS in July. The state is seeking more than $1.7 million for overpayment it made, citing a review of MaineCare claims between March 1, 2021, and Dec. 31, 2022, according to a letter the agency sent to the provider. The claims included payments for community support services, competency evaluations, behavioral health counseling and language interpretation services. 
USA Family Wellbeing had also received a notice of violation in 2024, which resulted in the company paying back more than $71,000 over the following year, according to DHHS.
USA Family Wellbeing has not had its payments suspended, according to DHHS.
The allegations raised in the DHHS documents appear to match similar accusations made in the confidential report inadvertently released by the attorney general’s office, which stated that Maine Connect Care and USA Family Wellbeing face allegations that included “phony billing” and “billing for noncovered services.”
That report, which the office has declined to discuss, also included homicide cases, alleged healthcare crimes, drug investigations and appeals. Most of the matters match what’s been filed publicly in court, but it appears some have not been made public.
The description in the report for a matter involving USA Family Wellbeing included an allegation of services being provided by an unlicensed person, and that the company was accused of a “potential theft of $1.58 million.”
The loss described in the description about Maine Connect Care “looks to exceed about $400,000,” the document stated.
Staff Writer Joe Lawlor contributed to this story.

title: UMaine football hosting Campbell for Homecoming game
text:
There is no shortage of local storylines on the college football front for Saturday.
The University of Maine’s disappointing football team will try to snap a six-game losing streak when it hosts Campbell University for its Homecoming game, Conference of New England rivals Husson University and the University of New England will square off in Bangor for the sixth annual Lobster Trap game, and Maine Maritime Academy could win its first game since 2017 when it entertains New England College.
The Maine Maritime Academy-New England College game will kick off at 11 a.m., while the Husson-UNE and UMaine-Campbell games start at 1 p.m.
In addition, 0-5 Colby will travel to take on 1-4 Hamilton at noon, 0-5 Bates will host 2-3 Middlebury at 1 p.m. and 0-5 Bowdoin will travel to play 5-0 Trinity at 1:30 p.m.
UMaine will bring an overall record of 1-6 and a Coastal Athletic Association mark of 1-3 into the game while 13th-ranked Campbell, picked eighth in the CAA preseason coaches poll, is 6-1 and 3-0 with its only loss coming to nationally ranked Football Bowl Subdivision team Florida.
It matches the 2019 team for the best seven-game start to a season.
The Black Bears have won their last nine Homecoming games since dropping a 21-10 contest to Yale in 2015.
But UMaine is 0-3 at home this season and is facing a Campbell team that boasts one of the nation’s most potent offenses.
The Fighting Camels are 11th in the country among 124 Football Championship Subdivision teams and first in the CAA in yards per game at 455 and 28th in the country and second in the CAA in scoring at 32.6 points per game.
UMaine is 120th in the country in points per game (14.4) and 111th in yards (281.9). And the Black Bears are last in the CAA in both.
Campbell coach Braxton Harris said he and his team are walking into a “hornet’s nest.”
“It’s a long trip for us, and most of our guys have been in the South, so it will probably be a little cooler than they’re used to,” Harris said. “We’re walking into a Homecoming crowd of a football team that has been really close to having some real big wins. They beat Towson in week one and were really close against Bryant in their last game.”
Campbell rallied for a 24-20 Homecoming win over Towson last weekend.
“Winning a road football game in the CAA is tough,” Harris said. “You can throw the records out the window. We just played a football team that hadn’t won this season, and I would argue they were better than a lot of teams we’ve played up until this point. This is going to be a huge challenge. We’ve got to be ready to play.”
UMaine has lost four of its six games by nine points or less.
UMaine head coach Jordan Stevens said the Fighting Camels are a very fundamentally sound football team that does a “tremendous job on offense starting at quarterback.”
Senior quarterback and McNeese State transfer Kamden Sixkiller has completed 67.1% of his passes for 1,899 yards and 15 touchdowns. The dual threat quarterback has also carried the ball 41 times for 196 yards and four TDs. Six different players have caught at least 15 passes led by Jyron Waiters’ 28 receptions for 342 yards and four TDs.
“He does an excellent job distributing the ball. They are one of the top offenses in scoring so we know we have to limit their points,” Stevens said. “I’m really impressed with how they finish their blocks and how hard their backs run. And, on defense, they swarm to the ball.”
J.J. Cowan has rushed for 471 yards and is averaging 6.3 yards per carry, and Jon Gullette is averaging 5.6 yards per carry on 43 carries and has also caught 19 passes for 133 yards.
UMaine’s defense is ranked 10th in the country on fourth down efficiency, holding opponents to a 30% conversion rate, and is 13th on third down, allowing a 30.4% conversion rate.
UMaine linebacker Sam Oppenheimer has continued to have a memorable season, ranking ninth in the nation in tackles with 73 and sixth in solo tackles with 42. He also has two interceptions. He was involved in a game-high 15 tackles in the loss to Bryant.
Linebacker Noah Carpenter and strong safety Jeremiah McGill have been involved in 53 and 50 tackles, respectively.
Charles Battaglia’s 48 tackles and A.J. Benton’s 37 pace Campbell.
Rashawn Marshall’s 410 yards on 96 carries leads UMaine. Nick Laughlin has caught 30 passes for 297 yards, and Evan Wallace has caught 21 for 213 yards.
Caden Drezek, who has completed 35 of 74 passes for 435 yards and two TDs, is likely to get the start for UMaine.
At the Winkin Sports Complex in Bangor, Husson has won two straight to improve to 2-4 overall and 2-1 in the CNE, while UNE of Biddeford is 1-5 and 1-2 after beating Maine Maritime Academy last week 62-14.
UNE has won the last two Lobster Trap games after Husson won the first three.

title: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez campaigns for Troy Jackson, touts shared progressive values
text:
PORTLAND, Maine - Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) traveled to Maine on Thursday to take the stage with Senate candidate Troy Jackson in Portland. The two took several questions from college students at the event hosted by “More Perfect University,” a progressive campus group, and touched on topics ranging from immigration enforcement to healthcare.
“They are sending ICE out in droves [in Maine]. Not just to intimidate the Somali community, the immigrant community, but to intimidate all of us,” Ocasio-Cortez said, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
“I hear it from people all the time who do not support Medicare for All. ‘Well, I like my private insurance.’ Fine, and I am going to do something better than your private insurance,” Jackson said.
Jackson and Ocasio-Cortez both argued that the money that is used to fund the ongoing war in Iran and ICE should be used to fund healthcare.
“How can we afford Iran? How can we afford Gaza? How can we afford these things when folks at home can’t eat, can’t go to the doctor or build a bridge to get there?” asked Cortez.
Ocasio-Cortez also spoke about higher education and called for all public colleges and universities to be tuition-free. She said higher education has become a “luxury” in 2026.
The two appeared to agree on nearly every topic discussed. From defunding ICE and ending the war in Iran. Ocasio-Cortez spent most of the evening speaking, with Jackson chiming in. The two also spent time taking jabs at Sen. Susan Collins and called her out again for her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
“Susan Collins, one of the only Republican female senators in a unique position to protect almost every woman in America, decided to declare open season on us instead,” Ocasio-Cortez said.
The two were also asked about funding rural healthcare and public transit. Jackson said he would like to see a rail system connecting Portland and Bangor eventually built using federal funds.

title: When a loved one refuses treatment: What families need to know
text:
(Aging Untold) — When an aging parent or loved one says no to medical treatment, it can feel alarming — but that decision is often rooted in something deeper than it first appears.
The Aging Untold hosts break down what’s really driving these moments and how families can respond with patience instead of panic.
“Slow down and listen”
When a loved one refuses care, the instinct for many families is to push back immediately. Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, says that reaction can make things worse.
“I think the first thing I would advise is to slow down. Take a deep breath and listen. Listen really carefully,” O’Rourke said. “What are they afraid of? What are they trying to avoid? What are they fighting for? Where are they emotionally? And then start there.”
O’Rourke cautioned against rushing toward a predetermined outcome.
“Don’t be quick to cut them off. Try to get a certain outcome in place. Just slow everything down,” she said.
She described working with a family where tensions boiled over.
“I worked with a family where they were in the middle of this discussion, and one of the kids just flipped out and called 911,” O’Rourke said. “And the ambulance came and she got in the ambulance, and the mother looked at me and she goes, ‘I don’t want to go. I don’t want to go to the hospital.’ And it was an awkward moment, but she got out of the ambulance.”
O’Rourke said the situation didn’t have to escalate the way it did.
“It was one of those things where it was a crisis when it didn’t need to be, if they just slow down and started listening earlier,” she said.
Understanding what’s really being said
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, agreed that slowing down is key and said families need to dig into the “why” behind a refusal.
“I think you’re right in terms of slowing down, listening and understanding, what is the person really saying?” Rogers said. “They’re not saying, ‘I don’t want to be treated’ necessarily. There’s something underlying that’s driving that value for them.”
Rogers said refusing a specific treatment isn’t the same as giving up.
“Not being treated and refusing treatment doesn’t mean that you’re saying, ‘I choose death,’” Rogers said. “You have to understand what is surrounding the decision that this person is making about how they want to live.”
Sometimes the person is looking at the medications along with the side effects and weighing all those different things, Rogers said.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck framed the decision as an act of self-determination.
“This is ultimately self-care in the most complex form. You’re taking care of yourself,” Cradduck said. “It may not line up with the way you would take care of yourself, but it’s the way I’ve chosen to. And maybe it’s based on seeing my own parent suffer through a treatment that I don’t want to have to endure.”
Clearing up misconceptions about hospice
Cradduck also pointed to hospice as an example of a widely misunderstood form of treatment.
“We see this one a lot where we think, oh, hospice, I’m not going to ever use hospice because they kill people. That’s what unfortunately a lot of people believe,” she said. “The reality is, to be part of hospice, you are already terminally ill. So hospice isn’t killing you. It’s providing comfort while you’re dying, while you’re going through that final sunset.”
Cradduck said this misunderstanding comes up often in counseling families.
“I’ve counseled with so many families where they’re like, ‘Oh, I would never have hospice,’ which is a form of treatment,” she said.
Rogers said hospice doesn’t mean the end.
“We were always taught hospice means the end ... but hospice means you get additional services, you get support, and it doesn’t mean it’s the end,” she said.
Cradduck added that belief systems can lead people to decline care that may benefit them.
“Based on belief systems, people will refuse treatments, and they’ll turn down something that maybe is to their benefit,” she said. “So sometimes just listening to why, and then giving good counsel, but honoring the person’s belief system regardless — I may not agree with you, but you have a right to choose your own destiny.”
Asking the right questions
The experts said families should make sure a loved one’s decision is based on accurate understanding, not a misconception.
“Asking questions to uncover what it is — so the questions behind the decisions and the opinions. Is there more information that could be provided? Is there more conversation that could be had that would make it a little bit easier to either understand their position, or for them to maybe make a different decision once they’re educated on it,” Ambrose said.
Rogers said that clarifying conversations give everyone a chance to understand each other.
“Clarify, because you could clarify whatever they’re saying. That’s your opportunity to clarify for misunderstanding,” the host said.
