title: Maine cannot afford to lose Sen. Susan Collins in Washington
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Timothy S. Hodgdon is president/CEO of Hodgdon Shipbuilding in East Boothbay. Hodgdon Shipbuilding was founded in 1816, four years before Maine became a state.
As a business owner in Maine, I want to express my strong support for Sen. Susan Collins in the upcoming election. I am increasingly concerned that backlash from the current political landscape could turn what should otherwise be a strong race for Sen. Collins into a much more difficult contest in November.
Here are the facts.
Sen. Collins has served Maine for decades, and during that time she has consistently worked to bring federal resources and opportunities back to our state. Her seniority and experience in Washington, and particularly her position as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, give Maine an important voice and critical influence when decisions are made regarding federal funding and priorities.
The Appropriations Committee plays a central role in determining discretionary federal spending, making this position particularly consequential for a state the size of Maine. That influence has produced significant, tangible results for Maine, which cannot be delivered by an inexperienced U.S. Senate replacement.
Sen. Collins’ work has supported BIW, UMaine, transportation/infrastructure projects and hundreds of other initiatives throughout all 16 Maine counties. According to Sen. Collins’ office, she has helped secure nearly $1.5 billion in Congressionally Directed Spending for 672 projects since 2021.
I believe Maine voters need to look carefully at what Sen. Collins’ position in the Senate means for our state and what will be lost if she is no longer representing Maine in Washington.
The televised debates between Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson raise a fundamental question: How many times must Sen. Collins correct the record before those corrections are given their due?
Throughout these debates, she has repeatedly addressed Jackson’s claims about her position on the Iran war, her voting record on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and her relationship with President Donald Trump (among other questionable statements).
Sen. Collins has explained that she voted nine times to end the Iran war, defended her decision to oppose the One Big Beautiful Bill Act at final passage and challenged what she considers misleading characterizations of her relationship with the president.
Yet Jackson frequently returns to the same accusations, seemingly disregarding the explanations and responses she has already provided. Vigorous debate and legitimate criticism are essential to our political process. But voters deserve more than repeated allegations and selective interpretations of a candidate’s record. They deserve a fair opportunity to hear the answers, consider the context and judge the facts for themselves.
When a candidate responds directly to an accusation, that response should be part of the discussion — not simply brushed aside as the same accusation is repeated. The real issue is not whether Sen. Collins’ record should be scrutinized; it absolutely should be. It is whether that scrutiny is being conducted fairly, accurately and with due regard for the facts.
Maine voters deserve a debate that informs rather than misleads, and that evaluates candidates on their complete records rather than on accusations repeated often enough to create an impression. It is also significant that Sen. Collins is the only Republican in either the House of Representatives or the Senate from New England, which results in an unhealthy partisan position, regardless of your party affiliation.
Replacing her with a first-term senator would represent a substantial loss of seniority, institutional knowledge, leadership and demonstrated ability to secure federal resources, an outcome that we cannot afford.
To say it frankly, there is no opponent who can fill Sen. Collins’ shoes as our senator from Maine. Her record, experience and performance all speak for themselves. Maine needs Susan Collins to stay in the Senate.

title: Maine's THC drink ban is coming Dec. 11. Here's what to know
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine's THC drink ban is coming Dec. 11. Here's what to know
Maine businesses that sell hemp-derived THC beverages are preparing for a major change as a federal law set to take effect Dec. 11 would remove many of the drinks from store shelves.
The law changes the federal definition of hemp and establishes new restrictions on hemp-derived products containing THC. Under the new limits, many currently sold THC-infused beverages will no longer be permitted.
The change could affect breweries, retailers, bars and restaurants that have added the drinks to their offerings.
Kai Adams of Sebago Brewing, which produces hemp-derived THC beverages under its Mystic Cove line, says the products have helped breweries adapt as consumer preferences shift away from traditional beer.
"It's been really helpful for the craft beer industry. You know, with a lot of declines in people drinking and a lot of younger people choosing many different alternatives to beverages. But we've done really well. And, we really want to continue to produce these," Adams said.
Adams says many consumers are unaware of the upcoming deadline. He is encouraging people who want to keep the beverages available to contact their elected representatives as he works toward introducing legislation to preserve the drinks.
The federal restrictions are scheduled to take effect Dec. 11, 2026. The law sets a limit of 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container for covered hemp-derived products, a threshold that would effectively prohibit many intoxicating hemp beverages currently on the market.

title: State plans public hearing on Central Maine Healthcare in Lewiston as concerns over Prime’s ownership deepen
text:
The state will hold a public hearing to determine whether Prime Healthcare Foundation is meeting staffing and care standards in operating Central Maine Healthcare, which includes Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston and several other facilities.
State Rep. Julie McCabe, D-Lewiston, requested the hearing in a letter Monday to the Maine Department of Health and Human Services. Over the past year, the state health department required Prime Healthcare Foundation, a nonprofit based in California, to make several commitments to maintain essential health services, safe patient volumes and trauma center status at Central Maine Healthcare before it could acquire the health system.
Compliance with those agreements is being called into question.
“The people of Lewiston deserve a hospital system that is safely managed and adequately staffed, that upholds the agreements entered into with the state of Maine, and that follows the laws of the state,” McCabe wrote. “Based on the many conversations I have had with healthcare providers and patients, it is my belief that Prime Healthcare is not currently abiding by their (agreement).”
A public hearing is “an appropriate step,” said Lindsay Hammes, Maine DHHS spokesperson, in an email Thursday. She said it will be scheduled in the next several weeks.
Central Maine Healthcare includes hospitals in Bridgton and Rumford and a number of physician practices. McCabe said changes at the health system, including workforce attrition, sterilization equipment issues and the premature termination of a contract with an emergency department physician group, which staffed 35 providers across the three hospitals, pose a “clear and present danger” to patients.
State officials have acknowledged the Lewiston hospital did not meet a requirement earlier this month intended to verify progress toward reestablishing trauma center status, a designation that lapsed before Prime took over — leaving just two destinations in Maine for around-the-clock emergency surgery.
EARLY TERMINATION
Central Maine Healthcare notified BlueWater Health last month that it was terminating early its three-year contract to staff three emergency departments in the Lewiston, Bridgton and Rumford hospitals, effective Jan. 12.
The departments were short 17 physicians and relying heavily on locum tenens, or temporary providers, when the Brunswick-based physician group signed the three-year contract in early 2025, said Dr. Jay Mullen, CEO of BlueWater Health. The group has since filled those vacancies and recruited 18 more physicians, nurses and physician assistants to Central Maine Healthcare.
Mullen said it’s difficult to retain board-certified emergency physicians because they can get jobs anywhere in the country, “so rural areas are always struggling.” Most of their recruits to Maine came from out of state.
With the termination, Mullen said 80% of the 35 providers will leave Central Maine Healthcare when their contract ends in January. Two-thirds will take roles elsewhere with BlueWater Health, which he said staffs emergency departments across New England and which recently signed a contract with St. Mary’s Regional Medical Center in Lewiston. Others are moving out of state.
One emergency department physician leaving the health system for another role with BlueWater Health, who asked to remain unnamed, said instability is driving her away.
“There is some fatigue of the chaos that seems to kind of be currently encircling Central Maine,” she said, “a lot of loss of the medical staff and nursing changes. I think a lot of members of my group would agree with me that people feel that they need to step away from Central Maine.”
A Central Maine Healthcare spokesperson said the health system is in ongoing discussions with BlueWater Health and Vituity, a California-based emergency physician group. “Regardless of the outcome of these negotiations,” the spokesperson said, “most physicians that have provided ED services at Central Maine Healthcare will have the opportunity to continue to do so with the firm that is selected.”
McCabe, the Lewiston lawmaker, said it was negligent for Central Maine Healthcare to terminate the BlueWater Health contract with only a few months notice and no arrangement to “fill the void.”
Hospitals are required by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to report the rate of emergency department visitors who leave without being seen by a physician. More than a year into the BlueWater contract, Central Maine Healthcare’s rate dropped from 7.2% to 3.5%. In the past three months, it’s climbed back up to 5.7%, according to data shared by McCabe and verified by Mullen.
The national benchmark is 2%.
“When you have increased wait times, people leave without being seen, and that doesn’t mean that they’re not sick. It just means that they gave up,” McCabe said. “And when you have those kinds of repeated interactions at the ED, you’re going to lose faith in your healthcare system.”
TRAUMA CENTER IN LIMBO
Maine’s health department regulates how ownership acquisitions, mergers and other major healthcare changes can happen in Maine, and by who.
To acquire Central Maine Healthcare, Prime Healthcare Foundation needed the state’s approval. One challenge: CMMC let its level three trauma center designation lapse in December 2025, a month after the state made it a mandatory condition of the acquisition.
The loss of a trauma center in Lewiston has impacted patients — sometimes with life-threatening conditions — who had to travel farther to reach the other trauma centers in Portland and Bangor. It’s also uprooted dozens of EMS agencies and increased trauma patient volumes at the other hospitals.
The state approved Prime Healthcare Foundation’s acquisition of the Maine health system earlier this year, but with the condition that CMMC must regain full trauma status by 2028. The hospital was also required to obtain a trauma manager — the person who leads the center and communicates with other hospitals ― by Oct. 2.
Hammes said on Oct. 6 that CMMC had made an offer to a candidate for the trauma manager position but that “hiring has not yet been completed.” The department, she said, “will be closely monitoring the outcome of the offer to assess compliance with the condition.”
On Thursday, she said the state had not received an update about the status of the offer and could not verify compliance.
A CMMC spokesperson has not responded to questions about the trauma manager requirement.
“We should be one of three trauma hospitals in the state, and from every indication, Prime doesn’t seem like they want that responsibility,” McCabe said. “I think our community is going to be, frankly, in danger if they are not able to adequately staff the emergency department, which provides life or death care.”
“We have many ER physicians who are very knowledgeable and interested in the care of trauma patients,” the BlueWater physician said. “I hope that there isn’t decreased momentum to gaining the level three trauma designation due to the departure of ER physicians who were ready and willing to be participatory in that process.”
Oct. 25 will mark the anniversary of the Lewiston mass shootings, which left 18 dead and more than a dozen wounded on a Wednesday night three years ago.
“On that night and in the days that followed, our teams demonstrated the critical role our hospitals and emergency services play in this community,” a CMMC spokesperson said. “We remain deeply proud of the extraordinary care they provided and mindful of our responsibility to be here for our communities every day.”
That night, it was trauma manager Tammy Lachance who made the call to secure blood from nearby hospitals, which “contributed in great measure to the survival of our operative patients,” said Dr. Richard King, a former CMMC trauma surgeon who responded to the emergency department within minutes of the shooting along with 30 other surgeons.
Lachance died after a battle with cancer last year. King hopes she is honored at CMMC this week.
It pains him to see the degradation of the trauma program they built, he said.
“Tammy was more than that one night,” King said. “She was the heart and soul of that trauma program for many years.”

title: Police officer who shot and killed 1-year-old boy in Mississippi has resigned, mayor says
text:
Police officer who shot and killed 1-year-old boy in Mississippi has resigned, mayor says
The police officer who shot and killed a 1-year-old boy in Mississippi when he fired into a moving vehicle while responding to a shoplifting call has resigned, the Senatobia mayor told The Associated Press Friday.
Sgt. Hunter Foster had been cleared of criminal wrongdoing by the Mississippi Attorney General's office earlier this week after its monthslong probe concluded his use of force had been justified.
On Thursday, the state released videos of the fatal shooting of Kohen Wiley, including Foster's body-worn camera footage of the June 14 encounter in a Walmart parking lot in Senatobia, about 40 miles south of Memphis, Tenn.
Senatobia Mayor Greg Graves confirmed Foster’s resignation Friday.
Foster's attorney Martin Zummach declined to comment when reached Friday. Zummach has said Foster had ‘no choice’ but to fire his weapon at the vehicle because it was moving at him.
Kohen's mother, Vellesiya Wiley, has disputed that her friend, who was driving, headed toward the officers.
Ben Crump, an attorney for Kohen's family, said the footage shows the fatal shot came from the side of the car, disputing that Foster was in imminent danger. An independent autopsy commissioned by the family concluded the same. An image of the vehicle shows its shattered right front passenger window. The family’s legal team called for the federal government to investigate the shooting.
Van Turner, another attorney representing Kohen’s family, has called for Foster to be de-certified as a police officer.
“What we need is for him to be de-certified so that he’s not able to go to another police department and do the same thing,” Van Turner said during a news conference Thursday.
Mississippi Department of Public Safety spokesperson Alex Gibert said Friday that Foster remained certified as a police officer.
Kohen would have celebrated his second birthday in early November.
The group of officers were at the Walmart store in response to an unrelated incident, according to a Mississippi Bureau of Investigation report. A Walmart employee then alerted them of two women running from the store.
The videos show Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, holding Kohen as she and her friend run across the parking lot and enter their vehicle. Five officers approach the parked car with guns drawn. The car reverses away and crashes into a parked vehicle nearby as officers yell for it to stop.
The vehicle then accelerates forward as Foster steps toward it, directly in front, with his gun drawn. The wheels turn away from him, and he appears to put his hands on the hood as he jumps out of the way. He fires his gun, shattering the window of the front passenger side, where Kohen was seated on his mother’s lap. The car continues to drive away.
Vellesiya Wiley has denied that she and her friend stole diapers from the store and they have not been charged, according to state and county court records.

title: UMF students can earn credits toward biotechnology master’s
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FARMINGTON — University of Maine at Farmington biology students can now begin working toward a master’s degree in biotechnology before finishing their undergraduate studies through a new partnership with Northeastern University.
The program, launched this fall, allows eligible UMF biology majors to take three graduate-level science courses that count toward their bachelor’s degrees and up to seven credits toward a master’s degree at Northeastern University’s Roux Institute in Portland.
The partnership is supported by a $400,000, three-year National Science Foundation grant awarded to UMF in 2023 to help smaller colleges develop partnerships, expand innovation and strengthen workforce opportunities.
“The life sciences sector is a growing industry in Maine that offers meaningful career opportunities to academically strong and motivated students throughout the state,” UMF President Joseph McDonnell said in an Oct. 6 news release.
“This new pathway between UMF and the Roux Institute provides our students a head start toward earning their master’s degree in biotechnology and developing the skills that will advance their careers and help support the state’s workforce needs,” he said.
The three courses, Theory and Methods of Scientific Inquiry, Biotechnology Laboratory and Biostatistics, will be taught by full-time, tenured UMF science faculty. They are the university’s first graduate-level science courses and have been approved to count toward degree requirements at both institutions.
Timothy Breton, UMF associate professor of biology and principal investigator for the federal grant, said the courses are intended to create opportunities for students while supporting the biotechnology industry in Maine and beyond.
“Life science and biotechnology industries are among the fastest growing sectors in New England, especially in Maine, and this pathway will help our students advance their careers in this expanding profession,” Breton said.
Students must maintain a grade point average of at least 3.0 through completion of their UMF bachelor’s degree and earn a B or better in each graduate course for the credits to count toward Northeastern’s master’s program. They must also meet Northeastern’s admission requirements.
The pathway does not automatically grant students a master’s degree. Those admitted to Northeastern must complete the university’s remaining graduate degree requirements.
The Roux Institute, Northeastern’s graduate campus and research center in Portland, focuses on technology, data science, life sciences and entrepreneurship, connecting academic programs with research and industry partnerships.
“We are excited to establish a clear pathway between UMF and the Roux Institute for UMF students interested in an advanced degree in the life sciences,” said Aileen Huang-Saad, director of life sciences, health and engineering programs at the Roux Institute.
“This partnership exemplifies how academic institutions can work together to offer students a diversity of choices for career advancement,” she said.
UMF students interested in the program can contact Breton at [email protected] or 207-778-7364.

title: Bystander jumps onto moving bus to help students during driver’s medical emergency
text:
ST. PAUL, Minn. (WCCO) — A bystander helped stop a bus carrying 19 middle schoolers Monday after the driver had a medical emergency, according to school officials in Minnesota.
Ebro Ahmed, 27, was taking a break outside his family business, Ya Bricks Snacks & Tobacco, in St. Paul’s Dayton’s Bluff neighborhood when he saw the bus moving through the streets with no hands on the wheel.
“I started yelling. I didn’t know what to do. The reason I started yelling was to get somebody’s attention,” Ahmed said.
Bystander describes boarding the bus
Ahmed said he ran toward the bus after noticing the door was open.
“It caught me by surprise because I was kind of confused about the door being open. So then I ran toward the bus and noticed he was having an emergency, so I just hopped on there,” Ahmed said.
“I wasn’t able to stop it at first, so I threw it in park, and it went in reverse by accident,” Ahmed said.
Ahmed assisted the driver while instructing students to call 911.
“It’s something you would never think would happen in real life,” Ahmed said.
Asked how he knew what to do, Ahmed said he drew on things he had seen before.
“TV shows, stuff like that. ‘Grey’s Anatomy,’ and TikTok,” Ahmed said.
School district response
In a statement, St. Paul Public Schools said there was a medical emergency on a contracted bus route from Battle Creek Middle School that likely made students late arriving home and that some children may have been upset by the situation. The district said its mental health team checked in with students afterward.
Ahmed said he and the students were alone when the incident happened.
“We were right here. No cars around, no adults around, just me alone with the kids,” Ahmed said.
Ahmed said the situation made him think of his own family.
“It’s scary. That could’ve been my sister, my brother, my daughter, my son. It could be my little cousin,” Ahmed said.
Ahmed said he wants to reunite with the driver and his family.
“It’s part of being human. We have feelings and emotions we’re supposed to feel. If I were to let him drive away, I would not be human anymore,” Ahmed said.
St. Paul Public Schools said the driver has been released from the hospital and is resting at home.

title: Levant corner store lowers gas prices to help community member fighting lung disease
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LEVANT, Maine (WABI) - A corner store in Levant is lowering gas prices to give back to the community.
Levant Corner Store and Ye Olde General Store in Carmel are donating five cents for every gallon of regular gas sold to Eva Gould, a community member with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a lung disease with an unknown cause that makes it hard to breathe.
“The community is bigger than I thought,” Gould said.
“Yeah. Our community is huge,” said Grace Gruder, Gould’s daughter.
Levant Corner Store General Manager Lance Allard said the store lowered gas prices for the event and then lowered them again to increase sales.
“We lowered it for the event and then still lowered it again just to jump up the sales. And it’s working,” Allard said.
The only cure for Gould’s condition is a double lung transplant.
“There’s so much testing, so much involved. My whole life has changed from not being able to work. You see things so differently,” Gould said.
“It’s made you value time more. You really learn that time is precious, valuable, and short. You learn that it’s really short,” Gruder said.
Gould travels to Boston for treatment, with most of the travel cost coming out of pocket. Allard said people are going out of their way to buy gas at the stores to help.
“People are going out of their way to get here and to help out. Obviously, the gas prices don’t hurt. But a lot of them are doing it just for the cause,” Allard said.
Allard said people have traveled from Winterport and Eddington just to support Gould.
Gould said the promotion is giving her and her family hope.
“Without that word, what do we have? I have to stay hopeful. There isn’t anything else to be. Or you can sit home and cry all day until you die. Or you can sit home and cry all day until you die,” Gould said.
Gould and Gruder said they rely on each other and the rest of their family to keep their hope alive.
“If I didn’t have her, I don’t know what I’d do,” Gould said.
“My family is my world,” Gruder said. “If we weren’t able to talk about it with each other and within our family, I feel like it would drive you crazy. It consumes your thoughts if you let it. So it’s nice to be able to lean on one another, talk to one another, talk to each other, have a family dinner, and cherish our time, you know?”
Gruder said the lower gas prices are helping the entire community, not just her family.
“So, the whole community really needs a break, so for Lance to be able to do that for our community, not only for us, but the whole community is really amazing, it’s really a blessing, and it shows that there are good people in the world, love thy neighbor, Lance, and the whole entire community has just been a triumph of love thy neighbor,” Gruder said.
The promotion runs through Oct. 31.
A GoFundMe is set up to donate to Gould directly.

title: DSA’s rise puts left flank at center of Democrats’ 2026 fight
text:
NEW YORK (Gray Media) - As Democrats hope to secure a majority in one, potentially both chambers of Congress, the rise of their left flank is in focus.
Democratic Socialists of America say they’re fighting for a democracy powered by everyday people, not capitalists. DSA members are now some of the most prominent voices in the Democratic Party, occupying roles from the Halls of Congress to the mayor’s mansion in New York City.
“For a long time, they were completely irrelevant,” said Lincoln Mitchell, a political expert at Columbia University. Mitchell says the organization’s roots trace back to the 1960s, but it only recently became a major player on the national stage.
“What DSA has done powerfully is to center working people and to center poor people in the story of urban America,” Mitchell said.
Sen. Bernie Sanders is often credited with igniting democratic socialism over the last decade. Mitchell says Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani brought the DSA into the mainstream by defeating established Democratic politicians.
“Among people today who are under 40 years old, socialism isn’t a bad word,” Mitchell said.
The duo uncovered an appetite for youthful energy combined with policies catering to American workers. The DSA and adjacent candidates are having a strong 2026. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed hopes to become the first Muslim U.S. Senator. A handful of House candidates are primed to win and grow the movement’s numbers in Washington. And figures like AOC and Mamdani rank as two of the most powerful endorsements in the election cycle.
“The energy is on the DSA left, and that is for certain,” Mitchell said.
The election on November 3rd will tell us a lot about not just the next two years, but potentially the next decade. The Democratic Socialists of America are a big part of the evolving political landscape, and they hope to be for a long time.

title: UMaine opens new sustainable aquaculture facility
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - The University of Maine hosted an open house Friday for its Sustainable Aquaculture Workforce and Innovation Center.
The new facility will support research on land-based fish farming, without the benefit of a nearby ocean.
The center aims to address problems in the seafood industry by researching how to farm fish, such as salmon, more sustainably.
The facility allows research across different scales to determine best practices for the future.
That research will give students the opportunity to gain hands-on experience while in college.
“I think one of the overwhelming feelings that students feel when they come in here, graduate, undergraduate students, and honestly even faculty, but focusing on the students right now, is just this sense of awe. Coming to this facility and seeing just what’s getting built here and what we’re going to have the capacity to do here, it really is awe-inspiring,” said Amber Johnston, Ph.D. candidate at UMaine.
“Workforce development programming here for professionals, we’ll be having undergraduate students working on capstone projects really as a part of this learner-centered R1, giving them hands-on engagement with research here at the university. And then finally, graduate student education, which will really allow graduate students to push forward the science that will impact ultimately both industry and other stakeholders,” said Matt Hawkyard, associate professor and fin fish nutritionist at UMaine.
Hawkyard said there should be fish in the building and programs fully moved in by next March.

title: Report of possible library cuts in Gray creates backlash
text:
As the Gray Town Council adopted its list of priorities for the 2027 fiscal year, rumors of major cuts to the town library spurred dozens of residents to attend the Oct. 20 council meeting in a show of support.
During a retreat organized by the Greater Portland Council of Governments, town councilors discussed multiple ideas for town priorities. One of the ideas was to cut public funding for Gray Public Library, and replace staff with volunteers. The proposal did not appear on the town’s final list of priorities, and council Chair Vincent Palange denied that it was ever seriously considered, claiming that it was one of several proposals thrown out by the retreat organizers and voted upon by attendees.
The proposed cuts attracted significant public reaction, filling the council chamber to capacity as residents gathered en masse to express support for the library.
Valerie Razsa, a member of the comprehensive plan committee, said when the committee surveyed residents, it found that the library was the most valued part of the community. Razsa, who does tutoring at the library, praised the staff for helping people of all ages. She said the amount of people showing up to support the library showed how much of a priority it was to the town.
Resident Debra Smith criticized the proposal to cut the library funding, saying that volunteers could not replace professional staff. Smith said that 38 public libraries, out of 257 statewide, are run by volunteers, and are often open for less than 12 hours a week in small, economically disadvantaged rural communities with a significantly smaller population than Gray.
Resident Christine Renaud highlighted the library’s role in the lives of lower-income patrons. Renaud said she regularly works with people at or below the poverty line, and recommends they go to the library to access services. Meanwhile, resident Erica Plant spoke about how the country is in a literacy crisis, with librarians on the front lines.
Sam Pfeifle, a Maine School Administrative District 15 school board member and candidate for state House, said the library is a place where residents can all come together, even in an age where people are spending more of their lives at home, and encouraged the town to prioritize community spaces so residents feel they’re getting something out of paying their property taxes.
“The way that we meet our friends and neighbors is through the rec program, through the library, through the services that the town provides,” said Pfeifle.
Some residents claimed the high turnout was due to misinformation spread by an organization called Grassroots Gray. Meg Barhite, president of Grassroots Gray, pushed back on the assessment, noting that cutting library funding was one of the items discussed in the publicly available notes from the council’s retreat. A Facebook post from the organization described the library cuts as a priority and encouraged residents to attend the Oct. 20 Town Council meeting.
Although the library will not be stripped of funding, one of the priorities on the council’s final list was to separate the recreation center from the library funding and offer “budget-neutral or profitable programming.”
Ultimately, the council’s list of priorities, without the library cuts, passed unanimously.

title: $5,000 reward offered for missing Gulf of Maine research vessel
text:
$5,000 reward offered for research vessel that went missing in Gulf of Maine
The unmanned vessel was monitoring a harmful algal bloom when researchers lost communication with it earlier this month
$5,000 reward offered for research vessel that went missing in Gulf of Maine
The unmanned vessel was monitoring a harmful algal bloom when researchers lost communication with it earlier this month
Researchers are offering a $5,000 reward for information leading to the recovery of an unmanned research vessel that was last seen monitoring a harmful algal bloom in the Gulf of Maine.
According to a notice from the Northeastern Regional Association of Coastal Ocean Observing Systems, researchers lost communication with a SeaTrac unmanned vessel on the night of Oct. 12.
The vessel was last reported 30 nautical miles southeast of Frenchman Bay, where it had been holding position to recharge.
A boat dispatched to the area a week later was unable to locate the vessel.
The yellow research vessel measures approximately 16 feet long and bears the markings "SeaTrac" on its bow and "Uncrewed Surface Vehicle" on the stern.
Reward eligibility will be determined by the vessel's operator team at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and the Northeastern Regional Association of Coastal Ocean Observing Systems.
Anyone with information is asked to contact Mike Brosnahan at mbrosnahan@whoi.edu or 508-289-5633.

title: Fat-free doesn’t always mean healthy: What to look for on food labels
text:
(Aging Untold) — Grabbing the “fat-free” option at the grocery store feels like the responsible choice, especially as we get older and start paying closer attention to our heart, our weight and our cholesterol.
But Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, explains why that label can be misleading — and what to check instead.
The biggest misconception about “fat-free”
“People think that fat-free is healthy. And really, fat free does not mean that it’s problem free,” Rogers said. “So if they’re removing the fat, they had to replace it with something else. So you have to look at the ingredients and look at the packaging.”
Rogers said the front of the package is designed to sell the product — not inform the shopper.
“Just remember this is about advertising,” she said. “So the package — the front of the package is all advertisement. And the back of the package is the ingredients, which tells the truth. That’s really what you want to know. If they took out something, what did they fill it with?”
She added that replacements for fat are often not healthy, even if they make a product taste better.
“Usually they fill it with something that’s not healthy. They made it taste good and all that, but it’s not healthy,” Rogers said.
A simple label-reading rule
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared her own personal rule of thumb for reading nutrition labels at the store.
“I’m a label reader,” O’Rourke said. “I eat anything with sugar being fifth and lower, and then I look at what’s above, and if I don’t understand it, I don’t eat it.”
Rethinking what food is for
Rather than focusing only on fat grams or calorie counts, Rogers said the better question is what is a food doing inside the body?
“We always thought about people looking at how much fat is in this food, or how many calories. Really, we have to get back to what does food do? It gives us energy,” Rogers said. “Why don’t you look at what is this food doing to my body? How is it helping me to stabilize my blood sugar? How’s it helping me with my hormones? That’s really what food is — it should be used as energy.”
Breaking down the different types of fat
Rogers said she used to find all the fat categories confusing, so she created a simple way to sort them.
“Monounsaturated fats — those are good fats. You want to eat them all day long. They help with the heart and cells,” she said. “That’s things like olive oil, avocados. Those are your healthy fats.”
She continued with polyunsaturated fats, which the body cannot produce on its own.
“Those are essential fats. That means your body can’t make it, so you have to get it from food,” Rogers said.
Saturated fats, she said, are OK in smaller amounts.
“Those are pretty good fats, but you want to do it in limitation. That’s your butter, your cream. They usually say no more than 10% of your total calories that day,” she said. “And then you have the trans fats — that’s just a no.”
Rogers compared the categories to family members and how welcome they are in your home.
“I had to classify it like a family. So you have those relatives that you want to come over — that’s your monos and your polys. And you have the other relatives that have boundaries. You have several relatives, they just can’t come,” she said.
Choosing food your great-grandparents would recognize
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said the simplest test for any product is whether it resembles real, recognizable food.
“The big thing is, when we’re looking at food, you want to be as close to natural food as possible. Would our great-grandparents recognize that as food?” she said. “They didn’t have to be nutrition experts, but today we kind of do. We want to be informed consumers.”
Key takeaways
- “Fat-free” isn’t always healthy. When fat is removed from a product, manufacturers replace it with something else — often sugar, sweeteners or starches.
- Flip the package over. The front is advertising; the ingredient list on the back tells you what’s actually in the product.
- Use simple ingredients. Choose foods close to what your great-grandparents would recognize is a simple way to eat more naturally.

title: 9 injured after distracted driver crashes into pedal tavern, police say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) — A distracted driver rear-ended a pedal tavern, injuring multiple people Thursday night in Nashville, Tennessee.
Ten of the 13 passengers were injured after the distracted driver hit the pedal tavern, according to the Metro Nashville Police Department.
The crash happened when a westbound Toyota RAV4 rear-ended the pedal tavern around 8:30 p.m. on Demonbreun Street in downtown Nashville, police said.
The driver of the RAV4 and the operator of the pedal tavern were not hurt. However, six people remained in the hospital as of Friday morning, with one in critical condition.
Nashville Pedal Tavern owners Pete Kootsikas, Angie Gleason and Brian Gleason released a joint statement Friday morning addressing the Thursday night crash involving one of their vehicles.
“Safety has been at the center of how we operate for 16 years, and we have proudly served hundreds of thousands of guests in Nashville. We are deeply saddened by what happened last night.”
Driver reported being distracted
The Metro Nashville Police Department said the RAV4 driver reported that he was distracted at the time of the crash. Police said they are not sure what distracted the driver.
Police spokesperson Kris Mumford said the injured passengers were an “older crowd,” but she was unsure where the victims are from.
Mumford said crashes involving pedal taverns are not common, adding that this is the first one she knew of.
“Of course it’s something you do worry about, but we’ll be investigating it, talking to the driver, and all of the patients have been transported to area hospitals. We hope they all recover well,” Mumford said.
“Pending review of the video footage on the pedal tavern and further investigation, the DA will be consulted for appropriate charges,” police said Friday morning.

title: School bus driver accused of DUI, evading police, using child as ‘shield’
text:
NORTH CHARLESTON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — A South Carolina woman is facing charges after police said she drove a school bus impaired and led police on a chase with her child in the vehicle before eventually using him as “a shield.”
Shakira Jones, 23, is charged with failure to stop for blue lights and sirens, driving under the influence and child endangerment.
North Charleston police said they received an alert at about 3:20 p.m. Thursday about a school bus driving erratically. Reports stated that the bus nearly hit another vehicle and that there were suspicions about the driver’s sobriety.
Officers found the bus and said they saw it traveling at around 65 miles per hour in a 45-mph zone and watched it make an improper turn, followed by multiple improper and erratic lane changes.
Police tried to initiate a traffic stop, but the bus sped up and did not stop.
Police said the bus led officers on a chase and continued driving erratically. Eventually, the driver sped into a parking lot where school staff were present. Staff members had to move out of the way to avoid the bus and the officers.
The bus came to a final stop, but the driver refused to exit, police said.
Officers were eventually able to see the driver and identify her as Jones.
A report states that officers readied their weapons and issued more commands, at which point Jones placed her child in front of her “in an attempt to shield herself from officers.”
Police were able to remove the child, and, after a brief struggle, officers brought Jones into custody.
Investigating officers reportedly found a bottle of prescribed amphetamines among Jones’ items, which were reportedly within arm’s reach of the driver’s seat.
Police said they performed field sobriety testing, which led officers to conclude that she had been driving while impaired.
Jones was booked into the Al Cannon Detention Center. No bond has been issued.

title: Lyme disease cases in Maine tracking ahead of last year
text:
Lyme disease cases in Maine so far this year are tracking slightly ahead of 2025, when the state set a record for the tickborne disease.
Megan Porter, health educator with the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention, said she can’t project whether 2026 cases will break the record, but the deer ticks that cause Lyme disease are currently active.
“Ticks are active anytime the temperature is above freezing,” Porter said. “The ticks are everywhere, so Mainers should take steps to prevent tickborne diseases.”
As of Oct. 20, the Maine CDC reported 3,976 Lyme disease cases so far this year. Through October 2025, the state had reported 3,763 cases of Lyme en route to logging a record of 4,257 cases last year.
Griffin Dill, who manages the University of Maine Cooperative Extension’s Tick Lab, said he expects there will be high levels of deer tick activity through mid-November.
Dill said deer ticks are now in their adult stage, and are currently searching for hosts, to prepare for laying eggs and surviving the winter. Despite the arid conditions — ticks prefer rainy and humid weather — the arachnids are still active, Dill said.
“They’re pretty well adapted to survive these adverse conditions,” Dill said. “It is by no means a booming year for tick activity, but we are not seeing a significant decrease in activity even though we’ve had dry weather.”
The lab receives thousands of tick submissions every year for identification and research.
The Maine CDC also reported that, through Oct. 20, there had been 1,223 anaplasmosis cases and 425 cases of babesiosis. The diseases, like Lyme, are transmitted to humans by deer ticks. Lyme and anaplasmosis are bacterial infections, while babesiosis is an infection caused by microscopic parasites.
In 2025, the state recorded a total of 352 cases of babesiosis and 1,604 cases of anaplasmosis, according to the Maine CDC.
Symptoms of the three diseases are similar, including fever, chills, fatigue, headaches and body aches, according to the U.S. CDC. Lyme can sometimes cause a bulls-eye rash. Lyme and anaplasmosis can be treated with a course of antibiotics, while babesiosis patients receive anti-parasitic medicine.
Porter said deer ticks are expanding their geographic range. They used to be mostly in coastal, southern Maine, but are now seen farther inland and Down East.
“We are seeing the ticks push into Down East, and increasing cases of tickborne disease in Western Maine,” Porter said.
Ticks are expanding their range due to climate change, scientists have said.
Porter said people can prevent tick bites by doing frequent checks after doing outdoor activities in tick habitat, tucking socks into pants and using repellent. After outdoor activities, Porter said, put clothes worn during the activity into the dryer on high, which will kill ticks.

title: State monitoring complaints of voter harassment in Lewiston
text:
Key Takeaways Key Takeaways are written by Maine Trust staff and highlight the most important points of this article so you can get the gist at a glance.
- Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said Thursday her office has received complaints of intrusive behavior at the polls in Lewiston.
- Despite confrontations between members of the public and a reporter over concerns of electioneering and intimidation, no one has been asked to leave City Hall for interfering with voting, according to officials.
- Volunteers have said confrontations have made for a bad voting experience and have even caused people to turn away from the polls.
LEWISTON — The Maine Secretary of State’s Office says it has received complaints regarding “intrusive filming, photography and harassment of voters” as early voting continues at City Hall.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said Thursday the city has taken steps to address the problem, and that her office is continuing to monitor the situation.
“All voters should be able to exercise their right to vote without feeling watched, questioned, or harassed, and we take these allegations seriously, particularly when it appears that voters were targeted for no other reason than their race or ethnicity,” Bellows said in a statement.
The complaints come as local Republicans and a right-wing media operation say they witnessed interpreters act inappropriately while they accompany residents to the polls.
House District 94 Republican candidate Janet Beaudoin, who faces Democrat Scott Harriman in the Nov. 3 race, said at the City Council meeting Tuesday that an interpreter said he’d tell the person he was helping to vote for her if she was a Democrat.
“It raised a serious concern about whether the voter was being encouraged to vote for a candidate,” she said. “Language assistance is a must for those who need it. I’m not disputing that. My concern is that interpreters are using their position near a voter to influence that person’s choice.”
The Maine Wire has come under scrutiny for its activities at the Lewiston polls. Several voters have claimed its reporters have been staking out the polls and harassing voters as they try to cast their ballots with the help of interpreters.
Videos have been circulating on social media showing a confrontation at the polls between local advocate and former city councilor Safiya Khalid and a Maine Wire reporter.
Steve Robinson, editor-in-chief of the Maine Wire, denies any wrongdoing, and said in a video podcast Tuesday that his organization’s presence is needed at the polls to make sure interpreters are acting appropriately.
The interpreters, Robinson said, are part of a “busing operation that is bringing in jobless Somali bums to vote.”
City Hall now has notices posted advising building visitors that since City Hall is a voting place, video recording and photography is prohibited within 15 feet of voters per state statute.
“As such, no videos or pictures may be taken in the Council Chambers or first floor of City Hall if a voter is within 15 feet,” the notice says, also providing that “voter selfies” are allowed as long as the voter is taking their own picture.
Many of those coming out early to vote do not speak English, so they are being accompanied by aides to help interpret their ballots.
City Clerk Kathy Montejo said it is common practice for groups including nonprofits to assist voters in getting to the polls and providing interpreting services, but that there is a state statute guiding that role.
Under the law, which is provided to aides at the polls, a voter has the right to select their aide and an aide cannot assist a voter unless their help is requested.
Aides cannot influence a voter’s choice or direct a voter to cast their vote in any way. They are informed before signing the absentee ballot as an aide that they are to read and translate out loud, and cannot discuss a ballot’s contents.
Thus far this election cycle, Montejo said she has not had to ask anyone, interpreter or otherwise, to leave the building.
Taste of Heritage owner Hussein Ahmed is one of many volunteers this year who said he is donating his time to shuttle people to the polls to vote. Ahmed said the general experience of voting this year has been so poor that several residents have turned back without voting, especially older voters.
Among others, he blames the Maine Wire’s presence at the polls as the root cause of the unease.
“They make the whole area so noisy, violating required distance, and they’re making it hard for the employees there,” Ahmed said. “People who look a certain way are being followed with cameras. It’s a very deliberate effort by a certain group of people. It’s really getting out of hand.
“This has never happened in all the time we have been voting. If someone could look into this we would appreciate it,” Ahmed continued. “I do this out of good will for my community — I want people to exercise their rights no matter who they vote for.”
Mayor Carl Sheline has encouraged residents to continue voting and to report all instances of harassment to the city clerk. He said in a Facebook post Thursday that the actions against interpreters at City Hall appear to be a “coordinated campaign of voter intimidation and suppression.”
“While people may hold different political opinions, everyone has the right to feel safe and secure when casting their ballot. Attempting to intimidate voters or suppress participation is the antithesis of democracy,” he said.
The ACLU of Maine reported Friday that it, along with other nonpartisan partners like the League of Women Voters of Maine, is monitoring the situation as the city and secretary of state are addressing the issue.
“We’re keeping our ear to the ground and paying close attention to make sure all eligible voters have the information and confidence they need to cast a ballot — no matter who it may be for,” ACLU of Maine spokesperson Samuel Crankshaw said.

title: Rhamondre Stevenson gives Patriots boost before half in loss to Bears
text:
CHICAGO — Rhamondre Stevenson and New England were in a bad spot. Then the right call at the right time provided a momentary lift for the Patriots.
Stevenson scored an unlikely touchdown on the final play of the first half Thursday night against the Chicago Bears. Stevenson’s fifth career TD reception trimmed New England’s deficit to 20-14 at the break, but the Bears held off the Patriots for a 30-24 victory.
“We’ve been working on that play for a long time and came in handy today, executed on that play,” Stevenson said. “So felt good to do that.”
Chicago opened a 13-point lead when it scored on Luther Burden’s 24-yard reception with 14 seconds left in the opening half. Kyle Williams returned the ensuing kickoff 25 yards to the New England 34.
Drake Maye then fired an 18-yard pass to A.J. Brown, and the Patriots (4-3) used their second timeout with 3 seconds to go.
On the next play, Stevenson slipped out of the backfield and Maye lobbed the ball over the head of Bears safety Cam Lewis. Stevenson ran away from Lewis and got a downfield block from DeMario Douglas before cutting past Bears cornerback Jaylon Johnson on his way to the end zone.
“I feel like it brought us some momentum, but obviously not enough,” Stevenson said. “We didn’t come out with the win.”
Stevenson’s 48-yard reception moved New England’s win probability from 10.2% to 24.5%, according to Next Gen Stats. The running back covered a total distance of 68.18 yards on the play, and he had a 4.3% chance of scoring.
“I think we could have rallied to the ball there and gotten him down,” Chicago coach Ben Johnson said.
Stevenson finished with 93 yards on five receptions, but had just 22 yards on six carries. The Patriots rushed for 70 yards on 17 attempts.
Any momentum that Stevenson generated for New England with his touchdown was erased by Chicago’s opening possession of the second half. The Bears (5-2) finished a nine-play, 72-yard drive with Caleb Williams’ 12-yard touchdown pass to Colston Loveland.
“We didn’t run the ball well enough,” Patriots coach Mike Vrabel said. “But we moved it however we needed to move it and sometimes you are going to have days like that. I thought we’d be able to run it a little better. We didn’t, but then our best players were putting the ball in good spots most of the time and making good decisions. That’s how it goes, we’d have liked to run the ball a little bit better. But it didn’t happen tonight.”

title: Cafe trains refugees, trafficking survivors in D.C. kitchen
text:
WASHINGTON (Aging Untold) — Emma’s Torch is a cafe and culinary school in Washington, D.C., that trains refugees, exiles and survivors of human trafficking.
Students at the cafe learn food preparation skills under timed kitchen conditions as part of their training.
On-the-job training
Students work through timed exercises such as julienne cutting chicken, with instructors telling them to have dishes “up by 10 minutes.”
Kerry Brodie founded the social justice nonprofit. The program lasts about 11 weeks and runs 40 hours a week.
“And that’s where our students are learning things like self-advocacy, English classes, resume crafts, interview prep, all of those things that are outside the kitchen,” Brodie said.
Brodie said 500 students have graduated from the program and 90% have jobs.
Rebuilding after loss
Nico came to the U.S. to rebuild his life.
He said he came to the United States with his two children and Emma’s Torch welcomed him and gave him new purpose.
“I learn new skills to know how to cook the best dishes in the world,” Nico said.
Nico said the program represents a second chance.
“You can begin a new life. You can believe in yourself,” Nico said.
Named for Emma Lazarus
The organization is named after Emma Lazarus, who wrote the words inscribed at the base of the Statue of Liberty: “Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free.”
Brodie described Lazarus as one of the unsung heroes of Jewish history and said the organization is meant to be a testament to that sentiment.

title: “All we have is each other”: Residents push forward over a year after Minnesota fire
text:
BRIMSON, Minn. (InvestigateTV) - In May 2025, about 30 miles north of Duluth, a 27-year-old man decided to have a campfire.
The weather was record warm, windy and dry with Red Flag warnings in place.
That campfire grew into the Camp House fire, torching thousands of acres of forest and more than 180 homes, cabins and outbuildings.
In the year since, the devastated residents of Brimson have gotten an unwanted crash course in disaster recovery.
What they learned -- don’t rely on leaders in St. Paul and Washington, D.C. for help. Rely on each other.
As flames began ripping across the terrain, Diane Knaffla enjoyed what she thought was a beautiful day outside her home of 36 years.
“I’m sitting under the big trees here and next thing I know my brother and nephew are tearing up the driveway, ‘Diane you gotta get out of here there’s a forest fire’”, said Knaffla. “I walked out in front of the house. I didn’t smell smoke, but when I looked that way it was orange smoke.”
Fifteen minutes later, the sheriff arrived and said it’s time to go. She left with little more than the clothes on her back in disbelief.
“It’s going to be here when I get back,” Knaffla thought. “It’s going to go around me. And yet I started to cry because looking in the rear view mirror, I thought, oh boy.”
Where a century-old home and 1,500 pine trees once stood now sits a modular house and a field.
“I love the woods,” said Knaffla. “Sitting outside under my trees was perfect for me.”
Three miles down the road, the fire took just about everything on Eric Radke’s property except for his lake view, his sense of humor, and his better half of 50 years.
“All we have is each other now,” Radke said about his wife, Sue. “The house had been here for 125 years. Why now? We just looked at it and thought this is that beautiful house we bought to retire in and we planned to live out here as long as we could stay in this part of the country, and it was just gone.”
The fires were still burning nearby on May 15, when state and federal leaders visited Brimson, pledging help in front of TV cameras. That included Governor Tim Walz, Rep. Pete Stauber, and Senators Amy Klobuchar and Tina Smith.
However, as fire victims would soon learn, that funding was to rebuild public infrastructure.
When it came to their homes and properties, it was solely up to their insurance. And insurance wouldn’t cover the cost of hauling out debris and dead trees or installation of new septic mounds, which the county required most to do.
The cost of all of that was north of $60,000 out-of-pocket for many.
After the flames were out, locals we spoke with say the recovery effort wasn’t led by elected leaders, but rather neighbors helping neighbors, and one community member in particular.
“It was extremely traumatic,” said Brimson resident Mikala Schliep.
Mikala Schliep was relatively new to the Brimson area when the wildfire broke out. She nearly lost her life.
“Closed the trunk of my car and then grabbed my dog and we were out the driveway, and it was just walls of fire on both sides of us going out,” said Schliep. “I was just screaming. It was so hot inside my car and I can’t see feet in front of me.”
After making it out just in time, and her home somehow being spared, Schliep’s devastation came from seeing the struggles of those who did lose everything.
“I just saw how much the community needed help and we weren’t getting it fast enough, at least by my standards, so that’s when we kind of stepped in,” said Schliep.
She started organizing drives, with Hugo’s Bar becoming an early drop off site for food, clothes and other necessities.
When donations overwhelmed that location, Bassett Hall became a one-stop shop for fire victims.
Eric Radke said much of his current wardrobe came from Bassett Hall.
Once everyone’s immediate needs were met, Schliep’s attention turned to cleanup and recovery, finding wreckers and volunteers to help haul out debris and downed trees, doing a lot of the work herself.
“People need to replace their septic systems, people need trees removed, and that’s where we wanted to start getting those funds and that’s where we started the non-profit side of it,” said Schliep.
She launched Brimson Strong, a non-profit aimed at raising money, obtaining grants and disbursing the funds to victims who might otherwise be out of luck.
“I did the grant writing for that,” said Schliep. “And that’s like a little win for me. I am severely dyslexic, like the worst degree you can be. So writing and reading has never come easy to me, but I’ve always been a great storyteller.”
And so far so good. The non-profit has given tens of thousands back to Brimson fire victims.
“I got a check for $5,000 for that,” said Diane Knaffla. “I’m almost getting choked up because of all that she’s done.”
“I’m still pretty new to Brimson,” said Schliep. “This place is so special and the people here are so strong and that’s why I fight so hard for it.”
Schliep and other residents we spoke with say the Red cross, United Way and St. Louis County provided much appreciate help immediately after the fire, but could only do so much.
Residents tell Northern News Now they also appreciate Rep. Natalie Zeleznikar, who they say has stayed in touch with residents.
Zeleznikar tells us she’d like the state to provide incentives for timber companies to haul out and utilize partially burned timber. She said that would significantly bring down costs for fire victim cleanup.
Here is a QR code to donate directly to Brimson Strong.
As for the the man cited for starting the fire, he’s only had to pay a $175 fine.
However, at least one of the people affected by the fire we spoke with plans to take him to small claims court.
The State of Minnesota announced exactly a year after the fire that it would allocate $250,000 for victims of the Camp House fire.

title: The Final Screen Tests for the Next James Bond Are Days Away
text:
The Final Decision on the Next James Bond Is Coming Soon
Years of speculation will soon come to an end, as Amazon are reportedly closing on making a decision in the next James Bond sweepstakes that have played out, very very slowly, since the company acquired MGM and thus gained control of the long-running Bond film franchise.
According to Variety, “final screen tests for Amazon MGM Studios‘ new 007 are set to happen in the next week ... beginning as early as Friday.”
They add that “who exactly will test is up in the air,” but they cite to specific finalists: Callum Turner and Jack Lowden.
Turner recently appeared in One Night Only and was previously seen in the romantic dramedy Eternity opposite Elizabeth Olsen and Miles Teller. Lowden is best known for his role on the streaming series Slow Horses; he also appeared in James L. Brooks’ Ella McCay. Turner is British; Lowden is Scottish. Their candidacy would suggest that Amazon is not looking to create a radically different Bond character, but rather to continue in the tradition started way back in 1962 when Sean Connery became the first James Bond in a big-screen 007 movie.
READ MORE: Every James Bond Movie, Ranked From Worst to Best
It’s now been five full years since Daniel Craig made his final appearance as James Bond in No Time to Die. Since then, there has been all sorts of behind-the-scenes wrangling over the future of the series. Amazon MGM eventually took full control of the franchise from its longtime stewards, Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli, and brought in producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman to oversee what will be the 26th official James Bond film.
They, in turn, brought in Dune’s Denis Villeneuve to direct the movie, which currently has a screenplay written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight.
Nothing is known yet about the approach this new movie is taking to Ian Fleming’s famous super-spy. The end of No Time to Die was a pretty conclusive farewell to the Daniel Craig version of the character; will Villeneuve start over from scratch with yet another “new” Bond? Will he make a period piece? Will the whole film just be a remake of Octopussy for some reason? At this point anything is possible...

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez campaigns for Troy Jackson, touts shared progressive values
Ocasio-Cortez and Jackson appeared to agree on all of the progressive policy points, including Medicare for All, abortion access and defunding ICE.
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) traveled to Maine on Thursday to take the stage with Senate candidate Troy Jackson in Portland. The two took several questions from college students at the event hosted by "More Perfect University," a progressive campus group, and touched on topics ranging from immigration enforcement to healthcare.
"They are sending ICE out in droves [in Maine]. Not just to intimidate the Somali community, the immigrant community, but to intimidate all of us," Ocasio-Cortez said, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
"I hear it from people all the time who do not support Medicare for All. 'Well, I like my private insurance.' Fine, and I am going to do something better than your private insurance," Jackson said.
Jackson and Ocasio-Cortez both argued that the money that is used to fund the ongoing war in Iran and ICE should be used to fund healthcare.
"How can we afford Iran? How can we afford Gaza? How can we afford these things when folks at home can't eat, can't go to the doctor or build a bridge to get there?" asked Cortez.
Ocasio-Cortez also spoke about higher education and called for all public colleges and universities to be tuition-free. She said higher education has become a "luxury" in 2026.
The two appeared to agree on nearly every topic discussed. From defunding ICE and ending the war in Iran. Ocasio-Cortez spent most of the evening speaking, with Jackson chiming in. The two also spent time taking jabs at Sen. Susan Collins and called her out again for her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
"Susan Collins, one of the only Republican female senators in a unique position to protect almost every woman in America, decided to declare open season on us instead," Ocasio-Cortez said.
The two were also asked about funding rural healthcare and public transit. Jackson said he would like to see a rail system connecting Portland and Bangor eventually built using federal funds.

title: Airbnb guests no longer have to wash dishes, strip the beds at checkout
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - Airbnb guests can say goodbye to checkout chores like washing dishes, stripping beds and taking out the trash under a new policy announced this week.
The short-term rental platform’s new rules limit hosts to “reasonable” checkout requests beginning on Nov. 20. Guests can still be asked to leave dishes in the sink, gather used towels and sort trash and recycling, but hosts generally cannot require chores typically handled by professional cleaners.
“Remember to think like a guest and keep in mind what you’d find unreasonable,” Airbnb tells hosts in a video announcing the new policy.
Checkout chores have been a recurring point of contention for Airbnb guests, particularly when they’re also paying cleaning fees. The company has previously acknowledged that those fees can create different expectations between hosts and travelers.
Airbnb said exceptions may apply in certain circumstances, such as requiring guests to put trash in animal-proof containers in areas with bears.
Hosts must now also disclose all house rules and requests in a designated section of their listing before guests book, according to Airbnb. They can no longer add extra requirements through messages, signs inside the property or other sections of a listing.
As part of the changes, Airbnb said it is standardizing house rules into seven categories, covering topics including overnight guests, quiet hours, pets, smoking and whether guests must lock up at checkout.
The changes build on Airbnb’s broader efforts to make booking a rental more predictable for travelers. In 2023, CEO Brian Chesky acknowledged that the variety of properties on Airbnb creates uncertainty among guests.
“A lot of guests have described booking Airbnb, once they check in, it’s a moment of truth. Is the house exactly what they expected?” he told The Associated Press. “We don’t want this to be a moment of truth. We want you to know exactly what you’re going to get before you book.”
