title: Obituary: Carolyn Diane Pollard
text:
RAYMOND – Carolyn Diane Pollard, 65, of Raymond, passed away on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026, surrounded by her family.
Carolyn was born on April 22, 1961, in Portland, the daughter of Bill and Anne (Whitney) Cordell. She spent her early years in Ashland, Ohio, before returning to Pownal, where she attended local schools. Her return to Maine reunited her with her large extended family in Gray, where she and her sister grew up surrounded by aunts, uncles, and cousins. Some of her cousins were so close that she considered them siblings.
Carolyn spent more than 30 years working in the insurance industry, building her career at Unum, where she was employed for over 15 years. She was also actively involved in the Group Underwriters Association of America, serving as a board member and as president in the early 2000s.
In 1997, Carolyn married Jeff Pollard, and together they raised two children, Christina and Jeffrey Jr. A weekend snowmobile ride led Carolyn and Jeff to a property in Roxbury, Maine, that would become known simply as “camp.” Over the years, camp became a special place filled with cherished memories, laughter, and time spent with family and friends.
Above all, Carolyn’s friends and family were her world. Her warm, inviting personality and remarkable ability to remember everyone’s name made her unforgettable to so many. Through her years of travel, she built friendships with people far and wide. No matter how much time had passed, she made a point of staying in touch, picking up right where she left off as though no time had passed at all. As her children grew, Carolyn found great joy in opening her home to them and their friends, hosting sleepovers complete with elaborate spreads and plenty of food. Making others feel welcome and creating lasting memories came naturally to her, and these moments reflected the love and care she so freely gave to those around her.
Carolyn is survived by her husband, Jeff Pollard of Raymond; her daughter, Christina Pollard of Standish; her son, Jeffrey Pollard Jr. of Raymond; her sister, Cheryl Croxford, and her husband, Curt, of Pittston; and many aunts, uncles, cousins, nieces, and nephews. She was predeceased by her parents, William Cordell and Anne (Whitney) Herrick.
A celebration of Carolyn’s life will be held at Spring Meadows on Thursday, October 29, from 3-7 p.m.
In lieu of flowers, the family requests that donations be made to the American Heart Association in
Carolyn’s memory.

title: DOJ sending election observers to polls in Portland and Lewiston
text:
The U.S. Department of Justice is sending election monitors to polls in Portland and Lewiston to oversee the Nov. 3 elections, the Maine Secretary of State’s office confirmed.
The Department of Justice has in recent years sent observers to other states on a smaller scale, usually in response to a civil rights violation. But this comes amid several efforts by the Trump administration to assert authority over the election and following an attempt to force Maine, among other states, to hand over voter information.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said she doesn’t expect the observers will have any impact on election processes.
“Any monitors are subject to the same laws and rules as any other observer at the poll,” Bellows told Maine Morning Star. “That means they can observe what’s taking place, but they may not interact with voters, handle ballots or equipment, or disrupt voting in any way.”
“We will monitor the monitors very carefully to ensure that they don’t cross any lines,” Bellows added.
This is the first time since Bellows became secretary of state in 2021 that federal election observers have been dispatched to Maine, which is among several states that were notified this week of the federal presence on Election Day.
The DOJ in August announced plans to send 1,000 election monitors to midterm election polling places nationwide, as first reported by Bloomberg. That’s significantly more than the 289 observers sent out for the 2022 midterm elections, and the 714 involved in the 2024 presidential election, CBS News reported.
Bellows said the DOJ observers will be among many other Election Day monitors, including those dispatched by the parties and nonpartisan groups including the League of Women Voters and ACLU.
They will dress in business casual clothing and won’t be allowed to use any DOJ identifiers. They also aren’t allowed to talk to voters inside polling places or to carry firearms.
The goal, according to letters sent by the DOJ, is to monitor for compliance with federal voting rights laws, including people with disabilities’ access to the ballot box, among other civil rights assurances.
Portland and Lewiston are Maine’s two most populous cities and are home to the state’s largest share of immigrants. In the weeks leading up to the election, President Donald Trump has launched an aggressive campaign against noncitizen voting, including attempts to purge voter rolls and send sensitive personal information to the Department of Homeland Security with the aim of flagging potential noncitizen voters.
Last year, the DOJ sued Maine after Bellows twice rejected requests from the Trump administration for Maine’s full, unredacted voter rolls — among other information. In May, a federal judge dismissed the administration’s lawsuit, following similar legal setbacks in other states.
Bellows said her office “will do everything in our power to ensure a positive voting experience for every citizen.” She added, “voter intimidation or interference is a crime, and we will hold the DOJ monitors to the same standards and expectations as anyone else who’s at the voting point on Election Day.”
She also pointed out that anyone who is concerned can cast a ballot at their municipal clerk’s office anytime during business hours before the end of early voting on Oct. 29.
There have already been reports of voter harassment in Lewiston. This week, an employee of the Maine Wire filmed members of the immigrant community at the city clerk’s office.
“We’ve been in close communication with the city clerk, and we understand the city of Lewiston has taken some measures to enforce order at the voting place,” Bellows said, noting the city has put up notices warning that filming or photography (outside of selfies) is prohibited at polling locations. “No one should be harassed or filmed without their consent by anyone, whether that person is purporting to be a member of the media, or there for partisan political purposes.”
The rightwing outlet alleged those seeking interpretation assistance were in some way violating voting rules. But Bellows said her office has not received a credible report that an interpreter is engaged in illegal electioneering.

title: ‘Neighborhood Nursing’: This program aims to be a national model for reinventing primary care
text:
BALTIMORE, Md. (InvestigateTV) — A pilot program called Neighborhood Nursing is providing basic primary care outside the traditional clinic setting in East Baltimore, setting up in a church and visiting apartment complexes and homes to reach residents.
The program’s services are open to anyone who lives in the area. Those services are free and funded for now largely through philanthropic donations.
How the program works
Stacye Cooper, a registered nurse with the program, said the goal is to be available in spaces where residents feel comfortable.
Cooper focuses on each patient’s physical condition, including blood pressure checks and diabetes management.
Terry Lindsay, a community health worker with the program, works to identify and address patients’ social needs, including help with rent, utilities and food.
“You might think, well, is that health? But that is health! And the trust comes from showing up over and over and from being in trusted spaces,” said Sarah Szanton.
Szanton is dean of the Johns Hopkins School of Nursing and leads the Neighborhood Nursing effort in partnership with three other universities in Maryland.
She would like to see the program expand beyond Maryland.
“The end goal is really to be in every state and for this to be how we do health care,” Szanton said. “Why are we here? We’re here to change the health of the nation.”
National primary care shortfalls
Nearly a third of Americans do not have a primary care provider, according to the National Association of Community Health Centers. That works out to more than 100 million people who are missing out on routine visits and screenings.
A 2026 “Health of U.S. Primary Care” report found that regular access to primary care is associated with lower hospitalizations and health costs, yet fewer than 5% of U.S. health care dollars are spent on primary care.
“We’ve really got it backwards,” Szanton said.
A model from Costa Rica
Szanton said Neighborhood Nursing was inspired by a public health care program in Costa Rica.
“It started in the mid-90s, and it’s based on having zones where everyone in a zone has the same nurse,” Szanton said. “Everyone in Costa Rica gets one visit a year and if you have higher risk for some reason you get two or three.”
Dr. Madeline Pesec, a physician and researcher at Harvard University’s School of Public Health, has studied the Costa Rican model with colleagues for years.
“It’s really impressive,” Pesec said. “To me, that is the secret sauce of Costa Rica, that they know exactly who their patients are.”
Pesec said Costa Rica has made progress in tackling infectious and chronic disease, which she said led to fewer deaths.
“We saw a 13% all-age, all-cause reduction in mortality. And we saw a 19% reduction in cardiovascular mortality, meaning diseases that come from heart attack or stroke,” Pesec said. “And the way you get those numbers down is by 10 years earlier, really working to control their blood sugar, working to control their blood pressure.”
Patients describe their experience
Edward Murray, 73, is one of the patients Neighborhood Nursing sees on a weekly basis.
“They make you feel comfortable. They talk to you. They don’t talk at you,” Murray said.
Cooper said she follows up when patients miss appointments.
“I’m looking around like, where is Mr. Murray? I’ll end up calling him. If he doesn’t answer his phone, I knock on his door. I know his apartment number,” Cooper said.
“It’s the love that they show,” Murray said.
Another couple, Maria and Brian, came in for a checkup a few weeks ago. In talking with Lindsay, it was revealed they had only recently secured housing after years living on the streets and had no furniture.
“We were basically sleeping on a rug in the living room in the apartment. So on the floor. And Terry ended up finding this Baltimore furniture bank, made an appointment for us. We got all three rooms of furniture for $350,” they said.
Asked what it means to help patients with needs beyond medical care, Lindsay said: “They look at us for all different types of advice. Sometimes it’s just being there for a person.”
Szanton said the program has served thousands of patients in the roughly three years since the pilot began.
“Oh it’s the reason to do it, right? It’s the feeling that we’re changing lives,” Szanton said.
Funding and expansion
Ann Greiner, who heads the Primary Care Collaborative, which advocates for primary care policy reform, said funding is one of the biggest challenges facing the system.
Greiner said expanding the program nationwide would require buy-in from federal and state lawmakers, health care providers and insurance companies.
“It’s not that there’s not enough money in our system. There is so much money in our system,” Greiner said. “It’s just, in my view, being spent on the wrong things. So we really need to have a reset.”
Szanton said the program is already in funding talks with policymakers.
“We see it kind of as a partnership between government and insurers,” Szanton said. “We’re not just offering it in Baltimore. We’re also at the same time working with policymakers.”
Cooper and Lindsay said they believe the program is reaching people who otherwise would not receive care.
“There’s so many people, if we weren’t here, they wouldn’t go to the doctor, they would not have these services. It’s our mission,” Lindsay said.
The Association of American Medical Colleges said primary care provider shortages are expected to worsen. By 2033, the AAMC projects a shortfall of more than 21,000 primary care physicians in the United States.

title: 2 ex-FBI officials charged with making false statements about Hunter Biden's laptop
text:
2 ex-FBI officials charged with making false statements about Hunter Biden's laptop
Two former FBI officials were charged on Friday with lying to Congress about their involvement in investigating Hunter Biden’s laptop in the run-up to the 2020 presidential election, the latest in a series of splashy and politically charged actions the Justice Department has undertaken ahead of next month's midterm contests.
Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, former top leaders of a since-disbanded task force set up to counter foreign election interference, surrendered to authorities and made their first appearance in federal court in Washington, where their lawyers pressed for a speedy hearing at which they could contest the allegations against them.
The prosecution, a rare Department of Justice criminal case against a former employee, revisits a tangled and peculiar saga that roiled the final weeks of the 2020 race. It also comes amid a broader, backward-looking effort by FBI Director Kash Patel, who before taking over the nation’s premier law enforcement agency was a harsh critic of it, to scrutinize high-profile episodes from the bureau’s recent past that for years have animated President Donald Trump’s conservative base.
Floris’ attorneys called her “a patriot” and said she has “served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years.”
“Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts,” her attorneys said in a statement. “It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election.”
A criminal complaint comes just before the midterms
The case was filed 10 days before the Nov. 3 elections via criminal complaint, which means prosecutors have not yet presented the case to a grand jury for an indictment. The Justice Department has repeatedly struggled in high-profile cases to convince grand juries in the nation’s capital to return indictments.
During the former FBI employees’ court appearance, both defense attorneys and the judge noted the unusual move to charge the case through a criminal complaint, which is more often used by prosecutors when they have an urgent need to take people into custody because, for example, they present a danger or a risk of flight.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui remarked that it is “rare that we have charges this old coming in this nature.” Faruqui set a preliminary hearing for next Tuesday over the objections of prosecutors, who pushed for more time given what the judge described as the “sword of Damocles” hanging over the defendants’ head.
The laptop discovery created turmoil in 2020 election
The revelation of the laptop’s existence in October 2020 injected a thorny storyline in the race between Trump, the Republican incumbent, and Biden’s father, Joe Biden, Trump’s Democratic challenger, who went on to win the race.
The complaint aims to build on longstanding congressional Republican complaints about the FBI’s handling of the laptop, including allegations that the bureau was not forthcoming to the public about its conclusion that the materials on it — including emails that showed discussions of the younger Biden’s foreign business dealings — were authentic and not the product of Russian disinformation.
The laptop’s contents were publicized by the New York Post, which said it had obtained from Trump ally Rudy Giuliani a hard drive of a computer dropped off by Hunter Biden at a Wilmington, Delaware, repair shop about a year earlier.
The curious circumstances of the laptop’s discovery raised concerns among Democrats and former intelligence officials about the possibility of Russian disinformation, particularly at a time when the Trump administration’s own intelligence community was assessing that Russia was attempting to interfere on Trump’s behalf in the election and as Giuliani had traveled abroad looking for dirt on the Bidens. Dozens of former U.S. intelligence officials signed a letter saying that the laptop bore the hallmarks of an “information campaign.”
But Trump’s then-director of national intelligence, John Ratcliffe, said in a letter to Congress that there was no proof foreign actors had anything to do with Hunter Biden’s laptop. The FBI under then-Director Chris Wray subsequently backed up that assessment.
Hunter Biden was subsequently charged with, and convicted of, gun and tax offenses during his father’s administration. Joe Biden pardoned him in his final weeks in office.
The case shines a light on an FBI task force on foreign intelligence
The complaint alleges that in their capacity as leaders of the Foreign Influence Task Force, Floris and Benavides were engaged in the investigations into Hunter Biden, and that Biden was a recurring subject at FITF meetings. Yet, the complaint says, both downplayed their firsthand knowledge of the laptop or involvement in investigations during 2023 congressional testimony. It accuses Benavides of making a false statement by telling lawmakers that he learned through Wikipedia that the FBI was in possession of the laptop.
“Lying to Congress by senior FBI officials strikes at the heart of our system. No one is above the law,” Patel said.
The case brings renewed attention to the work of the task force, which was established in the first Trump administration to police influence campaigns staged by Russia and other nations aimed at sowing discord, undermining democracy and spreading disinformation. The task force became a magnet of congressional Republican criticism during the Biden investigation and was disbanded in February 2025 by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi in one of her first acts on the job.
The Justice Department has made other splashy moves
As FBI director, Patel has presided over widespread firings of agents who were involved in investigations of Trump or who are perceived as being against the Republican administration's agenda.
He has also focused attention on years-old investigations like the Hunter Biden one that occurred before he became director and that have been the subject of grievances and complaints by Trump allies.
The Justice Department historically looks to avoid public and overt investigative acts in the direct lead-up to an election that involve candidates or that risk influencing an outcome. But officials in the last two weeks have made a series of bold moves in cases with political undertones, including a search of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s house in an immigration fraud investigation and a corruption indictment unsealed Thursday against powerful Democratic Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas.
Omar and Lucas are both Trump critics. Omar, who's from Minnesota, has called the search of her Washington home an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” Lucas has said she won't be intimidated or bullied by the federal government in its case against her and “will not back down.”

title: Fans are traveling from across the world for the World Series
text:
'Traveled for ... 24 hours': Fans travel from across the world for the World Series
Milwaukee Brewers fans are traveling in from around the world for the World Series. In each wave of travelers at General Mitchell International Airport, classic Brewers blue and gold shone through on Thursday.
Sister station WISN was there as fans arrived in Milwaukee on Thursday to see the city's first World Series game in more than four decades.
The Reed family traveled in from Maryland.
"I was 8 back in '82 when they lost to the Cards in seven," Earl Reed said. "I had always all along said for years, if they ever make it back to the World Series, I was coming."
Now, his whole family are die-hard Brewers fans.
"Super excited, super excited. It's my first World Series, so I can't wait. I can't wait," Melanie Reed said.
"I played volleyball at the University of Wisconsin, so big Wisconsin sports fan, this is super exciting," Sydney Reed said.
For Jacob Maurer, traveling back to Milwaukee for the World Series took a bit more planning.
"I'm traveling in from the country of Georgia. I just traveled for about 24 hours to get here," Maurer said. "When I was a kid, we were really bad. So it was more of just like a fun event to go to as a family. But as I've gotten older, it's been, like, deeper commitment to the team and stuff. I've been traveling for about the past seven years around the world. And so just by keeping track of them and been waiting for this my whole life."
Some fans have no connection to Milwaukee, besides their love for the Brewers, like Louis Bishop. He traveled to Milwaukee from Wilmington, North Carolina.
"In the early 2000s, I really started getting to baseball, and I didn't want to jump on any bandwagon. You know, in North Carolina, does it have a team that gets the closest at the time was the Braves, and I was like, you know, they had Miller Park. I like Miller Beer. They haven't — they've never won. The last time they went to the World Series was the year I was born. So that's where my fandom started," Bishop said.
Another fan told WISN he is returning to his home city after decades away to cheer on his hometown team.
"I grew up here in Milwaukee," Daniel Paul said after getting off his flight from Houston. "My sister has season tickets, so she called me and said after Game 4, she had a ticket for me, so I came back. I went to the NLCS a couple times when I lived out in California, and the Dodgers just beat us every single time, so my hopes — pretty low. But this year, we just have a team that is doing really good. When we won Game 4 against the Dodgers, I was super, super happy."
No matter where they're coming from, the Brew Crew is ready to see a World Series end in a ring for their team.

title: Federal judge orders Trump administration to halt noncitizen voting investigation in 9 states
text:
(AP) - A federal judge in California has ordered the Trump administration to halt investigations in nine states into whether noncitizens are registered to vote.
U.S. District Court Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin in Oakland found the government’s effort is relying on data that is full of errors and that it’s leading to intimidation of groups performing voter assistance efforts. She said it should be halted until polls close on Election Day, Nov. 3.
She put her ruling, which was made Wednesday, on hold until Friday to give the administration a chance to appeal.
The ruling applies to investigations in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.
It comes as the Trump administration has been hunting for noncitizen voters throughout the country in the months leading into the midterm elections. The administration has signaled that it’s a major problem, when in fact it’s quite rare, as even its own investigations have shown.
The lawsuit was filed by the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United, along with the Voto Latino Foundation, San Francisco and Santa Clara County.
In response to the ruling, the Department of Homeland Security issued an email statement Thursday saying it’s focused on “removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” while adding, “We have no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens.”
The judge based the decision to halt the investigation only on the unions’ assertion that the probe is harming voter assistance and mobilization efforts involving citizens. She did not find that union members’ right to vote was being infringed because most of them do that by mail and not in person. She said investigations don’t need to target U.S. citizens, use armed agents or intimidate citizens who are urging others to vote.
According to legal filings in the case, investigators were told to target naturalized citizens to see whether they had voted before they became U.S. citizens. The lists of voters to check came from sources that included state and local governments and publicly available information. Martinez-Olguin called them “voluminous and unreliable.”
“Even under the best conditions, there is a high likelihood of error in review because there is no federal database containing citizenship status of U.S. residents,” Martinez-Olguin wrote in her ruling. “The time limitations implemented during the Surge further exacerbate the risk of error.”
The Department of Justice has been demanding detailed and unredacted voter roll data from the states and has sued the 30 states that have refused to turn it over, losing each of those cases so far. The judge noted that for states that refused to share their records, the administration was trying to obtain them through “unreliable commercial versions of voter roll data.”
She said during a “surge” phase of the investigation starting in late August, agents were ordered to complete reviews of flagged individuals taking no more than 12 minutes per person to assess whether they were legally qualified to vote.
In their challenge, the plaintiffs said some U.S. citizens felt they were wrongly identified and investigated as part of the probe. Martinez-Olguin said those fears “are well understood as intimidation” that has chilled people from attending campaign events and working as poll monitors during the election.
Beau Tremitiere, a lawyer representing the unions and voter group, said in a statement that the ruling affirms the groups’ position.
“It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people’s homes weeks before an election,” Tremitiere said.
Details of the investigation, known as the “Unlawful Voter Initiative,” came to light last month after Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York and Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California released a whistleblower report about it.

title: Breezy Today... Beautiful Weekend Ahead
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Strong low pressure will continue to pull away from New England while strong high pressure builds in from the west today. This will keep the pressure gradient fairly tight over the area... in turn... keeping the breezy conditions going through much of the day with northerly winds gusting to 25-30 MPH at times. Otherwise expect a brighter and cooler day with abundant sunshine and high temperatures in the mid-40s to around 50° north and low 50s elsewhere. The gusty breeze will diminish this evening leading to a light wind overnight tonight. Clear skies combined with the light wind will allow for a colder night with nighttime lows dropping to the 20s in most spots. Coastal areas will be closer to... or a bit above 30°.
Strong high pressure will bring us some beautiful fall weather this weekend with lots of sunshine both Saturday and Sunday. The high will build to our south through the weekend... which will allow warmer air to return as the weekend progresses. After a cold start Saturday... temperatures will warm into the 50s for afternoon highs. A warmer west/southwesterly flow into New England will lead to a warmer day Sunday with highs topping off in the upper 50s to low 60s. This fantastic fall weather continues into next week too. A cold front is forecast to move through the state Monday afternoon but looks to be lacking moisture and will likely be more of a cloud producer than anything. Look for a mix of sun and clouds Monday with temperatures remaining on the milder side ahead of the front... with highs in the upper 50s to low 60s Monday afternoon. Colder weather will move in behind the front for Tuesday as high pressure builds in from Ontario. Tuesday will features lots of sunshine with high temperatures only in the 40s... with some upper 30s possible across the north. Temperatures will remain chilly Wednesday then moderate back to more seasonable levels later in the week. It looks like we could see some shower activity in the forecast late next week but at this point it doesn’t look like much and the forecast looks to be mainly dry into next weekend.
Rest of Today: Sunny... breezy... and cooler. Highs in the mid-40s to low 50s. North wind 10-20 MPH with gusts to 25-30 MPH possible.
Tonight: Clear and cold. Lows between 22°-32°... warmest along the coast. Light north/northwest wind.
Saturday: Sunny skies. Highs in the 50s. Light and variable wind.
Sunday: Sunny skies. Highs in the upper 50s to low 60s.
Monday: Mix of sun and clouds. Highs in the upper 50s to low 60s.
Tuesday: Mostly sunny and colder. Highs mainly in the 40s.

title: USPS raises some shipping rates ahead of holiday season
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — The U.S. Postal Service is temporarily raising prices on some package deliveries ahead of the holiday season. A shipping industry expert says the cost could eventually land on consumers’ receipts.
USPS said in a press release the temporary rates apply to some Priority Mail, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select shipments starting Oct. 4 and will stay in place through mid-January.
In its announcement, the Postal Service said the adjustment is “to help cover extra handling costs to ensure a successful peak season.”
Joseph DiSorbo, founder and CEO of SHIP.com, said the rate increase is tied to several factors.
“It’s probably tied to some diesel costs, but I also think it’s just tied to the USPS not really making money and they’re trying to get their financials correct,” DiSorbo said.
Impact on retailers
DiSorbo said small retailers under pressure from larger retailers may have to absorb some of the added costs, which would affect their margins in the short term.
“I would say on the small retailers, that are under pressure from the larger retailers, they might have to absorb some of those costs, which will put pressure on their margins, at least in the short term. I think ultimately it gets passed on to the end user consumer,” DiSorbo said.
DiSorbo said smaller retailers in particular may feel the squeeze.
“So I don’t think we’re going to see anytime soon, free shipping will disappear. But I think, it’s gonna over time have to be passed along to the consumer in some way, shape or form,” DiSorbo said.
What retailers and shoppers can do
DiSorbo said retailers should start planning now.
“I would be calling my shipper, whether it’s USPS or UPS or FedEx, and ask them, what are the plans for holiday season? What can I expect? So you can get out ahead of that. So then you can plan properly,” DiSorbo said.
For consumers, DiSorbo recommends waiting to shop.
“I would shop a little bit after Thanksgiving and see if I can get a great deal on something,” DiSorbo said.

title: Major toy companies did not disclose toxic chemicals in Maine
text:
Several manufacturers of popular children’s products disclosed using hazardous chemicals like cancer-causing formaldehyde in other states while failing to report those toxic ingredients to Maine regulators, public records show.
The findings highlight a vulnerability in the state’s public health oversight: laws designed to protect consumers rely on corporate self-reporting, allowing companies to reveal chemical hazards to regulators in some states while keeping local officials and families in the dark.
Investigators at Defend Our Health, a Portland-based advocacy group, uncovered the reporting gap while auditing filings in a multistate chemical clearinghouse shared by Vermont, Washington and Oregon.
In those three states, Crayola reported adding formaldehyde to more than 300 children’s products, including washable felt-tip markers, sticky tubs of finger paint and modeling clay, according to the clearinghouse.
Build-A-Bear Workshop, a retail chain where customers can assemble their own stuffed animals, disclosed the presence of phthalates, arsenic and heavy metals like mercury in toy accessories.
Yet neither company filed the required chemical disclosure documents with Maine authorities before offering those same product lines in local store aisles, according to Defend Our Health and state officials. Neither company replied to phone calls or emails asking why they did not disclose in Maine.
Emily Carey Perez de Alejo, executive director of Defend Our Health, said the discoveries alarmed her. She is the mother of a 4-year-old who regularly uses Crayola art supplies.
“Formaldehyde is a known carcinogen,” she said. “I’m beyond outraged that a trusted brand like Crayola thinks it’s OK to put something so dangerous in a product found in nearly every home and school in the country.”
Perez de Alejo contacted Crayola for an explanation. Initially, a representative told her by email Crayola had never added formaldehyde to its products. Then, after she cited the report filed in Vermont, Crayola told her that it had eliminated formaldehyde in 2025.
However, the company provided no documentation to verify the change, and disclosures in the multistate database continue to list formaldehyde as an active ingredient in Crayola products.
On its website, Crayola maintains that its entire product lineup is safe for children, pointing to third-party evaluations that found no toxic substances in quantities significant enough to harm humans.
Build-A-Bear appears to have removed mercury from all but one of its products, according to its 2025 filings in Vermont. Perez de Alejo recognized that as an improvement, and hoped that Defend Our Health’s calls to the company helped, but said its use in any product remains indefensible.
Enacted in 2008, Maine’s Kid-Safe Products Act protects children by identifying toxic chemicals in consumer products, requiring manufacturers to report their use and encouraging safer alternatives. Implementation rolled out gradually starting in 2011 as the state phased in reporting deadlines and sales bans for specific priority chemicals.
Defend Our Health’s safe kids campaign builds on its past work to track chemical risks in Maine.
After industrial contamination from forever chemicals, or PFAS, polluted local drinking water wells and devastated Maine farms, state lawmakers enacted groundbreaking bans on the use of PFAS-laden sludge fertilizer and PFAS in food packaging and consumer goods.
To help residents navigate store shelves following the consumer goods ban, Defend Our Health scoured the websites of hundreds of cookware manufacturers to compile a searchable directory that identifies thousands of noncompliant products.
The group applied that same strategy to children’s items, converting hard-to-navigate and often obscure regulatory spreadsheets into free searchable tools for parents and consumers.
Doctors say chemicals pose a higher risk to children because their bodies are still growing.
The American Academy of Pediatrics says formaldehyde can trigger severe allergies and increase cancer risks; phthalates can damage the hormone system and disrupt growth; and lead and mercury harm brain function and development.
Under Maine law, manufacturers must disclose any priority toxic additives within 30 days of starting to sell a product in the state. The Department of Environmental Protection confirmed neither Crayola or Build-A-Bear had filed a disclosure.
“If a manufacturer is selling a regulated children’s product that contains an intentionally added priority chemical in the state of Maine without filing a report, they are noncompliant with Maine law,” said Deputy Commissioner Dave Madore.
State officials can demand a certificate of compliance and halt sales of unreported products, he said. After being alerted by Defend Our Health, state officials contacted Crayola regarding those missing reports, he said. The agency did not know about Build-A-Bear’s missing reports.
Maine law permits the sale of products containing priority chemicals as long as manufacturers properly report them, but state regulators rely on those filings to construct legal cases for future bans, Madore said.
Prohibiting a chemical requires substantive evidence and legislative approval, Madore said.
The DEP is working on a way to make these chemical disclosures accessible to Maine residents.

title: Maine’s working waters are not dumping grounds for foreign corporations
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rock Alley is a Jonesport lobsterman and president of Protect Maine’s Fishing Heritage Foundation. Jason Faulkingham is a lobsterman from Beals.
We’ve spent our lives learning Maine’s waters.
If you work on the water, you learn to pay attention. You learn the tides, the bottom, the weather, how your gear moves. Families pass down their trade and their best spots from generation to generation.
For lobstermen and women, fishermen, clammers, wormers, shellfish growers and the businesses that depend on us, Maine’s bays are our workplaces. Clean water is not an abstract idea or slogan. It is the difference between making a living or losing one, and between a thriving community or a collapsing one.
That is why lawmakers and regulators should be paying close attention to the Conservation Law Foundation’s (CLF) lawsuit against Cooke Aquaculture.
A federal court in Maine recently allowed most of CLF’s Clean Water Act claims against Cooke to move forward. The court has not decided whether Cooke violated the law, but it has allowed allegations involving pollution, monitoring and reporting at Cooke’s open-net salmon farms to proceed.
CLF alleges that Cooke’s operations have discharged waste, uneaten feed, dead fish and other pollutants into surrounding waters and onto the seafloor. That matters to anyone whose livelihood depends on a healthy marine ecosystem. If pollution harms the bottom, it can affect the habitat and food sources that lobster and other fisheries depend on.
Outside the courtroom, this case raises a basic question for Maine: Who should carry the risk when a private corporation is given access to a public resource?
Industrial salmon farming is often sold as progress. We are told it means more seafood production, more efficiency and more jobs. I understand why those promises can sound appealing, especially in rural coastal communities like ours where every economic opportunity feels precious. Nobody who works on the water is against jobs. And Cooke employees are not the opposition.
Cooke is a multinational company operating in Maine’s communal waters, and the communities, not Cooke, pay the cost of any harms. A state lease may give a company permission to operate in a particular place, but that should not equate to Maine communities accepting pollution, escaped farm fish, weak monitoring or limited transparency as the cost of doing business.
The corporation may be headquartered elsewhere, but the environmental and economic consequences stay here. Mainers deserve that private industrial infrastructure have meaningful accountability to the people already working there.
We have seen this pattern before in other parts of the food system. Industrial production gets promoted as efficient and inevitable. Then operations consolidate, decision-making moves farther away from local communities and the costs are pushed onto the people who live nearby. Farmers, workers, rural towns and ecosystems are left to absorb the consequences while corporations keep expanding.
Lawmakers and regulators have an opportunity to keep that exact pattern from playing out on Maine’s coast.
Before leases are renewed or industrial salmon farming expands, we call on the commissioner of the Department of Marine Resources and the next governor and Maine Legislature to enforce stronger accountability, transparency and public input.
The burden should not fall on coastal residents to prove harm after the fact. Companies operating in public waters should face strong monitoring, clear reporting and real enforcement from the start, with that information easily accessible so communities can see what is being discharged, what regulators are tracking and how they are responding.
Accountability is not anti-business. It is the basic expectation that any company profiting from Maine’s waters should protect the resources and communities that make that business possible.
Protections for our waters only matter if they are enforced. Public hearings only matter if the voices of people most affected carry real weight. Oversight only matters if it is strong enough to prevent harm before it is too late.
The court’s decision to allow most of CLF’s claims to move forward should be a wake-up call. Our waters should not be treated like dumping grounds. Nor should permission to operate there be mistaken for ownership of a resource that belongs to all of us.
If a corporation wants access to Maine’s working waters, it should meet the highest standard, not the lowest one. That’s why CLF’s lawsuit matters. That’s why lawmakers must act now.
Maine’s working waters have sustained families for generations. Now is the time for our decisions to ensure they can support generations to come.

title: Rhamondre Stevenson gives Patriots boost before half in loss to Bears
text:
CHICAGO — Rhamondre Stevenson and New England were in a bad spot. Then the right call at the right time provided a momentary lift for the Patriots.
Stevenson scored an unlikely touchdown on the final play of the first half Thursday night against the Chicago Bears. Stevenson’s fifth career TD reception trimmed New England’s deficit to 20-14 at the break, but the Bears held off the Patriots for a 30-24 victory.
“We’ve been working on that play for a long time and came in handy today, executed on that play,” Stevenson said. “So felt good to do that.”
Chicago opened a 13-point lead when it scored on Luther Burden’s 24-yard reception with 14 seconds left in the opening half. Kyle Williams returned the ensuing kickoff 25 yards to the New England 34.
Drake Maye then fired an 18-yard pass to A.J. Brown, and the Patriots (4-3) used their second timeout with 3 seconds to go.
On the next play, Stevenson slipped out of the backfield and Maye lobbed the ball over the head of Bears safety Cam Lewis. Stevenson ran away from Lewis and got a downfield block from DeMario Douglas before cutting past Bears cornerback Jaylon Johnson on his way to the end zone.
“I feel like it brought us some momentum, but obviously not enough,” Stevenson said. “We didn’t come out with the win.”
Stevenson’s 48-yard reception moved New England’s win probability from 10.2% to 24.5%, according to Next Gen Stats. The running back covered a total distance of 68.18 yards on the play, and he had a 4.3% chance of scoring.
“I think we could have rallied to the ball there and gotten him down,” Chicago coach Ben Johnson said.
Stevenson finished with 93 yards on five receptions, but had just 22 yards on six carries. The Patriots rushed for 70 yards on 17 attempts.
Any momentum that Stevenson generated for New England with his touchdown was erased by Chicago’s opening possession of the second half. The Bears (5-2) finished a nine-play, 72-yard drive with Caleb Williams’ 12-yard touchdown pass to Colston Loveland.
“We didn’t run the ball well enough,” Patriots coach Mike Vrabel said. “But we moved it however we needed to move it and sometimes you are going to have days like that. I thought we’d be able to run it a little better. We didn’t, but then our best players were putting the ball in good spots most of the time and making good decisions. That’s how it goes, we’d have liked to run the ball a little bit better. But it didn’t happen tonight.”

title: The prison-based American Legion post helping incarcerated veterans rebuild lives
text:
ST. GABRIEL, La. (InvestigateTV) - American Legion Veterans Memorial Post 432 at Elayn Hunt Correctional Center was the first prison-based American Legion post in Louisiana, helping incarcerated veterans heal and rebuild their lives.
The program is recognized for a zero percent recidivism rate. No one from the post comes back to prison.
The members of the American Legion Veterans Memorial Post 432 maintain their connection to the military and find camaraderie among other inmates who are veterans.
Veterans reconnect with service identity
These organized meetings at Elayn Hunt started in 2018 and give veterans who are serving time a chance to reconnect to the part of themselves that chose to serve their country.
“I ended up going to Germany, to where I was transferred from Germany to Iraq. And so, I spent time in Desert Storm for about a year, a little over a year,” said Daren Kitchen, a Hunt inmate and veteran.
Kitchen has now been at Elayn Hunt for nine years; an experience he said has saved his life that was once consumed by drugs and crime.
“PTSD was never explained to me. So, it wasn’t until I was incarcerated here at Hunt that I went through my first PTSD class. And for all of those years, nobody...I didn’t think anybody understood... or I didn’t have anybody to relate to,” Kitchen said.
It’s a story Elayn Hunt program manager Dr. Lawton Searcy has heard time and time again on the prison grounds.
“I was astounded that we had some 60 to 70 incarcerated veterans here at Hunt. There were 3,500 within the state of Louisiana that were either incarcerated or on active parole,” Searcy said.
Veterans mentor younger inmates
Hunt inmate Frederick Reed joined the Army National Guard at 18 to pay for college. He’s now 55 and behind bars.
“I made a mistake and I ended up coming to prison. Things happened. But I’ve been able to transfer those skills that I learned through the military,” Reed said.
As part of its veteran’s program, Hunt has created a veteran’s dorm where former service members help to mentor young inmates trying to turn their lives around. Their art covers the walls, and military structure is on display.
“Incarcerated veterans are just, in a lot of ways, very different than what you may call a typical inmate. Because they do understand discipline. They do understand respect. But in suffering with PTSD, most... they’re trying to self-medicate,” Searcy said.
“I was trained for war, but I wasn’t trained for life after war. So, when I exited the military, I bounced all around. The drugs, the alcohol, the addictions,” Kitchen said.
Kitchen has found stability, partly due to the other veterans and Post 432.
American Legion supports incarcerated veterans
“We stand for the veterans that are still incarcerated. Because no veteran will ever be left behind again for any reason in the United States,” said Byron Comeaux, who is on the American Legion national executive committee.
His goal is to make sure that when veterans leave prison, they don’t come back.
“The minute you get out. The door lets you out and you’re right back in. This program has stopped that door from opening back up for the individuals because they have a sense of pride,” Comeaux said.
Warden Travis Day, who took over the facility plagued with problems earlier this year, sees the veterans as a valuable resource.
“I go home every night. These mentors are here 24 hours a day, seven days a week. They are in the dormitories. They are on the wall. They’re in the cafeteria,” Day said.
“We pretty much are doing what we... continuing the service that we have already started with our military service. We have just branched that over into helping those who are in our community,” Reed said.
“We know who’s being released from prison. And we can have an impact on who returns to our society, into our communities, around our families. So, I look forward to finding what’s the next thing that we can do to make this place better,” Kitchen said.
According to the American Legion, more than 107,000 veterans are currently incarcerated in the U.S. There are now more than 30 American Legion posts in correctional facilities.

title: What house is Maine’s oldest?
text:
Maine has one of the oldest housing stocks in the country, with hundreds of structures dating to pre-Revolutionary War times. But which home is actually the oldest?
It’s a little hard to pinpoint exactly when the first residence in Maine was built, State Historian Earle G. Shettleworth says. Countless historic homes have been lost to fires, Colonial warfare or age.
There are remains of a 17th- and 18th-century fishing village in Bristol, hints of 13,000-year-old Paleoamerican life in Rangeley’s western peaks, and an ever-present history of Indigenous tribes occupying Maine’s lands for thousands of years.
But possibly the oldest surviving English home in Maine is the McIntire Garrison House in York.
The dark two-story home sits in a salt marsh, unoccupied as it keeps watch over the York River, as it has for hundreds of years. But even its exact conception date has been debated.
Records show that the McIntire Garrison House was built sometime between 1707 and 1713, though the “legendary traditional date of construction is 1645,” according to an original nomination form that, in the 1960s, earned the house a spot on the National Register of Historic Places.
The Old York Historical Society’s Executive Director Catherine Duffy said locals may have incorrectly estimated the home’s age because dating technology wasn’t nearly as accurate as it is today.
In January 2024, researchers set out to get a final answer through a dendrochronological study, or the science of dating wooden artifacts through tree ring growth patterns. They took core samples from several of the home’s thick timbers and analyzed the rings under a microscope. The results showed that most of the timbers were felled primarily in the winter of 1712, with one piece dating to 1713. A plaque on the side of the home still reflects the nomination document.
The house remained in the McIntire family for more than 300 years until it was handed over to the historical society in 2024.
In the 1660s, Micum McIntire arrived in York County — then part of the Massachusetts Bay Colony — after being deported from England for supporting Scotland during the Third English Civil War, according to state records. He was sold as an indentured servant to work in New Hampshire sawmills, and one in South Berwick. He would stay there until 1668, when he found himself in York’s Scotland district.
It was there that he got his first land grant, married his wife, Dorothy, and had three sons, including John McIntire, who later built the home.
The name “Garrison” refers to a style of colonial architecture that originated in New England in the 17th-century. It’s both functional and aesthetic. The second floor juts out slightly over the ground floor, fortifying it against overhead attacks, and giving the home a sleek look.
The building was never officially used for anything other than a family home, though John’s granddaughter several generations later, Mary McIntire, set it up as a museum with classical furnishings and vignettes for visitors. A break-in in the 1960s or ’70s led the family to remove everything from the home.
It was used mostly for storage after a restoration in 1910, and the last McIntire moved out in the 1920s. But the family still holds yearly reunions in York, using their ancestral home as a centerpiece for the celebration, Duffy said.
“The fact that it’s remained in the same family line since the early 1700s is a pretty remarkable piece of history on its own,” Duffy said. Only a handful of other historic homes in the state can make that claim.
Duffy says the McIntire Garrison House is unsafe for visitors right now, but crews have been working on restoring it since 2025. They’re starting with a revamp of a cider house behind the residence, which dates to the early 1800s. Eventually, after lots of work in several phases, she hopes it’ll become an interactive glimpse into York’s history.
Archaeologist and Salem State University professor Dr. Emerson Baker says there are some other old houses that could one day dethrone the McIntire Garrison House, once they’re officially dated. Others have tried, like Bray House in Kittery which was proven to be close to 100 years younger than the owner claimed.
For now, the McIntire Garrison House remains the oldest English home in the state.

title: Meghan Markle’s father investigated for child pornography, reports say
text:
(Gray News) - Meghan Markle’s father Thomas Markle is allegedly being investigated for possession of child sexual abuse material, according to multiple reports.
The allegations against Markle Sr. were first reported Thursday by The Sun newspaper by his son.
Thomas Markle Jr. informed police that he allegedly found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images in boxes at his father’s home in the Philippines.
The Sun published a photo that it said showed Markle Jr. signing a sworn statement that he had submitted to police and quoted him as saying: “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.”
In a rare statement, Meghan said she was “deeply distressed” by her estranged father’s allegations, adding she was informed by police of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018, NBC News reported.
“The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” Meghan said. “My sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
Meghan said that she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.”
“I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed,” she said.
Markle Sr., 82, denied the reported allegations, calling them “sick lies.” He added they were “the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”
The Philippines’ Justice Department confirmed Friday that “the matter is under investigation” but otherwise declined to provide further details at this time.

title: Horses were a hit, part II
text:
For the second time this year, residents of St. Andrews Village Retirement Community got up close and personal with horses, this time on Friday, Oct. 23.
Back in mid-August, Ella Watts of Burke’s Island Farm in Boothbay, along with her father, Robbie, brought two horses to the Village where about 50 residents got to greet, brush and feed the Wattses’ horses, Jimmy and Marley. Ella also works at the Village and she and Resident Services Coordinator Sarah Hackler set up the visit.
On Friday, 11 residents took a field trip to Burke’s, located on Route 27, where Ella and Burke’s owner Amy Reny gave them a grand tour of the 12-year-old facility and the 16 horses being boarded there.
The hour-long visit under sunny but breezy conditions saw the residents view the paddocks, petting those horses who came to the fencing, and asking questions about the various horses on display. Ella and Amy then brought two horses – 26-year-old Ruby and Memphis – into the barn where the Village visitors got to meet them face-to-face.
The farm offers lessons for children and adults who compete at horse shows in the spring and summer. Ella also showed the visitors the riding facility – where it was decorated for the next day’s Halloween event. Ella, who works with mostly adults, explained that Amy, who works mainly with kids, has provided a safe and affordable place.
Many of the visitors related their experiences with horses when they were at a younger age to Ella, Amy and the newspaper.
As one of the three farm cats roamed around the barn, the visitors then walked down to the lower paddocks to meet Jimmy and Marley again. Amy also brought out for viewing the lone pony being boarded.
The nine women and two men from the Village, as well as their bus driver and Resident Services employee Kim Baxley, took many photos of the horses to relive their visit.

title: Cony football takes down rival Gardiner again
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
GARDINER — Another year, another win for the Cony Rams in Maine high school football’s oldest rivalry.
Cony closed out the regular season by defeating Gardiner 49-14 in a cross-class showdown Friday at Hoch Field. The win clinched the No. 2 seed in Class B North for the defending regional champion Rams and is Cony’s eighth consecutive victory in the rivalry.
HOW IT HAPPENED
• Anderson Noyes gashed Gardiner early. In his second game back for Cony (7-1) after suffering a leg injury in the preseason, the senior running back rushed for 112 yards and three touchdowns in the first half.
“It feels good running out there,” said Noyes, who ran for 109 yards and two scores in his return last week against Brunswick. “I’m glad to be back, and I’m just really happy for this team and the way they’ve been playing. I’m super proud of the guys.”
• Cony’s defense bent at times, but it didn’t break. You wouldn’t have expected a 35-point game given the total yardage — the Rams only outgained the Tigers 385-322. Yet when Cony needed big plays, it repeatedly made them to halt the home team’s drives.
On the first drive, Gardiner (3-5) drove to the red zone but came away empty as the Rams forced a missed field goal. Then, when the Tigers had first-and-5 from the Cony 25 midway through the second quarter, the Rams got a sack and tackled Justin Doody in the backfield. Davis Noyes then returned an interception for a score in the third quarter.
“We knew (Doody) was going to get the football with (Chase) McGrane still out — he’s the focal point of their offense, and he’s a really good runner,” said Cony coach B.L. Lippert. “We’ve got some pretty good players on defense, but they converted some third-and-shorts and fourth-and-shorts. When they got in the red zone, we did a better job of keeping them out.”
• The Rams didn’t throw the ball much, but their passing game was effective when it needed to be. Junior quarterback Drew Lindquist threw only one incompletion and had two touchdown passes in the third quarter, one a 68-yarder that hit Landen Perry in perfect stride to put Cony up 34-7.
WHAT IT MEANS
• Cony, which has not lost to Gardiner since 2017, continues its dominance of the rivalry. The Rams lead the all-time series 80-58-10. They will be the No. 2 seed in Class B North after Lawrence wrapped up an unbeaten regular season and the top spot in the region with a 60-6 victory over Messalonskee on Friday.
• Gardiner has lost four straight games after starting the season 3-1. The Tigers have had to reinvent their offense after losing McGrane, one of the state’s best tight ends, to a hand injury, and while the score certainly wasn’t what Gardiner hoped for Friday, coach Pat Munzing felt his team further established its post-McGrane identity.
“That’s what we’ve been kind of scouting for the past few weeks, to kind of figure out what works, and I think we’ve kind of found it,” Munzing said. “Coming into that Power-I and running some Wing-T stuff back-and-forth and being able to spread it right back out again, it gives teams an awful lot to prepare for.”
UNSUNG HERO
Cony’s Kingston Cox. Noyes is back in the RB1 role for Cony, but don’t forget about Cox, who shined early in the year in Noyes’ absence and bruised his way for some big runs Friday. He was also key to the Rams’ performance on defense.
NOTABLE QUOTABLES
• “We could have taken a few more shots — we liked some of the matchups out there — but when you play two high safeties, it opens up the box a little more for the run game. Anderson, Davis and Kingston ran really well, so we just kept feeding those guys.” — B.L. Lippert
• “(Lindquist’s touchdown pass to me) was right in the bread basket. That was great; I couldn’t have asked for better. … Drew has been working really hard in practice and doing great. When I get open, he finds me.” — Landen Perry
STAT LEADERS
• Cony: Anderson Noyes (14 carries, 131 yards, three touchdowns), Drew Lindquist (8 of 9, 159 passing yards, two touchdowns), Landen Perry (four catches, 131 yards, touchdown), Kingston Cox (nine carries, 79 yards)
• Gardiner: Justin Doody (25 carries, 198 yards, touchdown; 52-yard touchdown pass); Isaac Marquis (three catches, 92 yards, touchdown)
UP NEXT
• Cony: Bye to Class B North semifinals
• Gardiner: vs. Greely (7-1), 7 p.m. next Friday

title: New vaccine shown to cut melanoma risk

The vaccine is combined with the approved drug Keytruda.

title: Halloween Is The Deadliest Day For Child Pedestrians. Clear Walkways, Light Up Porches, And Ensure Costumes Don't Block Vision Or Movement
text:
Over 160 million folks go trick-or-treating each year in the US, and while Maine currently ranks as the 4th safest state in the nation for Halloween festivities, there are still some extra measures you can take to keep us at the top of that list this year.
Read More: Halloween Events In Orono Bring Trick-or-treating And Adult Fun
Second to opening presents on Christmas morning, kids LOVE to trick-or-treat, and seem to abandon all sense for that quest for candy. So it's up to the grownups in their lives to follow some simple rules, to ensure they make it home safe to enjoy all their holiday loot!
Here are 5 things to keep in mind as you head out the door with your kids this Halloween.
1.) Think Simplicity and Visibility when it comes to Halloween costumes.
When you're helping your kiddo pick the perfect pirate or princess costume, healthychildren.org says you should make sure the outfit fits your child well and doesn't keep them from seeing or being seen.
Halloween is the deadliest day for child pedestrians, so making sure your kids know the rules of the road, and can see and be seen by motorists is of the utmost importance on this day.
Reflective or light up clothing is best. And make sure there aren't any sharp accessories (like swords) that would injure someone.
2.) Choose your treats wisely.
While we may remember a time where folks handed out homemade fudge and popcorn balls on Halloween, people have made the migration towards individually wrapped candies, and with good reason.
Those candies often have ingredients on their wrappers, which is helpful for parents who have kids with food allergies or medical conditions like diabetes. (More on that in just a bit!)
It's also easier for helping kids to portion out their candy if it's in little fun-size helpings.
3.) Prepare the way for trick-or-treaters to visit.
Before those little ghosts and goblins make their way to your house to get those goodies, it's a really good idea for you to take a walk around your property to ensure that they have a safe path to travel. According to Mike Holmes of the Holmes Builder Network, there are some key things you'll want to keep an eye on.
"Clear leaves, hoses, toys and other tripping hazards from walkways. Check your driveway, sidewalks and steps for cracks or uneven surfaces and make sure stairs, decks, porches and handrails are secure. Turn on exterior and pathway lighting, replace burned-out exterior bulbs and use battery-operated lights instead of candles in pumpkins. Keep decorations away from stairs and walking paths."
"Use only outdoor-rated electrical decorations and extension cords outdoors, plug outdoor decorations into GFCI-protected receptacles, and keep extension cords out of driveways and walkways. Check electrical decorations for damaged cords or plugs."
Holmes also recommends making sure all the exits and doorways are clear. And don't forget to restrain pets so they don't feel anxious and try to jump on or bite your guests.
4.) Know where you're going and stay on a path.
If you can accompany your child around, that's the best.
But if they are old enough to go door-to-door by themselves, there are some things you want to make sure your kids know about and bring with them.
First, taking flashlights along is a must.
Second, stick to houses you're familiar with.
Third, make sure your children are familiar with traffic laws, and are paying attention to their surroundings and the road instead of electronics while they're out.
If you can go with a big group, there is a certain safety in numbers, too.
5.) Check all the candy BEFORE you eat it.
This can be one of the hardest parts of trick-or-treating; patience.
Law enforcement agencies also remind folks to check all the collected candy before letting kids eat it.
According to childrens.com/health, there 5 main reasons why you should absolutely inspect candy before kids consume it.
1.) Food Allergies: A lot of candies contain peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, wheat, and soy, that could all trigger something in the body of child with food allergies.
2.) Choking Hazards: Things like the dreaded gobstoppers, hard candies, gum, nuts, and small toys can easily block a young child's airway. Little kiddos (under 5) shouldn't really eat these, so you can throw those right out.
3.) Damaged or Tampered Packaging: If there are pinholes, tears, loose seals, or unusual colors and smells, chuck that stuff. It's not worth the risk.
4.) Cannabis and THC Edibles: It's become more of an issue nowadays that some package-free or lookalike products may contain THC or other intoxicating substances that mimic regular commercial sweets. As much as you don't want your kid to accidentally trip and fall down, you probably want avoid them accidentally tripping on a pot-laced goodie as well.
5.) Homemade Treats: Unwrapped or homemade goods (like baked treats) should generally be thrown away unless they come from a known, trusted source who prepared them.
A good rule of thumb is that anything that's not wrapped by the factory or isn't sealed should be tossed.
No candy bar or lollipop is ever worth taking a risk with a child's health or well-being. And if you think it's going to be too hard for your kiddo to resist, you could always back a small baggie of pre-checked candies for them to snack on on the way!
Read More: Touch-A-Truck & Treat Comes to Bangor’s Cross Insurance Center
Good luck out there, and we hope you have a safe and happy Halloween!

title: Maine State Museum’s grand reopening kicks off Saturday
text:
AUGUSTA — The Maine State Museum will host its first phase Grand Reopening Celebration on Saturday, Oct. 24. Doors will open at 10 a.m. with Maine humorist Gary Crocker, a welcome by Museum Director Bernard Fishman and a ribbon-cutting ceremony with the Kennebec Valley Chamber of Commerce. The ribbon cutting will be followed by a full day of fanfare and activities including vendors and musical acts, the L.L. Bean Bootmobile and special guests.
After a multi-year closure due to major renovations in its home in Maine’s Cultural Building, the museum will open its main and fourth floors to the public with new educational and exhibit spaces: “Beyond the Postcard: Stories of the Maine Experience”, “Vector: A Whale’s Life in the Gulf of Maine” and the Lunder Education Center. The fourth floor will also reopen with the new exhibit, “Maine Quilts: 250 Years of Comfort & Community”, and the popular returning exhibit, “At Home in Maine”, which will include new objects and upgrades. Beloved exhibits “Made in Maine” and “12,000 Years in Maine” will be returning in future phases.
“This is really a monumental time in our 190-year history,” Fishman said. “For the first time in decades, we were able to dig deep into our collections to show objects that have never been on display and make long-dreamt of exhibits and spaces become reality. Our new 4,130-square-foot whale gallery boasts the only display in the world of two humpback whales of this size and age, and our new Lunder Education Center is the first purpose-built education space for our visitors. We hope that our approach of infusing new technologies with museum collections and new stories will resonate with visitors in new ways.”
Fishman invites the public to come and see the changes and revisit the familiar exhibits. And to encourage visitors, Fishman announced, “We want to make the museum as accessible as possible by offering free admission through the end of the year.”
The museum will be open from 10 a.m. through 4 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 24. Regular museum hours are Tuesdays through Sundays, 10 a.m. through 4 p.m., closed on Mondays and state holidays. For more information and ways to support the museum visit MaineStateMuseum.org.

President Donald Trump is traveling to southwest Florida to rally supporters ahead of the midterm elections, with tight races in the state potentially influencing the balance of power.
President Donald Trump is visiting southwest Florida today to rally supporters as the midterm elections approach, with competitive races in the state drawing national attention.
Florida's gubernatorial race is extremely competitive, and Democrats believe they may have a chance to win the governor's seat for the first time in nearly 30 years. The state's Senate race is also tightening, according to an Associated Press analysis.
Many states expected to decide control of the Senate are seeing a significant boost in early voting. However, early voting is not up everywhere. In Iowa, where Trump traveled on Thursday, early voting is down about 6% compared to the same period four years ago.
During Trump's remarks in Iowa Thursday, Trump addressed farmers, focusing on the impact of tariffs, rising diesel prices, and fertilizer costs on the agricultural economy. He assured supporters that costs would decrease soon.
"We're going to have Iran finished very soon one way or the other," Trump said. "It's almost insignificant to me which way, but one way or the other, it's going to be done very soon, and your gasoline prices and your oil is going to come tumbling down."
Today, AAA reports that the average price for a gallon of regular gas is $4.29, which is about a 44% increase compared to when the war in Iran began at the end of February.
The president has a busy weekend ahead, with plans to travel to Georgia on Saturday and Michigan on Sunday to energize voters before they head to the polls next month.
