title: Bigfoot in Maine? Still No Proof in the Age of Smartphones
text:
Bigfoot in Maine? We’re Still Looking For Proof in The Age of Smartphones
We can send people to space, put tiny computers in our pockets, and get a notification when our macha is two minutes away.
But somehow, in 2026, we still don't have ANY undeniable proof that Bigfoot exists.
And here's the plot twist: Maine might be one of the best places to look for him.
A new 2026 study by Canada Sports Betting ranked U.S. states and Canadian provinces based on historical Bigfoot reports per 100,000 residents, forest coverage, and climate conditions.
The result? Maine landed among America's top 10 states for a potential Bigfoot sighting.
Which honestly tracks.
We have approximately a million acres of woods where something could be lurking, and half the time we're already blaming mysterious noises on something living in the trees.
But seriously, how have we not figured this out yet?
Come on, we have trail cameras, flocks, drones, satellite imagery, and people filming themselves eating chicken nuggets in their cars in 4K.
Yet Bigfoot apparently remains committed to keeping a low profile.
To be clear, these rankings are based on reported sightings and environmental factors, not scientific proof that Bigfoot exists.
Guys, no one's handed over a verified Sasquatch driver's license or a DNA sample that settles the debate.
Still, Maine's vast forests and remote stretches certainly leave room for the imagination.
So, if you're hiking, camping, or driving down a dark, wooded Maine road and spot something unusually tall and hairy crossing the street, maybe don't immediately assume it's a moose having a rough hair day.
Could Bigfoot be out there? We don't know. But if he is, Maine seems like a pretty good place to avoid people.
And honestly? Same, Bigfoot. Same.

title: Maine heating fuel prices rise to new record
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine heating fuel prices have surged to a record high, with the statewide average reaching $6.04 per gallon on Oct. 19 — up 83% from a year earlier, according to the latest weekly barometer.
The Maine Department of Energy Resources estimates that Maine residents will pay nearly $750 more to fill a 275-gallon oil tank than a year ago, before the Iran conflict that started this past February.
The previous record high for heating oil in Maine was set last month at $6.02 per gallon.
Maine uses more residential heating oil per capita than any other U.S. state and consumes significantly more per capita than other New England states.
More than 50% of Maine households rely on fuel oil for their primary heat source, according to the latest figures from the U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey.
That number has declined steadily since 2010, when usage was above 70%.
Propane use by Maine households has more than doubled since 2010, reaching 16% in 2024.
Electricity usage has been steadily climbing over the same period, from a low of just over 5% to 13.5% as more households, particularly those in new construction, have installed heat pumps.
Heating assistance measures
Gov. Janet Mills has called on Congress to increase heating assistance. In a letter to Maine’s congressional delegation, Mills said that current federal funding for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program is insufficient to meet the increased need caused by sharply higher home heating costs.
Earlier this week, the U.S. Department of Energy announced a rare release of oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve. The 315,000-barrel supply will be shared among the New England states and New York; it’s not yet clear how much will come to Maine.
“I encourage Maine people to stay informed of current prices, review incentive options through Efficiency Maine, and to contact their Community Action Agency if they need immediate relief,” said Celina Cunningham, acting commissioner of the Maine Department of Energy Resources.
Financial aid for heating is available through the Home Energy Assistance Program, administered by MaineHousing. Additionally, the Energy Crisis Intervention Program, which assists low-income households experiencing an urgent energy-related crisis, will open on Nov. 1.
Cunningham suggested that switching from oil or kerosene to energy-efficient heat pumps can save Maine households thousands of dollars annually, and encouraged homeowners to explore incentives available through Efficiency Maine.
The Department of Energy Resources offers a winter heating guide on its website. The guide includes weatherization tips and a summary of energy efficiency and home heating programs available through MaineHousing, Efficiency Maine, Community Action Agencies and other partners.

title: Inflation at the movies: Runtimes are longer, from 'The Odyssey' to 'You Can See Everything'
text:
Inflation at the movies: Runtimes are longer, from 'The Odyssey' to 'You Can See Everything'
Unfortunately for your bladder, movies are getting longer
Inflation at the movies: Runtimes are longer, from 'The Odyssey' to 'You Can See Everything'
Unfortunately for your bladder, movies are getting longer
Your bladder isn't lying. Movies are getting longer.
All kinds of films, from big-budget spectacles to art house dramas, are stretching their runtimes. It's an old saying that a short movie can feel long and a long movie can feel short. But data, not just bathroom runs, shows that runtime inflation is real at the movies.
Related video above: The death of the drive-in movie theater
After analyzing 36,431 movies released theatrically from 1980 to 2025, researcher Stephen Follows found that the average length of a wide-release movie has grown from 106 to 114 minutes.
For most who frequent the movie theater, this isn't surprising. It's become a regular feature of the pre-release anticipation of a movie: How long is it? When the official runtime of "The Odyssey" was released (173 minutes), for some it was as if Christopher Nolan had laid down a challenge as intimidating as the Cyclops.
But there's little evidence that long runtimes are dissuading moviegoers. They may even be a draw. "The Odyssey" is the second-highest-grossing movie of the year, with $1.8 billion in ticket sales, and the front-runner for best picture at the Oscars.
Still, the shift has changed the whole ecosystem around movies. Ahead of last year's Venice Film Festival, festival boss Alberto Barbera noted that movies running 2 hours and 15 minutes or 2 hours and 30 minutes had become "the new international standard."
This, Barbera said, can be a programming annoyance as well as a knock on an otherwise good film. The festival selection committee, he said, often sees films that would have benefited from being 10-20 minutes shorter.
This year, three films viewed as top Oscar contenders — "The Odyssey," "La Bola Negra" (159 minutes) and "You Can See Everything" (174 minutes) — all easily run more than 2 ½ hours. It's far from just the awards movies, though. The upcoming "Hunger Games" movie, "Sunrise on the Reaping," is 158 minutes long, a new high for the franchise. Any way you cut it, that's a lot of reaping.
The advent of streaming has led the movies to seek larger screens and longer runtimes. When the flat-screen enticements at home are so great, the movies strive to be bona fide events to get people to come out. Bigger is better, or so the thinking goes.
Clocking the 'Doomsday' runtime
No one knows this better than Joe and Anthony Russo, stewards of the "Avengers" movies including the upcoming "Avengers: Doomsday."
"The moviegoing experience is evolving," Joe Russo said in a recent interview. "Eventized cinema seems to be the draw to get people out of their homes. That can be premium storytelling, premium moviegoing experience, and length can certainly contribute to the feeling of an experience. In a lot of ways, it's the feeling of getting your money's worth."
"Doomsday" doesn't yet have an announced runtime, though that hasn't stopped a sizable cottage industry of coverage committed to pinning down its length. The Russos expect "Doomsday" to be closer to two and a half hours, slimmed down from the three-hour-long "Endgame" and relatively slender given that it contains a sizable portion of the Marvel Cinematic Universe.
For Russo, bigger is good, but not automatically better.
"It doesn't mean that you can't pack a punch in a shorter runtime," Russo said. "It's whatever the story requires. It's about squeezing the story into a diamond, and if that diamond ends up three-and-a-half hours, sure. If it ends up two-and-a-half hours, sure."
For some filmmakers, slowing down is important
The Japanese filmmaker Ryusuke Hamaguchi makes movies that are almost the diametric opposite of a superhero film, yet he has arrived at similar runtimes.
Hamaguchi's films are resolutely human-scaled; they move with the rhythm of life. His 2021 film "Drive My Car," the first Japanese film nominated for Best Picture, ran just under three hours. His movies are patient powerhouses that reject conventional movie plotting.
"Storytelling as an action, you're sort of forcing certain things to happen to make an interesting film," Hamaguchi said. "Oftentimes, when I watch other films, they say this is how it is and continue to push the plot forward. I find that to be uncomfortable."
Hamaguchi was speaking in an interview shortly after the Cannes Film Festival premiere of his latest film, "All of a Sudden." Contrary to its title, it runs 197 minutes. But the film, which Neon will release Nov. 25, is one of the gentlest and most enlightening movies of the year. Fittingly, it's about time.
Virginie Efira stars as the director of a Paris nursing home where she's introducing a more humane but time-consuming care technique called Humanitude. She encounters resistance from some staff but finds life improves for both the facility's patients and its employees.
For Hamaguchi, that message applies as much to movies as it does elder care.
"My own values and thoughts around filmmaking come into the film," he said. "I first learned about Humanitude in a different context and I decided to work within the field of caregiving. But when I started to research about it, I realized there were so many shared issues in common with the film industry."
The 90-minute movie may be nearly obsolete, but it's not gone
Not everyone shares the feeling that movies need to push closer to the three-hour mark. Polish filmmaker Paweł Pawlikowski has made three acclaimed films in a row, all 90 minutes or less. He's not necessarily against longer-running movies, but he sets out to distill his films down to their most potent elements.
"I love 'Lawrence of Arabia.' It felt proportionate to the film and the landscape," says Pawlikowski of David Lean's 327-minute 1962 epic. "But nowadays there are films where it's just too much. There are five endings and it's just showing off. I won't mention names but there are some really great directors doing it, too."
Pawlikowski's latest, "Fatherland," is a neat 82 minutes. Yet despite, or possibly because of its concision, "Fatherland" is an uncommonly rich experience, starring Hanns Zischler as the German Nobel Prize-winning novelist Thomas Mann and Sandra Hüller his daughter, Erika. They're on a road trip through Germany in the aftermath of World War II.
Pawlikowski is keenly aware that he's swimming against the long-movie current.
"It feels a bit controversial what I'm doing," Pawlikowski says, chuckling. "I'm quite aware that it's provocative to be so stripped down. I'm all into simplifying life, anyways. Stick to your friends. Like what you like. Try to be honest. If you can do that in film, or any kind of art form, it helps."

title: Portland aims to revamp century-old playground on Eastern Prom
text:
The city of Portland and the Portland Parks Conservancy are seeking community feedback as city officials work to modernize one of Portland’s oldest and most heavily used playgrounds.
Will’s Playground, located on the Eastern Promenade, was built in 1917, with regular updates through 2004. Its equipment, including swings that are more than 50 years old, is ready for an overhaul to meet modern standards of safety, accessibility and fun, according to a news release.
Following city funding awarded in 2025 to Portland’s Parks, Recreation and Facilities Department, a comprehensive redesign is underway.
“This site has been home to a playground for over 100 years, and we are excited to build a new playground here that will be a destination for all Portland families,” said Ethan Hipple, director of the Parks, Recreation and Facilities Department.
“The iconic site high on the bluffs of the Eastern Promenade, with panoramic views of the ocean and the islands, provides a uniquely Portland canvas for creating a playground beloved by children of all ages,” he added.
Updated equipment
Community members are invited to support this effort by participating in community engagement sessions. The first one is scheduled for Monday, Oct. 26, from 5 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. inside Merrill Auditorium’s rehearsal hall.
The renovation aims to create a landmark play area. Goals for the design include updated and site-specific equipment to replace aging structures; improved access and inclusivity; all-ages engagement by creating play spaces that appeal to and accommodate a wide range of age groups; protecting existing trees and leveraging scenic views; and year-round usability.
Playground specialists
The project is led by Reading, Mass., landscape architecture and engineering firm Weston & Sampson, with specialists in playground design, safety and accessibility, public engagement and civil engineering.
A working group includes representatives from Portland Public Schools, Friends of Eastern Promenade, Children’s Museum & Theatre of Maine, Trust for Public Land, Munjoy Hill Neighborhood Organization, TEMPOart, Portland Parks Commission, Natural Helpers, Boys and Girls Club and Portland Housing Authority.
Renovation timeline
The planned renovation will span several phases.
Community engagement, site assessment and initial concept and schematic design will run through this winter. Design development, permitting, construction documentation and fundraising will be conducted in 2027.
If funding is secured, contractor bidding and the contract award could happen in the winter of 2027 or spring 2028, with construction starting in 2028.

title: How Often Does It Actually Snow in Maine on Halloween?
text:
How Often Does It Actually Snow in Maine on Halloween?
If you grew up in Maine, wearing your Halloween costume over your winter clothes may not have felt uncommon.
👇 KEEP READING: Mainers Weigh In on What to Do With Leftover Halloween Candy 👇
However, historical weather records show that measurable Halloween snowfall is relatively uncommon in Maine and varies significantly by location.
The Northeast Regional Climate Center’s 2024 review found measurable snow on about 6% of Halloweens in Caribou.
Bangor and Portland had no measurable Halloween snowfall in the records covered by that review.
The National Weather Service’s “Halloween Weather over the Years” lists Bangor’s Halloween snowfall record as a trace, meaning too little to measure, compared with 7.6 inches in Caribou in 1959.
Measurable snowfall means enough snow fell to be recorded, while a trace means only a tiny amount fell, so a Halloween without measurable snow could still have included a few flakes.
Caribou’s northern location and colder fall climate also make Halloween snow more plausible there than in much of southern Maine.
Snow falling on Halloween differs from snow already on the ground, so snowfall totals alone don't tell us whether trick-or-treaters encountered snow left by an earlier storm.
The years covered by each location’s records also matter, because the findings describe the period reviewed rather than every Halloween in Maine’s history.
And there you have it! Halloween in Maine can certainly feel wintry, but the snowfall history looks very different depending on where you are in the state.

title: Halloween Is The Deadliest Day For Child Pedestrians. Clear Walkways, Light Up Porches, And Ensure Costumes Don't Block Vision Or Movement
text:
Over 160 million folks go trick-or-treating each year in the US, and while Maine currently ranks as the 4th safest state in the nation for Halloween festivities, there are still some extra measures you can take to keep us at the top of that list this year.
Read More: Halloween Events In Orono Bring Trick-or-treating And Adult Fun
Second to opening presents on Christmas morning, kids LOVE to trick-or-treat, and seem to abandon all sense for that quest for candy. So it's up to the grownups in their lives to follow some simple rules, to ensure they make it home safe to enjoy all their holiday loot!
Here are 5 things to keep in mind as you head out the door with your kids this Halloween.
1.) Think Simplicity and Visibility when it comes to Halloween costumes.
When you're helping your kiddo pick the perfect pirate or princess costume, healthychildren.org says you should make sure the outfit fits your child well and doesn't keep them from seeing or being seen.
Halloween is the deadliest day for child pedestrians, so making sure your kids know the rules of the road, and can see and be seen by motorists is of the utmost importance on this day.
Reflective or light up clothing is best. And make sure there aren't any sharp accessories (like swords) that would injure someone.
2.) Choose your treats wisely.
While we may remember a time where folks handed out homemade fudge and popcorn balls on Halloween, people have made the migration towards individually wrapped candies, and with good reason.
Those candies often have ingredients on their wrappers, which is helpful for parents who have kids with food allergies or medical conditions like diabetes. (More on that in just a bit!)
It's also easier for helping kids to portion out their candy if it's in little fun-size helpings.
3.) Prepare the way for trick-or-treaters to visit.
Before those little ghosts and goblins make their way to your house to get those goodies, it's a really good idea for you to take a walk around your property to ensure that they have a safe path to travel. According to Mike Holmes of the Holmes Builder Network, there are some key things you'll want to keep an eye on.
"Clear leaves, hoses, toys and other tripping hazards from walkways. Check your driveway, sidewalks and steps for cracks or uneven surfaces and make sure stairs, decks, porches and handrails are secure. Turn on exterior and pathway lighting, replace burned-out exterior bulbs and use battery-operated lights instead of candles in pumpkins. Keep decorations away from stairs and walking paths."
"Use only outdoor-rated electrical decorations and extension cords outdoors, plug outdoor decorations into GFCI-protected receptacles, and keep extension cords out of driveways and walkways. Check electrical decorations for damaged cords or plugs."
Holmes also recommends making sure all the exits and doorways are clear. And don't forget to restrain pets so they don't feel anxious and try to jump on or bite your guests.
4.) Know where you're going and stay on a path.
If you can accompany your child around, that's the best.
But if they are old enough to go door-to-door by themselves, there are some things you want to make sure your kids know about and bring with them.
First, taking flashlights along is a must.
Second, stick to houses you're familiar with.
Third, make sure your children are familiar with traffic laws, and are paying attention to their surroundings and the road instead of electronics while they're out.
If you can go with a big group, there is a certain safety in numbers, too.
5.) Check all the candy BEFORE you eat it.
This can be one of the hardest parts of trick-or-treating; patience.
Law enforcement agencies also remind folks to check all the collected candy before letting kids eat it.
According to childrens.com/health, there 5 main reasons why you should absolutely inspect candy before kids consume it.
1.) Food Allergies: A lot of candies contain peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, wheat, and soy, that could all trigger something in the body of child with food allergies.
2.) Choking Hazards: Things like the dreaded gobstoppers, hard candies, gum, nuts, and small toys can easily block a young child's airway. Little kiddos (under 5) shouldn't really eat these, so you can throw those right out.
3.) Damaged or Tampered Packaging: If there are pinholes, tears, loose seals, or unusual colors and smells, chuck that stuff. It's not worth the risk.
4.) Cannabis and THC Edibles: It's become more of an issue nowadays that some package-free or lookalike products may contain THC or other intoxicating substances that mimic regular commercial sweets. As much as you don't want your kid to accidentally trip and fall down, you probably want avoid them accidentally tripping on a pot-laced goodie as well.
5.) Homemade Treats: Unwrapped or homemade goods (like baked treats) should generally be thrown away unless they come from a known, trusted source who prepared them.
A good rule of thumb is that anything that's not wrapped by the factory or isn't sealed should be tossed.
No candy bar or lollipop is ever worth taking a risk with a child's health or well-being. And if you think it's going to be too hard for your kiddo to resist, you could always back a small baggie of pre-checked candies for them to snack on on the way!
Read More: Touch-A-Truck & Treat Comes to Bangor’s Cross Insurance Center
Good luck out there, and we hope you have a safe and happy Halloween!

title: Letter: Grocery store interaction showed Susan Collins’ integrity
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Recently, I was doing my grocery shopping when I noticed Sen. Susan Collins a few aisles over, doing hers. My first instinct was to leave her alone. I figured she must have people stopping her all the time with problems and requests, and she deserved a few quiet minutes like anyone else.
But I decided to walk over, introduce myself, and tell her I’m voting for her. I expected a quick handshake. Instead, we had a real conversation. She asked questions, she listened, and she was genuinely interested in what I had to say. Standing there in the middle of the store, it struck me how sincere I believe she is, and how much integrity she carries into every interaction.
Before we parted ways, she took down my name. The very next day, someone from her Senate office reached out to follow up with me. I was honestly amazed. That kind of care isn’t something you can fake.
That moment captured what I’ve always admired about Collins. I believe she is always working, always listening, and always delivering for Maine. I think she has never forgotten where she came from or the people who sent her to Washington and keep her there.
She has my vote, and I hope she has yours.
Shawn Spellman
Levant

title: Obituary: Irene M. Fenlason
text:
STARKS – Irene M. Fenlason, 77, a longtime resident of Starks, Maine, and recently of Portland, passed away peacefully on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026, at Gosnell Memorial Hospice in Scarborough. She found a place of peace after a struggle with a lingering illness, surrounded by the best wishes for her peace from her friends and family and capable assistance of her caretakers attending.
Irene was born in Waterville, Jan. 2, 1949, the daughter of Marion (Keast) and Lyle E. Fenlason. She grew up in North Anson and Skowhegan, attending public schools and graduating from Skowhegan High School in 1967. She then attended Colby College, graduating with a B.A. in English in 1971.
Shortly after graduating from college, and after a few years of itinerant waitressing, she went to work in the family business – Kennebec Auto Parts in Madison. For nearly 50 years she worked there as a clerk, manager and eventually the owner. She was extremely proud of her accomplishments and success in a “man’s” world. She also came to know many of the people and workers of Madison, Starks, and Anson and made her long term home in Starks as an independent person who had made her own way through life on her own terms.
Irene’s interests included pets – cats and dogs all her life and a horse of her own as a teenager – gardening, reading and collecting science fiction, stained glass making and participation in the affairs of her community, serving on the Starks planning board for several years. Like many of us, she also retained a strong affection for the works of Jane Austen – one of the many authors she studied in college.
Irene is survived by her brother, Bruce and his wife Judy Fenlason of Biddeford; a niece, Sara Fenlason and her wife Trisha Kirk of Minneapolis, Minn.; her special friends, neighbors and helpers Marc and Tracy Cowan of Starks; stepdaughter, Sandy Quimby Smith of Alabama; several cousins scattered over much of the eastern part of the country and memories of her successful life and career.
No services are planned at this time. Dennett, Craig & Pate Funeral Home, Saco are entrusted with her services.

title: 2 ex-FBI officials charged with making false statements about Hunter Biden’s laptop
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Two former FBI officials were charged Friday with lying to Congress about their involvement in investigating Hunter Biden’s laptop in the run-up to the 2020 presidential election, the latest in a series of splashy and politically charged actions the Justice Department has undertaken ahead of next month’s midterm contests.
Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, former leaders of a since-disbanded task force set up to counter foreign election interference, appeared in federal court in Washington, where their lawyers pressed for a speedy hearing to contest allegations their clients lied to lawmakers by saying that they did not participate in FBI investigations of Biden.
The prosecution, a rare Department of Justice criminal case against a former employee, revisits a tangled and peculiar saga that roiled the final weeks of the 2020 race. It also comes amid a broader, backward-looking effort by FBI Director Kash Patel, who before taking over the nation’s premier law enforcement agency was a harsh critic of it, to scrutinize high-profile episodes from the bureau’s recent past that for years have animated President Donald Trump’s conservative base.
Floris’ attorneys called her “a patriot” and said she has “served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years.”
“Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts,” her attorneys said in a statement. “It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election.”
Attorneys for Benavides accused the government of bringing “baseless criminal charges against him in a transparently political complaint.”
“This is another sad day for the Department of Justice,” his lawyers said in an emailed statement. “But now we are in court, and the truth will come out: Brad Benavides is a true patriot who devoted his career to protecting this country and its people. These charges are a disgrace.”
A criminal complaint comes just before the midterms
The case was filed less than two weeks before the Nov. 3 elections via criminal complaint, which means prosecutors have not yet presented the allegations to a grand jury for an indictment. The Justice Department has repeatedly struggled in high-profile cases to convince grand juries in the nation’s capital to return indictments.
During the former FBI employees’ court appearance, both defense attorneys and the judge noted the unusual move to charge the case through a complaint, which is more often used by prosecutors when they have an urgent need to take people into custody because, for example, they present a danger or a risk of flight.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui remarked that it is “rare that we have charges this old coming in this nature,” and over the objections of prosecutors who pushed for more time, set a preliminary hearing for next Tuesday, citing what he said was the “sword of Damocles” hanging over the defendants’ heads.
The laptop discovery created turmoil in 2020 election
The revelation of the laptop’s existence in October 2020 injected a thorny storyline in the race between Trump, the Republican incumbent, and Biden’s father, Joe Biden, Trump’s Democratic challenger who went on to win the race.
The laptop was publicized by the New York Post, which said it had obtained from Trump ally Rudy Giuliani a hard drive of a computer dropped off by Hunter Biden at a Wilmington, Delaware, repair shop about a year earlier.
The criminal complaint aims to build on longstanding congressional Republican complaints about the FBI’s handling of the laptop, including allegations that the bureau was not forthcoming to the public that the materials on it — including emails that showed discussions of the younger Biden’s foreign business dealings — were authentic and not the product of Russian disinformation.
The curious circumstances of the laptop’s discovery raised concerns among Democrats and former intelligence officials about the possibility of Russian involvement, particularly at a time when the Trump administration’s own intelligence community had assessed that Moscow that Russia was attempting to interfere in Trump’s favor in the election and as Giuliani had traveled abroad looking for dirt on the Bidens. Dozens of former U.S. intelligence officials signed a letter saying that the laptop bore the “classic earmarks of an Russian information operation.”
But Trump’s then-director of national intelligence, John Ratcliffe, said in a letter to Congress that there was no proof foreign actors had anything to do with the laptop. The FBI under then-Director Chris Wray subsequently endorsed that position.
Hunter Biden was charged with, and convicted of, gun and tax offenses during his father’s administration. Joe Biden pardoned him in his final weeks in office.
The case shines a light on an FBI task force on foreign intelligence
The complaint alleges that in their capacity as leaders of the Foreign Influence Task Force, Floris and Benavides were deeply engaged in the investigations into Hunter Biden, and that Biden was a recurring subject at FITF meetings.
Yet, the complaint says, both downplayed their firsthand knowledge of the laptop or involvement in investigations during 2023 testimony to lawmakers who were doing their own Biden investigation.
It accuses Benavides of making a false statement by saying he learned through Wikipedia that the FBI was in possession of the laptop, and says Floris falsely claimed to have had no knowledge of Hunter Biden having been the subject of discussions at FITF.
“Lying to Congress by senior FBI officials strikes at the heart of our system. No one is above the law,” Patel said.
The case brings renewed attention to the work of the task force, which was established in the first Trump administration to police influence campaigns staged by Russia and other nations aimed at sowing discord, undermining democracy and spreading disinformation. The task force became a magnet of congressional Republican criticism in part because of the Hunter Biden investigation and was disbanded in February 2025 by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi.
The Justice Department has made other splashy moves
As FBI director, Patel has presided over widespread firings of agents who were involved in investigations of Trump or who are perceived as being against the Republican administration’s agenda.
He has also focused attention on years-old investigations like the Hunter Biden one that occurred before he became director and that have been the subject of grievances and complaints by Trump allies.
The Justice Department historically looks to avoid public and overt investigative acts in the direct lead-up to an election that involve candidates or that risk influencing a political outcome. But officials in the last two weeks have made a series of bold moves in cases with political undertones, including a search of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s house in an immigration fraud investigation and a corruption indictment unsealed Thursday against powerful Democratic Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas.
Omar and Lucas are both Trump critics. Omar, who’s from Minnesota, has called the search of her Washington home an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” Lucas has said she won’t be intimidated or bullied by the federal government in its case against her and “will not back down.”

title: Mom who survived school shooting comforts son during school shooting in Oregon
text:
BEND, Ore. (CNN) - Parents in Bend are comforting their children after last week’s deadly shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School. One mother said she understands what her son experienced because she survived a school shooting herself.
Michelle, whose last name was withheld, said she found out about Thursday’s shooting when her fifth-grade son called and texted her from his Apple Watch, saying there was a shooter.
In the text message, Michelle told her son everything would be OK. She also told him about her own history of surviving a school shooting.
Michelle was a freshman at Granite Hills High School in El Cajon, California, when a gunman opened fire in 2001. Two teachers and three students were wounded.
Michelle said she was always nervous when she dropped her sons off at school, even before last Thursday’s shooting.

title: Lewiston to mark 3rd anniversary of mass shootings with weekend events
text:
LEWISTON, Maine (WMTW) - The Lewiston community will mark the third anniversary of the 2023 mass shootings this weekend with events honoring the victims, supporting survivors and remembering how the city came together in the aftermath.
The shootings on Oct. 25, 2023, killed 18 people and wounded 13 others at Just-In-Time Recreation and Schemengees Bar & Grille.
At the Maine Museum of Innovation, Learning and Labor, an ongoing exhibit preserves objects connected to the tragedy and the community’s response.
The exhibit includes the doors from Just-In-Time Recreation and a light fixture from Schemengees Bar & Grille that still bears bullet holes. It also features 3D-printed replicas of pumpkins that community members carved and left outside the bowling alley after the shootings.
“Unfortunately, October 25th, 2023 is a really important part of this community’s history now,” Maine MILL executive director Rachel Ferrante said. “And so we felt a responsibility to find a way to memorialize that.”
The museum’s memorial archive preserves objects and stories for future generations. The current exhibit, “Preserved,” is scheduled to remain on display through October 2027.
Other events are planned across Lewiston this weekend.
The third annual Lewiston Stronger Community Cornhole Tournament will take place Saturday, Oct. 24, at Just-In-Time Recreation. Two sessions are scheduled, from noon to 4 p.m. and from 5 to 11 p.m. Entry costs $20, with proceeds benefiting the Maine Resiliency Center.
A candlelight vigil hosted by the Maine Resiliency Center is scheduled for Sunday, Oct. 25, from 6 to 8 p.m. at Simard-Payne Memorial Park. Participants will gather at the park entrance before walking together to the Longley Bridge for the vigil.

title: Police reportedly assaulted by parents after ‘black magic’ reported in Charlotte neighborhood
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - Two parents were accused of assaulting police officers after the couple was reportedly engaging in “black magic rituals” at a house in North Carolina.
A criminal affidavit revealed the alleged incident happened on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at a home in east Charlotte.
The affidavit said Charlotte-Mecklenburg police were sent to the house after a concerned neighbor called 911. The document said the neighbor reported the parents were “performing black magic rituals,” “burning things,” and that there was “loud screaming.”
The neighbor also allegedly said the mother’s face was black and purple and she appeared to have been abused.
When police got to the neighborhood, they heard screaming and saw things being thrown inside the house.
Officers found both live and spent .22 rounds, broken items, and drops of blood on the front porch of the home.
As police walked toward the door, the affidavit said “the front door swung open,” and the two parents and four kids were staring out at them. The kids were aged 14, 11, 5, and 3 years old, according to the document.
What police found inside
Once inside the house, officers reportedly found the home in “complete disarray and in no shape for such small children.”
The affidavit said nearly every piece of decor and furniture was destroyed. Large knives, blow-torch lighters and other dangerous items were also reportedly left out in the open.
The document said the family made “non-sensical” statements to police, and at first told officers they were cleaning. They then allegedly claimed someone broke in and caused the damage.
Police assaulted by parents
At some point while police were inside the home, the affidavit said the father “began acting erratically” and tried to rub garlic and a Bible on the officers. While that was going on, the mother allegedly started “speaking fast and irate.”
Then, as police were looking around the house, both parents reportedly started screaming.
The father then started spraying down one of the kids with cologne and started moving toward a large butcher knife. The affidavit said a child then told police “she was not okay and was scared to be at the house.”
The affidavit said the father started throwing cloves of garlic at one of the officers. The mother then allegedly grabbed an officer’s neck, and when police tried to put the father in handcuffs, the mother tried to bite the officer’s leg.
Once outside, the mother allegedly spit at officers and spit inside the police car multiple times.
Parents charged
Court records identified the parents as 35-year-old Gabriel Antonio Santos-Funes and 33-year-old Maria Valladares.
Both parents were charged with several counts of misdemeanor child abuse, along with resisting an officer, assaulting a government employee, and other offenses.
Following their arrests, they were taken to the Mecklenburg County jail.

title: When a loved one refuses treatment: What families need to know
text:
(Aging Untold) — When an aging parent or loved one says no to medical treatment, it can feel alarming — but that decision is often rooted in something deeper than it first appears.
The Aging Untold hosts break down what’s really driving these moments and how families can respond with patience instead of panic.
“Slow down and listen”
When a loved one refuses care, the instinct for many families is to push back immediately. Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, says that reaction can make things worse.
“I think the first thing I would advise is to slow down. Take a deep breath and listen. Listen really carefully,” O’Rourke said. “What are they afraid of? What are they trying to avoid? What are they fighting for? Where are they emotionally? And then start there.”
O’Rourke cautioned against rushing toward a predetermined outcome.
“Don’t be quick to cut them off. Try to get a certain outcome in place. Just slow everything down,” she said.
She described working with a family where tensions boiled over.
“I worked with a family where they were in the middle of this discussion, and one of the kids just flipped out and called 911,” O’Rourke said. “And the ambulance came and she got in the ambulance, and the mother looked at me and she goes, ‘I don’t want to go. I don’t want to go to the hospital.’ And it was an awkward moment, but she got out of the ambulance.”
O’Rourke said the situation didn’t have to escalate the way it did.
“It was one of those things where it was a crisis when it didn’t need to be, if they just slow down and started listening earlier,” she said.
Understanding what’s really being said
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, agreed that slowing down is key and said families need to dig into the “why” behind a refusal.
“I think you’re right in terms of slowing down, listening and understanding, what is the person really saying?” Rogers said. “They’re not saying, ‘I don’t want to be treated’ necessarily. There’s something underlying that’s driving that value for them.”
Rogers said refusing a specific treatment isn’t the same as giving up.
“Not being treated and refusing treatment doesn’t mean that you’re saying, ‘I choose death,’” Rogers said. “You have to understand what is surrounding the decision that this person is making about how they want to live.”
Sometimes the person is looking at the medications along with the side effects and weighing all those different things, Rogers said.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck framed the decision as an act of self-determination.
“This is ultimately self-care in the most complex form. You’re taking care of yourself,” Cradduck said. “It may not line up with the way you would take care of yourself, but it’s the way I’ve chosen to. And maybe it’s based on seeing my own parent suffer through a treatment that I don’t want to have to endure.”
Clearing up misconceptions about hospice
Cradduck also pointed to hospice as an example of a widely misunderstood form of treatment.
“We see this one a lot where we think, oh, hospice, I’m not going to ever use hospice because they kill people. That’s what unfortunately a lot of people believe,” she said. “The reality is, to be part of hospice, you are already terminally ill. So hospice isn’t killing you. It’s providing comfort while you’re dying, while you’re going through that final sunset.”
Cradduck said this misunderstanding comes up often in counseling families.
“I’ve counseled with so many families where they’re like, ‘Oh, I would never have hospice,’ which is a form of treatment,” she said.
Rogers said hospice doesn’t mean the end.
“We were always taught hospice means the end ... but hospice means you get additional services, you get support, and it doesn’t mean it’s the end,” she said.
Cradduck added that belief systems can lead people to decline care that may benefit them.
“Based on belief systems, people will refuse treatments, and they’ll turn down something that maybe is to their benefit,” she said. “So sometimes just listening to why, and then giving good counsel, but honoring the person’s belief system regardless — I may not agree with you, but you have a right to choose your own destiny.”
Asking the right questions
The experts said families should make sure a loved one’s decision is based on accurate understanding, not a misconception.
“Asking questions to uncover what it is — so the questions behind the decisions and the opinions. Is there more information that could be provided? Is there more conversation that could be had that would make it a little bit easier to either understand their position, or for them to maybe make a different decision once they’re educated on it,” Ambrose said.
Rogers said that clarifying conversations give everyone a chance to understand each other.
“Clarify, because you could clarify whatever they’re saying. That’s your opportunity to clarify for misunderstanding,” the host said.

title: Federal judge orders Trump administration to halt noncitizen voting investigation in 9 states
text:
(AP) - A federal judge in California has ordered the Trump administration to halt investigations in nine states into whether noncitizens are registered to vote.
U.S. District Court Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin in Oakland found the government’s effort is relying on data that is full of errors and that it’s leading to intimidation of groups performing voter assistance efforts. She said it should be halted until polls close on Election Day, Nov. 3.
She put her ruling, which was made Wednesday, on hold until Friday to give the administration a chance to appeal.
The ruling applies to investigations in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.
It comes as the Trump administration has been hunting for noncitizen voters throughout the country in the months leading into the midterm elections. The administration has signaled that it’s a major problem, when in fact it’s quite rare, as even its own investigations have shown.
The lawsuit was filed by the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United, along with the Voto Latino Foundation, San Francisco and Santa Clara County.
In response to the ruling, the Department of Homeland Security issued an email statement Thursday saying it’s focused on “removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” while adding, “We have no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens.”
The judge based the decision to halt the investigation only on the unions’ assertion that the probe is harming voter assistance and mobilization efforts involving citizens. She did not find that union members’ right to vote was being infringed because most of them do that by mail and not in person. She said investigations don’t need to target U.S. citizens, use armed agents or intimidate citizens who are urging others to vote.
According to legal filings in the case, investigators were told to target naturalized citizens to see whether they had voted before they became U.S. citizens. The lists of voters to check came from sources that included state and local governments and publicly available information. Martinez-Olguin called them “voluminous and unreliable.”
“Even under the best conditions, there is a high likelihood of error in review because there is no federal database containing citizenship status of U.S. residents,” Martinez-Olguin wrote in her ruling. “The time limitations implemented during the Surge further exacerbate the risk of error.”
The Department of Justice has been demanding detailed and unredacted voter roll data from the states and has sued the 30 states that have refused to turn it over, losing each of those cases so far. The judge noted that for states that refused to share their records, the administration was trying to obtain them through “unreliable commercial versions of voter roll data.”
She said during a “surge” phase of the investigation starting in late August, agents were ordered to complete reviews of flagged individuals taking no more than 12 minutes per person to assess whether they were legally qualified to vote.
In their challenge, the plaintiffs said some U.S. citizens felt they were wrongly identified and investigated as part of the probe. Martinez-Olguin said those fears “are well understood as intimidation” that has chilled people from attending campaign events and working as poll monitors during the election.
Beau Tremitiere, a lawyer representing the unions and voter group, said in a statement that the ruling affirms the groups’ position.
“It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people’s homes weeks before an election,” Tremitiere said.
Details of the investigation, known as the “Unlawful Voter Initiative,” came to light last month after Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York and Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California released a whistleblower report about it.

title: Trump says he ordered the Justice Department lawsuit over Alaska’s US Senate race
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump on Friday said he told his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, kicking off what many fear could become a lengthy battle between the government and states over certifying an election where the president’s party is struggling.
“I’m the one that said do it,” Trump told reporters as he landed for a campaign rally in Florida.
The lawsuit, filed late Thursday, centers on one of the president’s longstanding complaints in the Senate race — the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan, who Republicans fear could siphon away votes from the incumbent in what’s likely to be a photo-finish contest with Democrat Mary Peltola, the state’s former congresswoman.
The second Sullivan, who is Daniel J. Sullivan from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg, has said he decided to run on his own, but Republicans have contended he is a Democratic plant to siphon votes away from their candidate.
The lawsuit by the Republican president’s Department of Justice in federal court in Alaska demands that the state be blocked from certifying a Peltola win if Daniel J. Sullivan remains on the ballot. “The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska,” the lawsuit says.
The legal challenge came 11 days before the Nov. 3 election and months after the final ballot was set. It is the latest example of the Department of Justice bolstering Trump’s political operation, targeting his enemies and suing Democratic-controlled states before the election.
At a forum in Anchorage Friday night, Peltola called the lawsuit “just flagrant, flagrant corruption in my opinion.” She told reporters that the legal fight was “another diversion from the issue that Alaskans want to talk about, which is affordability” and an example of how her Republican opponent was “using his connections in Washington, D.C., to manipulate the situation.”
“I am very concerned about Alaskans’ voices not being heard,” Peltola said.
Democrats and many voting rights advocates have long feared that the administration will try to block certification of elections that Trump’s party loses, much as he unsuccessfully tried to do when he lost the 2020 White House race to Democrat Joe Biden.
The Alaska Supreme Court rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, and the state’s Republican officials made the decisions about how to list him on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent. Alaska’s ranked choice voting system also will allow voters to select both of the men if confused.
Alaska’s other Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski, alluded to that in a social media post criticizing the lawsuit. “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot,” wrote Murkowski, who has endorsed the incumbent Sullivan. “The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit.”
Peltola and Sen. Sullivan were top vote-getters in nonpartisan primary
The senator received more than 68,000 votes in the August primary, while the challenging Sullivan got 4,107, about 2% of the total vote. Peltola, who had previously served one term in the House, was the top vote-getter in the nonpartisan primary. Both parties expect that whoever wins in November will do so by a tight margin in a state of 738,000 people.
The campaign for Sen. Dan Sullivan did not address whether the senator supports the Department of Justice’s intervention. “We’ll let the DOJ complaint run its course,” campaign spokesman Nate Adams said in a text message. “Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan’s strong record of delivering for Alaska.”
Daniel J. Sullivan, whose presence on the ballot is at issue in the lawsuit, did not respond to a request for comment.
“Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses,” said Devan Barber, executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.
In a statement Friday, the Department of Justice noted that Alaska’s election officials, who are Republicans, determined the other Sullivan’s campaign was an attempt to “mislead” voters and wanted him removed from the ballot. Both a state court and Alaska’s Supreme Court disagreed and kept the second Sullivan on the ballot.
“The Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters,” the department’s statement said.
Concerns about the Department of Justice’s role in the election had already reached a fever pitch this month after it filed an unusual, last-minute lawsuit demanding California segregate ballots from 20,000 voters who the Trump administration believed could be noncitizens. California said that it appeared many of those identified were indeed citizens and that they had no time to carefully investigate, as the administration threatened to prosecute the state’s election workers if there was illegal voting.
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche denied the action was a prelude to challenging certification of the midterm results in that state, adding that such a move may happen under a “doomsday” scenario but was unlikely.
“It is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process,” he told reporters Thursday in Virginia before the Alaska lawsuit was filed.
The lawsuit was signed by Associate U.S. Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who represented Trump allies and Jan. 6 defendants before becoming one of the top appointees at the department.
Constitution gives states the power to run elections
Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the lawsuit would likely only kick in if Republicans narrowly lose the Alaska Senate race and that it probably would not survive long. “The statute simply doesn’t let the Department of Justice enjoin certification,” Muller said. “The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month.”
The U.S. Constitution grants states the power to run their own elections. Elections for federal office like the Senate must comply with standards set by Congress. That division of power has frustrated Trump, who repeatedly has tried to seize control of election procedures through executive orders that courts have blocked.
The final step for a state election is formally certifying the winner, the act that the administration’s lawsuit seeks to prevent, it requests, “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan.”
The process in Alaska is complicated by the state’s ranked choice voting system, which Trump opposes, and many expect it to take weeks before a winner is known. Also on the state’s ballot is an initiative to repeal that system.
Trump has stepped up complaints about a ballot with dueling Sullivans
Trump has complained about Daniel J. Sullivan’s presence on the ballot, making reference to it during a rally in Alaska this month and in repeated social media posts, including one this week where he called it “CHEATING.”
“We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness,” the president wrote on Wednesday.
Clogging a ballot with third-party candidates to siphon off votes from the other major party is a long-standing tactic in the country’s two-party system. Republicans have been linked to an effort to persuade Ohio voters to support a socialist in that state’s Senate race, which could help Republican Sen. Jon Husted fend off a challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown.
___
Associated Press writers Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, Haven Daley in Anchorage, Alaska, Ali Swenson in New York and Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Obituary: Linda Mae Marchky Cronkhite
text:
BRUNSWICK – Linda Mae Marchky Cronkhite passed away peacefully on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, surrounded by her beloved caregiver, Béa Bonnaire Blakemore, close friends, and her cherished pets.
She is survived by her brother Lance Ray Marchky from Kelleys Island, Ohio, and his wife Susan Marie Marchky; and a nephew Andrew Marchky and wife Jill Marchky and great-niece Kelly Kennedy Wicker and great-nephew Russell Kennedy.
She was predeceased by her mother Kathleen Barbara Feyedelem and father Cecil Henry Marchky and sister Marla Jean Ridenbaugh.
Linda grew up in Sandusky, Ohio, alongside her parents, an older sister, and a younger brother. She spent her happiest childhood summers at her Hungarian grandmother’s farm on Kelleys Island on Lake Erie, developing a lifelong love for nature and animals. Guided by this deep compassion, she entered the Sisters of St. Francis of Sylvania convent directly after eighth grade. Known as Sister Edna from 1954 to 1968, Linda dedicated her early years to teaching first graders before earning her degree in nursing.
Her nursing career eventually took her to Brenham, Texas, where she served as the Director of Nurses at St. Jude Hospital. Linda was profoundly proud of her pioneering role there in racially integrating the hospital’s patients, ensuring equal care for all. In 1968, Linda made the decision to return to lay life, moving back to Ohio and later transitioning to Boston Children’s Hospital. It was in Boston that she met the love of her life, Dr. Leonard Wolsey Cronkhite Jr. The two were married in 1976.
Their shared journey took them to Milwaukee, where Leonard became the president of the Medical College of Wisconsin. Never one to stop learning, Linda earned her Ph.D. in philosophy from the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee and successfully led a major psychiatric unit. Though both were deeply devoted to their demanding careers, they always prioritized each other – frequently entertaining friends and traveling the world together. Following Leonard’s retirement, they moved to Brunswick in 1985, where they joined the Cumberland Club in Portland. Linda remained an active, vibrant member of the club, where she became legendary for her love of Halloween and the spectacular, unforgettable parties she threw.
Following Leonard’s passing in 1996, Linda was blessed to find companionship again. In 1998, she married Ashton Johnson, a dear, longtime friend of the couple. They shared many wonderful years together until Ashton’s passing in 2013. Linda will ultimately be laid to rest alongside her beloved Leonard in Arlington National Cemetery, honoring his service as a Major General in the U.S. Army Reserves.
Linda was truly the life of the party, bringing joy, energy, and a vibrant spirit wherever she went. She was a fierce animal advocate who gave back generously to her community, regularly supporting charities including MSMT, People Plus, Oasis Clinic, the Brunswick Humane Society, and the Tedford Shelter. In her later years, Linda found immense comfort and joy in her beautiful home, surrounded by a lush landscape of plants and flowers, the company of her dedicated live-in caregiver, and the pets they shared. Her warmth, generosity, and lively spirit will be deeply missed by all who knew her. There is a magical place that held a special spot in Linda’s heart and brought her immense joy for many years among the baby goats in pajamas, sunshine and likeminded, kindhearted people called Sunflower Farm which is located in Cumberland Center. In June of 2027, near the time of what would have been Linda’s 86th birthday, this is where we will be holding her celebration of life.
Friends and family are invited to visit 2-5 p.m., Saturday Oct. 24, 2026 at the Brackett Funeral Home, 29 Federal Street, Brunswick. Memories and condolences can be shared at http://www.brackettfh.com.

title: Calais council votes 4-3 to sign armory purchase agreement
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For more than two years the City of Calais has been waiting for the State of Maine to make a final determination on the use of the National Guard Armory on Calais Avenue. About three months ago, the city was notified that the state would be selling the armory and that the city would have the right of first refusal as required by state law, with the purchase and sale agreement received last month.
Following an executive session on October 8, the council voted 4-3 to authorize the city manager to sign the agreement on behalf of the city. Councillors Eddie Moreside, Michael Sherrard and Bill Quinn voted against the motion. The council committed to a public discussion on the purchase at a future council meeting to provide the public with details surrounding the decision. The closing would be December 31, pending final council approval.
During recent discussions on the purchase, councillors Sherrard and Moreside have protested the impact on local property taxes of the $578,000 purchase price, plus the future expenses to relocate from the city building on Church Street. City Manager Mike Ellis has provided the council with potential funding sources, including federal grants and congressional earmarks, although the deadline for applying to the delegation has passed for the current funding cycle.
Ellis has been requested by the council to complete a cost analysis of the renovation and relocation costs. Tentative plans include relocation of the recreation department and police department into the armory, which would require a dedicated entrance for the police. Additional renovations would be needed to relocate the staff from the current city building. Longer term plans include renovating the garage building on the property for the fire and EMS department and, potentially, the public works department.
Ladder truck funding accepted
The fire department was notified that they have received a $1 million grant from FEMA under the Assistance to Firefighters Grant Program. After mandated fees and administrative costs, the city has $952,381 in grant funding for the purchase of a new ladder truck to replace the current 41‑year‑old ladder. Following a discussion of various options and costs the council voted 5‑2 at the October 8 meeting to accept the funding, with councillors Sherrard and Moreside opposed due to the impact of the city share of between $350,000 to $600,000 on the local property taxes.
City financial consultant Hank Farrah provided the council with an update on the municipal enterprise funds. Enterprise funds are budget categories that operate separate from the general fund and are expected to be self‑funding. The ambulance fund has operated at a loss every year, with a deficit of $395,146 for fiscal year 2026 based on the unaudited financial statements and an accumulated deficit of $1,029,598. The water department showed an operating deficit of $59,126, and the sewer department $494,832. Farrah recommended that the city consider restructuring the city budget and at a minimum include the ambulance budget as part of the fire department in the general fund. Farrah noted that enterprise funds are intended to be self‑funded and not rely on property taxes but that he has found across his municipal clients that, due to the nature of ambulance reimbursements and payments, this is not a realistic model. Bringing the budget under the general fund improves the financial accounting, as the deficit is already paid by the city using the line of credit; however, the city has used a substantial amount of the available credit.
The council approved the change to a business zone for a small parcel at Baring and Boardman streets following a public hearing. The zone change was for a 40' by 40' parcel adjacent to the existing business zone to permit construction of a fiber optic connectivity station. The council also approved the local election warrant for the November 3 election.

title: $4 million fraud scheme: Influencer had hundreds of fake SNAP accounts, prosecutors say
text:
ATLANTA (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — An Atlanta social media influencer is accused of stealing millions of dollars in SNAP benefits, prosecutors said Wednesday.
Mercedes Reshard New, who goes by “Shawty Dred,” was indicted on federal charges for fraudulently obtaining more than $4 million in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia.
Fake accounts and fraudulent cards
Between January 2020 and July 2026, New allegedly controlled more than 350 fake SNAP accounts, which were created using stolen identities.
Prosecutors said New, 39, allegedly had SNAP EBT cards mailed to various metro Atlanta addresses and applied for his limited liability company, Shawty Dred LLC, to become an authorized SNAP retailer.
Between April 2024 and November 2025, New allegedly used fraudulently obtained EBT cards and a point-of-sale device associated with Shawty Dred LLC to steal more than $660,000 in SNAP benefits.
Store authorization revoked, arrest followed
In November 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture revoked New’s store authorization. About two weeks later, local police officers arrested New for allegedly selling SNAP benefits at a metro Atlanta store, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said.
Officers seized 14 EBT cards from New that had been issued to other people. New then allegedly had replacement cards mailed to his store address and other addresses in the Atlanta area.
Investigators said the scheme diverted $4.6 million in SNAP funds. The EBT debit cards were used to siphon around $4 million from the accounts.
Indictment and arrest
New has flaunted private jets, fancy cars and stacks of cash to his millions of followers on TikTok and Instagram, as he denounced others as “broke motherf****s,” prosecutors said.
On Oct. 7, a federal grand jury indicted New on 46 counts of mail fraud, 15 counts of aggravated identity theft and one count each of SNAP fraud and illegal transactions with access devices.
New was arrested on Oct. 13 and remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service pending further proceedings.
“New allegedly stole over $4 million meant for poor families who need help putting food on the table,” U.S. Attorney Theodore Hertzberg said in a statement. “My office is fully committed to rooting out abuses of the SNAP program and holding accountable criminal con artists and scammers who appallingly seek to profit by stealing taxpayer money meant to feed vulnerable Americans.”
New was previously arrested in 2022 after he allegedly exposed himself in public.

title: Fat-free doesn’t always mean healthy: What to look for on food labels
text:
(Aging Untold) — Grabbing the “fat-free” option at the grocery store feels like the responsible choice, especially as we get older and start paying closer attention to our heart, our weight and our cholesterol.
But Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, explains why that label can be misleading — and what to check instead.
The biggest misconception about “fat-free”
“People think that fat-free is healthy. And really, fat free does not mean that it’s problem free,” Rogers said. “So if they’re removing the fat, they had to replace it with something else. So you have to look at the ingredients and look at the packaging.”
Rogers said the front of the package is designed to sell the product — not inform the shopper.
“Just remember this is about advertising,” she said. “So the package — the front of the package is all advertisement. And the back of the package is the ingredients, which tells the truth. That’s really what you want to know. If they took out something, what did they fill it with?”
She added that replacements for fat are often not healthy, even if they make a product taste better.
“Usually they fill it with something that’s not healthy. They made it taste good and all that, but it’s not healthy,” Rogers said.
A simple label-reading rule
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared her own personal rule of thumb for reading nutrition labels at the store.
“I’m a label reader,” O’Rourke said. “I eat anything with sugar being fifth and lower, and then I look at what’s above, and if I don’t understand it, I don’t eat it.”
Rethinking what food is for
Rather than focusing only on fat grams or calorie counts, Rogers said the better question is what is a food doing inside the body?
“We always thought about people looking at how much fat is in this food, or how many calories. Really, we have to get back to what does food do? It gives us energy,” Rogers said. “Why don’t you look at what is this food doing to my body? How is it helping me to stabilize my blood sugar? How’s it helping me with my hormones? That’s really what food is — it should be used as energy.”
Breaking down the different types of fat
Rogers said she used to find all the fat categories confusing, so she created a simple way to sort them.
“Monounsaturated fats — those are good fats. You want to eat them all day long. They help with the heart and cells,” she said. “That’s things like olive oil, avocados. Those are your healthy fats.”
She continued with polyunsaturated fats, which the body cannot produce on its own.
“Those are essential fats. That means your body can’t make it, so you have to get it from food,” Rogers said.
Saturated fats, she said, are OK in smaller amounts.
“Those are pretty good fats, but you want to do it in limitation. That’s your butter, your cream. They usually say no more than 10% of your total calories that day,” she said. “And then you have the trans fats — that’s just a no.”
Rogers compared the categories to family members and how welcome they are in your home.
“I had to classify it like a family. So you have those relatives that you want to come over — that’s your monos and your polys. And you have the other relatives that have boundaries. You have several relatives, they just can’t come,” she said.
Choosing food your great-grandparents would recognize
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said the simplest test for any product is whether it resembles real, recognizable food.
“The big thing is, when we’re looking at food, you want to be as close to natural food as possible. Would our great-grandparents recognize that as food?” she said. “They didn’t have to be nutrition experts, but today we kind of do. We want to be informed consumers.”
Key takeaways
- “Fat-free” isn’t always healthy. When fat is removed from a product, manufacturers replace it with something else — often sugar, sweeteners or starches.
- Flip the package over. The front is advertising; the ingredient list on the back tells you what’s actually in the product.
- Use simple ingredients. Choose foods close to what your great-grandparents would recognize is a simple way to eat more naturally.

title: Why not ‘Mr. Jackson,’ Sen. Collins?
text:
I’m offended that Sen. Susan Collins has cast Troy Jackson’s telling her to “shut up” during their recent debate as reflecting his misogyny. This, from a senator who approved a Supreme Court justice facing credible complaints of sexual assault, a justice who went on to overturn Roe v. Wade?
I wonder, instead, what the senator’s repeatedly calling her opponent by his first name betokens.
Is she highlighting the name’s relative unusualness, casting him as “not one of us”? Is this a “social class” barb, suggesting that her more aristocratic upbringing entitles her to respect, while his does not? This inequality in naming sounds to me like the custom, in wealthy families, of calling adult servants by their first names. This is Maine, not the Antebellum South. Using language to demean and disrespect is not part of our usual discourse.
Despite the wishes of some, we all remain equal here. And we will stand judged by our behavior.
Gail Wasserman
Brunswick
