title: Eleni Richardson for South Portland School Board
text:
Eleni Richardson is a deeply engaged and effective leader, and I’m excited to support her for another term as an at-large member of the South Portland School Board. As a board member, she asks hard questions and keeps the well-being of students and teachers at the forefront of every discussion.
Apart from her board position, working long hours on her own time, Eleni has been essential to our community’s response to ICE detentions, serving as a critical bridge between volunteers and school staff trying to keep kids and families safe. She is exactly the kind of leader we need at a time when the school department and the city as a whole are facing complex challenges — someone who is collaborative and acts with conviction.
Chelsea Byun
South Portland

title: Kate Snyder knows what needs to happen in Portland
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I am proud to call Portland my home. We do have challenges ahead in addressing taxes, budgets and homelessness. Our schools continue to be a bright spot for our community. I am supporting Kate Snyder for the at-large City Council seat because of her vast and successful leadership as the city’s mayor and school board chair. She knows what needs to get done and how to accomplish the city’s future goals.
I do want changes but I also recognize how important it is to elect knowledgeable and proven leaders. I believe that important changes can happen if we elect a person like Kate, who has been committed to making our city a better place.
Bill Keefer
Portland

title: Cooper Flagg hurt in Mavericks’ win over Pacers
text:
INDIANAPOLIS — A jarring flagrant foul knocked Cooper Flagg awkwardly to the floor and eventually out of the game Friday night.
Now it’s unclear whether the Dallas star will miss any more time.
Last season’s NBA Rookie of the Year did not play in the second half of Dallas’ 121-105 victory Friday night over the Indiana Pacers after landing hard on his left shoulder after Aaron Nesmith tried to block his shot from behind to prevent a breakaway dunk.
Instead, Flagg landed hard on his shoulder.
“Cooper has left shoulder soreness, he’ll be evaluated in the next couple of days,” Mavericks coach Dusty May said before addressing whether Flagg needed an MRI. “I really don’t know. I saw him in the locker room, he’s in good spirits. We’ll know in the next couple days what’s next.”
Flagg, of Newport, did not speak to reporters following the game.
He was off to a fast start in his second pro season. Two days after scoring 32 points to become the highest scoring teenager in a season opener in league history, Flagg was on pace for his first triple double of the season. He finished with 14 points, five rebounds and six assists in 17 minutes.
But it was how he left that had everyone talking and scuffling as Mavericks players came to the defense of their hurting teammate.
Forward Naji Marshall confronted Nesmith under the basket, drawing players from both teams into a brief fray. After a replay review, the refs assessed double technical fouls to Nesmith and Marshall. Flagg then made 1 of 2 free throws and continued to rub his shoulder as he walked toward the locker room.
Two Mavericks players also appeared to leave the bench though May said he thought both went to check on Flagg, perhaps avoiding any disciplinary action from the league.
“Look, Nesmith is a great guy, a heck of a player. I’ve known him since he was in high school,” said May, who reached two NCAA Final Fours and won last year’s national championship just a few blocks away from Gainbridge Fieldhouse. “Obviously, an unfortunate play. Hopefully, Coop’s fine.”
Another brief scuffle broke out between the teams near midcourt in the second half though it led to technicals or flagrant fouls. Pacers coach Rick Carlisle noted that Indiana has now played two games that have resulted in multiple scuffles.

title: Man rescued after getting stuck in mud by Newport’s Sebasticook Lake
text:
A duck hunter was rescued from deep mud by Sebasticook Lake in Newport on Friday afternoon.
Newport Fire Chief Jeff Chretien said the man walked out on the lake bed to retrieve a duck he had shot when he became stuck.
The fire department responded around 12:40 p.m. Friday after a member of the nearby American Legion post spotted the man and called 911. Chretien said the man was with some friends who attempted to free him but had no luck.
First responders put ladders over the mud and walked across the rungs to where the man was stranded. They tied a rope around the man, who put his weight onto a jet sled he had with him. He had to kick his waders off, which were full of heavy mud, Chretien said.
From there, Chretien said, authorities were able to drag the man out until he could stand on the ladder rungs.
“It was great teamwork by all the rescuers,” he said.
The man was stuck for about an hour, Chretien estimated. There were no injuries — “just pride,” he said.

title: Family restaurant opens in Blue Hill after abrupt departure from Bucksport
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A restaurant that departed Bucksport’s Main Street last month after less than a year has opened its doors in downtown Blue Hill.
Stowaways Town Tavern has kept its menu and added a weekend breakfast at 40 Main St., formerly home to Sandy’s Blue Hill Cafe. After opening and closing three restaurants in Hancock County in the last several years, owner Rob DeGennaro said he’s in Blue Hill for the long term.
“People know us [here],” he said, noting his past restaurants in the area. “We just felt Blue Hill was … natural.”
The move marks a notable change for the dining scenes in Bucksport and Blue Hill, and also brings an eat-in breakfast option to its new area.
Stowaways’ extensive family-style menu offers large portions of dishes ranging from custom prepared fish to meatloaf to salads, with an accompanying bar menu including a range of frozen drinks inspired by DeGennaro’s past restaurants in Florida.
The original menu remains in Blue Hill with some additions, like barbecue ribs and steak options. A new weekend breakfast menu will have a new entree each week, like red velvet pancakes, blueberry stuffed French toast or crab benedict, served with a basket of muffins and popovers.
Stowaways first opened last October at the prominent corner building in Bucksport that previously housed MacLeod’s Restaurant for 45 years, until it closed in early 2025.
DeGennaro’s departure came amid a rent dispute with the building’s owner, George MacLeod, who owned the previous restaurant there. MacLeod previously told the River Observer newspaper that DeGennaro had missed deadlines to close on buying the building, then stopped paying rent and communicating with him.
DeGennaro said Thursday that the building needed more work than expected, which would drive up costs, and detailed complications around addressing it. He decided to focus on the Blue Hill location instead — where he was already planning to open a second Stowaways location. He is buying the new building, he said.
As for “rumors” about the reasons behind frequent moves — DeGennaro has closed restaurants in Castine, Stonington and Bucksport after short runs in recent years — he said building problems also arose in Stonington, where he was renting, and the closures were forced.
“Typically, when we open restaurants, we love them, we keep them,” he said. “So this one will be here for a long time.”
Sandy’s seats 90 people inside, more than the Bucksport location, with room for 20 outdoor patio seats.
The new location is open 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Wednesday through Friday this winter and 7:30 a.m. to 9 p.m. on weekends, and diners are encouraged to call ahead for seating. Gift certificates and coupons from Bucksport will be honored at the new location.

title: Obituary: Dalmon Ray Perry
text:
PHIPPSBURG – Dalmon Ray Perry, 78, of Phippsburg, passed away at home on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. He was born in Saco on July 29, 1948, the son of Arthur and Olive Perry. He grew up in Bath, graduating from Morse High School class of 1966. While attending Morse, he participated in basketball and track and held the school record for high jump several years after graduation. Illness prevented him from continuing his education at USM and led to his joining the Airforce. He was selected to attend language school in California, learning Chinese. Unfortunately, a motorcycle accident prevented him from continuing. His tour of duty included Labrador and Vietnam with him being honorably discharged in 1972 as a sergeant.
After his service, he drove for several construction companies, the USM women’s basketball team and the Harpswell school bus. He enjoyed being outside and meeting people. He also relished his time at the gym which helped him win many bodybuilding competitions. For 18 years he worked as a supervisor in the post office at the So. Portland distribution center. Dal loved golf and worked mowing the greens at both The Bath Country Club and the Mere Creek golf course. Not liking cold weather, he spent his winters golfing with his girlfriend in California. Loving the world of motorcycling (and it had to be a “Harley”), he belonged to two clubs – one in Maine and one in Palm Desert, Calif. “Aging” brought him into the world of books. He was a veracious reader, reading many books during the month. He also “enjoyed” his times with his girlfriend as he tried to win at Yahtzee and Phase 10.
Dalmon was predeceased by his parents and is survived by his son Ian (Samantha) of Phoenix, Ariz., his sister Linda, his girlfriend Linda, many cousins, and Oreo and Jake (two Boston Terriers he loved and helped raise).
A Mass of Christian burial will be held at St. Mary’s Church of All Saints Parrish, 144 Lincoln St in Bath on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026, at 11 a.m. Visiting hours will be held at Desmond Funeral Home in Bath on Thursday Oct. 22, 2026, from 4–6 p.m. Burial with military honors will be at Oak Grove Cemetery (middle school entrance) in Bath following mass. Please join the family back at the church after burial for fellowship, refreshments and memories.
To express your thoughts and condolences with the family, please visit http://www.desmondfuneralhomes .com
In lieu of flowers, please consider making a donation to your local Humane Society in Dalmon’s name.
He loved animals.

title: Father who killed Oregon school shooter describes deadly attack, taking down armed teen
text:
BEND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - In an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting, Kaylub Giamanco, 36, the man who took down the elementary shooter last week, described what he saw that day as he confronted the armed teen.
Giamanco explained in the interview about crawling through a damaged school building, hearing children crying for help and encountering the 16-year-old shooter at Silver Rail Elementary School.
The Oregon father, whose two daughters were at the school at the time of the shooting, said panic set in after seeing the gunman throwing a rifle over a fence at his daughters’ school.
He said he opened his center console, where his gun was, repeating “no, no, no, no, no.”
Giamanco said he then moved toward the school building after hearing children pleading for help and hearing gunfire. He said he army-crawled faster, thinking it could be the last thing he ever did.
The father said he moved low past a recycling bin and into a corridor toward the doors, then crawled through the bottom of a broken-out window onto a rug in a small entryway with stairs. He said the special-needs classroom was to his left.
Giamanco said he got to his hands and knees, checked his weapon to confirm a live round was chambered, then looked through a window into the classroom.
He noted seeing a teacher on the left struggling with the gunman holding a rifle on the right. He said both were turned sideways to him, with the shooter not knowing he was there.
Giamanco said he then pushed the door open, stepped in and fired.
The 36-year-old called his mother after what occurred.
“I just had to take the life of what I think might be a child because he went into my daughters’ school with a gun,” he recalled telling her.
Giamanco said she told him to calm down, that he did the right thing and saved lives.
Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher were killed in the school shooting last Thursday. The teen shooter was identified as a former student of the school, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II.
Police said John blasted his way through locked doors with a shotgun and attacked a special-needs classroom.
Another student was critically injured and a teacher was injured and hospitalized.
Police have said Giamanco was carrying his gun legally in his truck and have credited him and the unarmed teacher who confronted the gunman with saving lives.

title: Jayson Tatum bounces back to lift Celtics past Knicks
text:
BOSTON — Jayson Tatum scored 25 of his 36 points in the second half, including seven of his team’s final eight to help the Boston Celtics hold off the New York Knicks 107-103 on Friday night.
Paul George and Neemias Queta added 15 points apiece to help fend off a late rally by the defending NBA champion Knicks.
New York fell to 0-2 after losing its season opener to the Philadelphia 76ers.
Karl-Anthony Towns had 22 points to lead five Knicks in double figures. OG Anunoby finished with 20 points, 10 rebounds and eight assists. Deuce McBride scored 20 points and Jalen Brunson added 19.
In a game that featured 12 lead changes and four ties, Boston outscored New York 33-24 in the third quarter to increase a one-point halftime lead to 10.
The Celtics’ edge grew as high as 91-79 before a 12-3 Knicks run cut it to 94-91 on a Towns putback dunk.
New York got it back to 99-96 on Josh Hart’s 3-pointer before Queta turned it over, leading to a floater by Brunson. But Tatum responded with a 19-footer on Boston’s next possession that made it 101-98 with 1:11 remaining.
It was 103-98 when Anunoby hit a pair of free throws with less than a minute left. Tatum then drained a 3 from the wing.
Mitchell Robinson finished with four points, four rebounds and a block after struggling with early foul trouble throughout his first matchup against the Knicks team that he helped win last season’s title. Robinson was the only member of New York’s regular rotation who didn’t return to the team.
It didn’t stop him from making his presence felt opposite the team with whom he spent his first eight NBA seasons. During one sequence in the fourth quarter Robinson swatted away a layup attempt by Towns. Following a miss by Mikal Bridges, Robinson then was the recipient of an alley-oop from Derrick White.
The game was scrappy on both sides, but Queta was the only Celtics player to attempt a free throw through two-plus quarters. That didn’t change until Tatum went to the line with 3:21 remaining in the third.

title: Grand Canyon adds new dog to help reduce wildlife interactions with visitors
text:
GRAND CANYON, AZ (InvestigateTV) — Each year, there are dangerous encounters between Grand Canyon visitors and wildlife such as elk. So the park created a new program to reduce these interactions, with the introduction of their newest employee, Blue, the Catahoula dog.
Around 5 million people visit the Grand Canyon, and wildlife biologist Brady Dunne said people get too close to wildlife.
“Every time someone calls for an incident, I’m the one who responds,” said Dunne. “I graphed out that data, and just year after year has climbed exponentially.”
He said they track at least 12 guest and wildlife interactions that are classified as dangerous each year, but those are only the ones recorded.
Dunne said one of the reasons there are so many interactions is the number of elk and their adaptive behaviors.
“Right now, we have the most elk we’ve ever had, and the highest percentage of those elk are habituated,” he said.
He created a program using Blue, the 18-month-old Catahoula Leonberger dog, to teach the elk not to go into populated areas.
Blue is one of only two dogs in the country with this job right now.
“So I’m going to try out using a spotted wolf that we call blue,” Dunne said. “Over time, it’s called aversive conditioning. Over time, they say a wolf lives at the El Tovar, I’m not going to come drop my calf there.”
Blue chased elk away from the local school on Monday.
“So we move her across the road, and we push her into the woods, and she goes into her own where she belongs,” Dunne said.
Blue never touches the elk, and Dunne said the goal isn’t to chase the animals out of the park but to move them away from areas with the most people.
They collared nine elk, so they’ll collect data on how efficient the program is.
Dunne is hopeful the project will make a positive impact, protecting elk and visitors.
“Really, what I like most about it is Blue is a symbol for people to see, to think to themselves, ‘should I approach this elk? Oh wait a second, maybe I’ll be true to Blue and I won’t pursue,’” he said.
It’s important to remember that wildlife can be aggressive when we do not respect their space. Visitors should stay at least 25 yards away from large animals like bison and elk.

title: Stillwater And I-95 Exit 186 Gets New Lane Markings Monday As Bangor Tackles Crash Hotspot
text:
It's been a particular bone of contention with many who ride the roads in Bangor; Stillwater Avenue, especially at the intersection of I-95, can get kind of confusing. Since they redid the exit off-ramp in that area, first you couldn't turn left off the ramp...then you could.
Read More: What Makes Route 2A In Maine America's Most Haunted Road
Maine personal injury lawyers, Hardy, Wolf & Downing say that section of road has seen it's fair share of accidents the past few years.
"The intersection/area of Stillwater Avenue and Interstate 95 (Exit 186) in Bangor is consistently ranked as one of the most crash-prone and high-traffic commercial zones in the city."
Historically, between 2022 and 2024, an average of 50 crashes have taken place at that spot. According to the Maine DOT, last year there were 64 crashes that resulted in 14 people being injured.
Bangor City Officials say the traffic pattern is about to change...again.
On Monday, the Maine DOT, who recently redesigned that intersection, will start painting new markings so that folks will know where to go.
"New pavement markings and traffic pattern lines will be painted on Monday, Oct. 26, weather permitting. Work is expected to be completed by the end of the day."
They're asking that people allow a little extra travel time and go slowly through that section as folks get used to the new pattern. They encourage motorists to travel with caution through the area, as there will be workers and painting equipment on the scene as they work on the project.
The Maine DOT also suggests that drivers follow the directions on both the signs that are posted along the way, and that the workers provide.

City officials are hopeful that reworking that intersection will improve both traffic flow and safety in that area.

title: Buxton voters approve temporary ban on data centers in Maine town
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BUXTON, Maine - Voters in Buxton have approved a temporary ban on data centers as the town joins a growing list of southern Maine communities that have passed similar moratoriums.
Buxton’s moratorium, which passed Wednesday night, restricts data center development for 180 days.
In April, the Maine Legislature passed a bill that would have put a temporary moratorium on data centers in the state.
It would have been the first of its kind in the U.S.
The legislation would have also required the Maine Department of Energy Resources to create the Maine Data Center Coordination Council to ensure the state is ready for data centers.
Governor Mills vetoed the bill.

title: These are the most popular baby names of 2026, new report says
text:
These are the most popular baby names of 2026, new report says
The 2026 baby-name list is here, and a few familiar favorites have some fresh company.
Olivia and Noah held on to the top spots in BabyCenter’s 2026 rankings of most popular baby names.
Eliana made the year’s biggest move among girls. It jumped five places to No. 2 after debuting in the top 10 last year at No. 7.
Related video above | The most popular and fastest-rising U.S. baby names of 2025
Amelia slipped to No. 3, Charlotte rose to No. 4, and Sophia, Isabella and Emma each fell in the rankings.
Evelyn returned to the top 10 at No. 9 after dropping out in 2024, while Mia stayed at No. 10 and Ellie slipped to No. 11.
The boys’ top five stayed exactly the same for the third year in a row: Noah, Liam, Oliver, Elijah and Mateo.
Elias leaped eight places to No. 7, making the top 10 for the first time, and Leo returned to the list at No. 10. Asher and Luca fell just outside it, at No. 11 and No. 12.
There was movement farther down the charts, too. Magnolia rose 40 places to No. 88 among girls, the only new girl name in the top 100.
Four boys’ names made their top-100 debuts: Milo, Stetson, Archer and Dean, which landed at No. 100. Dean is appearing in BabyCenter’s top 100 for the first time this century.
The rankings also point to a taste for longer names: 29% of the top girl names and 31% of the top boy names have at least seven letters. E was the most common first initial among girls’ names in the top 100, while J led for boys.

title: Hear from the man who jumped onto runaway school bus carrying 19 students
text:
Good Samaritan who jumped aboard runaway bus carrying 19 students shares his story
Ebro Ahmed, hailed as a hero for jumping aboard a school bus while its driver was having a medical emergency, shares his story
Good Samaritan who jumped aboard runaway bus carrying 19 students shares his story
Ebro Ahmed, hailed as a hero for jumping aboard a school bus while its driver was having a medical emergency, shares his story
Surveillance cameras at Ya Bricks Snacks and Tobacco were rolling when Ebro Ahmed jumped aboard a runaway school bus carrying 19 students in St. Paul, Minnesota.
Ahmed told WCCO he was working outside his family’s store in the Dayton’s Bluff neighborhood on Monday when he saw a bus moving down the street with its door still open.
"It caught me by surprise because I was kind of confused about the door being open,” Ahmed told WCCO’s Frankie McLister.
The 27-year-old knew something wasn’t right, so he started yelling to get anyone’s attention.
“So then I ran toward the bus and noticed he was having an emergency, so I just hopped on there,” he said.
Try as he might, Ahmed was unable to get the bus to stop by way of the brakes, so he threw it into park.
As he helped the driver, he told the students to call 911.
In a statement, St. Paul Public Schools said the medical emergency occurred on a contracted bus route from Battle Creek Middle School, according to WCCO, which reported that mental health providers at the school provided support for students who were shaken up by the situation.
While the move was heroic, Ahmed says the situation has made him reflect on his life and loved ones.
“It's something you would never think would happen in real life.” he said, later adding, "It's scary. That could've been my sister, my brother, my daughter, my son. It could be my little cousin,” he said. 
It’s also made him reflect on looking out for neighbors and strangers alike.
"It's part of being human. We have feelings and emotions we're supposed to feel. If I were to let him drive away, I would not be human anymore,” he said.
Ahmed said he would like to reunite with the driver and meet his family.
St. Paul Public Schools said the driver was released from the hospital and is resting at home, WCCO reported.

title: Man used sledgehammer to remove head of Iwo Jima monument soldier, police say
text:
QUANTICO, Va. (WUSA) — A man is accused of beheading one of the Marines depicted on the Iwo Jima statue in Quantico, Virginia.
The Prince William County Police Department said officers were called to the statue late Tuesday night.
Officers found 27-year-old Miguel Alonso Maldonado Soriano vandalizing the monument with a sledgehammer, according to police.
Police said Soriano caused hundreds of thousands of dollars in damage to the statue and removed the head of one of the depicted soldiers.
Soriano was arrested and faces charges of felony destruction of property, trespass with intent to damage property and felony injury to a monument.
He was held without bond pending a court appearance.
There is no word on a motive.

title: Why protein is a game-changer for healthy aging
text:
(Aging Untold) — Protein does more than fuel muscle — it supports strength, healing and independence as we get older. But older adults can fall short on their daily needs, especially when appetite shrinks or meals get smaller.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, breaks down why protein matters so much with age and how to get enough of it.
Protein supports more than muscle
“Protein is the raw building blocks that your body is using for muscle, for strength, for inflammation, for healing and for independence,” Rogers said. “So you need protein, but you also need strength training to utilize it.”
As the body ages, it naturally becomes more frail — losing muscle and gaining fat, a condition known as sarcopenia, Rogers said.
“So your body tends to break down tissue more and not build it as fast,” Rogers said.
Illness and surgery raise protein needs
Rogers said chronic conditions, infection, inflammation, surgery or wounds can push the body into what’s called a catabolic state.
“Meaning they’re breaking down tissue faster [than] they’re rebuilding it,” Rogers said. “And if you get too catabolic ... you need much more protein to heal, then you’re going to have poor wound healing and all that. So it’s really, really important.”
How much protein do you actually need?
Rogers said protein needs are typically calculated in grams per kilogram of body weight.
“The general recommendation is about 0.8 to 1g/kg, sometimes 1.8 or more,” Rogers said. “If you’re older you’re going to need more, depending on that condition.”
She cautioned that protein intake should be discussed with a primary care doctor first.
“There’s going to be certain states that you cannot afford that much protein, like kidney disease and things like that,” Rogers said.
Timing and source matter
Rogers said eating protein slows digestion, which helps avoid blood sugar spikes.
“It’s really important to know the source of your protein also, because some of those protein shakes spike your insulin,” Rogers said. “So you want to get a good source.”
Rogers and aging expert Amy O’Rourke recommend eating protein first thing in the morning to help stabilize glucose, then spreading intake throughout the day for a steady source of energy.
“If you don’t have a great appetite, go in small meals throughout the day and then think variety,” O’Rourke said. “Maybe you don’t want to eat your protein. Maybe you want to drink your protein. Maybe you want to have a glass of milk. Maybe you want to have string cheese.”
Don’t skip protein to save money
O’Rourke said cost shouldn’t be a reason to cut back.
“What you’ll pay in debilitation in your body is a lot more expensive than maybe that milk would cost,” O’Rourke said.
O’Rourke also cautioned against relying only on protein shakes without reading labels or considering overall diet balance.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said balance is important.
“We’ve got to have balance, and we’ve got to actually consider and talk about these things with doctors,” Cradduck said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose added that fitness trainers and nutritionists could provide information as well.
“Fitness trainers may be able to give you some guidance on protein as well. Nutritionist[s too]. But no matter what age you are, there’s so many different choices, say for protein powders, and so you have to do some investigating and due diligence on your part,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.
Key takeaways
- Protein supports independence. It helps maintain the muscle strength needed for everyday tasks like climbing stairs or grocery shopping.
- Aging changes how the body uses protein. Older adults are more prone to sarcopenia — muscle loss paired with increased fat—and the body rebuilds tissue more slowly.
- Timing and source matter. Eating protein in the morning and spacing it throughout the day helps stabilize blood sugar and energy; not all protein sources are equal.
- Don’t cut protein to save money. Variety — including milk, string cheese or protein shakes with good labels — can help meet needs without overspending.

title: Major toy companies did not disclose toxic chemicals in Maine
text:
Several manufacturers of popular children’s products disclosed using hazardous chemicals like cancer-causing formaldehyde in other states while failing to report those toxic ingredients to Maine regulators, public records show.
The findings highlight a vulnerability in the state’s public health oversight: laws designed to protect consumers rely on corporate self-reporting, allowing companies to reveal chemical hazards to regulators in some states while keeping local officials and families in the dark.
Investigators at Defend Our Health, a Portland-based advocacy group, uncovered the reporting gap while auditing filings in a multistate chemical clearinghouse shared by Vermont, Washington and Oregon.
In those three states, Crayola reported adding formaldehyde to more than 300 children’s products, including washable felt-tip markers, sticky tubs of finger paint and modeling clay, according to the clearinghouse.
Build-A-Bear Workshop, a retail chain where customers can assemble their own stuffed animals, disclosed the presence of phthalates, arsenic and heavy metals like mercury in toy accessories.
Yet neither company filed the required chemical disclosure documents with Maine authorities before offering those same product lines in local store aisles, according to Defend Our Health and state officials. Neither company replied to phone calls or emails asking why they did not disclose in Maine.
Emily Carey Perez de Alejo, executive director of Defend Our Health, said the discoveries alarmed her. She is the mother of a 4-year-old who regularly uses Crayola art supplies.
“Formaldehyde is a known carcinogen,” she said. “I’m beyond outraged that a trusted brand like Crayola thinks it’s OK to put something so dangerous in a product found in nearly every home and school in the country.”
Perez de Alejo contacted Crayola for an explanation. Initially, a representative told her by email Crayola had never added formaldehyde to its products. Then, after she cited the report filed in Vermont, Crayola told her that it had eliminated formaldehyde in 2025.
However, the company provided no documentation to verify the change, and disclosures in the multistate database continue to list formaldehyde as an active ingredient in Crayola products.
On its website, Crayola maintains that its entire product lineup is safe for children, pointing to third-party evaluations that found no toxic substances in quantities significant enough to harm humans.
Build-A-Bear appears to have removed mercury from all but one of its products, according to its 2025 filings in Vermont. Perez de Alejo recognized that as an improvement, and hoped that Defend Our Health’s calls to the company helped, but said its use in any product remains indefensible.
Enacted in 2008, Maine’s Kid-Safe Products Act protects children by identifying toxic chemicals in consumer products, requiring manufacturers to report their use and encouraging safer alternatives. Implementation rolled out gradually starting in 2011 as the state phased in reporting deadlines and sales bans for specific priority chemicals.
Defend Our Health’s safe kids campaign builds on its past work to track chemical risks in Maine.
After industrial contamination from forever chemicals, or PFAS, polluted local drinking water wells and devastated Maine farms, state lawmakers enacted groundbreaking bans on the use of PFAS-laden sludge fertilizer and PFAS in food packaging and consumer goods.
To help residents navigate store shelves following the consumer goods ban, Defend Our Health scoured the websites of hundreds of cookware manufacturers to compile a searchable directory that identifies thousands of noncompliant products.
The group applied that same strategy to children’s items, converting hard-to-navigate and often obscure regulatory spreadsheets into free searchable tools for parents and consumers.
Doctors say chemicals pose a higher risk to children because their bodies are still growing.
The American Academy of Pediatrics says formaldehyde can trigger severe allergies and increase cancer risks; phthalates can damage the hormone system and disrupt growth; and lead and mercury harm brain function and development.
Under Maine law, manufacturers must disclose any priority toxic additives within 30 days of starting to sell a product in the state. The Department of Environmental Protection confirmed neither Crayola or Build-A-Bear had filed a disclosure.
“If a manufacturer is selling a regulated children’s product that contains an intentionally added priority chemical in the state of Maine without filing a report, they are noncompliant with Maine law,” said Deputy Commissioner Dave Madore.
State officials can demand a certificate of compliance and halt sales of unreported products, he said. After being alerted by Defend Our Health, state officials contacted Crayola regarding those missing reports, he said. The agency did not know about Build-A-Bear’s missing reports.
Maine law permits the sale of products containing priority chemicals as long as manufacturers properly report them, but state regulators rely on those filings to construct legal cases for future bans, Madore said.
Prohibiting a chemical requires substantive evidence and legislative approval, Madore said.
The DEP is working on a way to make these chemical disclosures accessible to Maine residents.

title: Meet the candidates: Tipping and Kenney discuss issues facing UMaine students
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This election season, Orono residents and University of Maine students registered to vote locally will help decide whether incumbent Democratic Sen. Mike Tipping or Republican challenger Leo Kenney will represent Maine Senate District 8 in Augusta.
The Maine Campus interviewed both candidates to understand their perspective on issues affecting the UMaine community, including the university system’s budget deficit and how to address the rising cost of living for students.
Maine Campus: What do you believe is the most pressing issue facing University of Maine students and residents of District 8, and what specific actions would you take to address that issue?
Tipping said that navigating the “increasing costs of tuition, housing and food” is a core concern in District 8. He added that he has made various efforts to address these challenges, including introducing a bill to help Pell Grant recipients afford the cost of attendance and passing a new tax on real estate transfers over $1 million, which “puts that money toward more affordable housing.”
Kenney said the greatest issue is “a lack of opportunity” and jobs that encourage students to stay in the state of Maine. Referencing reports in 2025 that Maine’s average residential electric bills rose more than 36% in a single year, he added that “high energy costs are a major deterrent for companies deciding where they want to invest and grow.” Through reexamining Maine’s energy policies, Kenney said he will “make sure Maine ratepayers aren’t paying more than they should to benefit out-of-state developers.”
Also touching on the issue of affordability, Kenney said he would explore implementing a supplemental Homestead Exemption to help support first-time homeowners and retirees living on fixed incomes. He added that he would “support efforts to increase the supply of housing, so more young people and families can afford to rent or buy in Maine.”
Maine Campus: The University of Maine System is facing a budget deficit and potential faculty and staff layoffs. What role should the state legislature play in addressing these challenges, and would you support increasing state appropriations to the UMaine System?
Tipping said it is clear that “for the past five decades, the state has been systematically underfunding our universities,” and, despite him introducing a bill last year to increase funding for UMaine by $9 million annually, he said the current situation exemplifies why “there is a lot more we need to do.”
“The State of Maine used to cover more than 70% of the costs of the UMaine System. Now it covers just 40% and a majority of the costs are paid by students through tuition,” said Tipping. “Our public universities are the greatest engines of opportunity we possess and we should be investing in them, not defunding them.”
Kenney said it is important to maintain the university’s programs and workforce, describing it as “central” to keeping young people in Maine, but emphasized the importance of “thoroughly” examining the system’s finances before making a decision about increased state appropriations.
“What I can commit to is making sure the university has the support it needs to protect its programs, students and jobs while using public dollars responsibly,” said Kenney. “I’d want to work with UMS leaders, faculty and students to understand the problem before deciding how the state should help.”
Maine Campus: Why do you believe you are well suited to represent District 8 and the interests of the University of Maine community? What efforts have you made while campaigning to connect with voters on campus?
Tipping pointed to his work with student organizations, including a bill he introduced to grant two elected student representatives seats on the UMS Board of Trustees. He said the bill was developed in partnership with UMaine’s student government, with students helping make decisions about the legislation.
Tipping also said he previously served as president of his college student union and has attended various events on campus during his campaign, including a recent joint town hall with Matt Dunlap.
Kenney said his experience as a UMaine graduate, business owner and longtime member of the Orono Town Council and school board makes him well suited to represent the district.
“I was born and raised here, and the University of Maine has always been my backyard,” said Kenney.
Kenney added that he has connected with students through sporting events, club activities, Greek life and canvassing. He said he understands student concerns about “affordability, future jobs and wanting to stay in Maine” and that he will “bring these concerns to Augusta.”
Maine Campus: What is one policy or legislative priority on which you disagree with your opponent, and why should voters in District 8 favor your approach?
Tipping said he opposes Kenney being in favor of “building seven or eight new data centers in Maine.” He added that, in contrast to his opponent, he supports a moratorium on new data centers “until we have a better understanding of their environmental impact and effect on electricity rates for Maine people.”
“I also helped pass the law ensuring that data centers no longer receive state tax subsidies,” said Tipping. “I don’t believe Maine taxpayers should have to pay to subsidize Amazon and Google.”
Kenney said that Tipping voting to support the state’s budget growth each time since taking office has helped exacerbate “housing, energy and everyday costs” and that he would not have supported those proposed increases.
“I believe a more careful approach to spending would help keep Maine affordable for families, students and young people who want to build their lives here, and I would work with colleagues on both sides to find that balance,” said Kenney.
Maine Campus: Is there anything else you’d like to share with the UMaine community ahead of Election Day?
Tipping said that students have the right to vote where they attend college and that registering in Orono does not affect their tuition or financial aid. He also emphasized the importance of student participation, noting that his previous state Senate race was the closest in Maine.
“Your vote makes a big difference here,” said Tipping. “This is an important election. Turnout will be high and you should make sure your voice is heard.”
Kenney said he is “fortunate to have grown up in Orono” and that “the thousands of young people who join our community each year are what make Orono such a vibrant place to live.”
Both candidates encouraged students to vote, noting that early voting is available at the Orono Town Office through Oct. 29, with Election Day voting scheduled for Nov. 3 at the New Balance Field House. To learn more about the upcoming election, students can visit UMaine UVote’s guide or information listed on the Town of Orono’s website.

title: Rape suspect wanted by NYPD for nearly a decade arrested in Westbrook
text:
Man wanted by NYPD for nearly a decade arrested in Westbrook, Maine
A man who has been wanted by the New York City Police Department (NYPD) for the last eight years has been arrested in Westbrook.
The Westbrook Police Department announced on Friday that officers noticed some suspicious activity near an ATM on Main Street at about 3:30 a.m. on Tuesday.
As police spoke with multiple people at the scene, they determined that one of them was Christhian Hernandez Vega, a 30-year-old man wanted by the NYPD for rape.
Vega was arrested as a fugitive from justice and taken to the Cumberland County Jail, pending extradition to New York.

title: Buxton voters approve temporary ban on data centers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Buxton voters approve temporary ban on data centers in Maine town
Voters in Buxton have approved a temporary ban on data centers, as the town joins a growing list of southern Maine communities that have passed similar moratoriums.
Buxton's moratorium, which passed during a special meeting held Wednesday night, restricts data center development for 180 days, retroactive to Aug. 12.
The cities of Sanford and Westbrook, as well as the town of Gray, have approved temporary pauses on data centers that halt applications and construction while local rules are reviewed.
On April 15, the Maine Legislature passed a bill, LD 307, that would have put a temporary moratorium on data centers in the state — a moratorium that would have been the first of its kind in the United States. The legislation would have also required the Maine Department of Energy Resources to create the Maine Data Center Coordination Council to ensure the state is ready for data centers.
Gov. Janet Mills, however, vetoed the bill on April 24. When the bill was passed, a spokesperson for Mills said the governor agreed with lawmakers that the rapid growth of large-scale AI data centers warrants careful evaluation of impacts on public resources, the environment and Maine ratepayers. But Mills also supported an exemption to the law for the proposed data center at the former Jay paper mill, which was not included in the bill passed by the Legislature.
There were not enough votes in the Maine Legislature to override the governor's veto. But on April 29, the same day legislators held that vote, Mills signed an executive order to establish a 15-person Data Center Advisory Council, which will make recommendations on large-scale data center development in Maine. The council must deliver policy recommendations and strategies to the governor and Legislature by Jan. 29, 2027.
In June, Jay officials announced that the owners of the former paper mill put plans to build a data center at the site on hold because the developer backed out of the project.

title: Donald Trump to lift some Canadian tariffs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
President Donald Trump’s administration is planning to lift tariffs on some Canadian imports at the end of the month.
The Wall Street Journal reported Friday afternoon that the change is to help Sen. Susan Collins’ reelection bid. Collins’ office and the White House separately confirmed the changes to the tariffs shortly after.
The change is aimed at benefiting the blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed industries, according to a statement from Collins’ office.
It played into the dueling themes of Collins’ toss-up race with Democrat Troy Jackson. She has built her campaign around her ability to negotiate with those around the Republican president while highlighting her disagreements with him on tariffs and other major issues. Jackson has sought to tie her to the unpopular Trump in a Democratic-leaning state.
Collins’ statement said she had stressed the burdens of high costs on Maine businesses and families to key members of the Trump administration.
“I will continue working directly with [federal] officials to seek additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner,” she said.
The tariff exemptions would apply to packaging materials such as cardboard boxes, plastic crates, bags and film; refrigeration and the machinery used to clean, sort, fill, seal, label and wrap farm and food products; and edible seaweed and algae.
Trump imposed tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian goods in August after trade talks collapsed. Canada answered with its own tariffs last month, though it backed down on a planned 25% levy on Maine lobster before they took effect.
Collins has voted several times to end Trump’s tariffs on Canada while lobbying for item-by-item relief. The administration exempted Canadian road salt and cement in September after she pressed U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
“This is not China we are dealing with,” Collins said in August. “It is Canada, our best friend.”
At a debate last week, Collins cited those exemptions and one for pulp as proof her clout delivers for Maine. Jackson said he would not give her credit for pulling a few items off the tariff list “when we should have never had a list.”
Maine Democratic Party spokesperson Misha Linnehan said Trump knows Collins’ campaign “is in trouble because of her unyielding support for his disastrous agenda.”
“Now, he’s playing politics with our trade policy when Maine businesses and families are already reeling from the chaos of his trade wars,” Linnehan said.
The race is one of a handful that could decide control of the U.S. Senate. The most recent public poll, by Fox News, found the candidates tied at 49% with less than two weeks until Election Day.
Jackson, who was joined by U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at a rally in Portland on Thursday, has held a slight edge in other recent polls. But Collins trailed in every single one in 2020 before handily beating Democrat Sara Gideon.

title: Marshall Faulk diagnosed with Parkinson's disease
text:
Hall of Famer Marshall Faulk diagnosed with Parkinson's disease
Hall of Fame running back and Southern University coach Marshall Faulk has been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.
Faulk revealed his diagnosis on the podcast "The Caring Neurologist" on Wednesday, telling the host, "I want to help as many people as I can."
Video above: Marshall Faulk describes how the Saints' Domecoming game was a sign of the city being reborn
The 53-year-old Faulk said he was not experiencing "issues" beyond hand rigidity and a few tremors, thanks to medication. He doesn't believe the symptoms have gotten worse in the 18 months he's been dealing with the disease.
Faulk initially dismissed the hand rigidity he experienced while golfing as normal nerves but grew concerned when it continued even when he was not competing.
"I just thought it was normal nerves when putting and stuff like that. But it started to be times where I was playing, but I wasn't in a match, and it would still do that. And I was like, 'Wow, is that something, is that normal?' And the doctor was literally like, 'You need to go get checked,'" Faulk said on the podcast.
Faulk is in his first season as Southern's coach after serving as running backs coach at Colorado. He played 12 NFL seasons with the Indianapolis Colts and St. Louis Rams, and was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2011.
The New Orleans native grew up a Saints fan and worked at the Louisiana Superdome as a child. He attended San Diego State University and finished second in the Heisman Trophy voting in 1992. He was also a Heisman finalist in 1991 and 1994.
Faulk was a first-round draft pick of the Colts in 1994 and was named to the All-Rookie Team. In the years to come, he set numerous records leading up to his MVP season in 2000, the same year the Rams beat the Tennessee Titans in the Super Bowl.
He finished his illustrious career with 12,279 rushing yards, 100 rushing touchdowns, as well as 767 receptions for 6,875 receiving yards and 36 receiving touchdowns.
Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder that affects the dopamine-producing neurons in a specific area of the brain called the substantia nigra, according to Parkinson.org. Symptoms generally develop slowly over years. The progression of symptoms is often a bit different from one person to another due to the diversity of the disease. People with Parkinson's may experience tremors, pain in the hands, slowness and paucity of movement, limb stiffness, gait and balance problems.
The disease affects 10 million people worldwide.
The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Maine duck hunter rescued after getting stuck chest-deep in mud
text:
A Maine duck hunter had to be rescued from chest-deep mud Friday after he got stuck trying to retrieve a bird.
The man was roughly 300 feet from shore in Sebasticook Lake when the Newport Fire Department responded around 12:45 p.m., Chief Jeff Chretien said. The man was not injured.
Chretien has never had to rescue a person from mud in more than 26 years, but he said the firefighters all thought on the fly. They came up with the idea of throwing ladders on top of the mud to walk on, which worked.
Once they got close enough to the man, they threw a rope and a sled and they got him free of the mud, Chretien said. He was pulled in the sled to the ladders before walking back to shore.
“We had a hard time getting him out,” Chretien said. “His waders were full. I bet his waders weighed 400 pounds by the time we got him out of it.”
The lake’s water level was low because the dam drained in early September as it does every year, Chretien said.
The dead duck was in the water about another 100 feet from where the man was stuck, Chretien said. Typically the only way for a person to go out and retrieve a duck is by canoe or kayak, he said.
A firefighter let the man borrow a kayak to go retrieve the duck after the rescue, Chretien said. A Maine game warden asked the man to retrieve the duck.
“If you do something dumb, you still shot an animal,” Chretien said. “It’s your job to take care of it.”

title: Trump at South Florida rally revives the idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran
text:
Trump at South Florida rally revives the idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran
President Donald Trump on Friday told a rally for candidates in South Florida that U.S. warships returning from the Middle East could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war, his latest suggestion of taking an interventionist approach to the nearby country.
Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days ahead of midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the U.S. war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries.
"We'll do a little stopover," Trump said. "Actually, what we're going to do with Cuba is, we're going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They'll raise up their hands. And then we're going to send (Secretary of State) Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal."
Both Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would "be next" in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.
In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of U.S. military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island's former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous U.S. presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that "it looks like I'll be the one that does it."
Rubio told reporters separately that Cuba has been a national security threat for years because of its ties to U.S. adversaries and that Trump is intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wants to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the U.S. could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island's current government.
Moments after Trump spoke at the rally, Rubio posted on social media that "now is the time" for action on Cuba, addressing his post "to those who seek to create positive change" and urging them "to seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA."
Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a Sept. 29 interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.
"The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn't have a functional economy and it's governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that's never worked," Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.
"We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they're facing," he said. "We're never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear."
Rubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. But the U.S. side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.
During his address to the United Nations General Assembly last month, Trump said Rubio — son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba's socialist leadership — was "deep into negotiations with Cuba," saying he would "not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep."
Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries "will make a deal," adding, "I don't think we'll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly."
Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington's decades-long economic embargo against Havana.
Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk, and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have migrated, many to the United States.
___
Kinnard reported from Columbia, S.C., and can be reached at http://x.com/MegKinnardAP. AP Diplomatic Writer Matthew Lee contributed from Washington.

title: Inside the high-tech lab where fake patients help save real lives
text:
NEW ORLEANS (InvestigateTV) - The patient is struggling to breathe. Monitors are beeping. Medical students are checking lung sounds, reading vital signs and preparing for the next step.
But this is not a real emergency room.
The simulators can speak, breathe, blink, show a pulse and change condition based on what students do next.
The goal is to give future doctors hands-on practice before they face life-or-death moments with real patients.
“Before it used to be you practiced on patients. Now you practice on plastic before you even touch a patient,” said Dr. Peter DeBlieux, assistant dean for LSU Health New Orleans’ Center for Advanced Learning and Simulation.
Behind the scenes, a simulation team controls the patient’s voice, vital signs and medical outcome in real time. If students miss something, the patient can get worse. If they respond correctly, the patient can stabilize.
The training is not limited to medical students. Doctors, nurses and other health professionals also train at the center, often in teams meant to mirror the pace and pressure of a real hospital.
“Since 2000, LSU has invested millions in the space of simulation, not just for medical students and not just for residents in training but also we have practicing physicians across the country that come to do simulation training here,” DeBlieux said.
DeBlieux said the technology has changed dramatically over the past 25 years, moving from basic CPR mannequins to simulators that can connect to ventilators, monitors and other equipment. LSU Health New Orleans says some simulators can cost up to $200,000 each.
“You can create a rare disease and then standardize it so that everyone in the class may not ever see it in a hospital setting or in a clinic setting, but can practice and train in this setting,” DeBlieux said.
The center has also had to rebuild. Its first simulation center opened in 2000, but Hurricane Katrina flooded the facility and destroyed equipment. LSU later rebuilt the center with more space and more advanced technology.
After each scenario, students go through a debrief to review what worked and what did not. Then they do it again.
“This simulator we have, it blinks, it breathes, it talks,” fourth-year medical student Lindzi Paul said. “It was a really good experience.”
Fourth-year medical student Aysha Gibson said the training feels real.
“You really take it personally if you’re able to save this patient or treat this patient properly,” Gibson said.
Gibson said the technology could help shape the future of medical care.
“I think this technology really will help form the next generation of doctors,” Gibson said.
DeBlieux said the benefit extends beyond the classroom.
“So for over 25 years, all of the LSU graduates in New Orleans have benefitted from training in simulation, which means our community has benefitted,” DeBlieux said.
The center plans to add artificial intelligence and virtual reality headsets as it raises money for the next step in medical training.

title: Maine’s youngest children need Head Start. A proposed federal rule puts it at risk.
text:
Deirdre Burns Mondor, MD, MPH, is a primary care pediatrician in York County.
The first few years of a child’s life shape much of what comes after. By the time a child starts kindergarten, the brain has already done a remarkable amount of growing, and the experiences and relationships of those early years help set the course for learning, behavior and health for years to come.
As a pediatrician, I see the difference a strong start makes, and I see how hard it can be to catch up without one.
Last year, Head Start marked its 60th anniversary. In that time, it has transformed the lives of more than 40 million children nationally. It has lasted because it is more than a classroom. Along with early learning, Head Start connects children and families to healthcare, developmental screening, nutrition and support for parents. Research shows that, by age 2, children in Early Head Start show stronger cognitive, language and social-emotional skills than their peers who aren’t in the program.
Here, Head Start is a federal-state-local partnership investing in Maine’s children, families and workforce. It prepares children for school success, supports working families and brings federal dollars into Maine communities. Maine also puts in its own money to support program expansion, and that investment strengthens Head Start’s ability to reach more children.
For a pediatrician, one part of that work especially stands out: supporting children with delayed milestones or disabilities. Head Start is a key partner in the early identification of special needs and ensures children with developmental needs receive support as early as possible.
Last year, 217 preschoolers and 46 infants and toddlers in Maine Head Start were newly identified as eligible for special education or early intervention services. A delay caught at age 2 instead of age 5 can mean years of help that change the course of a child’s schooling.
A proposed federal rule would pull in the other direction.
The Department of Health and Human Services has proposed stripping away many of the standards at the heart of Head Start. It would drop the requirement to screen every child within weeks of enrolling, and the requirement to make sure a problem, once found, is followed up and treated. It would also end the requirement to check, within 90 days, whether each child has a regular doctor and dentist.
Each of these standards matters. Together, they are what make Head Start work. The harm of this proposal is cumulative. Weakening several parts of the program at once means children are less likely to get the support they need, and the families facing the most barriers will feel it first.
We could expect a delay in children receiving appropriate medical care to address issues that directly affect academic performance and behavior in the classroom (e.g., hearing deficits, sleep apnea, asthma, to name a few).
Not only does early intervention improve the confidence and performance of children in the classroom, but identifying deficits and providing services prior to kindergarten is proven to save costs for our schools and communities in the long-run.
After 60 years, Head Start remains one of the best examples we have of an early investment that pays off for children, families and communities. I urge Sen. Collins, Sen. King, Rep. Pingree and Rep. Golden to ask HHS to rescind this proposed rule and protect the standards that give Maine’s youngest children a strong start.

title: Obituary: Terry Lee Welch
text:
WINTER HAVEN, Fla. – Terry Lee Welch, 78, passed away on Oct. 14, 2026, in Winter Haven, Florida, following a brief illness.
Terry was born on March 27, 1948, in Gorham, to Andrew Dionne and Arlene (Shane) Dionne. She attended Gorham schools and, after raising her family, pursued her passion for hairstyling by attending Headhunters School of Hair Design. She earned her cosmetology license in 1987 and spent the next 35 years serving countless loyal clients from her home salon. Terry loved her work and treasured the many friendships she built along the way.
In 1971, she married Henry “Skip” Welch, and together they raised their family in Westbrook. After retiring in 2011, they moved to Florida. Although they enjoyed their Florida home, Maine always remained close to Terry’s heart. For many years, they returned each summer to Sebago Lake, continuing the tradition until 2023, when Alzheimer’s disease made travel and caregiving more challenging.
Terry was an enthusiastic bingo player, Scrabble enthusiast and devoted Texas Hold’em competitor. She enjoyed participating in tournaments and played in casinos throughout the United States and the Bahamas. Whether competing in a major casino tournament or playing in the semi-weekly $10 Texas Hold’em games at her retirement community clubhouse, she loved the excitement, camaraderie, and competition.
Above all, Terry was a kind and caring soul. She treated everyone she met with warmth, respect, and compassion and was always willing to help those in need, especially family members and those less fortunate. Anyone who knew Terry knew that if she saw someone asking for help at a traffic light, she would roll down her window, offer a smile, and hand over a few dollars without hesitation.
Terry’s greatest joy in life was her family. She was a devoted mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother who took immense pride in her children and the people they became. Her family’s guiding principle was simple: “Always be kind. It’s not that hard.” Having become a mother at a young age, Terry was blessed to watch all of her grandchildren grow into adulthood, and she was immensely proud of each of them. A close-knit family that cared deeply for one another meant everything to her, and she cherished the strong bonds they shared.
The last three years of Terry’s life were marked by the challenges of Alzheimer’s Disease, yet she faced them with remarkable grace and determination. She continued to embrace life, finding joy in everyday moments. Her quick wit and sharp sense of humor remained with her until the very end. Simple pleasures, including her regular trips to Wendy’s for lunch and Dairy Queen for a vanilla cone, brought her happiness and became cherished rituals until her stroke.
Terry is survived by her loving husband of 55 years, Henry “Skip” Welch; her children, Denise Usher and her husband Jeff of Buxton, Debbie Strout and her husband Scott of North Yarmouth, Jeff Morris and his wife Nerine of Gorham, and Marcie Aube and her husband Jason of Gorham; her grandchildren, Nichole, Shawna, Andrew, Ackelia, Josh, and Matt; and her great-grandchildren, Asyia and Kane. She is survived by her brother Larry and his partner Sandra from Arizona, and her sister Jeannette and her husband Sherrill from Gorham. She was predeceased by her parents; her brother, Harland; and her sisters, Virginia, Helen, and Kate.
A special thanks to her best friend Carolyn Mooney, who was always there to take her to bingo, get her nails done, take her to lunch, or provide caregiving support whenever it was needed.
A private graveside service for family will be held at a later date.

title: Bodycam video shows moments leading up to officer shooting HeeHaw, a beloved pet donkey
text:
CEDARTOWN, Ga. (Gray News) — Body camera video has been released of a police shooting in August that killed a beloved pet donkey.
Video from Cedartown police shows a 1-year-old donkey named HeeHaw trotting toward officers. According to an incident report, an officer tried to scare HeeHaw away with a Taser, but police said he kept coming back.
One officer then fired one shot that killed the animal.
HeeHaw was shot in his own pasture. Officers were on the property searching for a local missing child. Police said the child was later found at a church near the pasture where HeeHaw was killed.
HeeHaw’s owner, Hannah Israel, said her farm is “definitely not the same” without her beloved pet.
Israel told ANF that HeeHaw was simply saying “hello” to the officers because he loved people. The body camera video shows him running toward the officers while braying.
“That would be normal for him because he’s saying hi. That’s what donkeys do. That’s just being a donkey,” Israel told ANF.
Israel said she had bottle-raised HeeHaw from birth inside her home. The baby donkey participated in petting zoos at their farm and mobile petting zoos around the community.
Israel said HeeHaw loved all animals and people, and that he never knew a stranger.
Israel is now suing the officer who shot HeeHaw, identified as Trenton Garner. The lawsuit alleges that officers entered Israel’s pasture without permission and shot HeeHaw without justification.
Garner is fighting the lawsuit. His lawyers said he reasonably believed that HeeHaw posed an immediate threat to another officer. They also said they did not need a warrant to search the pasture.
The shooting has sparked outrage online. The family has started a GoFundMe to help pay for legal fees.

title: Florida officer took possession of man’s home after finding him dead 4 years ago, police say
text:
(AP) - A Florida police officer who found a man dead during a welfare check in 2022 is accused of taking possession of the man’s home and impersonating him for years while fixing up the place, authorities said.
The officer said he took possession of the property weeks after discovering the homeowner’s body to “prevent squatters from taking control of it,” according to a court document he filed.
Investigators in South Florida have accused Lauderhill police officer Brian Sguros of carrying out a “complex scheme” to take control of the $400,000 home. They say he made it appear the man was still alive by using his identification to pay taxes on the property and obtain permits to make repairs.
Sguros was arrested this week and charged with five felonies, including official misconduct and criminal use of deceased personal identification. He appeared in court at a brief hearing on Wednesday and then dashed away from reporters outside.
Messages seeking comment were left Thursday with one of his attorneys and Sguros, who has been suspended from his job.
Court documents in a related civil case show that the officer’s attempt to take possession of the two-story house in a tidy neighborhood just outside Fort Lauderdale became known after a real estate group bought the house from the man’s relatives in 2025.
Sguros said in an affidavit that in August 2022 — less than a month after he found Dennis West dead inside the Lauderhill home — he took possession of the property and spent the next 2 1/2 years making repairs, spending more than $200,000 of his own money.
He said the house had been filled with trash, that its roof was partially collapsed and that the structure was unstable.
Sguros said in another court document that he took over the property “believing that by cleaning, securing, and restoring a dangerous and abandoned residence he was acting lawfully and responsibly to protect the surrounding community.”
He argued that he made no attempts to hide what he was doing.
But investigators with Broward County Sheriff’s Office said the deception began when the officer told the county medical examiner that he was friends with West, who had died of natural causes, and that the man had no family, which was not true.
Sguros paid taxes and utilities at the home in West’s name, and forged his signature to get permits for work at the home, the sheriff’s office said. Investigators said Sguros also used his access to law enforcement databases to find information about West.
The officer in February 2025 filed paperwork with the county appraiser stating his possession of the home. But after the real estate group later acquired deeds to the property, he filed a civil case against the company seeking to be reimbursed for the money he spent on repairs.

title: US tourist in Italy falls 1,000 feet to death on mountain hike
text:
US tourist in Italy falls 1,000 feet to death on mountain hike
A Florida woman died after plunging more than 1,000 feet while hiking in the Italian Dolomite mountains, according to police in the northern city of Trentino.
Her death on Saturday was announced late this week after her next of kin were notified, police say.
Michelle Alejandra Rubio-Leiva, who was 36 and from Miami, was on vacation with family members on the Forcella Pordoi trail, a high-altitude site in the Sella group of the Dolomites, when she fell, police told CNN.
The UNESCO World Heritage Site, known for its sweeping views and zig-zag canyon, is only accessible by cable car and reaches 9,344 feet at its highest.
Rubio-Leiva’s sister, who was with her at the time, alerted emergency services, which dispatched a team of specialists from the Trentino Alpine and Cave Rescue Services and a rescue helicopter to descend to the spot from where her body was eventually recovered.
The two women had left the trail to reach a steep exposed spot on an upper cliff to take a picture when Rubio-Leiva slipped and fell into the canyon below, according to emergency workers who described the accident to local media. Rubio-Leiva’s family members were airlifted to Canazei while her body was retrieved, the local carabinieri told CNN. The recovery operation lasted several hours.
The hiking area is extremely dangerous and known for steep inclines, loose gravel and falling rocks, according to the Italian Alpine Rescue unit, which told CNN that more than 80 people died in the Dolomites in 2026 so far.

title: Susan Collins uses Troy Jackson’s ‘shut up’ debate line in new ad
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins is out with a new ad capitalizing on her opponent Troy Jackson’s debate comment telling her to “shut up.”
“Troy has something to say to Maine women. Shut up,” the ad’s narrator says.
It is airing with the race a coin flip less than two weeks out. The Republican senator and Jackson were tied at 49% among likely voters in a Fox News poll released Thursday. The ad references a comment Jackson made during a debate Oct. 15, after Collins said a person disrupting the event was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters.”
Jackson responded: “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.”
He added later that he didn’t regret the statement and that he had no idea who the person interrupting the debate was. The Sunrise Movement, a progressive group, later claimed the protester as a member. He was not among the supporters Jackson invited.
Collins’ campaign has tied the remark to Jackson’s temper as Maine Senate president. She told Fox News host Sean Hannity the next day that it was telling.
“I thought about the reputation that Troy Jackson has in Augusta, particularly when he is dealing with women with whom he disagrees,” Collins said.
Jackson campaign spokesperson Maggie Amjad called the new ad part of a series of personal attacks.
“Maine women know which candidate is fighting for them, and it’s Troy Jackson,” Amjad said in a statement.
Collins, the only Republican running this year in a state Kamala Harris carried in 2024, is seeking a sixth term. Jackson, a Democrat, is a former Maine Senate president and logger.
Collins has not led a public poll since late September, but she trailed in every one in 2020 before handily beating Democrat Sara Gideon. Decision Desk HQ, the BDN’s election results partner, gives Jackson a 56% chance of winning.
BDN writer Michael Shepherd contributed to this report.

title: Police reportedly assaulted by parents after ‘black magic’ reported in Charlotte neighborhood
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - Two parents were accused of assaulting police officers after the couple was reportedly engaging in “black magic rituals” at a house in North Carolina.
A criminal affidavit revealed the alleged incident happened on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at a home in east Charlotte.
The affidavit said Charlotte-Mecklenburg police were sent to the house after a concerned neighbor called 911. The document said the neighbor reported the parents were “performing black magic rituals,” “burning things,” and that there was “loud screaming.”
The neighbor also allegedly said the mother’s face was black and purple and she appeared to have been abused.
When police got to the neighborhood, they heard screaming and saw things being thrown inside the house.
Officers found both live and spent .22 rounds, broken items, and drops of blood on the front porch of the home.
As police walked toward the door, the affidavit said “the front door swung open,” and the two parents and four kids were staring out at them. The kids were aged 14, 11, 5, and 3 years old, according to the document.
What police found inside
Once inside the house, officers reportedly found the home in “complete disarray and in no shape for such small children.”
The affidavit said nearly every piece of decor and furniture was destroyed. Large knives, blow-torch lighters and other dangerous items were also reportedly left out in the open.
The document said the family made “non-sensical” statements to police, and at first told officers they were cleaning. They then allegedly claimed someone broke in and caused the damage.
Police assaulted by parents
At some point while police were inside the home, the affidavit said the father “began acting erratically” and tried to rub garlic and a Bible on the officers. While that was going on, the mother allegedly started “speaking fast and irate.”
Then, as police were looking around the house, both parents reportedly started screaming.
The father then started spraying down one of the kids with cologne and started moving toward a large butcher knife. The affidavit said a child then told police “she was not okay and was scared to be at the house.”
The affidavit said the father started throwing cloves of garlic at one of the officers. The mother then allegedly grabbed an officer’s neck, and when police tried to put the father in handcuffs, the mother tried to bite the officer’s leg.
Once outside, the mother allegedly spit at officers and spit inside the police car multiple times.
Parents charged
Court records identified the parents as 35-year-old Gabriel Antonio Santos-Funes and 33-year-old Maria Valladares.
Both parents were charged with several counts of misdemeanor child abuse, along with resisting an officer, assaulting a government employee, and other offenses.
Following their arrests, they were taken to the Mecklenburg County jail.
