title: InvestigateTV+: Perimenopause still poorly understood
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Experts say the transition period before menopause—perimenopause—is still poorly understood, leaving many women blindsided by dozens of symptoms and a frustrating search for answers. InvestigateTV+ takes an in-depth look at the knowledge gap, why diagnosis can be difficult and the complicated history of one of the most effective treatment options.
Plus, after a campfire sparks a massive Minnesota wildfire, we follow one community’s road to recovery and the neighbors who stepped up to help families rebuild.
Perimenopause still poorly understood
Perimenopause is defined as the phase when the ovaries gradually produce less estrogen. It can begin anywhere from eight to 10 years before menopause.
The most common signs of perimenopause, like those of menopause, are hot flashes, weight gain and mood changes, in addition to at least 31 other symptoms, according to doctors.
It remains under-recognized both among the medical community and the women who experience it.
Recovering after a wildfire
A campfire grew into the Camp House fire, torching thousands of acres of forest and more than 180 homes, cabins and outbuildings.
In the year since, the devastated residents of Brimson have gotten an unwanted crash course in disaster recovery.
Where fake patients save real lives
The patient is struggling to breathe. Monitors are beeping. Medical students are checking lung sounds, reading vital signs and preparing for the next step.
But this is not a real emergency room.
At LSU Health New Orleans, students are training on high-tech medical simulators built to look, feel and respond like people in crisis.
The cats helping volunteers
Giving time through volunteer work can make a big difference for the cause, but also for the volunteer. Research shows volunteering can offer benefits for mental health.
The Mayo Clinic says it can reduce stress and increase feel-good hormones in the brain. Volunteering can also provide purpose.
At the Cat Alliance Team Sanctuary in Sherwood, Oregon, it’s hard to tell the difference between who’s helping and who’s being helped. The volunteers say they get so much out of their time there.

title: $5K reward offered for missing drone boat in Gulf of Maine
text:
A $5,000 reward is being offered for a missing drone boat in the Gulf of Maine.
The drone boat went missing about 30 nautical miles southeast of Frenchman Bay, where it was awaiting recharge, on the night of Oct. 12, according to the Maine Lobstermen’s Association.
When a boat was dispatched that week to search for the yellow uncrewed vessel, there was no sign of it, likely indicating the drone boat is adrift in the gulf. It is equipped with float bags, which would prevent it from sinking.
The drone boat, which is about 16 feet long and 4.5 feet wide, was monitoring a harmful algal bloom in the Gulf of Maine.
The drone has markings reading “Uncrewed Surface Vehicle” and “SeaTrac.”
It is operated by a team from Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in Massachusetts and Northeastern Regional Association of Coastal Ocean Observing Systems in New Hampshire.
The lobstermen’s association advised anyone who spots the drone boat to report its location and not attempt to recover it. Anyone who tries to recover it does so at their own risk and should exercise caution and not remove the drone boat from the water.
Sightings can be reported to Mike Brosnahan at mbrosnahan@whoi.edu or 508-289-3633.

title: L.C.S. Hosts 3rd Annual Anti-Bullying Color Run
text:
LIMESTONE, Maine (WAGM) - Two county schools turned bullying awareness into a colorful afternoon today. This afternoon LCS hosted their 3rd annual “Too Cool to be a Bully” Color Run. Every student at Limestone Community School and Dawn F. Barnes Elementary took part. Students ran laps behind the school while getting covered in colored powder. Kids say it’s a fun way to promote bullying awareness. And over the last three years, they say it’s made a real impact.
“It’s a run just to show that we don’t accept bullying here and we should just all be kind. It’ll affect so many and sometimes we see it and we don’t even notice it. I feel like it honestly helps. I feel like there’s definitely a lot less bullying going on here at our two schools as there has been in the past,” said Charlotte Tibbert, one of the LCS Color Run participants.
“It’s a big problem and I think that it might not help as much as we want it to, but it’ll help a little bit. If there’s something going on, cyberbullying, talk to somebody about it,” added Landyn Richardson, another participant.
Limestone and Caswell students ended the day with a little bit of color to remind them to be kind to one another.

title: Meghan Markle’s father investigated for child pornography, reports say
text:
(Gray News) - Meghan Markle’s father Thomas Markle is allegedly being investigated for possession of child sexual abuse material, according to multiple reports.
The allegations against Markle Sr. were first reported Thursday by The Sun newspaper by his son.
Thomas Markle Jr. informed police that he allegedly found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images in boxes at his father’s home in the Philippines.
The Sun published a photo that it said showed Markle Jr. signing a sworn statement that he had submitted to police and quoted him as saying: “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.”
In a rare statement, Meghan said she was “deeply distressed” by her estranged father’s allegations, adding she was informed by police of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018, NBC News reported.

Meghan said that she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.”
“I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed,” she said.
Markle Sr., 82, denied the reported allegations, calling them “sick lies.” He added they were “the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”

title: 2 Maine healthcare providers accused of violations by state
text:
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services took action against two Portland behavioral health companies that receive federal funds through MaineCare, according to records from the agency’s program integrity unit.
DHHS suspended Medicaid payments to Maine Connect Care earlier this year and another company, USA Family Wellbeing, has received violation notices for alleged overbilling, according to letters sent to the providers.
Both providers were included in a confidential list of criminal division cases the Office of the Maine Attorney General accidentally sent on Oct. 8 to reporters and other recipients outside the office. Neither company appears to have been charged in state or federal court, according to a review of online records. A spokesperson for the attorney general’s office said Thursday that she had no information to share about either company.
Neither company responded to calls and emails on Thursday seeking comment.
The attorney general’s document says the office got not response to “multiple inquiries” it made to federal prosecutors about whether these two matters, “along with a group of other matters/investigations with similar allegations,” would be pursued federally. A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Maine said he could not comment under federal policy.
The U.S. Centers for Medicaid and Medicare announced this month that it was auditing the state for fraud; its administrator, Dr. Mehmet Oz, and Vice President JD Vance have both accused Maine officials of turning a blind eye to fraud.
Maine has suspended payments to at least five providers this year, according to information the state shared in August. DHHS spokesperson Lindsay Hammes said in an email Thursday that the department refers cases to law enforcement, including the attorney general’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit, any time it’s made aware of a credible allegation of MaineCare fraud.
She said the department doesn’t provide information about those referrals to protect the integrity of the investigations.
DHHS suspended Medicaid payments to Maine Connect Care on Jan. 30, according to a letter the agency sent via certified mail. The letter stated that DHHS is required to suspend payments when there’s been an allegation of fraud, and that the suspension will last either until it’s been determined there was no fraud, or until any criminal or civil prosecutions have resolved.
The letter said there have been “general allegations” of billing for services not rendered, billing for individuals who aren’t eligible for MaineCare reimbursements, and billing for services provided by unlicensed individuals.
USA Family Wellbeing, meanwhile, has appealed a notice of violation that it received from DHHS in July. The state is seeking more than $1.7 million for overpayment it made, citing a review of MaineCare claims between March 1, 2021, and Dec. 31, 2022, according to a letter the agency sent to the provider. The claims included payments for community support services, competency evaluations, behavioral health counseling and language interpretation services. 
USA Family Wellbeing had also received a notice of violation in 2024, which resulted in the company paying back more than $71,000 over the following year, according to DHHS.
USA Family Wellbeing has not had its payments suspended, according to DHHS.
The allegations raised in the DHHS documents appear to match similar accusations made in the confidential report inadvertently released by the attorney general’s office, which stated that Maine Connect Care and USA Family Wellbeing face allegations that included “phony billing” and “billing for noncovered services.”
That report, which the office has declined to discuss, also included homicide cases, alleged healthcare crimes, drug investigations and appeals. Most of the matters match what’s been filed publicly in court, but it appears some have not been made public.
The description in the report for a matter involving USA Family Wellbeing included an allegation of services being provided by an unlicensed person, and that the company was accused of a “potential theft of $1.58 million.”
The loss described in the description about Maine Connect Care “looks to exceed about $400,000,” the document stated.
Staff Writer Joe Lawlor contributed to this story.

title: Daycare operator arrested after viral video seemingly shows kids fighting in her home
text:
SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WNDU/Gray News) - A daycare operator is facing charges after a viral video allegedly showed kids fighting inside her home in Indiana.
Tysharae Jones, 29, faces charges of battery with injury to a person under 14, neglect of a dependent resulting in bodily injury and contributing to the delinquency of a minor.
Police said the fight happened in June 2026. The special victims unit with the prosecutor’s office has been handling the case.

title: Maine cannot afford to lose Sen. Susan Collins in Washington
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Timothy S. Hodgdon is president/CEO of Hodgdon Shipbuilding in East Boothbay. Hodgdon Shipbuilding was founded in 1816, four years before Maine became a state.
As a business owner in Maine, I want to express my strong support for Sen. Susan Collins in the upcoming election. I am increasingly concerned that backlash from the current political landscape could turn what should otherwise be a strong race for Sen. Collins into a much more difficult contest in November.
Here are the facts.
Sen. Collins has served Maine for decades, and during that time she has consistently worked to bring federal resources and opportunities back to our state. Her seniority and experience in Washington, and particularly her position as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, give Maine an important voice and critical influence when decisions are made regarding federal funding and priorities.
The Appropriations Committee plays a central role in determining discretionary federal spending, making this position particularly consequential for a state the size of Maine. That influence has produced significant, tangible results for Maine, which cannot be delivered by an inexperienced U.S. Senate replacement.
Sen. Collins’ work has supported BIW, UMaine, transportation/infrastructure projects and hundreds of other initiatives throughout all 16 Maine counties. According to Sen. Collins’ office, she has helped secure nearly $1.5 billion in Congressionally Directed Spending for 672 projects since 2021.
I believe Maine voters need to look carefully at what Sen. Collins’ position in the Senate means for our state and what will be lost if she is no longer representing Maine in Washington.
The televised debates between Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson raise a fundamental question: How many times must Sen. Collins correct the record before those corrections are given their due?
Throughout these debates, she has repeatedly addressed Jackson’s claims about her position on the Iran war, her voting record on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and her relationship with President Donald Trump (among other questionable statements).
Sen. Collins has explained that she voted nine times to end the Iran war, defended her decision to oppose the One Big Beautiful Bill Act at final passage and challenged what she considers misleading characterizations of her relationship with the president.
Yet Jackson frequently returns to the same accusations, seemingly disregarding the explanations and responses she has already provided. Vigorous debate and legitimate criticism are essential to our political process. But voters deserve more than repeated allegations and selective interpretations of a candidate’s record. They deserve a fair opportunity to hear the answers, consider the context and judge the facts for themselves.
When a candidate responds directly to an accusation, that response should be part of the discussion — not simply brushed aside as the same accusation is repeated. The real issue is not whether Sen. Collins’ record should be scrutinized; it absolutely should be. It is whether that scrutiny is being conducted fairly, accurately and with due regard for the facts.
Maine voters deserve a debate that informs rather than misleads, and that evaluates candidates on their complete records rather than on accusations repeated often enough to create an impression. It is also significant that Sen. Collins is the only Republican in either the House of Representatives or the Senate from New England, which results in an unhealthy partisan position, regardless of your party affiliation.
Replacing her with a first-term senator would represent a substantial loss of seniority, institutional knowledge, leadership and demonstrated ability to secure federal resources, an outcome that we cannot afford.
To say it frankly, there is no opponent who can fill Sen. Collins’ shoes as our senator from Maine. Her record, experience and performance all speak for themselves. Maine needs Susan Collins to stay in the Senate.

title: Airbnb guests no longer have to wash dishes, strip the beds at checkout
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - Airbnb guests can say goodbye to checkout chores like washing dishes, stripping beds and taking out the trash under a new policy announced this week.
The short-term rental platform’s new rules limit hosts to “reasonable” checkout requests beginning on Nov. 20. Guests can still be asked to leave dishes in the sink, gather used towels and sort trash and recycling, but hosts generally cannot require chores typically handled by professional cleaners.
“Remember to think like a guest and keep in mind what you’d find unreasonable,” Airbnb tells hosts in a video announcing the new policy.
Checkout chores have been a recurring point of contention for Airbnb guests, particularly when they’re also paying cleaning fees. The company has previously acknowledged that those fees can create different expectations between hosts and travelers.
Airbnb said exceptions may apply in certain circumstances, such as requiring guests to put trash in animal-proof containers in areas with bears.
Hosts must now also disclose all house rules and requests in a designated section of their listing before guests book, according to Airbnb. They can no longer add extra requirements through messages, signs inside the property or other sections of a listing.
As part of the changes, Airbnb said it is standardizing house rules into seven categories, covering topics including overnight guests, quiet hours, pets, smoking and whether guests must lock up at checkout.
The changes build on Airbnb’s broader efforts to make booking a rental more predictable for travelers. In 2023, CEO Brian Chesky acknowledged that the variety of properties on Airbnb creates uncertainty among guests.
“A lot of guests have described booking Airbnb, once they check in, it’s a moment of truth. Is the house exactly what they expected?” he told The Associated Press. “We don’t want this to be a moment of truth. We want you to know exactly what you’re going to get before you book.”

title: $5K reward offered after uncrewed vessel goes missing off Maine coast
text:
A research team has reestablished communication with an uncrewed vessel that it had lost track of in the Gulf of Maine on Oct. 12.
The vessel, a SeaTrac USV, was located roughly 90 miles off the coast of Gloucester, Massachusetts, the Northeastern Regional Association of Coastal Ocean Observing Systems said in an update Friday night.
The SeaTrac was about 30 miles southeast of Frenchman Bay when the project team lost contact with it, according to a notice from the regional association that was shared by the Maine Lobstermen’s Association.
Researchers had offered a $5,000 reward for the public’s help locating the vessel, which was monitoring a harmful algal bloom in the Gulf of Maine.
The team plans to recover the vessel on Sunday, according to Friday’s update.

title: What house is Maine’s oldest?
text:
In our series AskME, we explore your questions about Maine's history, culture and customs. What have you been wondering? We’ll work to find an answer. Explore the questions, or submit your own, at pressherald.com/ask-me.
Maine has one of the oldest housing stocks in the country, with hundreds of structures dating to pre-Revolutionary War times. But which home is actually the oldest?
It’s a little hard to pinpoint exactly when the first residence in Maine was built, State Historian Earle G. Shettleworth says. Countless historic homes have been lost to fires, Colonial warfare or age.
There are remains of a 17th- and 18th-century fishing village in Bristol, hints of 13,000-year-old Paleoamerican life in Rangeley’s western peaks, and an ever-present history of Indigenous tribes occupying Maine’s lands for thousands of years.
But possibly the oldest surviving English home in Maine is the McIntire Garrison House in York.
The dark two-story home sits in a salt marsh, unoccupied as it keeps watch over the York River, as it has for hundreds of years. But even its exact conception date has been debated.
Records show that the McIntire Garrison House was built sometime between 1707 and 1713, though the “legendary traditional date of construction is 1645,” according to an original nomination form that, in the 1960s, earned the house a spot on the National Register of Historic Places.
The Old York Historical Society’s Executive Director Catherine Duffy said locals may have incorrectly estimated the home’s age because dating technology wasn’t nearly as accurate as it is today.
In January 2024, researchers set out to get a final answer through a dendrochronological study, or the science of dating wooden artifacts through tree ring growth patterns. They took core samples from several of the home’s thick timbers and analyzed the rings under a microscope. The results showed that most of the timbers were felled primarily in the winter of 1712, with one piece dating to 1713. A plaque on the side of the home still reflects the nomination document.
The house remained in the McIntire family for more than 300 years until it was handed over to the historical society in 2024.
In the 1660s, Micum McIntire arrived in York County — then part of the Massachusetts Bay Colony — after being deported from England for supporting Scotland during the Third English Civil War, according to state records. He was sold as an indentured servant to work in New Hampshire sawmills, and one in South Berwick. He would stay there until 1668, when he found himself in York’s Scotland district.
It was there that he got his first land grant, married his wife, Dorothy, and had three sons, including John McIntire, who later built the home.
The name “Garrison” refers to a style of colonial architecture that originated in New England in the 17th-century. It’s both functional and aesthetic. The second floor juts out slightly over the ground floor, fortifying it against overhead attacks, and giving the home a sleek look.
The building was never officially used for anything other than a family home, though John’s granddaughter several generations later, Mary McIntire, set it up as a museum with classical furnishings and vignettes for visitors. A break-in in the 1960s or ’70s led the family to remove everything from the home.
It was used mostly for storage after a restoration in 1910, and the last McIntire moved out in the 1920s. But the family still holds yearly reunions in York, using their ancestral home as a centerpiece for the celebration, Duffy said.
“The fact that it’s remained in the same family line since the early 1700s is a pretty remarkable piece of history on its own,” Duffy said. Only a handful of other historic homes in the state can make that claim.
Duffy says the McIntire Garrison House is unsafe for visitors right now, but crews have been working on restoring it since 2025. They’re starting with a revamp of a cider house behind the residence, which dates to the early 1800s. Eventually, after lots of work in several phases, she hopes it’ll become an interactive glimpse into York’s history.
Archaeologist and Salem State University professor Dr. Emerson Baker says there are some other old houses that could one day dethrone the McIntire Garrison House, once they’re officially dated. Others have tried, like Bray House in Kittery which was proven to be close to 100 years younger than the owner claimed.
For now, the McIntire Garrison House remains the oldest English home in the state.

INDEPENDENCE, Mo. (KCTV/Gray News) - A man in Missouri is accused of killing his girlfriend while she visited him in the hospital, according to authorities.
James F. Lawson was charged with second-degree murder in the death of Jessica Cyrus.
The shooting happened as Cyrus visited Lawson at Centerpoint Medical Center on Oct. 22.

Investigators say hospital surveillance showed Lawson in a wheelchair facing the victim as she struggled to breathe and bent forward, while Lawson appeared to reach at his pants and hip area with a dark object in his right hand.

title: Boothbay Fire Department celebrates life-saving equipment upgrade with ribbon-cutting ceremony
text:
The Boothbay Fire Department recently hosted a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the Boothbay Center Station to celebrate the arrival of its new Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA). SCBA equipment, which is worn by firefighters, is essentially highly technical air packs, allowing firefighters to breath clean air while operating in extremely volatile and dangerous environments. The event served as an opportunity to thank the elected officials, local businesses, residents, and department members who made this critical safety upgrade a reality.
Distinguished guests in attendance included Chuck Mahaleris from Senator Susan Collins' Office, Scott Wilkinson from Senator Angus King's Office, Ken Desmond, President of the Maine State Federation of Firefighters, and Boothbay Town Manager Dan Bryer. Regional support was also on display, with Fire Chief Gerry Gamage of Southport and firefighters from a number of other departments in attendance.
In 2025, the department was awarded a $228,000 grant from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the Assistance to Firefighters Grant (AFG) program to fund the procurement of new Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus
The acquisition of this transformative grant was bolstered by the advocacy of Maine's senior senators, Susan Collins and Angus King. Collins and King were instrumental in the nearly 9-month submission and award process, working hand-in-hand with Boothbay Fire and writing letters of support to FEMA and the AFG team. Throughout the 8-month federal review period, both Collins and King, alongside their dedicated staff, provided crucial assistance by responding to the department's questions and ensuring the extensive application was received and thoroughly reviewed at the highest levels.
“Firefighters put their lives on the line every day to protect our communities, and it is essential that they have the equipment they need to do their jobs safely and effectively,” Senator Collins. “That is why I led the enactment of the bipartisan Fire Grants and Safety Act, legislation that reauthorized the grant programs that help fire departments purchase lifesaving equipment like these new breathing apparatuses. I am pleased that the Boothbay Fire Department secured this funding, which will better protect their firefighters as they respond to emergencies and work to keep Mainers safe.”
“This new equipment represents an investment in the safety of Boothbay’s firefighters and the entire community, ensuring our first responders have the resources they need to carry out their job for years to come,” said Senator King. “It is a tremendous example of what can be accomplished when federal support, local leadership, and the community come together for the safety of all. I’m grateful to everyone who worked to make this critical investment a reality.”
During his address, Boothbay Fire Chief Tim Pinkham highlighted the critical nature of replacing the department's 21-year-old, failing gear. "These SCBA units are designed to operate in the harshest conditions and environment imaginable, with zero visibility and temperatures routinely running between 500 and 800 degrees," Pinkham said. He described the department's emergency responses as a "zero fail mission," emphasizing that the new gear is the single most important piece of life-saving equipment firefighters rely on to rescue trapped individuals and protect property.
While the grant was awarded specifically to Boothbay Fire, the benefits of this state-of-the-art equipment extend far beyond the town's borders. The Boothbay peninsula operates within a tightly integrated mutual aid system, meaning major emergency responses frequently rely on collaboration between neighboring departments. By upgrading to these highly reliable SCBA units, Boothbay Fire enhances the safety and operational readiness not only for its own crew but also for its mutual aid partners in Boothbay Harbor, Southport and Edgecomb. The presence of the neighboring fire chiefs and firefighters at the ceremony underscored this unified, regional approach to emergency response and community safety.
Acquiring the new equipment was a major undertaking that began in 2024. A dedicated group of Boothbay firefighters spent over 700 hours writing the grant application and evaluating key SCBA manufacturers. The meticulous 40-page application detailed the region's economic status and critical infrastructure, such as Bigelow Labs, Washburn & Doughty and Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens. Following the award, the department spent hundreds of additional hours issuing requests for proposals before ultimately selecting the new packs from the 3M Scott company.
While the FEMA grant covered the bulk of the cost, securing the award required a local match of funds. Boothbay firefighters volunteered their time to led a fundraising effort to cover the $12,500 required co-pay. With the generous support of local businesses and residents, the department successfully raised the needed funds. This resulted in no local funds from the town of Boothbay being required.
Boothbay Town Manager Dan Bryer said “Congratulations to the Boothbay Fire Department on this well-deserved $228,000 award that will save money for our local taxpayers. And thank you to our firefighters for your dedication, and service to our community.”
Before officially cutting the ribbon, the celebration featured a live demonstration of the new SCBA equipment. A team of Boothbay firefighters—including the husband-and-wife team of Assistant Chief Alex Arsenault and Lieutenant Chantalle Arsenault, competed in a gear-donning drill. Officiated by Ken Desmond, the drill showcased the speed and precision required to safely equip for an emergency. As the firefighters raced, Chief Pinkham pointed out the significant financial investment in personnel safety, noting that fully outfitting a single firefighter with Personal Protective Equipment and a new SCBA unit costs over $18,000.
The ceremony highlighted the immense dedication of the region's first responders, bringing attention to the fact that 82% of Maine fire departments are volunteer based, and the vast majority of firefighters have full time jobs in a range of occupations, answering the call 24/7, 365 days a year. The acquisition of these SCBA units secures the safety and capability of the Boothbay Fire Department for the next decade.

title: Vienna Union Hall Association holds Halloween Dance, October 31
How Often Does It Actually Snow in Maine on Halloween?
text:
How Often Does It Actually Snow in Maine on Halloween?
If you grew up in Maine, wearing your Halloween costume over your winter clothes may not have felt uncommon.
👇 KEEP READING: Mainers Weigh In on What to Do With Leftover Halloween Candy 👇
However, historical weather records show that measurable Halloween snowfall is relatively uncommon in Maine and varies significantly by location.
The Northeast Regional Climate Center’s 2024 review found measurable snow on about 6% of Halloweens in Caribou.
Bangor and Portland had no measurable Halloween snowfall in the records covered by that review.
The National Weather Service’s “Halloween Weather over the Years” lists Bangor’s Halloween snowfall record as a trace, meaning too little to measure, compared with 7.6 inches in Caribou in 1959.
Measurable snowfall means enough snow fell to be recorded, while a trace means only a tiny amount fell, so a Halloween without measurable snow could still have included a few flakes.
Caribou’s northern location and colder fall climate also make Halloween snow more plausible there than in much of southern Maine.
Snow falling on Halloween differs from snow already on the ground, so snowfall totals alone don't tell us whether trick-or-treaters encountered snow left by an earlier storm.
The years covered by each location’s records also matter, because the findings describe the period reviewed rather than every Halloween in Maine’s history.
And there you have it! Halloween in Maine can certainly feel wintry, but the snowfall history looks very different depending on where you are in the state.

title: 6 arrested in $1.2 million Walmart fraud scheme after dozens of packages found piling up
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PEORIA, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — What began with a Walmart driver’s tip about dozens of packages piling up at a home in Arizona led investigators to a million-dollar fraud scheme that stretched to Southeast Asia.
Authorities in Arizona said a Walmart driver told them on Aug. 22 that he’d delivered 30 to 50 packages under different names to the same Peoria-area home in just a couple of days.
Days later, a customer reported that someone had hacked their Walmart account and used it to buy items.
According to court documents, those two reports sparked a two-month investigation that ended Thursday morning with six arrests.
How it happened
Investigators say the group placed about 15,500 orders on Walmart.com using hacked customer accounts and stolen credit and debit card numbers.
They reportedly altered delivery addresses to get around fraud alerts.
“Without that delivery driver, I don’t know if it would have come across our radar,” Peoria police officer William Kennedy said.
Police linked 11,364 orders worth more than $768,000 to six drop houses in Mesa, Avondale, Glendale and Peoria, according to court paperwork.
In total, investigators put the fraud at about $1.23 million.
The merchandise was reportedly funneled through two boba shops in Peoria and Tolleson, before being driven to California to be shipped to Vietnam in containers through U.S. Cargo Shipping LLC.
“Like your average shopper who gets stuff for the dogs, the kids, their house, all those types of items were coming to those houses,” Kennedy said.
So far, police say Walmart has confirmed $57,501 in chargeback losses tied to two victims, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed 203 customers with $8,821 in unauthorized purchases.
Police shared photos showing some of the $25,000 worth of Walmart merchandise recovered in the investigation. Officers also seized $35,000 in cash and $45,000 in gold bars.
Finding the ringleader
Investigators identified 30-year-old Hoài Nguyen Nguyen as the organizer of the illegal operation, which included at least nine other people.
Nguyen denied any involvement in the crimes and told police he was only an employee for U.S. Cargo Shipping LLC, the company he is believed to be the owner of.
Two other suspects reportedly told police Nguyen recruited them to accept packages under different names, track them and load them into his van and U-Haul trailer for drives to California in exchange for a cut of the shipment values.
Search warrants were served across the Valley with help from SWAT teams, Homeland Security Investigations and Walmart investigators.
Ten people were detained; four were released.
Six people were booked into Maricopa County Jail on charges including fraud, identity theft, computer tampering and trafficking in stolen property:
- Thien Tran, 42
- Uy Vu Phan, 55
- Minh Ngọc Nguyen, 57
- Hie Xuan Le, 24
- Hoài Nguyen Nguyen, 30
- Hailey Hang Nguyen, 26
All six face charges of fraudulent schemes and artifices, possession of an access device violation, computer tampering for fraud, aggravated taking of identity and trafficking in stolen property in the first degree, according to court records.

title: Parkinson’s doesn’t always start with a tremor — here’s what to watch for
text:
(Aging Untold) — When most people picture Parkinson’s disease, they picture a tremor. But the disease often begins long before that, with subtle changes that are easy to miss — and easy to dismiss.
The early signs most people miss
“Most people think that when they think of Parkinson’s, you think of tremors. But signs really do, in fact, occur much earlier, very subtle signs like the loss of smell is a big one. And constipation or the changes in the handwriting,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Rogers explained what’s happening inside the brain during those early stages.
“What’s going on is there is a misfolding of these abnormal proteins that they start to form these things called Lewy bodies,” she said. “And they accumulate and they damage the dopamine-producing neurons in a part of the brain called the substantia nigra.”
By the time tremors appear, Rogers said, significant damage has often already been done.
“The problem is, by the time you see tremors, you’ve probably damaged 50% to 70% of those dopamine secreting neurons,” she said.
Real-life examples of early warning signs
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said she’s seen those early signs play out with people she’s worked with — sometimes missed, and sometimes caught in time.
“I remember a client of mine was telling me that her husband’s writing started to get smaller and smaller and smaller, and then his arm — like when he walked, one arm moved and the other one didn’t,” O’Rourke said. “Two very common symptoms that if she had brought him to the doctor, something could have been done.”
O’Rourke also recalled a different kind of story — one of long-term resilience.
“I was watching this university professor teach a class, and in the middle of the class he said, ‘You know, I have Parkinson’s and I’ve had it for 15 years,’” she said. “He began to tell us about the life that he built and all the support network that he used to continue living his life with Parkinson’s.”
Rogers pointed to another early sign that’s often overlooked.
“I think the one sign that people miss is that acting out dreams during the middle of REM sleep,” she said. “That can be an early sign as well too.”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck also drew a distinction between a typical tremor and one that could signal something more serious.
She said essential tremors, which can happen if you’re active, writing or you’re doing something for a long time, are not out-of-the-ordinary things.
“It’s when you’re at rest and you see that tremor, especially early on. If you see anything, then there’s something neurological going on that you need to have checked out,” Cradduck said.
She added that tremors aren’t a guarantee, even in advanced cases.
“Not every presentation of Parkinson’s, even in an advanced stage, has tremors,” she said.
Movement and community make a difference
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said staying active is one of the most powerful tools available to people living with Parkinson’s.
“There are really great examples out there of people that have just thrown themselves into boxing, dance, water exercise, rock climbing, urban pole walking — all kinds of really great exercise sets promoted within the Parkinson’s community,” Ambrose said. “It really makes a huge difference for those that are able to and choose to do that.”
O’Rourke also praised the support systems available nationwide.
“I think the Parkinson’s community has done a phenomenal job with all the support and care that they offer all across the country — the Parkinson’s Movement Disorder Alliance, the Michael J. Fox Foundation, the Parkinson’s Voice Project,” she said. “I’ve spoken at a lot of the Parkinson’s groups, and they bring in education ranging from housing to finances to legal. They really give both the caregiver, the family and the person with Parkinson’s a lot of support.”
Rogers pointed to Michael J. Fox’s role in raising awareness of the disease.
“Michael J. Fox really brought awareness to Parkinson’s,” she said.
Cradduck agreed, calling Fox a pioneer.
“I believe that he has been a pioneer in showing the resilience of the human body and what you can go through and what you can still do and what you can still accomplish,” she said.
Resources
Key takeaways for Parkinson’s patients and families
- It’s a diverse spectrum. Parkinson’s looks different in everyone and can start years before tremors show, with early signs like sleep issues or loss of smell.
- Movement is medicine. Consistent exercise like boxing, dance or balance training protects brain function and helps preserve independence.
- Never walk alone. Isolation makes Parkinson’s harder. Joining a support community is just as important as medical treatment.

title: Freeport football shuts out Lisbon in regular-season finale
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
FREEPORT — It didn’t take long for Andrew Thomas to settle in at quarterback in his first game back from a hand injury.
On Friday’s fourth play, the senior found his way into the end zone for a 26-yard touchdown run, setting the tone for Freeport in its 34-0 win over Lisbon in a Class D South regular-season finale.
“It was so amazing being back,” said Thomas. “Sam (Willard) fit the spot so well, and I’m glad of everything he’s done for the team the past three weeks, but I’m so glad to be back.”
The Falcons were dominant on the ground, scoring five rushing touchdowns.
“I’m so glad to be with my O-lineman, who work so hard every single play — shout out Jaden Best,” Thomas said. “It was just an awesome feeling to get a goose egg, too. Couldn’t have a better senior night.”
HOW IT HAPPENED
Thomas scored just over two minutes into the first quarter, and after Lisbon (5-3) turned it over on downs, Freeport (6-2) scored again, this time on a 10-yard run by Keegan Haveran.
Willard’s 8-yard touchdown run extended the Falcons’ lead to 20-0 before halftime.
Lisbon reached the Freeport 10 late in the third quarter, but Greyson Quigg tackled Greyhounds quarterback Jaxson Roy-Thompson for a 5-yard loss on third down, and a fourth-down pass fell incomplete.
The Falcons padded their lead with a 9-yard run by Landon Clark and an 11-yard run from Devon Crone.
WHAT IT MEANS
With the win, Freeport locks up the No. 1 seed in Class D South. The Falcons will have a bye into the semifinals.
“Everyone goes back to zero tomorrow,” Freeport coach Paul St. Pierre said. “So, it’s great to get the rest, it’s great to get the home game, but it’s not going to mean anything in two weeks, and I guarantee whoever we’re playing isn’t going to care that we were No. 1.
“And at that point, they won’t, but we’re going to enjoy it for a night, and I’m really proud of these guys for working hard all season, in the offseason, and they gave themselves a chance tonight and they made me proud.”
Lisbon will be the No. 4 seed, a notable improvement after missing the playoffs the last two seasons.
“Tonight wasn’t great, but the coaching staff, our first goal was to have a winning season be able to host a home playoff game and go from there,” Lisbon coach Walter Polky said. “And we have. Either way, we were going to host a game no matter what … These seniors haven’t had a winning season their whole high school career, and that was one of our main goals.”
UNSUNG HERO
Freeport’s Ben Gaddis had an interception on the final play of the game. The Falcons may have already been up by five touchdowns, but the junior’s heads-up play was a perfect representation of the Falcons’ defensive effort.
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Freeport: Andrew Thomas (11 rushes, 130 yards, touchdown), Sam Willard (seven rushes, 80 yards, touchdown)

title: InvestigateTV+: Perimenopause still poorly understood
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Experts say the transition period before menopause—perimenopause—is still poorly understood, leaving many women blindsided by dozens of symptoms and a frustrating search for answers. InvestigateTV+ takes an in-depth look at the knowledge gap, why diagnosis can be difficult and the complicated history of one of the most effective treatment options.
Plus, after a campfire sparks a massive Minnesota wildfire, we follow one community’s road to recovery and the neighbors who stepped up to help families rebuild.
Perimenopause still poorly understood
Perimenopause is defined as the phase when the ovaries gradually produce less estrogen. It can begin anywhere from eight to 10 years before menopause.
The most common signs of perimenopause, like those of menopause, are hot flashes, weight gain and mood changes, in addition to at least 31 other symptoms, according to doctors.
It remains under-recognized both among the medical community and the women who experience it.
Recovering after a wildfire
A campfire grew into the Camp House fire, torching thousands of acres of forest and more than 180 homes, cabins and outbuildings.
In the year since, the devastated residents of Brimson have gotten an unwanted crash course in disaster recovery.
Where fake patients save real lives
The patient is struggling to breathe. Monitors are beeping. Medical students are checking lung sounds, reading vital signs and preparing for the next step.
But this is not a real emergency room.
At LSU Health New Orleans, students are training on high-tech medical simulators built to look, feel and respond like people in crisis.
The cats helping volunteers
Giving time through volunteer work can make a big difference for the cause, but also for the volunteer. Research shows volunteering can offer benefits for mental health.
The Mayo Clinic says it can reduce stress and increase feel-good hormones in the brain. Volunteering can also provide purpose.
At the Cat Alliance Team Sanctuary in Sherwood, Oregon, it’s hard to tell the difference between who’s helping and who’s being helped. The volunteers say they get so much out of their time there.

title: School bus driver accused of DUI, evading police, using child as ‘shield’
text:
NORTH CHARLESTON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — A South Carolina woman is facing charges after police said she drove a school bus impaired and led police on a chase with her child in the vehicle before eventually using him as “a shield.”
Shakira Jones, 23, is charged with failure to stop for blue lights and sirens, driving under the influence and child endangerment.
North Charleston police said they received an alert at about 3:20 p.m. Thursday about a school bus driving erratically. Reports stated that the bus nearly hit another vehicle and that there were suspicions about the driver’s sobriety.
Officers found the bus and said they saw it traveling at around 65 miles per hour in a 45-mph zone and watched it make an improper turn, followed by multiple improper and erratic lane changes.
Police tried to initiate a traffic stop, but the bus sped up and did not stop.
Police said the bus led officers on a chase and continued driving erratically. Eventually, the driver sped into a parking lot where school staff were present. Staff members had to move out of the way to avoid the bus and the officers.
The bus came to a final stop, but the driver refused to exit, police said.
Officers were eventually able to see the driver and identify her as Jones.
A report states that officers readied their weapons and issued more commands, at which point Jones placed her child in front of her “in an attempt to shield herself from officers.”
Police were able to remove the child, and, after a brief struggle, officers brought Jones into custody.
Investigating officers reportedly found a bottle of prescribed amphetamines among Jones’ items, which were reportedly within arm’s reach of the driver’s seat.
Police said they performed field sobriety testing, which led officers to conclude that she had been driving while impaired.
Jones was booked into the Al Cannon Detention Center. No bond has been issued.

The California-based retailer is opening 30 new stores in 16 states in the coming weeks and months.
The popular grocery chain currently has stores in 42 states and Washington, D.C.

title: Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, ‘distressed’ by allegations her father had child sex abuse images
text:
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, ‘deeply distressed’ by allegations her father had child sex abuse images
Prince Harry’s wife, Meghan, said Friday she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former home. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to London police in 2018.
Meghan, also known as the Duchess of Sussex, issued the statement after The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, reported that her brother found the images while clearing out the home of their father, Thomas Markle Sr., in the Philippines.
“I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed," Meghan said in a statement.
She also addressed the letter sent to the Metropolitan Police Service’s Royal and Specialist Protection unit, which later shared its contents with her.
“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father, and I was given assurances that these were being investigated. I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.”
Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits,” married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.
Thomas Markle Sr., a retired television lighting and photography director, did not attend the wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan’s estrangement from her father. While some reports suggested she had shunned him in favor of her new royal status, Meghan said her decision to distance herself was intended to protect her children.
“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” Meghan said in her statement.
Thomas Markle Sr. was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S.
The Sun reported that Thomas Markle Jr. recently found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s former home in the Philippine city of Cebu when he was clearing out the property.
Markle Jr. told the newspaper that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the Federal Bureau of Investigation in the U.S.
“I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now,” Markle Jr. told The Sun. “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.”
In comments to the Daily Mail, the 82-year-old Markle denied the allegations.
“I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me," he was quoted by the Daily Mail as saying. "I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”

title: Lyme disease cases in Maine tracking ahead of last year
text:
Lyme disease cases in Maine so far this year are tracking slightly ahead of 2025, when the state set a record for the tickborne disease.
Megan Porter, health educator with the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention, said she can’t project whether 2026 cases will break the record, but the deer ticks that cause Lyme disease are currently active.
“Ticks are active anytime the temperature is above freezing,” Porter said. “The ticks are everywhere, so Mainers should take steps to prevent tickborne diseases.”
As of Oct. 20, the Maine CDC reported 3,976 Lyme disease cases so far this year. Through October 2025, the state had reported 3,763 cases of Lyme en route to logging a record of 4,257 cases last year.
Griffin Dill, who manages the University of Maine Cooperative Extension’s Tick Lab, said he expects there will be high levels of deer tick activity through mid-November.
Dill said deer ticks are now in their adult stage, and are currently searching for hosts, to prepare for laying eggs and surviving the winter. Despite the arid conditions — ticks prefer rainy and humid weather — the arachnids are still active, Dill said.
“They’re pretty well adapted to survive these adverse conditions,” Dill said. “It is by no means a booming year for tick activity, but we are not seeing a significant decrease in activity even though we’ve had dry weather.”
The lab receives thousands of tick submissions every year for identification and research.
The Maine CDC also reported that, through Oct. 20, there had been 1,223 anaplasmosis cases and 425 cases of babesiosis. The diseases, like Lyme, are transmitted to humans by deer ticks. Lyme and anaplasmosis are bacterial infections, while babesiosis is an infection caused by microscopic parasites.
In 2025, the state recorded a total of 352 cases of babesiosis and 1,604 cases of anaplasmosis, according to the Maine CDC.
Symptoms of the three diseases are similar, including fever, chills, fatigue, headaches and body aches, according to the U.S. CDC. Lyme can sometimes cause a bulls-eye rash. Lyme and anaplasmosis can be treated with a course of antibiotics, while babesiosis patients receive anti-parasitic medicine.
Porter said deer ticks are expanding their geographic range. They used to be mostly in coastal, southern Maine, but are now seen farther inland and Down East.
“We are seeing the ticks push into Down East, and increasing cases of tickborne disease in Western Maine,” Porter said.
Ticks are expanding their range due to climate change, scientists have said.
Porter said people can prevent tick bites by doing frequent checks after doing outdoor activities in tick habitat, tucking socks into pants and using repellent. After outdoor activities, Porter said, put clothes worn during the activity into the dryer on high, which will kill ticks.

title: Officers rescue woman from burning car
text:
Off-duty officers rescue woman from burning car
Off-duty officers rescue woman from burning car
Two off-duty state parks peace officers rescued a woman from a burning car after it crashed in Sutter County, California, on Friday morning, according to the California Department of Parks and Recreation.
California State Parks said Dylan Ayache and Ryan Gray were driving down Highway 70 from Butte County around 6:40 a.m. when they saw a car turned over and fully engulfed in flames near the Nicolaus exit. They were the first trained responders on the scene and quickly pulled the woman to safety.
The woman, a 46-year-old from Plumas Lake, was taken to a hospital for treatment and released later that day, California State Parks said.
The Sutter County Fire Department and California Highway Patrol also responded, officials said.

title: Vance blamed Biden for gas prices. PolitiFact says otherwise
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JD Vance blames Biden for gas prices, but PolitiFact says Iran War is the bigger cause JD Vance blamed Biden for expensive gas, but fact-checkers say that’s false. Experts say the war in Iran is the main reason prices are high now. JD Vance blames Biden for gas prices, but PolitiFact says Iran War is the bigger cause JD Vance blamed Biden for expensive gas, but fact-checkers say that’s false. Experts say the war in Iran is the main reason prices are high now. This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com. JD Vance falsely blames Biden policy for high gas prices. Iran War is mainly to blame. If your time is short - Market forces and global events like pandemics and wars tend to influence refinery production more than presidential policy, and the most obvious cause of today’s high gasoline prices is the war in Iran, which was launched by President Donald Trump. - California, not the U.S., has lost 20% of its oil refining capacity; the nation’s refining capacity has been largely stable. - Climate change and energy policies introduced by former President Joe Biden could play a long-term role in nudging refinery operators to cut back or shut down facilities, experts say. As the Trump administration faces voter pushback over high gasoline prices, Vice President JD Vance tried to shift the blame to former President Joe Biden. During a CBS News town hall Oct. 17, Vance said, “The biggest reason why gas prices are so high is because when Joe Biden was president, we had about 20% of American refining capacity that went offline. We’re slowly bringing that online, but it does take a little bit of time. And because we shut down so much refining capacity, we were more susceptible to the shocks that we’ve seen in the Middle Eastern energy crisis.” Vance’s office did not respond to our questions for this article. But while California has lost 20% of its gasoline refining capacity, national refinery capacity has remained relatively stable. Twenty percent is “not a correct statistic in terms of national refinery capacity,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, which tracks U.S. gasoline prices. What’s more, presidential policy is one of many factors that shape U.S. refining capabilities, multiple oil industry experts told PolitiFact, and the most obvious cause of today’s high gasoline prices is the war in Iran, which was launched by President Donald Trump, not Biden. “The biggest factor influencing high gasoline prices is the elevated cost of crude oil, caused by the reduction in ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and damage to export and pipeline facilities in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries,” said Hugh Daigle, a professor with the University of Texas at Austin’s petroleum and geosystems engineering department. How could Biden’s policies have made a difference? Energy market experts said some of Biden’s policies — notably efforts to combat climate change, which involve transitioning away from fossil fuels and toward cleaner, renewable energy — likely contributed to some refiners’ decisions not to greenlight new refineries or to expand existing ones. In particular, California’s stringent environmental policies help explain why two refineries shuttered there. The timing is less clear than Vance made it sound: The closure of a Phillips 66 refinery in Los Angeles was announced two weeks before Trump won reelection in 2024. Valero announced the closure of its refinery in Benicia, California, in April 2025, when Trump was president. Both facilities closed during Trump’s second term. How does the refining economy work? Biden’s policies are not considered the prime culprit for today’s high gasoline prices, experts said. The bigger factors shaping U.S. refining capacity are market-driven, experts said. They include: The current and expected demand for fuel. The growth of electric cars — partially nudged by government policy but also driven by consumers’ decisions — has put some downward pressure on demand for gasoline, and thus the demand for refining. And as more people work from home, they have to drive less often. Foreign refining capacity. The more foreign refining capability there is, the less pressure for oil companies to rely exclusively on U.S. refiners. “Since 2019, global refining capacity has shrunk by about 1 million barrels a day while demand has grown by about 4.5 million barrels a day,” said Skip York, a fellow at Rice University’s Center for Energy Studies. U.S. refiners are busy right now because 3 million barrels a day are offline in Russia and the Middle East because of Ukrainian and Iranian attacks. Much of the Russian and Middle Eastern refinery capacity is geared toward producing diesel. As a result, York said, U.S. refiners have switched some of their production from gasoline to diesel — which has further hiked gasoline prices for U.S. drivers. Refinery profitability. When Phillips 66 announced it was closing the Los Angeles refinery, the company said that in addition to concerns about California regulations, it made the decision despite the facility being profitable. There were “more attractive projects in the company’s portfolio,” York said. U.S. and world events. During recessions, there is less demand for gasoline, so refinery use tends to drop. “The big drop in U.S. refining capacity utilization happened in spring of 2020, during the initial wave of COVID shutdowns,” said Clark Williams-Derry, an energy finance analyst at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. How does U.S. refinery capacity today compare with the Biden era? Despite disruption driven by the COVID-19 pandemic, wars and market factors, U.S. refinery usage has remained relatively stable under both Biden and Trump, data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration shows.
In 2021 and 2022, deferred maintenance and supply-chain breakdowns during the pandemic undercut refinery capacity. U.S. refining capacity has been at historically normal levels ever since, Daigle said.
Williams-Derry calculated how many refineries’ last dates of operation fell during Trump’s two terms and compared it with how many shut down during Biden’s term. He found that the amount of refining capacity lost from shutdowns under Trump quadrupled the amount lost under Biden. “Personally, I don’t think that politics had much to do with any of these closures,” Williams-Derry said. He cited a Phillips 66 facility in Belle Chasse, Louisiana, that was 50 years old in 2021 when it suffered hurricane damage. “Phillips tried to sell it but couldn’t find a buyer, so it turned it into a terminal and closed the refinery,” he said. Why are gasoline prices high now? The most obvious cause of high gasoline prices today is the start of the war in Iran. Prices spiked immediately after the war began Feb. 28 and have remained high since.
“Reduced refinery capacity would contribute somewhat to higher gasoline and diesel prices today, but this is by no means the biggest reason why gasoline prices are so high today,” said Kenneth Gillingham, a Yale University economist who specializes in energy and environmental issues. Our ruling Vance said, “The biggest reason why gas prices are so high is because when Joe Biden was president, we had about 20% of American refining capacity that went offline.” Vance’s statement is inaccurate on multiple levels. California, not the U.S., lost 20% of its refining capacity. The national outlook has been largely stable. Market forces and global realities influence refinery production more than presidential policy does, and the most obvious cause of today’s high gasoline prices is the war in Iran, which was launched by Trump, not Biden. We rate the statement False. This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com. It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: The cat sanctuary helping volunteers find mental wellness
text:
SHERWOOD, Ore. (InvestigateTV) - Giving time through volunteer work can make a big difference for the cause, but also for the volunteer. Research shows volunteering can offer benefits for mental health.
The Mayo Clinic says it can reduce stress and increase feel-good hormones in the brain. Volunteering can also provide purpose.
At the Cat Alliance Team Sanctuary in Sherwood, Oregon, it’s hard to tell the difference between who’s helping and who’s being helped. The volunteers say they get so much out of their time there.
The sanctuary houses 140 cats. Every room has 15 to 25 cats. One room has more feral cats because it will be their forever home.
The cats may not appear to be picture perfect pets. Hobbit was born with no eyelids. Tommy has an underbite. One cat was adopted once, but kept attacking the other cat, so the sanctuary took him back.
Every cat has a story and a name. Reatha Larson knows them all.
“I manage the kitties that live here. Most of them are unadoptable. That’s what we were built for because most rescues take in the adoptable ones,” Larson said.
Running a sanctuary with 140 cats is a lot of work. To keep it running smoothly, Larson relies on her team of volunteers.
Elizabeth Lindemann has been volunteering for about two years.
“I will help with the water and the food, and if the staff needs help with litter boxes, I will do that,” Lindemann said. “I consider myself another set of eyes for the kitties.”
As much as Lindemann does to help the cats and the shelter, she said what she’s gotten back is more.
“For me personally, it has helped me be calm and has helped me with a sense of accomplishment and build a community. It has helped me step out of my comfort zone,” Lindemann said.
Volunteering has been shown to reduce stress, improve self-esteem and offer a sense of purpose. Lindemann said this opportunity to serve has provided all of that, and it came at the right time in her life.
“I think sometimes for an older person, for whatever their background, their mental health can go like this,” Lindemann said, waving her hands up and down like a wave.
“Volunteering helps my mental health in a way that there is stability, there’s a connection outside of myself,” Lindemann said.
That connection propels the cycle of the volunteers helping the shelter, the shelter helping the cats, and the cats helping the volunteers.
“Volunteering reinforces that I’m needed here and I’m contributing to the world,” Lindemann said.
The sanctuary is always looking for more volunteers. Larson said it’s a great activity for parents and kids to come in together.

title: Sargent Family Community Center marks 10 years in the community
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - The Sargent Family Community Center is celebrating 10 years at its current location and looking back at the memories made during those years and beyond.
The center has compiled four binders of photos, along with more photos displayed across two tables and additional images in the back. Some photos date back to the 70s when the William Haskell Recreation Center was still open on Main St.
Director Steven Samson says he hopes community members will come in and try to find a picture of themselves.
“You might find an old picture of yourself back playing in elementary basketball or soccer or hockey here. It’s a really cool exhibit we have here,” Samson said.
Community members reflect on center’s history
Kevin Sipe was there for the beginning of the Sargent Family Community Center and, before that, the William Haskell Recreation Center. Sipe said looking through the photos was a trip down memory lane.
“And then all the little kids, these cute little photos of kids who are now in their 40s or 50s,” Sipe said.
Sipe has lived in the community most of his life. He said the center has continued a tradition that started before the current building opened.
“The rec center historically, because it’s a free place for kids to go and because a lot of our programs are free or at very low cost, has been really the center of the community,” Sipe said.
New display highlights visitor feedback
Near the entrance, a wall lists what visitors say they enjoy most about the center.
“They’re going to look over on their left, and we’ve asked people, ‘What is something you enjoy doing here?’ There are a lot of lists of different little items that people really enjoy. It’s fascinating to see all the different opportunities provided to our community,” Samson said.
The center currently offers programs for people of all ages, including toddler time, youth sports, after-school activities, and programs for older residents.
Anniversary celebration planned
The community is invited to celebrate the anniversary at the rec center tomorrow, Saturday 24th from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Admission is free, and the center will provide food, drinks, games, crafts, and bounce houses.

title: Bigfoot in Maine? Still No Proof in the Age of Smartphones
text:
Bigfoot in Maine? We’re Still Looking For Proof in The Age of Smartphones
We can send people to space, put tiny computers in our pockets, and get a notification when our macha is two minutes away.
But somehow, in 2026, we still don't have ANY undeniable proof that Bigfoot exists.
And here's the plot twist: Maine might be one of the best places to look for him.
A new 2026 study by Canada Sports Betting ranked U.S. states and Canadian provinces based on historical Bigfoot reports per 100,000 residents, forest coverage, and climate conditions.
The result? Maine landed among America's top 10 states for a potential Bigfoot sighting.
Which honestly tracks.
We have approximately a million acres of woods where something could be lurking, and half the time we're already blaming mysterious noises on something living in the trees.
But seriously, how have we not figured this out yet?
Come on, we have trail cameras, flocks, drones, satellite imagery, and people filming themselves eating chicken nuggets in their cars in 4K.
Yet Bigfoot apparently remains committed to keeping a low profile.
To be clear, these rankings are based on reported sightings and environmental factors, not scientific proof that Bigfoot exists.
Guys, no one's handed over a verified Sasquatch driver's license or a DNA sample that settles the debate.
Still, Maine's vast forests and remote stretches certainly leave room for the imagination.
So, if you're hiking, camping, or driving down a dark, wooded Maine road and spot something unusually tall and hairy crossing the street, maybe don't immediately assume it's a moose having a rough hair day.
Could Bigfoot be out there? We don't know. But if he is, Maine seems like a pretty good place to avoid people.
And honestly? Same, Bigfoot. Same.

title: Why walking is a step toward healthy aging
text:
(Aging Untold) — Walking is one of the simplest tools we have for healthy aging, and the benefits add up even in short bursts.
The Aging Untold hosts break down how to make every step count, why muscle loss happens faster than most people realize, and why using a walker or cane is nothing to be embarrassed about.
Start small, stay consistent
“Steps count by just doing it. You’ve just got to jump in and do it. You don’t have to go out and run a marathon. You just start small and just start moving,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Rogers said walking reflects the health of the entire body — it draws on muscle strength, balance, heart health and oxygenation.
“So how many times you see people — how far can they walk, that distance when they start gasping for breath? That’s oxygenation. That’s heart health,” Rogers said. “What about these people with chronic lung diseases like COPD and all that? They need that oxygenation. That’s one of the first signs you see in them — their ability to walk.”
Rogers said gait, or the way someone walks, can also be a clue to neurological issues.
“That can be a clue that something else is going on in your body,” she said. “It’s your body’s report card.”
Rogers cited a randomized trial showing that people who did aerobic exercise three times a week for 40 minutes increased their hippocampal volume, the brain’s memory center.
“So walking, all that, is more than just an exercise — that’s a ‘brain-cize,’” she said.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said the idea of hitting 10,000 steps a day can feel overwhelming, but it doesn’t have to be the goal.
“I like to tell people consistency beats intensity,” O’Rourke said. “If you can’t walk or have difficulty walking, try just lifting your knees up from the chair, maybe walking to the front door and back, maybe walking for five minutes, 10 minutes and just extending the amount of time.”
O’Rourke suggested turning walking into a friendly challenge.
“Maybe it is that you set up a competition with somebody to say, let’s take a walk and see how far we can walk, and then keep track of how many miles you’re building up,” she said. “But don’t start too big, because you’ll set yourself up for failure.”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck also advised pacing walks so there’s enough energy to get back.
“When you’re going out and you’re going to see how far you can walk, make sure that you can walk back,” Cradduck said.
Muscles weaken faster than people expect
Cradduck said muscle loss can happen quickly, even in healthy older adults.
“I don’t think people realize just how quickly muscles atrophy,” Cradduck said. “You take somebody that’s a little older and they go into the hospital and they’re bedbound for a week in the hospital for a urinary tract [infection], and then all of a sudden they’re not able to walk.”
Cradduck said people who are unable to walk should still try to keep their legs moving, such as with foot or leg pumps.
She added that walking also supports cognition because it requires multiple coordinated steps in the brain.
“There’s a lot of brain steps in taking a step,” she said. “The foot has to move a certain way, and the leg has to move a certain way. The balance has to happen.”
For people who are immobile, Rogers said placing their legs on a vibrating plate can help.
“Really it’s about circulation,” she said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said mobility is tied to independence.
“Just think of mobility as freedom,” she said. “It gives you your independence, your ability to move.”
Don’t let pride stand in the way of using a walker
Ths hosts said strength and fitness training help maintain walking ability over time, and that avoiding long periods of sitting matters too.
“Every hour, get up,” O’Rourke said. “If you’re working, get up, take a walk. Even standing up, sitting down — just start somewhere.”
Cradduck said fear of falling, including concerns about hip fractures, often causes people to stop walking altogether — which can do more harm.
“I will tell anyone: use a walker, use a support system,” Cradduck said. “It is no different than me having glasses on my face right now so I can see. This is something that I need as an aide. A walker, if that keeps you moving and keeps you going, and it keeps your brain healthy, keeps your heart healthy, and it keeps you from falling, don’t be embarrassed by it.”
Cradduck said people are more likely to draw sympathy from inactivity than from using mobility aids.
“People are going to feel sorry for you when you’re lying in the bed, unable to move — not when you’re walking around using a walker for safety,” she said.
Ambrose said the stigma around walkers is often self-imposed. Her 12-year-old grandson had his birthday party at a roller-skating rink in Chicago and kids used PVC pipe skating aids that resembled walkers.
“So they’re using it as tools,” Ambrose said. “I like to say we’re an evolved species. We’re supposed to use tools. We wear eyeglasses when we need them. We wear hearing aids when we need them, and we use walkers, wheelchairs, walking sticks — whatever we need, when we need them.”
O’Rourke said pride and ego often get in the way.
“I think pride gets in the way, ego gets in the way, and you can see it when someone’s not using a walker and they’re afraid of falling,” she said. “They’re almost putting themselves at risk for falling more. They do more harm.”
Ambrose also said home environment matters for staying active, especially during bad weather.
“Think about your environment,” she said. “What can I do so I can walk inside my home? Or if you moved to independent living, you can walk hallways. So think about where you live — that’s going to matter too.”
Key takeaways
- Strength training protects your walking gait.
- Mobility aids are tools, not weaknesses. Walkers, canes and wheelchairs support independence and safety, similar to glasses or hearing aids.
- Consistency beats intensity. Keep moving by turning chores into exercise.
- Stand up hourly and park farther away to prevent rapid muscle atrophy.
