title: Brunswick families living in hotels after town condemns unsafe mobile homes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BRUNSWICK — Since moving into their mobile home in Brunswick more than a year ago, Kristie Miquelon and Eric Harris have noticed sagging floors, water damage, leaky windows and other hazards.
A few months ago, Harris’ foot went straight through the floor in their living room. Then, in August, Miquelon’s asthma nebulizer caught fire, burning the cord.
“The problems just kept building, and building, and building,” Miquelon said.
Fed up with what they describe as improper maintenance of their rental unit, the family reported their living situation to town officials, who condemned their home and three others in the mobile home park known as Zoe Court. It’s been nearly a month since then and Miquelon, Harris and their 6-year-old — and some of their neighbors — have been living in a hotel while they await repairs and figure out their next steps.
Brunswick’s code enforcement office and fire department completed an inspection of the 20-plus homes in Zoe Court in late September after receiving Harris and Miquelon’s reports of overheating outlets, cords burning up when plugged in and holes in the floors, said Deputy Fire Chief Josh Shean.
Last week, Brunswick issued the park’s owners, Massachusetts-based Hekla Ventures, an $800 citation for failing to submit plans to correct eight code violations, Shean said.
The structural and electrical issues inspectors found in the homes presented safety issues, Shean said Wednesday.
“Three of (the homes) had structural concerns where there was visible sagging in the floors,” he said.
One unit was condemned because it had no running water or heat. Shean said the residents of the unit owned their home, and had moved in in March with the expectation that there were no issues with the heat or water.
In addition, some of the homes had unstable exterior stairs, water heaters that didn’t meet code and electrical work done without permits, Shean said.
Deb Crocker, Brunswick director of human services, said there were maintenance issues throughout the entire park, where the mobile homes date to the 1970s.
The town moved residents from the four condemned homes to hotel rooms after the failed inspections using a mixture of funding from Maine Housing and the town’s General Assistance program, said Crocker.
Most of the mobile home units in Zoe Court are rented, town officials said. In traditional mobile home parks, residents own their home and rent the lot they stay on.
The units were not registered under Brunswick’s rental registry, Shean said, which tracks landlord and property information for code enforcement purposes.
Miquelon and Harris, at 11 Zoe Court, were paying about $1,500 a month in rent for their now-condemned home. That doesn’t include utilities like heat — which escapes the home through gaps in the windows.
“If you’d have told me this place was $750 a month with nothing included, that would be a little bit (better). Propane is not cheap; they want at least $500 every time they deliver, and I don’t have that type of money every time we need heat,” Miquelon said.
One of the condemned trailers was repaired in a matter of days, Shean said. Authorities reinspected that home and tenants were allowed to move back in. The remaining three households, though, were still living in hotels this week.
Miquelon and Harris said issues they’ve reported to management in the past have been sloppily fixed, or not at all.
A home test kit detected mold in the home, confirming the family’s suspicions about constant illnesses they say they experienced while living at Zoe Court. Nearly a month after moving out, the floor under their bathroom flooring is still wet.
“I’m always wheezing, tight chest, and then it’s been like ever since we’ve been out of here and in the hotel, I can breathe,” said Miquelon, who has asthma. “I haven’t had to use my nebulizer at all. I barely use my inhaler.”
Hekla Ventures, a private holding company, has owned the park since 2022, according to the Cumberland County Registry of Deeds. The company did not respond Friday to a request for comment.
Crocker, the town’s human services director, said it’s been extremely destabilizing for families to uproot their lives and move to hotel rooms, especially those with children.
“You can’t cook a meal like you could at home. There’s so many inconveniences with staying in a hotel,” she said.
Miquelon gets up early for work at the Dunkin’ in Topsham and the family shares one car, so they’ve been relying on friends to take their daughter to school while living at the hotel. She’s doing remarkably well despite the circumstances, Miquelon said.
“She’s starting to get tired of the hotel because we’re just in one room,” Miquelon said.
She and Harris are looking for a new place and receiving legal representation from Pine Tree Legal Assistance. They hope to stay in the Brunswick area — where their daughter goes to school and Harris coaches high school football — but it’s difficult to find a rental they can afford.
Given the extent of the damage, the family says they can’t see themselves moving back into Zoe Court once repairs are completed.

title: Classes canceled in Rockland after 'unexpected death' of staff member
text:
Classes canceled at Oceanside High School in Rockland after 'unexpected death' of teacher
Counseling and support services available at the school from noon to 2 p.m. Friday
Classes canceled at Oceanside High School in Rockland after 'unexpected death' of teacher
Counseling and support services available at the school from noon to 2 p.m. Friday
Regional School Unit 13 (RSU 13) officials canceled classes at Oceanside High School on Friday following the "unexpected death" of a teacher.
In a letter that was shared publicly by the school district, Oceanside High School Principal Jesse Bartke notified families that school officials learned late Thursday afternoon that world language teacher Megan Thill had passed away unexpectedly.
The faculty page on the Oceanside High School website indicates that Thill taught German, Spanish and an intro to world languages class.
In his letter to families, Bartke said the school is preparing to welcome students back on Monday.
"We also want to express our gratitude to our wonderful community of support who offered services, food, care, and encouragement," Bartke said.
In a notice to the community that was shared on Facebook, officials said that counselors will be available at the school from 12 to 2 p.m. on Friday for students who might need emotional support.
Bartke encouraged parents and guardians who need support talking with their child about their grief to use the following resources:
- 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: Call or text 988. TTY users need to dial 711 first. The line is available in Spanish at 1-888-628-9454. There is also an online chat option.
- Maine Crisis Line: Call or text 1-888-568-1112. TTY users need to dial 711 first. There is also an online chat option.
- Call 211 for the 211 Maine health services directory and assistance program. TTY users need to dial 711 first. Many languages are supported.
- NAMI Teen & Young Adult HelpLine: Text "FRIEND" to 62640, call 1-800-950-6264 or email helpline@nami.org.
- NAMI Maine Helpline: Call or text 1-800-464-5767 or email helpline@namimaine.org.
In addition, Bartke said parents and guardians who anticipate that their child will need additional support upon their return to school on Monday should email the school-based mental health clinician, Dr. Rebecca Roveto, at RRoveto@RSU13.org. Parents and guardians are also welcome to contact their child's counselor or administrator by email or phone on Monday.
The Belong Church in Rockland is also opening its doors to RSU 13 community members seeking a "calm, quiet place" to process what the church called the "sudden passing of a beloved staff member." The church was open Friday from 8 a.m. to 12 p.m.
RSU 13 officials said students attending Maine Career and Technical Education programs were still able to go to school on Friday if they arranged their own transportation.

title: The cat sanctuary helping volunteers find mental wellness
text:
SHERWOOD, Ore. (InvestigateTV) - Giving time through volunteer work can make a big difference for the cause, but also for the volunteer. Research shows volunteering can offer benefits for mental health.
The sanctuary houses 140 cats. Every room has 15 to 25 cats. One room has more feral cats because it will be their forever home.
The cats may not appear to be picture perfect pets. Hobbit was born with no eyelids. Tommy has an underbite. One cat was adopted once, but kept attacking the other cat, so the sanctuary took him back.
Every cat has a story and a name. Reatha Larson knows them all.
“I manage the kitties that live here. Most of them are unadoptable. That’s what we were built for because most rescues take in the adoptable ones,” Larson said.
Running a sanctuary with 140 cats is a lot of work. To keep it running smoothly, Larson relies on her team of volunteers.
Elizabeth Lindemann has been volunteering for about two years.
“I will help with the water and the food, and if the staff needs help with litter boxes, I will do that,” Lindemann said. “I consider myself another set of eyes for the kitties.”
As much as Lindemann does to help the cats and the shelter, she said what she’s gotten back is more.
“For me personally, it has helped me be calm and has helped me with a sense of accomplishment and build a community. It has helped me step out of my comfort zone,” Lindemann said.
Volunteering has been shown to reduce stress, improve self-esteem and offer a sense of purpose. Lindemann said this opportunity to serve has provided all of that, and it came at the right time in her life.
“I think sometimes for an older person, for whatever their background, their mental health can go like this,” Lindemann said, waving her hands up and down like a wave.
“Volunteering helps my mental health in a way that there is stability, there’s a connection outside of myself,” Lindemann said.
That connection propels the cycle of the volunteers helping the shelter, the shelter helping the cats, and the cats helping the volunteers.
“Volunteering reinforces that I’m needed here and I’m contributing to the world,” Lindemann said.
The sanctuary is always looking for more volunteers. Larson said it’s a great activity for parents and kids to come in together.

title: Officer who shot and killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley resigns
text:
SENATOBIA, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) - The police officer who shot and killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley in a Walmart parking lot in June has resigned from the force, attorneys for the Wiley family told Action News 5.
Former Senatobia police officer Hunter Foster’s body-camera footage was just released Thursday by the Mississippi Department of Public Safety.
The video shows him running out of the store with other officers after a Walmart employee told him that accused shoplifters were on the run. Within 13 seconds, Foster’s gun was aimed at the car with Wiley inside it.
Body-camera audio captures officers shouting “Stop the car. Stop. Stop.” Gunfire is also heard along with breaking glass and screeching brakes as the car continued moving.
Three shots were fired, all from Foster’s weapon.
The shots injured the driver and killed Wiley, who was in his mother’s arms in the front passenger seat.
Kohen Wiley’s grandmother, LaSandra Williams, said she has seen the video.
“I’m having a difficult time understanding the word justified. I just don’t understand,” Williams said.
Williams, her family and their attorneys have reviewed the footage. Attorney Ben Crump addressed the shooting at a news conference Thursday.
“America, our society must have more empathy for human life,” Crump said.
The family’s legal team said Foster has resigned from the Senatobia Police Department. Crump said he wants Foster decertified.
Crump said, “The bullet that killed Kohen Wiley was not justified. This decision sends a message that a Black baby boy, his life, is not as valuable as the white diapers that he is wrapped in.”
The Mississippi Attorney General’s Office ruled the shooting justified based on the investigation conducted by the Department of Public Safety.
The state’s investigation found the driver drove into the officers, and the video supports that finding. Several officers drew their guns, but only Foster opened fire.
Attorney Van Turner said the fight for justice for Kohen Wiley is not over.
“We’re going to petition the Department of Justice to open an investigation to make sure that we get justice for this baby. It just won’t end here. We have to take it all the way to the top,” Turner said.
Kohen Wiley’s mother said she held her baby up in the air to show officers a child was in the car.
Action News 5 slowed multiple body-camera videos down to see if it was easy to spot her and her child in the front seat, but it was not, especially given how quickly the incident escalated.

title: Woman charged after Facebook threat at Trump during planned trip to Alabama-Georgia game
text:
LAUDERDALE COUNTY, Ala. (WAFF/Gray News) — An Alabama woman faces federal charges after investigators said she posted a threat against President Donald Trump on Facebook ahead of his planned trip to the Alabama-Georgia college football game.
The charges against Megan Lorraine Utz, of Florence, were filed Oct. 8 in federal court in Alabama.
Threat posted after game announcement
According to investigators, around Oct. 5, a social media account under the name “Kase Utz” made a threatening comment in response to a Facebook post about Trump’s plan to attend the game that said, “He’s not allowed in my stadium! I’ll put a bullet through him if he dares.”
Investigators said the account was linked to Utz by matching the profile photo to her driver’s license photo, including a distinctive neck tattoo. Records from the social media company also matched her birthday and pointed to Florence.
Arrest followed foot chase
On Oct. 6, FBI and Secret Service agents with police went to the Salvation Army in Florence, where Utz was last known to be staying. Workers said she left in a light-blue pickup and might be at a nearby house.
Agents said they found the truck on Midway Street. Utz briefly opened the front door, then shut and locked it, and later ran on foot. Officers caught her about two blocks away.
Utz was arrested on a separate local warrant for harassing messages. Officers took an iPhone from her.
Investigators say she agreed to talk
Investigators said they read Utz her rights and she agreed to talk. She told them she suffered 18 concussions and had taken several prescription medications.
When asked about the post, Utz said she wanted her phone checked for hacking and blamed malware for the message. Utz asked officers, “How am I going to shoot him?”
Officers sent the phone to an FBI forensics lab for examination.
Prior police encounters noted in court file
The court file also mentions earlier run-ins with police, including a 2024 local warrant over harassing messages, a recent theft report where she was listed as a suspect and being removed from a rehab facility and the Salvation Army.
Utz will be arraigned in Birmingham on Nov. 4.

title: Bucksport appoints new deputy police chief
text:
Bucksport has a new deputy police chief, the latest appointment in a handful of recent staffing changes in its public safety departments.
The Town Council appointed Daniel Harlan, a sergeant who’s worked for the town for 15 years in total, to the role Thursday.
“No question in my mind he’s the right man for the job,” Town Manager Jacob Gran said. “We have, or will have, three very fine gentlemen in our public safety leadership positions, and I look forward to seeing what they accomplish together.”
Bucksport’s three public safety leaders are its deputy fire chief, deputy police chief and public safety director, who oversees the town’s in-house police and fire departments. Public Safety Director David Winchester was appointed in September. Deputy Fire Chief Michael Denning has held his position for decades and plans to retire at the end of the year.
The town’s public safety director, Sean Geagan, retired from that role in July after 37 years to become coordinator of student behavior and school safety at the local school district, RSU 25.
After evaluating its staffing structure amid budget conversations, the town decided to keep the public safety director position and appointed deputy police chief David Winchester in September.
Harlan was previously an officer in Bucksport, became a sergeant with Hancock County and then moved to become a patrolman in Brewer in February 2024, the Bangor Daily News previously reported. He was sworn in as a Bucksport sergeant that September.

title: A Sneak Peek Inside the Renovated Maine State Museum
text:
A Sneak Peek Inside the Renovated Maine State Museum
It is hard to believe that it has been over six years since the Maine State Museum closed its doors.
Fortunately, the wait is almost over! The museum will reopen to the public on Saturday, October 24th!
When and Why Did The Museum Close?
Initially, the museum closed because of the COVID-19 pandemic. Like nearly all non-essential public facing spaces, the museum closed its doors in order to "flatten the curve".
However, the museum remained closed.
Why?
Well, it was decided that the closure was the perfect time to start some much needed updates to the museum. In addition to a series of needed structural repairs being made to the building and an asbestos removal project, the museum exhibits went through a significant overhaul.
About the Maine State Museum Renovations
When the museum reopens the public will have a chance to experience the history of Maine through "Beyond the Postcard". Basically, the story of Maine life will be told through the stories of people who lived here. For example, Cornelia "Fly Rod" Crosby, an outdoors influencer 120 years before we had influencers. Also, Alvin O. Lombard, who invented a motorized log hauler.
Then, of course, there is Vector the humpback whale. We have heard so much about the museum's new acquisition: a whale skeleton. She is even more impressive in person than you think! Next to Vector is the skeleton of a juvenile whale.
The new children's area has a lot of interactive experiences and contains the last operating Maine switchboard, which operated in Bryant Pond until the early 1980s.
The museum's upper-level is dominated by a massive display of Maine quilts. Some of them date back to the early 1800s.
Only about half the museum will open on Saturday. Just the top floors. The lower levels, which include the 12,000 Years In Maine & Made in Maine exhibits, will open at a later date. Probably sometime in the next year.
According to Maine State Museum Director Bernard Fishman, the lengthy renovation project cost about $3 million and much of the money came from donations by organizations and companies. These include the Lunder Foundation, the Alfond Foundation, the Betterment Fund, Avangrid, Kennebec Savings Bank, Hammond Lumber, and Bangor Savings Bank.
The Maine State Museum Will Be Free Through 2026
Thanks to a grant from Avangrid, the museum will be free through December 31st. And, also thanks to Avangrid, the museum will be free one Saturday a month through 2027.

title: Aging Untold: Why walking is a step toward healthy aging
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we share practical ways to walk smarter, improve stability and boost your stamina with every step.
We also discuss what it really means when an aging loved one refuses medical treatment and how families can navigate that choice with compassion and support.
Then, a survivor shares his journey with ocular melanoma, underscoring the eye exam that can catch rare conditions early.
Walking, even in short bursts, is a tool for healthy aging.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said walking reflects the health of the entire body, and it can also provide clues to neurological issues.
Walking draws on muscle strength, balance, heart health and oxygenation, she said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said mobility is tied to independence.
“Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck says that people who have difficulties with walking should still try to keep their legs moving with foot or leg pumps. Muscle loss can happen quickly, even in healthy older adults.
Hearing that an aging loved one is refusing medical treatment can be difficult.
Rather than push back, aging expert Amy O’Rourke says to slow down, take a deep breath and listen to figure out what they are afraid of, trying to avoid or fighting for.
Rogers said the person is sometimes looking at the medications along with the side effects and weighing all those different things.
The Aging Untold experts said families should make sure a loved one’s decision is based on accurate understanding, not a misconception.
Ocular melanoma affects only five or six out of every million people each year. Ryan Gibson is one of them.
When he lost his right eye to the rare cancer, the decision before him was whether to blend in with a normal-looking prosthetic or make a statement. Gibson chose to make a statement.
He uses his prosthetic eye as a conversation starter to raise awareness about ocular melanoma.
At Emma’s Torch, a cafe and culinary school in Washington, D.C., students learn food preparation skills under timed kitchen conditions. The students are refugees, exiles and survivors of human trafficking.
Kerry Brodie founded the social justice nonprofit to help the students with self-advocacy skills, English classes, resume writing, interview prep and more.

title: Legendary LSU basketball coach Dale Brown dies at 90
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - Dale Brown, the legendary LSU men’s basketball coach who transformed the Tigers into a national contender and coached some of the biggest names in college basketball, died on Oct. 23.
He was 90.
Brown spent 25 seasons leading the LSU men’s basketball program from 1972 to 1997, compiling 448 victories and guiding the Tigers to two NCAA Final Four appearances.
Brown led LSU to four Southeastern Conference regular-season championships, 13 NCAA Tournament appearances and Final Four appearances in 1981 and 1986.
Among the players he coached were future NBA Hall of Famer Shaquille O’Neal, Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf, formerly known as Chris Jackson, and LSU standout Rudy Macklin.
He remains the winningest head coach in LSU men’s basketball history.
His death came just two days after LSU announced he had been selected to receive the 2027 John R. Wooden Legends of Coaching Award, recognizing his accomplishments and impact on college basketball.
Dale Brown’s family remembers his love for Louisiana
In a statement following his death, Brown’s family remembered him as a man who put others first and developed a lasting connection with Louisiana.
“We have lost the most loving and most loved man any of us has ever known,” the family said.
“Dale Brown always put others first. He always led with the heart. He was always a great humanitarian before anything else.”
The family also reflected on the relationship Brown built with the state during his decades at LSU.
“Dale long ago fell in love with Louisiana. And the people of Louisiana loved him right back. We are forever grateful for that.”
Tributes pour in following Brown’s death
Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry joined those mourning Brown’s death, crediting the longtime coach with transforming LSU basketball.
“Saddened to hear the news of Coach Dale Brown’s passing.
He put LSU Basketball on the map and his impact will be felt for decades to come.
Sharon and I join the Brown family and the LSU community in mourning this monumental loss.
While we will miss him, I’m confident that his legacy will be carried on both on and off the basketball court. May he rest in peace," Landry wrote on X.
Sports journalist Marc J. Spears also remembered Brown, reflecting on their conversations over the years.
“Rest in Peace to an extraordinary human in Dale Brown, the legendary former LSU men’s basketball coach, who passed today at 90. Truly appreciated his conversations on basketball and life. Thank you for your time and wisdom coach,” Spears wrote on X.
A legendary career at LSU
Brown arrived in Baton Rouge in 1972 and worked to build a basketball program capable of competing with the nation’s best.
He traveled across Louisiana promoting LSU basketball and encouraging fans to support the Tigers.
His efforts helped LSU capture its first SEC regular-season championship since 1954 when the Tigers won the title in 1979.
Two years later, Brown led LSU to the 1981 Final Four. The Tigers returned to college basketball’s biggest stage in 1986.
Brown was named the Associated Press National Coach of the Year in 1981 and earned SEC Coach of the Year honors four times.
He was inducted into the National Collegiate Basketball Hall of Fame, Louisiana Sports Hall of Fame and LSU Athletic Hall of Fame.
In 2022, LSU officially unveiled Dale Brown Court inside the Pete Maravich Assembly Center. The court was renamed Dale Brown/Sue Gunter Court in 2023 to recognize both former LSU basketball coaches.
Brown reflected on his life and legacy
During a 2025 interview with WAFB investigative reporter Chris Nakamoto, Brown reflected on his coaching career, the lessons he learned from his mother and how he hoped to be remembered.
Brown recalled a game against undefeated, top-ranked Kentucky in Baton Rouge when all five of his starters had fouled out.
Facing what appeared to be an impossible situation, Brown said he called a timeout and encouraged his remaining players to believe they could win.
“From now on you are not substitutes, you are backups,” Brown recalled telling his players.
Brown said LSU went on to win the game.
But when Nakamoto asked Brown what he hoped people would remember about him after 90 years, the former coach turned to lessons from his childhood.
“I was taught by my mother to do things that are right. And to stand up for what’s right,” Brown said. “I don’t care if anyone disagrees with me. I’m not trying to get into an argument.”
He also recalled his mother’s advice about the importance of character over appearances.
“If you spend too much time polishing your image, you will tarnish your character and be an unhappy man,” Brown said, recalling her words. “So you say what’s in your heart.”
Brown was born Oct. 31, 1935, in Minot, North Dakota. He died eight days before his 91st birthday.

title: Lawrence football rumbles through Messalonskee in regular-season finale
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
FAIRFIELD — For four years, Brady Richards asked to carry the ball. On Friday night, he got his chance.
“I would always tell Coach (Pete) Curtis, ‘I’m ready. Give me the rock,'” Richards said.
The senior offensive lineman scored his first high school touchdown on a 3-yard run, the most memorable of many scores in the Lawrence football team’s 60-6 win over Messalonskee in a Class B North matchup at Keyes Field.
“It was awesome,” Richards said. “My heart was pounding.”
The Bulldogs (8-0) gained 302 of their 389 yards in the first half, highlighted by senior running back Keegan Littlefield, who ran for 150 yards on seven carries and scored a touchdown. Junior quarterback Jackson Dangler had 60 yards on three carries, scoring two touchdowns.
Seven ball carriers had 30 or more yards rushing for the Bulldogs.
“When you have the (offensive) line we do, anybody can kind of carry the ball,” said Curtis, Lawrence’s first-year head coach. “The backs are good, but the line helps.”
Lawrence built a 42-6 lead by halftime, and since both teams are heading to the B North playoffs, the Bulldogs and the Eagles pulled their starters and played their backups for most of the final two quarters. Kayleb Gerow, Maddock LePage and Talan Ward each had touchdown runs in the second half for Lawrence.
Ready for his moment
Richards, a 6-foot-4, 250-pound lineman, was notified on Thursday that he might get a carry in Friday’s game, so he got some practice reps for his big moment.
“The last seven weeks, (Curtis) really hasn’t talked about (getting the ball) at all,” Richards said. “On Thursday, he said, ‘We’re putting you in.'”
With the Bulldogs up 20-0 late in the first quarter, Richards’ number was called. He lined up at fullback, took a handoff from Dangler, ran over a couple of Messalonskee defenders and walked into the end zone, throwing both arms in the air in celebration before he was mobbed by his teammates.
Richards said the last time he had scored a touchdown was in eighth grade.
“Everyone came up to me, patting me on the back, giving me hugs, it was just amazing,” Richards said.
Keeping up the fight
Messalonskee (4-4) had 120 yards in the first half, most coming at the end of the second quarter when the Eagles put together a 76-yard drive that ate up 4:49 and was punctuated by a 1-yard touchdown plunge from senior quarterback Fin Minkel.
Minkel finished with 33 rushing yards on six carries.
Leader of the pack
With the win, the Bulldogs wrap up the No. 1 seed in the Class B North playoffs. This means Lawrence earns a bye and has a week off before the semifinal round.
“It’s good to get their bodies rested,” Curtis said. “We’re still going to have practice and they’re still going to be running, but probably limited contact. … We told the kids during the preseason, (the goal) is to just climb the mountain and get better and better each day, and I think we’ve done that.”
Cony (7-1) will be the No. 2 seed, followed by No. 3 Skowhegan (5-3) and No. 4 Fryeburg Academy.
Messalonskee enters the playoffs as the No. 5 seed, with Brunswick (2-6) holding the sixth and final seed in the tournament.
Statistical leaders
• Lawrence: Keegan Littlefield (7 carries, 150 yards, TD); Jackson Dangler (3 carries, 60 yards, 2 TDs); Hunter Curtis (2 carries, 30 yards, TD); Jaiden Hebert (5 carries, 26 yards, TD)
• Messalonskee: Fin Minkel (6 carries, 33 yards rushing, TD; 64 yards passing); Malachi Cusano (5 carries, 26 yards); Peter McLaughlin (2 of 7 passing, 33 yards)

title: Legendary LSU basketball coach Dale Brown dies at 90
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - Dale Brown, the legendary LSU men’s basketball coach who transformed the Tigers into a national contender and coached some of the biggest names in college basketball, died on Oct. 23.
He was 90.
Brown spent 25 seasons leading the LSU men’s basketball program from 1972 to 1997, compiling 448 victories and guiding the Tigers to two NCAA Final Four appearances.
Brown led LSU to four Southeastern Conference regular-season championships, 13 NCAA Tournament appearances and Final Four appearances in 1981 and 1986.
Among the players he coached were future NBA Hall of Famer Shaquille O’Neal, Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf, formerly known as Chris Jackson, and LSU standout Rudy Macklin.
He remains the winningest head coach in LSU men’s basketball history.
His death came just two days after LSU announced he had been selected to receive the 2027 John R. Wooden Legends of Coaching Award, recognizing his accomplishments and impact on college basketball.
Dale Brown’s family remembers his love for Louisiana
In a statement following his death, Brown’s family remembered him as a man who put others first and developed a lasting connection with Louisiana.
“We have lost the most loving and most loved man any of us has ever known,” the family said.
“Dale Brown always put others first. He always led with the heart. He was always a great humanitarian before anything else.”
The family also reflected on the relationship Brown built with the state during his decades at LSU.
“Dale long ago fell in love with Louisiana. And the people of Louisiana loved him right back. We are forever grateful for that.”
Tributes pour in following Brown’s death
Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry joined those mourning Brown’s death, crediting the longtime coach with transforming LSU basketball.
“Saddened to hear the news of Coach Dale Brown’s passing.
He put LSU Basketball on the map and his impact will be felt for decades to come.
Sharon and I join the Brown family and the LSU community in mourning this monumental loss.
While we will miss him, I’m confident that his legacy will be carried on both on and off the basketball court. May he rest in peace," Landry wrote on X.
Sports journalist Marc J. Spears also remembered Brown, reflecting on their conversations over the years.
“Rest in Peace to an extraordinary human in Dale Brown, the legendary former LSU men’s basketball coach, who passed today at 90. Truly appreciated his conversations on basketball and life. Thank you for your time and wisdom coach,” Spears wrote on X.
A legendary career at LSU
Brown arrived in Baton Rouge in 1972 and worked to build a basketball program capable of competing with the nation’s best.
He traveled across Louisiana promoting LSU basketball and encouraging fans to support the Tigers.
His efforts helped LSU capture its first SEC regular-season championship since 1954 when the Tigers won the title in 1979.
Two years later, Brown led LSU to the 1981 Final Four. The Tigers returned to college basketball’s biggest stage in 1986.
Brown was named the Associated Press National Coach of the Year in 1981 and earned SEC Coach of the Year honors four times.
He was inducted into the National Collegiate Basketball Hall of Fame, Louisiana Sports Hall of Fame and LSU Athletic Hall of Fame.
In 2022, LSU officially unveiled Dale Brown Court inside the Pete Maravich Assembly Center. The court was renamed Dale Brown/Sue Gunter Court in 2023 to recognize both former LSU basketball coaches.
Brown reflected on his life and legacy
During a 2025 interview with WAFB investigative reporter Chris Nakamoto, Brown reflected on his coaching career, the lessons he learned from his mother and how he hoped to be remembered.
Brown recalled a game against undefeated, top-ranked Kentucky in Baton Rouge when all five of his starters had fouled out.
Facing what appeared to be an impossible situation, Brown said he called a timeout and encouraged his remaining players to believe they could win.
“From now on you are not substitutes, you are backups,” Brown recalled telling his players.
Brown said LSU went on to win the game.
But when Nakamoto asked Brown what he hoped people would remember about him after 90 years, the former coach turned to lessons from his childhood.
“I was taught by my mother to do things that are right. And to stand up for what’s right,” Brown said. “I don’t care if anyone disagrees with me. I’m not trying to get into an argument.”
He also recalled his mother’s advice about the importance of character over appearances.
“If you spend too much time polishing your image, you will tarnish your character and be an unhappy man,” Brown said, recalling her words. “So you say what’s in your heart.”
Brown was born Oct. 31, 1935, in Minot, North Dakota. He died eight days before his 91st birthday.

title: HIGH SCHOOL SOCCER PLAYOFFS PREVIEW
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - The Maine Principals’ Association soccer tournament is underway, with several county teams competing for championships across Classes B, C, D and the 8-person bracket.
Class B boys
The Caribou Vikings play Saturday in a preliminary matchup against Medomak Valley. The Vikings are the 8 seed and finished the season with a record of 4-8-2. The Vikings had two wins over Fort Kent earlier this year. The winner of Saturday’s match will face top seed John Bapst, which is undefeated.
The Presque Isle Wildcats are the 4 seed and received a bye into next week’s quarterfinals. They finished the season with a record of 8-5-1, including wins over Foxcroft Academy and Caribou. They will face the winner of the 12-5 matchup between Skowhegan and Erskine.
Class B girls
The Presque Isle Lady Wildcats are the 3 seed and earned a bye. They finished the season with a record of 9-3-2, with two wins over Orono and a win over previously undefeated Fort Kent. They will face the winner of the 11-6 matchup between Lawrence and Skowhegan.
Class C boys
The Fort Kent Warriors are the 3 seed and will face 6 seed Washington Academy. The Warriors finished the season 7-6-1, including wins over Madawaska and Washington Academy.
Class C girls
The Fort Kent Lady Warriors are the top seed, finishing with a record of 11-1-2. Their only loss was against Class B’s Presque Isle. They will face 8th-seeded MCI Saturday at 2 p.m.
The Houlton Lady Shires are the 5 seed. The Lady Shires finished the season with a record of 7-7, including a win over Central. They face 5th-seeded Central High. Star player Ava Ezell said it would mean a lot to the team to make a deep run.
Class D boys
Top seed Madawaska finished the season with a 12-2 record, with their only losses against Class C’s Fort Kent. Madawaska has two wins over Central Aroostook this season. The Owls face 8 seed MSSM in an all-county quarterfinal matchup.
The 2 seed Central Aroostook Panthers have a record of 11-3. Central Aroostook swept both Washburn and Easton this year. They will face 7th-seeded Penobscot Valley.
Defending champion and 3 seed Fort Fairfield has a record of 6-6-2, with a win over Central Aroostook this season. The Tigers face 6th-seeded Washburn. The Beavers finished 4-8-2, including two wins over Hodgdon. They play Tuesday at 3 p.m.
5th-seeded Easton is taking on 4th-seeded Hodgdon. Easton finished 8-6 on the year, including two wins over Hodgdon. Hodgdon finished 9-4-1 and swept Easton during the regular season.
Class D girls
7th-seeded Washburn is taking on 2 seed Fort Fairfield. Washburn finished with a record of 7-7. The Lady Tigers finished the year with a record of 12-2, with their only losses against Central Aroostook and Madawaska. Fort Fairfield plays Washburn next Tuesday at 1 p.m.
6 seed Van Buren takes on 3 seed Central Aroostook next Wednesday at 2 p.m. in an all-county quarterfinal. Central Aroostook finished 11-3 this season, including wins over Ashland and Fort Fairfield. Van Buren finished with a record of 9-5, including a win over Ashland this season.
4 seed Ashland, led by coach Peter Belskis, is taking on 5 seed Madawaska. Ashland finished 9-4-1, and Madawaska went 10-4. Ashland’s star player Addie Labelle was injured earlier in the year, and Sadie Trams has stepped up. Madawaska has a win against Fort Fairfield this season.
8-person bracket
The Wisdom Lady Pioneers are the 2 seed with a record of 12-2. Sisters Madi and Ellie Cyr have played all year for the team. They are looking to return to the state title game. Wisdom awaits the winner of the 7-10 matchup between George Stevens and Penobscot Christian.

title: Pope Leo XIV cancels Assisi trip on doctors' advice as he recovers from surgery
text:
Pope Leo XIV cancels Assisi trip on doctors' advice as he recovers from surgery
Pope Leo XIV will miss a planned trip to Assisi next week after doctors advised against the helicopter journey to the Italian town as he recovers from thoracic surgery, the Vatican said Friday.
The pope had been due to attend a gathering on Tuesday marking the 40th anniversary of St. John Paul II’s World Day of Prayer for Peace.
In a statement, the Vatican said Leo, 71, was advised not to travel “to facilitate his recovery” from the surgery to treat his lung cancer last week. The pope will instead send a message to organizers, Christian and other religious leaders, and guests attending the event, titled “Disarmed and Disarming Peace.”
In a separate statement, the pope's doctors said a follow-up chest X-ray confirmed he was recovering well. However, given the short time that has elapsed since the operation, they recommended as a precaution that he not make the trip to Assisi by helicopter.
The Vatican said Leo wanted to express his closeness to participants and reaffirm his belief that the “spirit of Assisi,” dialogue and the search for words and gestures of peace remain valuable resources at a time of conflict.
The Assisi meeting commemorates the landmark interfaith peace gathering convened by St. John Paul II in 1986.
The cancellation is the latest change to Leo’s schedule since he had part of one lung removed last week in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
The pope will need no further treatment for lung cancer after tests confirmed the disease was localized, the Vatican said Wednesday.
The Vatican has said the pope’s activities will be guided by medical advice during his recovery.
Leo returned to the Vatican last Saturday, as his surgeon said there are “no clinical reasons” to prevent a planned trip to Latin America next month.
Thoracic surgeons often advise patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery — which would give the pope just the interval needed to make his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, depending on his recovery.
The trip will involve a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes.
In his public appearances since returning to the Vatican, Leo appeared in good health, speaking with a strong and clear voice.

title: Where the candidates in Maine stand on taxes and tariffs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Your Choice, Your Voice: Where the candidates for office in Maine stand on tariffs and taxes
Maine's Total Coverage asked viewers what issues they are most interested in learning more about heading into the midterm election.
After hundreds of submissions, one of the top issues on voters' minds is taxes and tariffs. Maine's Total Coverage asked all the candidates for governor and congressional office about their stance on the issue.
Gubernatorial candidates
The race for the Blaine House began with two crowded primaries. Republican Bobby Charles was the winner of a seven-way ranked-choice voting primary and Democrat Hannah Pingree won in a five-way race. Independent Rick Bennett, who left the Republican Party last year, was the only independent who got the required number of signatures to get on the November ballot.
As it relates to taxes, in the last legislature there were new taxes on things like cigarettes, marijuana, paint, streaming services, fishing licenses and millionaires.
"I will drill down on tax expenditures and make them accountable," Bennett said. "These are special tax deals that are given for public purposes. But often we don't even know what the real value of those are. They may be a special break for a given company. It might be a tax program."
"An 80% increase in spending by this governor and this legislature in just eight years. They've gone from $7.1 billion to almost $14 billion," Charles said. "That is where the problem is. The problem is in the spending. We can bring those other taxes down. If we can get the spending back down again."
Property taxes are the consensus for the gubernatorial candidates. Pingree said she has a plan to lower those taxes.
"I've proposed to double the homestead exemption, to increase the property tax fairness credit," Pingree said. "I think we need to look at how we tax second homes owned by non-Maine residents at a higher rate. That's going to require a bipartisan conversation."
Senate candidates
The highly-anticipated Senate race has been closely watched for months. Senator Susan Collins is seeking a historic sixth term in Washington. Democrat Troy Jackson replaced Graham Platner as the party's nominee in late July after Platner dropped out following a sexual assault allegation he denies.
Since July, there's been a back-and-forth battle between Jackson and Collins on a variety of issues, including tariffs.
Collins says she has strongly opposed tariffs with Canada, pointing to the close relationship between the country and Maine. Recently, the senator says she's been able to get several products taken off the list, including cement, pulp and road salt.
"In the tiny town of Frenchville of 900 people in northern Maine, the new tariff would have added $10,000 to their expenses this winter," Collins said. "So I was very glad to convince the administration to do away with that tariff, and believe me, I'm continuing to pressure them to come back to the table with Canada and negotiate in a better way."
Jackson says there are still more tariffs on the table to worry about. Criticizing Collins, Jackson says the senator should be doing more as the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee to block certain tariffs.
"What about all the other tariffs that are on? How much money is that going to cost the town of Presque Isle, the town of Frenchville, all the people that work in the farming and fishing and forestry industry," Jackson said. "I mean, all those people, parts, everything that comes out of Canada, our products go to Canada. I mean, that's what's actually going to cost people."
Candidates for Congress in Maine's 1st District
The race for Maine's 1st Congressional District is a rematch. Army veteran Ron Russell is challenging Congresswoman Chellie Pingree for her seat in Washington.
Pingree has held the congressional seat for nearly two decades. Russell ran against her back in 2024, but lost.
Russell secured the Republican nomination back in June, defeating newcomer Joshua James Pietrowicz.
When it comes to tariffs, the two candidates are quite divided. Russell says the tariffs with Canada are only temporary, saying President Donald Trump is using tariffs as a power very well.
"He's using it just to make a point because we know Canada has tariffs against us that prevent the sale of dairy products, as an example, so that will soon pass," Russell said.
Congresswoman Pingree disagrees, calling the tariffs a nightmare. She says that Maine businesses that do cross-border trading are hurting. Pingree also says she's fighting back against the administration.
"Congress has the authority to tariff," Pingree said. "Congress should take back that authority and stop allowing the president to do them, especially in the manner that he's done them, which are arbitrary, sometimes used as punishment, sometimes just a threat."
Candidates for Congress in Maine's 2nd District
Maine's 2nd Congressional District began when Congressman Jared Golden still planned to run for his seat.
Former two-time Republican Governor Paul LePage got in the race to take on Golden. LePage was uncontested in the primary. Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap filed paperwork to primary Golden.
Golden eventually left the race, and three other candidates got in to primary Dunlap.
Dunlap won in a four-way ranked-choice voting primary in June to take on LePage.
On tariffs, Dunlap said tariffs have a purpose, specifically when they target an industry because of unfair competition overseas. He added that Pres. Donald Trump's tariffs hurt Mainers.
"We pay the tariff. Canada doesn't pay the tariff," Dunlap said. "I think that's something that the president would like people to think that we're punishing Canada somehow. We're actually punishing our own citizens, and then they reciprocate by having tariffs on all kinds of different things that we depend on the export of."
LePage agreed that tariffs have a purpose, breaking a little with Trump.
"Tariffs are good if you don't have an income tax because that's how you would pay for goods and services," LePage said. "I don't agree with both of them. So one of them has got to go. Preferably the income tax."

title: More tribal leaders step into Maine’s fraught Senate race
text:
Amid a bruising and expensive knock-down-drag-out U.S. Senate race in Maine, Wabanaki leaders are stepping into the fray. It hasn’t been entirely smooth.
Chief William Nicholas Sr., of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Motahkomikuk (Indian Township), told the Portland Press Herald on Friday that he’s endorsing the five-term Republican incumbent Susan Collins.
He joins Chief Amkuwiposohehs “Pos” Bassett of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik (Pleasant Point), who announced his support for Collins last week in what seems to be a first for the senator. Democrat Troy Jackson, Collins’ opponent, picked up his first tribal endorsement in the Senate race from the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians chief and tribal council on Monday.
Jackson was endorsed by the Mi’kmaq Nation when he ran in the Democratic primary for governor this spring.
Maliseet Chief Clarissa Sabattis noted Jackson’s long-standing commitment to tribal sovereignty in a statement announcing her endorsement.
“From championing clean drinking water initiatives to his role in creating the commission to reexamine the 1980 Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act, Troy has consistently proven that he listens to indigenous voices and stands with the Wabanaki people,” she said.
Nicholas praised Collins’ directing of federal dollars to his community and her responsiveness.
“Every time we’ve had an issue in our community and she’s been called upon, she’s personally stepped up,” Nicholas said.
He rattled off a list of projects — 335 heat pumps, 70 hybrid hot water heaters, 230 doors and exterior and storm doors and at least 10 single-family homes — that Collins has helped fund. He was touched by the senator’s visit to the reservation this summer.
“It’s hard to turn away from an ally and a friend who has done so much for this community,” Nicholas said.
As both sides fire volleys of nasty accusations at one another, Nicholas felt compelled to cut through the noise.
“People are going to base their information on what they’re seeing,” he said. “But you know, every time somebody turns on a heat pump, somebody helped us with that.”
Collins said in a statement Friday afternoon that she was honored by the endorsement and looks forward to continuing to work with the tribe.
Although Collins has not championed tribal sovereignty in the way some Wabanaki leaders would hope, Nicholas is backing Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree to address the issue at the state level.
Nicholas was careful to state that he personally is endorsing Collins as tribal chief — but that he does not speak for the entire community, which remains divided.
His counterpart in Sipayik, Bassett, drew criticism when he alone penned an endorsement letter on behalf of the tribe.
After the Collins campaign celebrated what they billed as the endorsement of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Pleasant Point, several tribal members questioned the chief’s authority to make a unilateral endorsement without consulting the tribal council.
“Absent direction by the tribal community or its governing body, the chief does not have the authority to speak for the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik,” tribal member Gail Dana, who narrowly lost the election for chief against Bassett last month, wrote in an opinion column in the Bangor Daily News.
Council member Adam Newell said he was blindsided by the announcement.
At a minimum, Newell said, Bassett should have consulted the council in advance. He voiced his objections to the chief directly and on Facebook, where he sought to distance himself from the divisive race.
“It’s a new thing for tribes to start doing it,” he said, warning “it’s a slippery slope for me.”
The campaign referred questions to Bassett, who did not respond to a request for comment.
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.

title: Man used sledgehammer to remove head of Iwo Jima monument Marine, police say
text:
QUANTICO, Va. (WUSA) — A man is accused of beheading one of the Marines depicted on the Iwo Jima statue in Quantico, Virginia.
The Prince William County Police Department said officers were called to the statue late Tuesday night.
Officers found 27-year-old Miguel Alonso Maldonado Soriano vandalizing the monument with a sledgehammer, according to police.
Police said Soriano caused hundreds of thousands of dollars in damage to the statue and removed the head of one of the depicted soldiers.
Soriano was arrested and faces charges of felony destruction of property, trespass with intent to damage property and felony injury to a monument.
He was held without bond pending a court appearance.
There is no word on a motive.

title: Longtime EMTs’ retirement ends Maine’s only all-volunteer ambulance service
text:
DENNYSVILLE, Maine (WABI) - Maine is losing its only ambulance service made up entirely of volunteers. The Dennys River Ambulance Service will stop operating on Nov. 30 due to a lack of volunteers.
Dennys River EMS has served the towns of Pembroke and Dennysville and the Edmund, Marion and Cathance townships since 1966.
Wayne and Roberta Seeley have been EMTs with the Dennysville Volunteer Fire Department for more than 50 years. The couple, now in their 80s, is retiring, and with no other volunteers to take their place, the ambulance service is retiring as well.
“I feel really bad about it stopping because people like to see somebody come that they know,” Roberta Seeley said. “And now they’re going to have strangers come in and some of the older people aren’t going to really care for this.”
New faces aren’t going to be the only adjustment for residents. With Lubec and Eastport as the closest alternatives, residents will see a delay in response and transport time.
“That service may not even be at their station,” noted EMT Cierra Seeley. “They may be on another call and not have a second crew. So that’s just going to add more time.”
Brent Ellinwood, another volunteer EMT for Dennys River, added that other services are going to charge the towns money to come, meaning taxes will go up.
In its heyday, Dennys River Ambulance had about 12 volunteers. The service is now down to six, a number officials say isn’t enough to stay operational.
“You’d have to have 10 or 12, I would say, to run and have them on duty 24 hours a day, seven days a week,” Wayne Seeley said. “People are not volunteering like they used to anymore.”
Cierra, the Seeleys’ granddaughter, said the family considered every option before reaching this point.
“It’s heartbreaking. We were really hoping to keep it going, but without the volunteers, we can’t. We’ve thought of every scenario,” she described. “I don’t think people are going to realize what they had with us here until we’re actually gone and they call.”
Rick Petrie, a longtime EMT and member of the legislative EMS Commission, said the closure reflects larger problems, calling it “a warning about the sustainability of the EMSs in the state of Maine and nationally.”
Petrie cited full-time employment and the extensive training process are among the reasons volunteerism is down, but that’s not the only reason stations are struggling.
“The EMS system in Maine and nationally is flawed,” Petrie said. “It’s based on a flawed model that’s many years old, has never been updated, has never been looked at, and the net result is no ambulance service in the state of Maine responding solely on 911 calls is not being subsidized.”
According to Petrie, to fund a fully-staffed ambulance service, they would need to respond to about 2,500 paying calls a year. In Dennysville, they get about 100.
“It isn’t happening because the people don’t care,” Petrie said. “It’s because we built a system 40 or 50 years ago that we’re still relying on, and the system doesn’t work anymore. It’s broken and it doesn’t work.”
While the Seeleys are retiring from EMS work, their service with the Dennysville Volunteer Fire Department will continue.
As EMTs, they have delivered medical equipment such as crutches and hospital beds to residents’ homes. They said that despite the ambulance service closing, they will continue providing these resources to their neighbors.

title: Maine DHHS will hold public hearing on Prime Healthcare
text:
Maine’s Department of Health and Human Services will hold a public hearing on Prime Healthcare as part of its review of the organization. The state approved Prime Healthcare Foundation’s purchase of Central Maine Healthcare earlier this year, and the company has since been the subject of numerous complaints and concerns.
Democratic Rep. Julie McCabe requested the public hearing. She represents Lewiston, home to Central Maine Healthcare’s flagship hospital.
McCabe said concerns about Prime include staff turnover, the firing or suspension of 20 nurses involved in unionization efforts, and the cancellation of a contract with an emergency department physician group.
Central Maine Medical Center is also facing potential termination from Medicare because of infection control issues. McCabe said patients and providers deserve an opportunity to share their experiences with Maine’s Department of Health and Human Services.
“Through the public hearing process, the Commissioner will be able to learn more critical information about what is going on in our community and be able to have a much clearer idea of Prime’s culpability and will be able to make more informed enforcement decisions,” McCabe said.
DHHS spokesperson Lindsay Hammes said the department is “taking its subsequent review of the Certificate of Need approval for Prime Healthcare Foundation, Inc. seriously and agrees that a public hearing is an appropriate step.”
Hammes said the hearing will be scheduled in the coming weeks.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Marshwood football bounces back to beat Kennebunk in finale
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SOUTH BERWICK — Marshwood High’s football team showed the grit and poise that has defined its season in a 32-16 win Friday against Kennebunk to earn the top playoff seed in Class B South and a bye into the regional semifinals.
The Hawks rebounded from their lone poor effort this season, a 37-14 home loss to Biddeford. They also bounced back during Friday’s game. Kennebunk led 10-0 in the first half and 16-8 early in the third quarter. Plus, Marshwood’s top player, running back/linebacker Greg Castoras, was on the sidelines in street clothes, wearing a coach’s headset with a video tablet in his hands, encouraging teammates.
“They responded to some adversity. We had a tough game last week and we had some tough conversations about the film, and how we practiced,” said Marshwood’s interim head coach, Andrew Elwell. “We needed that reality check. I needed that reality check. And I could not be more proud of the kids.”
Marshwood, with a 35-man roster, finishes the regular season at 7-1. With a welcome week off, the Hawks are hopeful to have Castoras back in two weeks when they host the winner of the No. 4 vs. No. 5 quarterfinal, likely Falmouth vs. Westbrook.
“We just put our heads down and worked,” said Michael Sbrizza, the Hawks’ senior quarterback/safety/punter/kicker. “That’s all it comes down to really. Work, work, work. It’s all about the process. And I think it showed here tonight.”
Kennebunk, at 6-2, will also get a bye into the regional semifinals. Biddeford (5-3) had an opportunity to jump to No. 2 but was beaten 44-8 by Cheverus (3-5), which needed the win to earn a playoff spot.
“Any time you can advance a week without playing, that’s obviously a benefit,” said Kennebunk coach Keith Noel. “After tonight, it gives us a chance to get back to basics. Which we’ve got to go and do. Get some guys a little healthier and be ready to play in two weeks.”
TAKING THE FOURTH
Early in the third quarter, both teams scored on long touchdown runs. Kennebunk’s Bradley Farrell took the third scrimmage play of the half 43 yards to put the Rams up 16-8. Farrell also had a 66-yard score in the first half.
On the next possession, Sbrizza turned a QB sneak into a 39-yard score, and Noah Goodwin’s conversion rush knotted the game at 16-16.
Both defenses stepped up after that, resulting in five consecutive three-and-outs, three by Kennebunk.
Marshwood appeared headed for another punt when, on the first play of the fourth quarter, Goodwin took the second handoff on an inside criss-cross counter — a staple play in the wing T offense for both teams — and went 24 yards on second-and-17. Later in the drive, on third-and-15, Sbrizza connected with Parker Ferrer for a 21-yard gain to the Rams 7.
On fourth-and-goal, Goodwin capped the 11-play drive, scoring from the 1.
Sbrizza, as he had done throughout the game, cued up a squib kickoff. This one caromed off a front-line Kennebunk player and was recovered by Marshwood’s Harrison Ames. The Hawks then put together a 10-play touchdown drive.
When Goodwin scored from the 10 and Jon Buttrick added the 2-point conversion, Marshwood led 32-16, only 1:40 was left in the game, and Kennebunk had not run a play in the fourth quarter.
UNSUNG HERO
Buttrick, a 5-foot-7, 150-pound junior, stepped into Castoras’ starting role on both sides of the ball. He had a team-high 17 carries for 59 yards, including an 11-yard first-half touchdown. On defense, he had multiple tackles for loss, including a sack.
Buttrick grew up playing football but said he initially chose not to play this year to focus on wrestling. He said Elwell was constantly recruiting him during school. He joined the team after the second game of the season.
“The first couple of weeks, I was mostly a practice player, helping out as much as I can,” Buttrick said. “Definitely, my role was very small. Castoras, our best guy out there, went down last week. Basically, Thursday, I found out (I’d be starting). I wasn’t too surprised. I was of the mindset, ‘Next guy up.'”
STATISTICS
• Kennebunk: Peter Landenberger (13 carries, 81 yards), Bradley Farrell (four carries, 109 yards, two TDs), Giovanni D’Elia (3 of 11 passing, 35 yards), Blake Morris (35-yard field goal)
• Marshwood: Noah Goodwin (13 carries, 71 yards, two TDs), Michael Sbrizza (12 carries, 71 yards, TD; 2 of 11 passing, 30 yards, one INT), Jon Buttrick (17 carries, 59 yards, TD)

title: Why not ‘Mr. Jackson,’ Sen. Collins?
text:
I’m offended that Sen. Susan Collins has cast Troy Jackson’s telling her to “shut up” during their recent debate as reflecting his misogyny. This, from a senator who approved a Supreme Court justice facing credible complaints of sexual assault, a justice who went on to overturn Roe v. Wade?
I wonder, instead, what the senator’s repeatedly calling her opponent by his first name betokens.
Is she highlighting the name’s relative unusualness, casting him as “not one of us”? Is this a “social class” barb, suggesting that her more aristocratic upbringing entitles her to respect, while his does not? This inequality in naming sounds to me like the custom, in wealthy families, of calling adult servants by their first names. This is Maine, not the Antebellum South. Using language to demean and disrespect is not part of our usual discourse.
Despite the wishes of some, we all remain equal here. And we will stand judged by our behavior.
Gail Wasserman
Brunswick

title: When health changes your sex life, intimacy doesn’t have to disappear
text:
(Aging Untold) — Health changes don’t just affect the body — they can reshape confidence, connection and communication between partners.
The Aging Untold experts tackle the questions many couples are afraid to ask out loud: When is it safe to resume sex? What if it isn’t? And what should you ask your doctor?
Start with what’s changing — and why
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first step is figuring out what’s behind the change.
“What’s changing it and why is it changing?” Cradduck said.
Cradduck noted that competency and consent are the first things to consider.
“Is it a matter of competency and consent? And if it is, then it’s off the table,” Cradduck said. “I’m not talking about lucidity. I’m saying if somebody cannot consent, then sex is off the table at that point. It’s not consensual.”
Cradduck added that for physical issues, like erectile dysfunction, a doctor can often help.
“Seeing a doctor can absolutely take care of it, and take care of things that are before, that are coming after,” Cradduck said. “There’s a lot of reasons to change, and there’s a lot of things that happen. We know with women, we have our own issues as we’re post-menopausal.”
Cradduck encouraged couples not to let embarrassment stop the conversation.
“Don’t be embarrassed by it, and say, ‘Hey, this isn’t working,’ or ‘This is hurting,’ or ‘This is something I want to participate in, but I’m not in the mood to,’” Cradduck said.
Intimacy and sexuality aren’t the same thing
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said one of the biggest misconceptions couples carry is treating intimacy and sexuality as interchangeable.
“I think one of the biggest misconceptions is that intimacy and sexuality are the same — and they’re not,” Rogers said. “Intimacy is that connection, and sexuality is an expression of that connection.”
Rogers said the best time to talk about these changes is before a health crisis hits.
“I think the best time for people to have these kinds of discussions is before a crisis,” Rogers said. “These are things we need to be talking about when we’re younger, because we know we’re going to age. We know there’s going to be a trajectory for different chronic conditions that may interfere. Perhaps if we start to take the time to discuss it early, we have a better understanding, the communication.”
When you’re exhausted from caregiving, intimacy can look different
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said intimacy is ultimately about feeling seen.
“To me, intimacy is feeling seen and understood and loved,” she said. “So when I think about that, I think talking is so important, and really honest conversations.”
O’Rourke acknowledged that caregiving fatigue can get in the way of a partner’s desire for sex.
“If you’re the caregiver and you’re taking care of somebody, you’re going to be tired a lot,” she said. “Maybe the other person wants to have sex, and maybe you’re just so exhausted you just can’t do it.”
Her suggestion: bring back date night.
“Go back to that,” O’Rourke said. “Set aside some time, just the two of you, no caregiving job in front of you, and talk. And maybe intimacy for you guys is just going to be holding hands. Maybe it’s going to be watching a TV show with your arms wrapped around each other. Maybe it’s going to be just a little bit of cuddling at night. So you can replace a few things until maybe you get back to possibly having sex again.”
A husband’s question: dementia, desire and what’s OK
Cradduck shared a story from a husband who called her with what he described as an awkward question. His wife had dementia, and he said she wanted to have sex.
“He said, ‘This is going to be an awkward conversation,’” Cradduck said. “I said, ‘Shoot it, I’m good.’”
Cradduck said the couple had a decades-long love story — high school sweethearts who found each other again later in life, only for her to later be diagnosed with dementia.
“He said, ‘She wants to have sex,’” Cradduck said. “And I said, ‘Do you want to have sex with her?’ And he said, ‘Well, of course I do. But is it OK?’ And I’m like, ‘Absolutely, it’s OK. She wants to.’”
Cradduck said the husband handled all of his wife’s care tasks — bathing her, helping her use the toilet — and she offered him a practical way to separate his roles.
“I did tell him, if you want that separation between your caregiving and your intimate life, wear gloves when you’re caregiving so that touch is clinical, and then touch her with your bare hand when you’re her husband,” Cradduck said. “That helped him, because he was having trouble himself moving from ‘I’m the caregiver’ to ‘I’m the husband.’ It gave him that separation.”
Understanding consent when cognitive decline is involved
Rogers said cognitive decline adds complexity to questions of consent.
“Do you guys see a difference when you bring cognitive decline into it for the person? That can be a whole different avenue to explore, because now you’re looking at that consent. When do they know, and how do you even broach that?” Rogers said.
Cradduck explained that consent and lucidity are not the same thing.
“If she’s not able to consent, if she’s not able to agree to what’s happening, or if she’s uncomfortable in those actions, then that’s not consent,” Cradduck said. “If she is not a willing participant, that’s not consent. And lucidity and consent are not the same thing. You can have moments of cognitive impairment and still be consensual in this relationship.”
Cradduck added that cognitive impairment can also lower inhibitions, which can change how a person expresses desire.
“Sometimes cognitive impairment also takes away some inhibitions,” Cradduck said. “So some people become more amorous.”
Rogers noted that consent for someone with dementia can shift moment to moment.
“I’ve seen people with dementia, and they change. They might outburst, ‘Don’t touch me,’ and then everything is fine,” Rogers said. “You have to be consenting at the time of whatever that emotion is.”
Cradduck added that you have to respect it if the consent gets removed in the midst of things.
O’Rourke also recalled a moment from working as a nursing home administrator, when a caregiver ran down the hall to report that a couple living together was about to be intimate.
“They’re about to do it. What do we do?” O’Rourke recalled the caregiver asking. “And I said, ‘You shut the door.’”

title: State releases footage of police shooting of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley
text:
SENATOBIA, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) - The Mississippi Department of Public Safety released new footage from the fatal shooting of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley.
The new video shows body camera footage of the officer who fired shots into the vehicle.
Wiley was shot and killed by a Senatobia Police Officer on June 14 in a Walmart Parking lot.
WARNING: Some viewers may find the footage difficult to watch.
Wiley’s family is pushing to have the Department of Justice open an investigation into his death.
Video shows law enforcement officers in the store’s loss prevention office being interrupted by a store employee saying, “two women are running.” Moments later, video shows law enforcement officers running after Wiley and the other woman as both get into the car.
Officers are then seen in front of the car as the driver backs out of the parking spot. Officers can be heard telling the driver to stop with guns drawn.
The driver is then seen driving toward officers, hitting one and crossing into the next parking lot aisle, striking a parked vehicle and later driving off.
Action News 5 received other footage from Darkhorse Press two days after Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch’s office determined the officers’ actions that day were justified.
That footage includes five videos: three body-camera videos from Senatobia officers and two surveillance videos from Walmart.

title: Homeowner targeted in key fob car theft. Here’s how to protect yourself
text:
ST. LOUIS (KMOV/Gray News) - A car was recently stolen in the St. Louis area and the victim believes thieves used a technique called a relay attack to take it.
Car theft victim Sherri Brown said her vehicle was stolen even though the car was locked and the key fobs were inside the house.
Vehicle taken overnight
Brown’s 2017 Nissan Maxima was stolen sometime Sunday night or early Monday morning. The vehicle was parked on an off-street parking pad beside her house. When she woke up Monday, it was gone.
“No signs of forced entry, no broken glass. Not any signs of forced break-in,” she said.
How a relay attack works
One thief stands next to a house with a device that captures the signal from a key fob inside. It boosts the signal strength enough that a car parked in the driveway picks it up like the key fob is right next to it.
The door unlocks, and the thieves can get in, push the button and drive away.
“Nissan Maximas, to my knowledge, are not known to be heavily stolen cars. And that method is not easy to do, but it can happen,” Brown said.
Protecting key fobs
Key fobs can be protected by keeping them in a signal-blocking holder. They are sold online by Home Depot and Best Buy. Brown regularly uses one, except Sunday night.
“I had planned on going out that evening, so I left my keys in my purse versus putting them back in the key fob protector,” Brown said.
The theft of her car comes at a time when extra expenses forced her to cut costs. She only has liability insurance.
“I own the car, it was 10 years old, and I thought that was something realistic to cut from my budget temporarily. So, wrong choice I guess,” Brown said.
If a signal-blocking holder is not used for key fobs, it’s recommended they be kept as far away as possible from the exterior of the home.
Citywide auto theft trends
St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department crime statistics show vehicle thefts are dropping. In the Tower Grove South neighborhood, auto thefts are down 13% so far this year. Citywide auto thefts have declined 15% over this time last year.
