title: Penobscot County Commissioners endorse a nearly 28% budget hike
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Penobscot County Commissioners recommended a 27.6% budget jump for 2027 after a divisive budget meeting Friday.
The spike stems from rising maintenance costs, cost of living adjustments, employee benefit costs and interest payments, according to budget documents. All but one department, the unorganized territory administration, have a proposed increased budget for 2027 compared to 2026, but it does not fully fund county departments, County Administrator Blair Tinkham said.
Penobscot County’s budget spike comes one year after County Commissioners David Marshall, Andre Cushing and Dan Tremble approved a more than 15% budget hike that mostly stemmed from a need to fully fund the Penobscot County Jail, which has drained roughly $11 million from county reserve funds since 2022. It’s unclear how the surge will increase the tax commitment for county residents, but it is likely to create a roughly $50 jump per county resident from this year’s commitment.
Although taxes will go up, not every community will see the same increase on their tax bills because local taxes are dispersed among school, municipal and county budgets. Last year’s jump saw some Greater Bangor communities pay hundreds of thousands in additional tax to the county, which equated to taxpayers paying roughly six cents more per $1,000 in property value.
The amount to be raised through taxes, which still needs to be approved by the county’s budget advisory committee, rose to roughly $36 million from this year’s $29 million.
Although expenses rose, four proposed positions – employees in the finance department, administrator’s office, maintenance department and emergency management agency – will not be funded. A grant manager, sheriff’s deputy and one additional maintenance employee, which were not included in last year’s budget, were funded.
The county will also not pay back funds borrowed from its unorganized territory department that the county used this year to cover expenses when it did not have enough cash on hand. Departments will also be funded at 85% of their requested expenditures.
In total, more than $2 million was removed from a first budget proposal that fully funded all departments.
Although monies were cut from the initially proposed budget, some funds were also added.
County commissioners want to raise additional money through taxes for the jail that exceed limits set by state law. County officials hope that the legislature will raise those limits in January, allowing them to raise an additional $3 million to fund the jail.
The county is proposing raising roughly $15 million for funding the Penobscot County Jail, a $3 million jump from the current budget. The spike is more than the yearly 4% increase allowed under state law, but Tinkham said the county is allowed to recoup funds from previous years when the county undertaxed municipalities. The county did not tax towns the amount it could for jail operations since 2022, he said.
The recommended amount is more than is required to fund jail operations and would allow the county to add $1 million to its depleted reserves.
The additional $1 million, which was brought forward as a motion from Cushing, divided commissioners before being approved. Cushing’s motion initially failed because Marshall and Tremble did not second it. After saying he wanted the motion’s failure reflected in the meeting minutes, Tinkham said the increase is the only way to bring in a large amount of revenue in one year.
“I want to be on record saying, I don’t like the number, but it is the mechanism for us to start recouping our fund balance,” Tinkham said.
In a second attempt, Marshall seconded Cushing’s motion. With Tremble voting against, the motion passed 2-1.
While the $15 million figure will be recommended to the budget committee, it will be accompanied by a narrative outlining that it’s unclear if the additional million dollars will be legal under the state’s 4% increase cap. Tinkham, who said he believes it is legal, will ask a municipal lawyer for an opinion. If it’s found to be illegal, the county will remove the additional funding, he said, but keep the $14 million figure.
In his understanding, Tinkham said, if the county commissioners and county budget advisory committee pass the jail budget increase, it will be legally binding.
The roughly 28% increase was one of five options brought before the commissioners in a meeting Thursday afternoon. The options varied from a nearly 32% spike to a roughly 22% jump.
Commissioners Marshall and Cushing voted to recommend the budget increase Thursday with Tremble voting against.
When sharing the multiple options with commissioners Thursday, Tinkham told commissioners he believes the only reason not to fully fund county operations and departments is political backlash. Disagreements between Commissioners Marshall and Tremble reflected the difference between keeping taxes low and appeasing taxpayers, or fully funding the county.
“I know there’s no question about what the staff’s doing and the work they’re doing, but the people in my district in Bangor are paying $6 a gallon to heat their house, and the other city services are going up, county services going up. They just can’t keep taking these hits,” Tremble said Thursday.
Tremble voted against all but four departmental budgets Friday. The ones he voted for did not have increased capital reserve funding.
“[The lowest] options now before us sounds like, well, we’re just going to kick it down the road again this year, but just a little less further,” Marshall said Thursday.
Thursday and Friday’s meetings, which were the most divisive of the past year and were rare occurrences of commissioners not voting unanimously, come on the heels of a year of commissioners and county officials enacting a hiring freeze, working on plans to change the county’s budget year from a calendar cycle to a fiscal year system, and searching for additional revenue to offset rising costs. Additionally, commissioners have been planning to build a new jail.
Funding for plans or engineering for a new Penobscot County Jail are not included in the budget.
A staff hiring freeze coupled with a $1 million cut to the 2026 proposed budget from the county’s budget committee have led to employees being overworked, Tinkham said when advocating for departments to be fully funded, which would have led to nearly 32% budget hike.
“I think it’s misunderstood how invaluable these services are and how much stress this full-time workforce has had to sacrifice to meet the operational needs of what they provide for Penobscot County,” Tinkham said Thursday.
The budget will be sent to the county’s budget advisory committee for approval. The committee will meet on Nov. 4 and 5.

title: More tribal leaders step into Maine’s fraught Senate race
text:
Amid a bruising and expensive knock-down-drag-out U.S. Senate race in Maine, Wabanaki leaders are stepping into the fray. It hasn’t been entirely smooth.
Chief William Nicholas Sr., of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Motahkomikuk (Indian Township), told the Portland Press Herald on Friday that he’s endorsing the five-term Republican incumbent Susan Collins.
He joins Chief Amkuwiposohehs “Pos” Bassett of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik (Pleasant Point), who announced his support for Collins last week in what seems to be a first for the senator. Democrat Troy Jackson, Collins’ opponent, picked up his first tribal endorsement in the Senate race from the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians chief and tribal council on Monday.
Jackson was endorsed by the Mi’kmaq Nation when he ran in the Democratic primary for governor this spring.
Maliseet Chief Clarissa Sabattis noted Jackson’s long-standing commitment to tribal sovereignty in a statement announcing her endorsement.
“From championing clean drinking water initiatives to his role in creating the commission to reexamine the 1980 Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act, Troy has consistently proven that he listens to indigenous voices and stands with the Wabanaki people,” she said.
Nicholas praised Collins’ directing of federal dollars to his community and her responsiveness.
“Every time we’ve had an issue in our community and she’s been called upon, she’s personally stepped up,” Nicholas said.
He rattled off a list of projects — 335 heat pumps, 70 hybrid hot water heaters, 230 doors and exterior and storm doors and at least 10 single-family homes — that Collins has helped fund. He was touched by the senator’s visit to the reservation this summer.
“It’s hard to turn away from an ally and a friend who has done so much for this community,” Nicholas said.
As both sides fire volleys of nasty accusations at one another, Nicholas felt compelled to cut through the noise.
“People are going to base their information on what they’re seeing,” he said. “But you know, every time somebody turns on a heat pump, somebody helped us with that.”
Collins said in a statement Friday afternoon that she was honored by the endorsement and looks forward to continuing to work with the tribe.
Although Collins has not championed tribal sovereignty in the way some Wabanaki leaders would hope, Nicholas is backing Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree to address the issue at the state level.
Nicholas was careful to state that he personally is endorsing Collins as tribal chief — but that he does not speak for the entire community, which remains divided.
His counterpart in Sipayik, Bassett, drew criticism when he alone penned an endorsement letter on behalf of the tribe.
After the Collins campaign celebrated what they billed as the endorsement of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Pleasant Point, several tribal members questioned the chief’s authority to make a unilateral endorsement without consulting the tribal council.
“Absent direction by the tribal community or its governing body, the chief does not have the authority to speak for the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik,” tribal member Gail Dana, who narrowly lost the election for chief against Bassett last month, wrote in an opinion column in the Bangor Daily News.
Council member Adam Newell said he was blindsided by the announcement.
At a minimum, Newell said, Bassett should have consulted the council in advance. He voiced his objections to the chief directly and on Facebook, where he sought to distance himself from the divisive race.
“It’s a new thing for tribes to start doing it,” he said, warning “it’s a slippery slope for me.”
The campaign referred questions to Bassett, who did not respond to a request for comment.
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.

title: Inside the high-tech lab where fake patients help save real lives
text:
NEW ORLEANS (InvestigateTV) - The patient is struggling to breathe. Monitors are beeping. Medical students are checking lung sounds, reading vital signs and preparing for the next step.
But this is not a real emergency room.
At LSU Health New Orleans, students are training on high-tech medical simulators built to look, feel and respond like people in crisis.
The simulators can speak, breathe, blink, show a pulse and change condition based on what students do next.
The goal is to give future doctors hands-on practice before they face life-or-death moments with real patients.
“Before it used to be you practiced on patients. Now you practice on plastic before you even touch a patient,” said Dr. Peter DeBlieux, assistant dean for LSU Health New Orleans’ Center for Advanced Learning and Simulation.
Behind the scenes, a simulation team controls the patient’s voice, vital signs and medical outcome in real time. If students miss something, the patient can get worse. If they respond correctly, the patient can stabilize.
The training is not limited to medical students. Doctors, nurses and other health professionals also train at the center, often in teams meant to mirror the pace and pressure of a real hospital.
“Since 2000, LSU has invested millions in the space of simulation, not just for medical students and not just for residents in training but also we have practicing physicians across the country that come to do simulation training here,” DeBlieux said.
DeBlieux said the technology has changed dramatically over the past 25 years, moving from basic CPR mannequins to simulators that can connect to ventilators, monitors and other equipment. LSU Health New Orleans says some simulators can cost up to $200,000 each.
“You can create a rare disease and then standardize it so that everyone in the class may not ever see it in a hospital setting or in a clinic setting, but can practice and train in this setting,” DeBlieux said.
The center has also had to rebuild. Its first simulation center opened in 2000, but Hurricane Katrina flooded the facility and destroyed equipment. LSU later rebuilt the center with more space and more advanced technology.
After each scenario, students go through a debrief to review what worked and what did not. Then they do it again.
“This simulator we have, it blinks, it breathes, it talks,” fourth-year medical student Lindzi Paul said. “It was a really good experience.”
Fourth-year medical student Aysha Gibson said the training feels real.
“You really take it personally if you’re able to save this patient or treat this patient properly,” Gibson said.
Gibson said the technology could help shape the future of medical care.
“I think this technology really will help form the next generation of doctors,” Gibson said.
DeBlieux said the benefit extends beyond the classroom.
“So for over 25 years, all of the LSU graduates in New Orleans have benefitted from training in simulation, which means our community has benefitted,” DeBlieux said.
The center plans to add artificial intelligence and virtual reality headsets as it raises money for the next step in medical training.

title: Brackett Hopes to Maintain Momentum in Bid for Seventh Term as Sheriff
text:
Running unopposed for his seventh consecutive term as sheriff, Todd Brackett, D-Nobleboro, hopes to strengthen the community’s connection to and understanding of law enforcement while the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office adapts to changing times.
Growing up, Brackett wanted to be a game warden. However, he was introduced to county law enforcement after graduating from high school and found that he enjoyed the constantly shifting demands of the job.
“Every day you went to work, you didn’t know where you were going to be or what you were going to be doing, and who you were going to get to meet,” he said.
Brackett has worn many hats during his nearly 40–year career in law enforcement. While attending the University of Maine at Augusta, he worked as a corrections officer at the Kennebec County Jail, where his duties included prisoner transport and booking and receiving.
In 1986, he began working as a deputy sheriff at the Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office, serving as a canine handler with his partner, Cliff, before moving to the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office in 1988.
Lincoln County residents elected Brackett as sheriff in 2002 and he has held the office since.
Brackett said this experience has given him “a really good sense of what’s going on” in the region and he hopes to maintain momentum on recent initiatives, such as the citizens’ advisory committee established in recent years. He said increased public scrutiny of law enforcement in recent years motivated him to create a committee that represented Lincoln County and could offer new perspectives.
“My goal was to put together a diverse group … diversity and age, race, sexual orientation, geographic locations around the county, and political affiliations,” Brackett said. “The citizens’ advisory committee has come to me with ideas that I hadn’t considered, (and) listening to that kind of feedback is important.”
If reelected, Brackett plans to continue the committee, which he said was a “fantastic platform” for candid conversations. The committee assisted with policy discussions on hiring a behavioral health liaison, responses to political demonstrations, and most recently, the sheriff’s office’s stance on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity.
Debates over the extent to which local law enforcement collaborates with ICE have grown in recent months, especially following the fatal shooting of a Colombian man in Biddeford in July. Brackett said his office does not assist ICE in deportation operations.
“I don’t have any interest in stopping people because they look like they’re from away and to check their immigration status,” he said. “That’s not my job, that’s not my staff’s job, and they’re not going to do it. That’s my policy.”
At the same time, Brackett said ICE has a role in certain criminal cases where the sheriff’s office does not have the resources to respond to a serious situation.
“For me, it’s trying to find a balance,” Brackett said. “We don’t have time to do immigration enforcement, we can’t keep up with the (regular) enforcement we have to do right here in Lincoln County, (and) we have no statutory authority to do (immigration enforcement).”
According to Brackett, public safety challenges confronting Lincoln County today are complex and include increased traffic volume, elder fraud, domestic violence, and substance abuse.
“We continue to have a drug problem in Lincoln County,” he said. “Since 2024, it’s been over 441, as of May 1, overdoses in Lincoln County alone, and that’s way too many.”
Brackett said one initiative he is most proud of from his tenure as sheriff is the introduction of a full–time recovery coach and clinician who focus solely on substance use work, as well as increasing partnerships with local organizations to provide more prevention and recovery resources.
“What we find with substance use disorder, if you’re addicted to a substance and you have an underlying mental health issue, that’s fairly common, so we call that a co–occurring disorder,” he said. “Everybody plays a key role and staying connected to that is really crucial.”
However, he said that “fluctuating services” within Lincoln County affect the sheriff’s office’s ability to respond to substance abuse adequately. He voiced concern about the pause of addiction psychiatry services at MaineHealth Behavioral Health in Damariscotta.
“Even now, some services are shrinking, with MaineHealth taking the intensive outpatient program from Damariscotta, moving it to Rockland and Brunswick,” Brackett said. “The services will still be available, but it’s really going to cause a problem for access for folks who struggle with issues right here in Lincoln County, especially if they don’t have transportation.”
Brackett said crimes dealt with by his staff often relate back to substance abuse, making the issue a top priority.
“A lot of these things are intertwined, it’s not just a drug case and a burglary case and a fraud case, oftentimes they’re overlapped,” he said. “So trying to get to the root cause of that through addressing substance use disorder, you know, is how we can hopefully make a bigger impact.”
If reelected, Brackett will also work to increase the LCSO’s visibility with schools. He said increasing deputies’ engagement with students helps connect the sheriff’s office to youth and educates students about law enforcement.
“Elementary schools in particular, (we) have lunch with the kids and go and play ball with them at recess or whatever they’re doing,” Brackett said. “While that’s not a full–time school resource officer, it’s keeping our deputies involved in the schools.”
Even with deep knowledge of these areas, Brackett said Lincoln County faces new challenges in the future. He cited today’s partisan political climate as an example.
“Five or six years ago, you would never see every weekend, vigils (and) gatherings downtown on the bridge,” he said. “What’s happening in the world, what’s happening in our country, what’s happening around our state … all of which can have an impact on Lincoln County from a public safety perspective.”
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

title: New Standish resident closes on local Habitat for Humanity’s 100th affordable home
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Michelle Demers and her 11- and 12-year-old children moved in with her parents in Hollis in recent years after she left a bad relationship, she said. Despite working full time as a phlebotomist at Maine Health Maine Medical Center in Biddeford, she could not afford housing for her family.
Now, Demers’ children are talking about the colors they want to paint their new bedrooms. She picked up the keys Thursday to her own three-bedroom house in Hunters Haven subdivision off Nature’s Way in Standish. It’s the 100th home that Habitat for Humanity of Greater Portland, a nonprofit organization that builds affordable housing, has helped a Mainer buy since its first in 1987.
“Me and my kids will finally have a place to call home. This is ours. It’s like a happy ending,” Demers, 41, said.
Habitat for Humanity of Greater Portland built about two or three houses for residents in need each year until 2022, and has since built an average of eight per year. Demers’ home is one of 12 houses that will be completed in Standish by the end of 2026, following an eight-home subdivision in South Portland last year and preceding a nine-home neighborhood in Gray planned for next year.
A recent survey of 824 Mainers by the Siena Research Institute and Maine Trust for Local News found an overwhelming 85% of people have negative feelings about the availability of affordable housing in the state. That struggle is what Habitat is combating.
Applicants must prove they are in need of affordable housing, but make at least $40,000 a year and meet other financial metrics to show they can pay off a reasonable mortgage.
Then, they are required to dedicate 275 volunteer hours toward helping build houses for the program, as well as take financial education and homeowners courses.
Demers applied to the program in February and was accepted in April. Many of her volunteer hours, called “sweat equity hours,” were spent building her own home and the homes of her future neighbors in the Hunters Haven subdivision.
“It was a great experience, because you get to learn all these things that you’ve never done before,” Demers said. “I’ve never done siding, or flooring, or putting insulation in. I got to meet some really great people.”
Chad Mullin, executive director of Habitat for Humanity of Greater Portland, said most of the homes the organization builds have a market value of around $475,000, but they typically sell them for $300,000 to $325,000, adjusting price based on what the owner can afford. Many owners also qualify for USDA Rural Development loans, making purchasing a home even more accessible.
Mullin said that two of the homeowners in the Standish subdivision applied to the program twice, and one applied three times before being accepted because their financial situation was initially not secure enough, but later improved. The organization connects rejected applicants with financial counselors who can sometimes help them eventually qualify.
“Housing is such a key component to who we are as people,” Mullin said. “When people have decent shelter — affordable, adequate, safe, warm places to live — they have a basic foundation to build their lives on.”
Demers said she looks forward to moving into a neighborhood of people who successfully went through the program. She heard several of her neighbors are also single mothers.
“Everybody knows what everybody went through,” Demers said. “Hopefully we can all kind of get to know each other, maybe help each other out.”

title: Cafe trains refugees, trafficking survivors in D.C. kitchen
text:
WASHINGTON (Aging Untold) — Emma’s Torch is a cafe and culinary school in Washington, D.C., that trains refugees, exiles and survivors of human trafficking.
Students at the cafe learn food preparation skills under timed kitchen conditions as part of their training.
On-the-job training
Students work through timed exercises such as julienne cutting chicken, with instructors telling them to have dishes “up by 10 minutes.”
Kerry Brodie founded the social justice nonprofit. The program lasts about 11 weeks and runs 40 hours a week.
“And that’s where our students are learning things like self-advocacy, English classes, resume crafts, interview prep, all of those things that are outside the kitchen,” Brodie said.
Brodie said 500 students have graduated from the program and 90% have jobs.
Rebuilding after loss
Nico came to the U.S. to rebuild his life.
He said he came to the United States with his two children and Emma’s Torch welcomed him and gave him new purpose.
“I learn new skills to know how to cook the best dishes in the world,” Nico said.
Nico said the program represents a second chance.
“You can begin a new life. You can believe in yourself,” Nico said.
Named for Emma Lazarus
The organization is named after Emma Lazarus, who wrote the words inscribed at the base of the Statue of Liberty: “Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free.”
Brodie described Lazarus as one of the unsung heroes of Jewish history and said the organization is meant to be a testament to that sentiment.

title: State releases footage of police shooting of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley
text:

title: UMaine goalie Wickstrom Stumer shuts out Colgate
text:
ORONO, Maine — University of Maine junior goalie Petter Wickstrom Stumer had a memorable debut at Alfond Arena on Friday night.
The Canisius University transfer from Stockholm, Sweden, made 24 saves and the Black Bears received goals from senior left wing Tanner Klimpke, sophomore defenseman Loic Usereau and junior right wing Lee Parks to beat Colgate University 3-0 in a hard-fought contest.
It was the second career shutout for the 6-foot-6 Wickstrom Stumer.
UMaine is now 3-2 while Colgate fell to 0-5.
The teams will play again Saturday at 4.
Reid Dyck made 34 saves for Colgate.
Usereau collected his second goal of the season at the 3:32 mark of the second period.
Isa Parekh slid the puck over to him at the top of the left circle and Usereau wristed the puck past the glove of Dyck, who was effectively screened by UMaine sophomore center Jaden Lipinski.
Colgate had a decided edge in offensive zone time in the middle period but only managed to put three shots on goal.
UMaine was credited with seven shots on goal.
Klimpke staked UMaine to a 1-0 lead on the power play with 5:28 left in the first period.
It was his third goal of the season and all three have come on the power play.
Owen Fowler made a cross-ice pass to Sully Scholle, who fired a one-timer from the circle to the right of Dyck.
Dyck made the save but the puck squirted free at the edge of the crease and Klimpke jammed it under Dyck.
Parks extended his goal-scoring streak to four games by finishing a nifty cross-ice feed from longtime friend Will Gerrior in the third period.
Both goalies were sharp in the first period.
Wickstrom Stumer made 12 saves and Dyck had 13.
Wickstrom Stumer had a pair of instances where he had to make multiple saves during goalmouth scrambles.
Dyck made a superb left pad stop on Charlie Russell’s one-time wrister from the middle of the low slot and he had a few more solid positional stops including a glove save off Will Gerrior, who broke in down the left wing.

title: Saco seeking community input as city creates open space plan
text:
The city of Saco is embarking on an effort to create an open space plan — and wants residents to weigh in.
Working in tandem with the Saco Conservation Commission, the plan will guide how Saco cares for, connects and expands the outdoor places that contribute to the community’s environment and quality of life.
A public interactive listening session next week will provide an opportunity for community members to learn more about the plan and share their ideas, priorities, concerns and experiences. The session will begin at 6 p.m. Tuesday in the Deering Room at Dyer Public Library.
In a news release Thursday, City Planner Charles Tetelman said residents’ input will help the city identify priorities and turn them into practical actions.
“People experience Saco’s open spaces in different ways,” Tetelman said. “We want this plan to reflect that range of experience.”
Under the plan, open space includes more than just public parks. It also encompasses trails, conservation lands, forests, farms and other working lands, natural areas, waterfront access and land set aside through development. While not all of those areas are open to the public, they all provide environmental, agricultural or community value, the city said in its release.
Saco already has a robust Parks and Recreation Department, Tetelman said in an email Thursday, as well as ongoing dedication to maintaining trails and working with the conservation commission to publicize those trails and encourage people to explore them.
But the plan will build on those efforts by helping the city understand how they work together, where there are gaps and what the community wants to prioritize, Tetelman added.
“As Saco grows, we want a shared understanding of our conservation and open space needs, along with the tools available to balance those needs with other community priorities,” he said.
Mayor Jodi MacPhail said the open space plan will help pave the way for existing locations and help identify future possibilities.
“These spaces are for the residents and visitors to enjoy,” MacPhail said. “Their input is vital to help the city make these spaces for everyone.”
As the plan progresses, it will bring together existing information, new analysis and resident input to determine what Saco’s open space inventory currently looks like; where people can access those places and what makes accessibility difficult; and how open spaces support wildlife, water quality, climate resilience, agriculture and recreation.
It will also help understand where there are opportunities to protect land, improve connections or increase access, and what actions the city can realistically take.
Several other communities in southern Maine have their own open space plans or guidelines, including Biddeford, Cumberland, Falmouth and Kittery. Yarmouth adopted a plan in 2019, and Gorham unveiled its own in June.

title: Maine’s youngest children need Head Start. A proposed federal rule puts it at risk.
text:
Deirdre Burns Mondor, MD, MPH, is a primary care pediatrician in York County.
The first few years of a child’s life shape much of what comes after. By the time a child starts kindergarten, the brain has already done a remarkable amount of growing, and the experiences and relationships of those early years help set the course for learning, behavior and health for years to come.
As a pediatrician, I see the difference a strong start makes, and I see how hard it can be to catch up without one.
Last year, Head Start marked its 60th anniversary. In that time, it has transformed the lives of more than 40 million children nationally. It has lasted because it is more than a classroom. Along with early learning, Head Start connects children and families to healthcare, developmental screening, nutrition and support for parents. Research shows that, by age 2, children in Early Head Start show stronger cognitive, language and social-emotional skills than their peers who aren’t in the program.
Here, Head Start is a federal-state-local partnership investing in Maine’s children, families and workforce. It prepares children for school success, supports working families and brings federal dollars into Maine communities. Maine also puts in its own money to support program expansion, and that investment strengthens Head Start’s ability to reach more children.
For a pediatrician, one part of that work especially stands out: supporting children with delayed milestones or disabilities. Head Start is a key partner in the early identification of special needs and ensures children with developmental needs receive support as early as possible.
Last year, 217 preschoolers and 46 infants and toddlers in Maine Head Start were newly identified as eligible for special education or early intervention services. A delay caught at age 2 instead of age 5 can mean years of help that change the course of a child’s schooling.
A proposed federal rule would pull in the other direction.
The Department of Health and Human Services has proposed stripping away many of the standards at the heart of Head Start. It would drop the requirement to screen every child within weeks of enrolling, and the requirement to make sure a problem, once found, is followed up and treated. It would also end the requirement to check, within 90 days, whether each child has a regular doctor and dentist.
Each of these standards matters. Together, they are what make Head Start work. The harm of this proposal is cumulative. Weakening several parts of the program at once means children are less likely to get the support they need, and the families facing the most barriers will feel it first.
We could expect a delay in children receiving appropriate medical care to address issues that directly affect academic performance and behavior in the classroom (e.g., hearing deficits, sleep apnea, asthma, to name a few).
Not only does early intervention improve the confidence and performance of children in the classroom, but identifying deficits and providing services prior to kindergarten is proven to save costs for our schools and communities in the long-run.
After 60 years, Head Start remains one of the best examples we have of an early investment that pays off for children, families and communities. I urge Sen. Collins, Sen. King, Rep. Pingree and Rep. Golden to ask HHS to rescind this proposed rule and protect the standards that give Maine’s youngest children a strong start.

title: Independent Rick Bennett pushes common-ground politics in Maine governor bid
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Independent candidate for governor Rick Bennett says it’s time for a different kind of politics — one that starts with common ground.
Bennett says running without a party label lets him focus on Maine as a whole. He says Maine politics should start with shared values and compromise, not division.
He says voters are tired of toxicity and dark money in the other races.
Budget focus
Bennett also pointed to partisan dysfunction in Augusta, saying the state budget hasn’t been seriously reviewed in six years or had a public hearing. He wants to change that.
“Obviously, the next governor is going to have to get serious about the budget that you mentioned. We’re looking at a one billion dollar plus shortfall,” Bennett said. “That means that revenue growth, although it’s going to continue up, is going to be outstripped by expense growth which is going to continue up higher.”
Bennett says he would bring both parties together to pass a consensus, current-services budget to build a better Maine.
Voters head to the polls in 11 days on Election Day.

title: Why protein is a game-changer for healthy aging
text:
(Aging Untold) — Protein does more than fuel muscle — it supports strength, healing and independence as we get older. But older adults can fall short on their daily needs, especially when appetite shrinks or meals get smaller.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, breaks down why protein matters so much with age and how to get enough of it.
Protein supports more than muscle
“Protein is the raw building blocks that your body is using for muscle, for strength, for inflammation, for healing and for independence,” Rogers said. “So you need protein, but you also need strength training to utilize it.”
As the body ages, it naturally becomes more frail — losing muscle and gaining fat, a condition known as sarcopenia, Rogers said.
“So your body tends to break down tissue more and not build it as fast,” Rogers said.
Illness and surgery raise protein needs
Rogers said chronic conditions, infection, inflammation, surgery or wounds can push the body into what’s called a catabolic state.
“Meaning they’re breaking down tissue faster [than] they’re rebuilding it,” Rogers said. “And if you get too catabolic ... you need much more protein to heal, then you’re going to have poor wound healing and all that. So it’s really, really important.”
How much protein do you actually need?
Rogers said protein needs are typically calculated in grams per kilogram of body weight.
“The general recommendation is about 0.8 to 1g/kg, sometimes 1.8 or more,” Rogers said. “If you’re older you’re going to need more, depending on that condition.”
She cautioned that protein intake should be discussed with a primary care doctor first.
“There’s going to be certain states that you cannot afford that much protein, like kidney disease and things like that,” Rogers said.
Timing and source matter
Rogers said eating protein slows digestion, which helps avoid blood sugar spikes.
“It’s really important to know the source of your protein also, because some of those protein shakes spike your insulin,” Rogers said. “So you want to get a good source.”
Rogers and aging expert Amy O’Rourke recommend eating protein first thing in the morning to help stabilize glucose, then spreading intake throughout the day for a steady source of energy.
“If you don’t have a great appetite, go in small meals throughout the day and then think variety,” O’Rourke said. “Maybe you don’t want to eat your protein. Maybe you want to drink your protein. Maybe you want to have a glass of milk. Maybe you want to have string cheese.”
Don’t skip protein to save money
O’Rourke said cost shouldn’t be a reason to cut back.
“What you’ll pay in debilitation in your body is a lot more expensive than maybe that milk would cost,” O’Rourke said.
O’Rourke also cautioned against relying only on protein shakes without reading labels or considering overall diet balance.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said balance is important.
“We’ve got to have balance, and we’ve got to actually consider and talk about these things with doctors,” Cradduck said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose added that fitness trainers and nutritionists could provide information as well.
“Fitness trainers may be able to give you some guidance on protein as well. Nutritionist[s too]. But no matter what age you are, there’s so many different choices, say for protein powders, and so you have to do some investigating and due diligence on your part,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.
Key takeaways
- Protein supports independence. It helps maintain the muscle strength needed for everyday tasks like climbing stairs or grocery shopping.
- Aging changes how the body uses protein. Older adults are more prone to sarcopenia — muscle loss paired with increased fat—and the body rebuilds tissue more slowly.
- Timing and source matter. Eating protein in the morning and spacing it throughout the day helps stabilize blood sugar and energy; not all protein sources are equal.
- Don’t cut protein to save money. Variety — including milk, string cheese or protein shakes with good labels — can help meet needs without overspending.

title: Lewiston to mark 3rd anniversary of mass shootings with weekend events
text:
Lewiston to mark 3rd anniversary of mass shootings with weekend events
The Lewiston community will mark the third anniversary of the 2023 mass shootings this weekend with events honoring the victims, supporting survivors and remembering how the city came together in the aftermath.
The shootings on Oct. 25, 2023, killed 18 people and wounded 13 others at Just-In-Time Recreation and Schemengees Bar & Grille.
At the Maine Museum of Innovation, Learning and Labor, an ongoing exhibit preserves objects connected to the tragedy and the community’s response.
The exhibit includes the doors from Just-In-Time Recreation and a light fixture from Schemengees Bar & Grille that still bears bullet holes. It also features 3D-printed replicas of pumpkins that community members carved and left outside the bowling alley after the shootings.
“Unfortunately, October 25th, 2023 is a really important part of this community's history now,” Maine MILL executive director Rachel Ferrante said. “And so we felt a responsibility to find a way to memorialize that.”
The museum’s memorial archive preserves objects and stories for future generations. The current exhibit, “Preserved,” is scheduled to remain on display through October 2027.
Other events are planned across Lewiston this weekend.
The third annual Lewiston Stronger Community Cornhole Tournament will take place Saturday, Oct. 24, at Just-In-Time Recreation. Two sessions are scheduled, from noon to 4 p.m. and from 5 to 11 p.m. Entry costs $20, with proceeds benefiting the Maine Resiliency Center.
A candlelight vigil hosted by the Maine Resiliency Center is scheduled for Sunday, Oct. 25, from 6 to 8 p.m. at Simard-Payne Memorial Park. Participants will gather at the park entrance before walking together to the Longley Bridge for the vigil.

title: We must right the ship of state, by voting for Democrats
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Ron Phillips is the retired founder and CEO of Coastal Enterprises, Inc., a community investment company based in Brunswick.
On Nov. 3, whatever our party leanings or voting habits, we must ask not only who is on the ballot in these midterm elections, but also what is on the ballot. In these perilous times, I believe we need to flip the U.S. House and the Senate to restore the word as well as the spirit of the U.S. Constitution. It’s the guardrail of our democracy.
With their experience, values and inclusive approach to governing, I believe we can trust the Democratic ticket to right the ship. At the top of the ballot are four crucial Democratic votes: Chellie Pingree and Matt Dunlap for the U.S. House in the 1st and 2nd Districts, Troy Jackson for the U.S. Senate, and Hannah Pingree for governor. Please vote for them, and other Democrats.
In my view, the very heart of the U.S. Constitution is on the chopping block: Specifically, Articles I, II and III that set forth the powers, and the limits, vested in the executive, Congress and the judiciary. Those are the three big reasons I see to vote Democratic. With the current administration, those branches are tested, challenged, and even thrown under the bus, and the American people wonder, “what’s next?”
There is mounting evidence that the Trump administration is concentrating power in the executive branch. Take the war with Iran. After the blood-soaked tragedy of Vietnam, Congress passed the War Powers Act of 1973 to reassert that Congress, not the commander in chief, holds the power to take the nation to war. I believe the destruction and threats to Iran, an ancient civilization, could have been avoided based on agreements already in force on nuclear weapons.
Congress also holds the power of the purse. Yet one estimate puts the funds the administration has cut, frozen or rescinded or withheld at $177 billion, for agencies and programs such as USAID, the National Institutes of Health, Supplementary Assistance Program for children, Medicaid and the Department of Education. Perhaps we should focus on who has the authority to impose tariffs. Congress does. All this while over $4 trillion in estimated tax cuts over the next 10 years favor the wealthy and other sectors.
Then there is the very serious weakening of voting procedures, which are the purview of the states. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 protects all of us, including Black and Indigenous Americans and other minorities from historic marginalization, intimidation, and access.
The latest flex of executive muscle portends even a greater threat to our Constitution. Banning news outlets from White House briefings is a blatant violation of the First Amendment, a cornerstone of ours or anyone’s democracy. The world is taking note.
There’s much more to talk about, from Ukraine, the Palestine-Israeli War, or immigration and ICE, to America’s unfavorable standing in the world. We could end this opinion on the sheer corruption of the present administration: self-dealing, and family and friends raking in billions, all in broad daylight. Or on the demolition of the White House’s East Wing, or the threatened destruction of the Kennedy Center, a memorial to an assassinated president, because Trump was prohibited from putting his name on it.
If none of this sways a Maine voter, consider character. The president’s speech is replete with expletives, demeaning language and falsehoods.
With some 88 criminal charges, indictments and criminal counts brought against him, and even with the Supreme Court’s questionable 2024 ruling in Trump v. United States granting him a level of immunity while president, we might go back to 1950 for guidance. In that year, in response to Wisconsin Sen. Joseph McCarthy’s Red Scare tactics, Maine Sen. Margaret Chase Smith, speaking as a senator, a woman, a Republican and an American, stood up in that venerable chamber and delivered her famous Declaration of Conscience speech.
Not to say that there are Republicans or others — even Democrats — who see eye to eye on government policy choices. But this time, we have three big reasons to vote Democratic. Or maybe we need just two: The U.S. Constitution as a whole, with due process and all the rest, and Margaret Chase Smith’s conscience.

title: Homeowner targeted in key fob car theft. Here’s how to protect yourself
text:
ST. LOUIS (KMOV/Gray News) - A car was recently stolen in the St. Louis area and the victim believes thieves used a technique called a relay attack to take it.
Car theft victim Sherri Brown said her vehicle was stolen even though the car was locked and the key fobs were inside the house.
Vehicle taken overnight
Brown’s 2017 Nissan Maxima was stolen sometime Sunday night or early Monday morning. The vehicle was parked on an off-street parking pad beside her house. When she woke up Monday, it was gone.
“No signs of forced entry, no broken glass. Not any signs of forced break-in,” she said.
How a relay attack works
One thief stands next to a house with a device that captures the signal from a key fob inside. It boosts the signal strength enough that a car parked in the driveway picks it up like the key fob is right next to it.
The door unlocks, and the thieves can get in, push the button and drive away.
“Nissan Maximas, to my knowledge, are not known to be heavily stolen cars. And that method is not easy to do, but it can happen,” Brown said.
Protecting key fobs
Key fobs can be protected by keeping them in a signal-blocking holder. They are sold online by Home Depot and Best Buy. Brown regularly uses one, except Sunday night.
“I had planned on going out that evening, so I left my keys in my purse versus putting them back in the key fob protector,” Brown said.
The theft of her car comes at a time when extra expenses forced her to cut costs. She only has liability insurance.
“I own the car, it was 10 years old, and I thought that was something realistic to cut from my budget temporarily. So, wrong choice I guess,” Brown said.
If a signal-blocking holder is not used for key fobs, it’s recommended they be kept as far away as possible from the exterior of the home.
Citywide auto theft trends
St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department crime statistics show vehicle thefts are dropping. In the Tower Grove South neighborhood, auto thefts are down 13% so far this year. Citywide auto thefts have declined 15% over this time last year.

title: Latino voters could decide control of Congress. Here's what's shaping their choices
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Latino voters could decide control of Congress. Here's what's shaping their choices
New polling shows Democrats with a substantial lead among Latino voters ahead of the midterms. But interviews in Texas reveal sharply different views on immigration, economic concerns and frustration with both political parties.
Latino voters could decide control of Congress. Here's what's shaping their choices
New polling shows Democrats with a substantial lead among Latino voters ahead of the midterms. But interviews in Texas reveal sharply different views on immigration, economic concerns and frustration with both political parties.
Before a recent trip, Gloria Suarez's husband asked her a question she never expected: Did she have her birth certificate?
For Suarez, a Texas voter, the question reflects how President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement policies have affected her sense of security.
"I never dreamed there would be a day when I would have to prove my citizenship in this country," Suarez told Hearst Television.
"I think immigration issues are extremely important. What's happening right now is critical. I think we all feel under threat," she said.
But another Latino voter in Texas sees those same enforcement policies very differently.
"I think that's the best thing that can happen," said Diana Escamilla, who strongly supports the president's immigration crackdown. "It's just a shame that it came to this point. So many invaders."
Escamilla has spent nearly her entire life along the Rio Grande in South Texas, a region once considered a Democratic stronghold.
"It was always 'pull the palanca' — pull the lever. All Democrat, across the board," she recalled.
Their opposing views illustrate the complicated political landscape facing Republicans and Democrats ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Latino voters could help determine control of Congress.
Their disagreement also reflects the divide over one of Trump's signature policies.
A new Pew Research Center survey found 62% of Latino registered voters believe the Trump administration is doing too much when it comes to deportations.
But among Latino voters supporting Republican congressional candidates, 47% say the administration is doing about the right amount, while another 33% believe it isn't doing enough, according to the Pew survey.
Even some Republicans have warned that immigration enforcement could hurt their party.
Rep. María Elvira Salazar, who represents a heavily Latino district in Miami, delivered that message in a September campaign advertisement filmed outside the White House.
"The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today," Salazar said.
Yet some voters who helped elect Trump remain firmly committed to Republicans.
Mike Mendez, who had not been particularly engaged in politics before voting for Trump in 2024, said he plans to stick with the party.
Asked whether he was still voting Republican, Mendez responded without hesitation.
"Of course. Definitely," Mendez said.
But when asked whether Trump could maintain his support among Latino voters without appearing on the ballot himself, Mendez was less certain.
"It's hard to say right now," he said, pointing to the emotions surrounding immigration enforcement and how it is portrayed in the media.
The economy could matter even more
Despite the intense debate over immigration, another issue ranks even higher among Latino voters heading into November: the economy, according to polling.
Pew Research found 86% of Latino registered voters consider the economy very important to their congressional vote, compared with 64% who say the same about immigration.
Economic concerns cross party lines, with majorities of Latino voters supporting both Democratic and Republican congressional candidates identifying the economy as a top priority.
Pew found 80% are very concerned about gas and energy prices, while 74% believe Trump's policies have made economic conditions worse.
Matthew Wilson, a political scientist at Southern Methodist University, believes economic dissatisfaction could ultimately prove more damaging to Republicans than immigration enforcement.
"If President Trump and Republicans experience losses among Latino voters in this cycle, and I think they will, it's going to be more about economic dissatisfaction and economic unease than it is about immigration related issues," Wilson said.
But Democrats also face questions about whether they're connecting with voters.
Candace Valenzuela, a former Biden-Harris official now running for county commissioner as a Democrat, acknowledged that her party failed to connect with some voters in 2024, while Trump delivered a message that resonated.
"When it doesn't seem like you are offering anything that looks like empowerment, they're not going to want to vote for you," Valenzuela said.
What's at stake in November
With competitive congressional races across the country, Latino voters could play a consequential role in determining which party controls the House.
In closely contested districts with sizable Latino populations, even relatively small changes in turnout or political support could make the difference between victory and defeat.
Trump won 46% of Latino voters in 2024, compared with 51% for Kamala Harris, according to a national exit poll conducted by Edison Research. It was one of the strongest showings for a Republican presidential candidate among Latino voters in decades.
But new polling suggests Republicans face a difficult test: maintaining those gains without Trump on the ballot.
An October Reuters/Ipsos poll found Hispanic registered voters favoring Democratic congressional candidates 52% to 26%.
A separate Equis Research poll showed a similar gap, with Democrats leading 57% to 31%.
The 2024 presidential exit poll and 2026 congressional preference surveys measure different contests and are not directly comparable.
A warning for both parties
But beyond individual policies and political promises, some Latino voters say their frustration comes down to whether politicians are listening.
At a small Dallas diner, voters, community leaders and politicians gather on the first Saturday of each month to discuss issues ranging from schools and health care to government spending.
Joe Valdez, who attends the gatherings, says politicians often pay attention to Latino communities during election season, only for that attention to disappear afterward.
"Many of us feel like they love us before elections ... but after the election ... ya no te conozco," Valdez said, using a Spanish expression meaning "I don't know you anymore."
New polling also raises questions about how connected Latino voters feel to the parties they support. Among Latino voters backing Democratic congressional candidates, just 42% say the Democratic Party cares about people like them a great deal or quite a bit. Among those supporting Republicans, 43% say the same about the GOP.
For Valdez, the choice comes down to the individual candidate rather than party affiliation.
"I vote the person. Not necessarily whether they're Republican or Democrat or independent," he said. "I listen to what they have to say."

title: Retro reigns at Maine’s only analog photo booth
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — It’s a simple way to preserve a memory. It’s a TikTok trend, a trip back in time, and a test of patience.
Maine’s only working analog photo booth arrived in the Old Port over the summer, captivating locals and tourists.
Dylan Jackson, 20, of Portland, and Mika Reed, 20, of Farmington, glued their eyes to a tiny television screen on top of the booth in Gritty McDuff’s Brew Pub. It showed a grainy livestream of what was happening inside the machine: a circular mechanism called a “spider assembly” rotated a strip of photographic paper and dipped it into vats of chemicals, gradually revealing images of their smiling faces.
The process takes four minutes — plenty of time for anticipation to build. Jackson and Reed grabbed their strip when the machine spit it out, visibly joyous at the result.
“I think it’s so cool that you get to watch your photos develop,” Jackson said.
The machine is believed to be one of about 270 analog photo booths still operating in the world, according to its technician, Margaret Skiff. Invented in 1925, the device had its heyday in the 1940s and ’50s. Back then, they were ubiquitous at variety stores, arcades, fairs, bus stations and other high-traffic commercial areas.
Digital versions quickly took over in the 1990s, but Skiff said a small community of dedicated technicians work to preserve the old-school machines, and now they are experiencing a comeback.
For some, the vintage booths are a destination.
“Every time we find a new one, we always go,” said Kainoa CW, a student at Mount Holyoke College. “I see pictures of people who have been doing this since they were young, and they have a whole collection now, and I’m like, ‘That’s gonna be me when I’m older.'”
Many people who crowded the pub’s front alcove on a recent Saturday for the one-of-a-kind photos said they are pursuing more physical keepsakes instead of containing all of their memories in their phone. Some said they think the analog machines produce better black-and-white pictures than their digital successors.
“If we go any other place, we could get a regular strip or something, but the fact that it’s analog is the pull for sure,” said Khang Nguyen, 26, of Boston. “It just captures a different type of energy.”
Each strip is $8, and the Portland machine only accepts card payments. Adjust the stool for height, flip the background to black or white depending on your clothing or skin tone, and be ready to pose and change positions for the four rapid-fire photographs.
Skiff, a 28-year old Portlander who also runs popular TikTok, Instagram and YouTube accounts, decided she wanted to get involved with analog photo booths after using one during a trip to New York City. Late last year, she reached out to people on Facebook in hopes of finding one to buy, and in the spring started conversations with Wesley Landson, a Massachusetts-based restorer of the booths.
Landson had revived the dilapidated booth after buying it from a Mainer, and was searching for a technician to operate it for him in Portland. He taught Skiff the ropes in a few days, and in July she unveiled it at Off Track Pizza. She moved it to Gritty McDuff’s in September, where there is more space, Skiff said. It has gone through 10,000 strips since settling in the city.
“I think I had some idea of how popular it was going to be, but the response has just been so much greater than we expected,” Skiff said.
Maintaining an analog photo booth is no simple job, and there is a lot of room for error, according to Skiff. It’s essentially a mini darkroom — the chemicals and photo paper need replacement every week or two, which takes about two hours.
After switching those parts out, Skiff poses for a couple of test strips. If anything is off with the machine’s alignment, temperature, aperture, or the camera’s focus, the photos may turn out off-color, scratchy or show white light patches, telling her where to make adjustments so that the strips appear “crispy.”
Monitoring the livestream of the inner workings of the machine from her phone, Skiff has shown up within minutes of noticing something is wrong to make quick fixes before people walk away with imperfect strips.
“People that love it really appreciate the nostalgia and the physical aspect of it,” Skiff said. “And it’s the anticipation, of ‘Oh, we only get one, and we didn’t see it on a screen. We have no idea how these pictures are going to turn out.’ I think they’re some of the best pictures you’ll take of yourself.”
The booth, and other booths like it in other states, have gone viral on social media. Many of its visitors say they knew about it from TikTok or Instagram.
Nikayla Speltz and Rahul Sharon, from Minnesota, had just gotten engaged on a trip to Acadia National Park, Baxter State Park and Portland, and came to the booth for pictures to celebrate. They said it’s nearly impossible to use the only analog photo booth back at home without waiting for hours in long lines at the state fair.
“It’s a cool way to capture a moment,” Speltz said. “Film feels like this special thing again.”

title: 10 Classic Horror Movies That Bombed on Release
text:
10 Beloved Horror Classics That Bombed on Release
Calling any movie an “instant classic” is a bit of a cliché at this point, but there are certainly plenty of movies that fit the bill—films that live up to the hype, make tons of money in theaters, and become beloved cultural touchstones for decades afterward. There are a lot of horror movies out there destined to become classics, movies like The Exorcist, Jaws, and Halloween that legions of fans return to again and again because of their visceral scares and blockbuster fun.
Not all horror classics have this kind of immediate undeniable success. In fact, a lot of scary movies considered iconic today were massive bombs in their time, either due to a botched release strategy or the simple fact that audiences just weren’t ready for them yet. It can be difficult to imagine, but your favorite horror movie, the one you watch every October during spooky season, might be one of these, a huge financial disappointment that might have languished in obscurity if it weren’t for a few dedicated fans, or a slow yet inevitable reappraisal.
A lot of these movies did badly because they’re somewhat controversial. Others were simply up against more popular movies that people at the time liked better. And a few of them were simply ahead of their time, full of cultural commentary we only fully understood years later. These movies were nearly forgotten, or might have only been remembered for how much money they lost. Glad we’ve all come around to how great these are.

title: Grand Canyon adds new dog to help reduce wildlife interactions with visitors
text:
GRAND CANYON, AZ (InvestigateTV) — Each year, there are dangerous encounters between Grand Canyon visitors and wildlife such as elk. So the park created a new program to reduce these interactions, with the introduction of their newest employee, Blue, the Catahoula dog.
Around 5 million people visit the Grand Canyon, and wildlife biologist Brady Dunne said people get too close to wildlife.
“Every time someone calls for an incident, I’m the one who responds,” said Dunne. “I graphed out that data, and just year after year has climbed exponentially.”
He said they track at least 12 guest and wildlife interactions that are classified as dangerous each year, but those are only the ones recorded.
Dunne said one of the reasons there are so many interactions is the number of elk and their adaptive behaviors.
“Right now, we have the most elk we’ve ever had, and the highest percentage of those elk are habituated,” he said.
He created a program using Blue, the 18-month-old Catahoula Leonberger dog, to teach the elk not to go into populated areas.
Blue is one of only two dogs in the country with this job right now.
“So I’m going to try out using a spotted wolf that we call blue,” Dunne said. “Over time, it’s called aversive conditioning. Over time, they say a wolf lives at the El Tovar, I’m not going to come drop my calf there.”
Blue chased elk away from the local school on Monday.
“So we move her across the road, and we push her into the woods, and she goes into her own where she belongs,” Dunne said.
Blue never touches the elk, and Dunne said the goal isn’t to chase the animals out of the park but to move them away from areas with the most people.
They collared nine elk, so they’ll collect data on how efficient the program is.
Dunne is hopeful the project will make a positive impact, protecting elk and visitors.
“Really, what I like most about it is Blue is a symbol for people to see, to think to themselves, ‘should I approach this elk? Oh wait a second, maybe I’ll be true to Blue and I won’t pursue,’” he said.
It’s important to remember that wildlife can be aggressive when we do not respect their space. Visitors should stay at least 25 yards away from large animals like bison and elk.

title: Teacher accused of selling pills to student in classroom, police say
text:
MONTGOMERY, Ala. (WSFA/Gray News) - An Alabama teacher is accused of selling pills to a student in a classroom, according to authorities.
Langston Carter, 30, was taken into custody Thursday after Montgomery police were called to L.E.A.D. Academy.
Court records say a student was found with two pills containing 5 milligrams of oxycodone hydrochloride and 325 milligrams of acetaminophen. The student told officers he got the pills from Carter, his teacher.
The student said he paid $10 for the pills after Carter allegedly offered to sell them to him on multiple occasions. He was told to send the money via Cash App to Carter’s girlfriend, but he had to ask another student to send it because he didn’t have an account. Investigators later verified the transaction, court filings state.
After the money was sent, Carter gave the student the pills in the classroom, according to court documents.
L.E.A.D. Academy confirmed Thursday that students were placed on lockdown that afternoon at the direction of the Montgomery Police Department “to ensure integrity of the investigation.”
Court filings say after hearing the accusations, a K-9 officer conducted an open-air sniff outside Carter’s vehicle. The K-9 indicated an odor, and police opened the trunk where they reported finding a sling-style bag containing:
- 6.9 grams of marijuana
- a digital scale
- empty plastic bags
- 18.9 grams of mushroom-infused gummies
- nineteen 5-milligram oxycodone hydrochloride and 325-milligram acetaminophen pills
- a loaded Beretta 9 mm handgun
- other narcotics-related items
In a statement posted Friday morning, the school confirmed the teacher, now identified in court records as Carter, has been fired.
Montgomery police said Carter faces multiple felony charges, including possession of a firearm on school property, two counts of unlawful distribution of a controlled substance and first-degree possession of marijuana.
He is being held in the Montgomery County Detention Facility on $300,000 bond.

title: Woman who resurrected Eastport’s iconic mustard company dies
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Nancy Raye, the third generation-owner of Raye’s Mustard who helped the company survive the death of Maine’s sardine industry and grow to an international business, has died.
Fourth-generation owners Kevin and Karen Raye, her cousin and his wife, announced her death on social media Friday. Their post did not give her age or birthday, but she was born in 1940.
Raye ran the business from 1990 to 2005, a period her family called pivotal as the sardine industry declined and “spelled doom” for Raye’s Mustard, which supplied mustard to be packed into cans with sardines at area canneries. Nancy Raye moved home to Eastport from California to save the business, pivoting to focus on specialty and gourmet mustards for retail.
“With her native positivity and ‘can-do’ spirit, she made it her mission to save Raye’s Mustard, and she succeeded,” the Rayes wrote.
Raye’s grandfather, J. Wesley Raye, started the business in 1900 after returning home from the Spanish-American War, according to Bangor Daily News archives.
He saw an opportunity to improve mustard-making and went on to supply the many sardine packing operations that then lined the coast in Maine and New Brunswick — virtually all of them, the BDN previously reported — and ran the company until his death in 1948.
He was succeeded by his son, H. Wadsworth Raye, and then H. Wadsworth Raye’s son, Donald, until Nancy Raye’s return home.
The mustard stood apart from conventional offerings because it was freshly ground, keeping full flavor in the finished product, Raye told the BDN. She described a “cold-ground” process that grinds mustard seeds, vinegar, water and spices are mixed by hand in wooden vats before being ground on massive granite wheels in a shaft-powered mill.
As the sardine industry declined, Raye’s reached a turning point, Nancy Raye previously said: expand into retail or shut down. As consumer tastes changed and fishery regulations tightened, the dozens of sardine canneries that had lined the coast in the 1950s began to close, the last one shuttering in 2010.
Raye’s, meanwhile, already sold mustard from the factory to locals, and within a year at the helm Nancy Raye had opened a shop while developing a gourmet reputation and new markets: a gift shop, a takeout stand, international buyers, and mail orders.
The market was limited only by imagination and capital, she told the BDN in 1993, and when people tasted it, it sold itself.
Today, the company offers an extensive line of specialty mustards, ground on the same stones, and also runs a museum in Eastport.
“Nancy has done a tremendous job elevating it from a small factory for sardines to a real namesake of fine mustards all over the world,” then-City Manager Bud Finch said when she sold the business — by then, the nation’s last traditional stone-ground mustard mill — to her cousins in 2005.
Nancy Raye was also focused on keeping it in the family.
“I like to take something old and make it work. I guess I don’t really fit into the disposable age,” she told the BDN in 1992. “There are values here that I want to maintain, and at the same time, I want to make our mustard competitive in today’s market.”

title: The Israeli army says 2 soldiers were killed in West Bank attack
text:
JERUSALEM (AP) — The Israeli army says two soldiers were killed in an attack in the occupied West Bank on Friday morning that also left two suspected gunmen dead in violence that is likely to heighten political tensions and security concerns ahead of Israel’s parliamentary election next week.
The army said two soldiers, Staff Sgt. Ron Yonatan Roytman and Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem, were killed and three others were lightly wounded during an attack by Palestinian gunmen. The attack took place near the Yehuda Junction outside the West Bank city of Hebron.
The army said it had prevented a “terror attack against Israeli civilians” and that the two suspects, both Palestinians from Hebron, were armed with an M16 rifle and a handgun.
It said the men arrived at an Israeli military position in the morning, triggering an exchange of fire lasting approximately 20 minutes, after which the gunmen were killed by Israeli troops. The army said its forces prevented the men from advancing further where the attack could have resulted in civilian casualties.
The military set up roadblocks and closures in Palestinian towns in the area.
Israeli voters will decide next Tuesday whether to grant Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu yet another term as prime minister — or usher in a new era of Israeli politics. The election comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza.
Israel’s government has warned of potential attacks by the country’s “enemies” in the lead-up to the election.
Netanyahu holds an emergency meeting
Netanyahu’s office said it had instructed security forces to immediately cordon off Hebron and prepare for a full closure of the West Bank, starting Friday.
The prime minister also held an emergency meeting of his Security Cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies, blaming Hamas for Friday’s attack.
“Our brave soldiers thwarted this attack with courage and determination,” he said, without elaborating on what the planned attack entailed.
“I commend them for their actions and wish our wounded a speedy recovery,” he added.
Earlier Friday, Israel’s far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for extremist views, said that the attack shows that Israel needs to restrict the Palestinians’ freedom of movement in the West Bank.
“The lives of the residents of Judea and Samaria, of the settlers, the lives of the soldiers, the lives of the police officers, the lives of our fighters are a million times more important than freedom of movement,” he said, using an Israeli reference to the West Bank.
Dozens are arrested in West Bank security operations
Following the shooting on Friday, the army said soldiers and Israeli security and intelligence agencies conducted dozens of operations in the West Bank and apprehended dozens of people, including those affiliated with Hamas and Islamic Jihad militant groups.
It also said it had located weapons, including M16 rifles and submachine guns.
Eyal Zamir, the Israeli army’s chief of staff, said a “large quantity of ammunition was found” in a vehicle used by the gunmen.
“This ammunition was intended to be used in a larger-scale attack,” he added.
Palestinian life is ‘impossible,’ says US congressional candidate
Closures of the West Bank are becoming more common. It was the fourth time in the past month that Israel had imposed restrictions across the territory, shutting gates and checkpoints connecting Palestinian villages to major roads.
Roads in the territory remain open to Israeli drivers, including settlers, who can still travel through the area but may face delays.
U.S Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander, who was in the West Bank on Friday, said the Israeli army’s closure following the attack was an example of Israel enforcing an apartheid system on Palestinians.
“It’s part of the effort to take more control, to make Palestinian life impossible,” Lander, who was detained by Israeli forces on Wednesday, said in an interview.
Yishai Fleisher, an international spokesperson for Hebron’s Jewish community and a political candidate for the far-right Otzma Yehudit, or Jewish Power, party, said Israel had the right to defend itself from a “hostile majority.”
“We are tired of the weapons and the brainwashing and incitement that is next door,” he said.

title: China earthquake: Powerful quake collapses hundreds of homes in Tibet
text:
Powerful earthquake in China’s Tibet collapses hundreds of homes and kills at least 16 people
A magnitude 7 earthquake hit China's Tibet region on Thursday evening, killing at least 16 people, injuring 46 and collapsing hundreds of homes in the northern regional city of Nagqu, official media said.
Search and rescue efforts continued following the collapse of at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials. Among the injured, 11 people were in serious condition and the other 35 sustained minor injuries, the media office said.
More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies including 1,000 prefabricated housing units, around 3,000 tents and folding beds, as well as flashlights and winter clothing arrived in the region.
China’s official news agency Xinhua said on Friday that communication in part of the region has been down. Local railway authorities have taken emergency actions to halt trains passing through the region.
The earthquake also caused rockfalls that have forced local authorities to close a section of National Highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua.
Intermittent snows are expected in the earthquake region over the next three days, Xinhua said.
It was the biggest earthquake in the region in the last five years, China's national broadcaster CCTV said.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10:33 p.m. local time, with its epicenter 191 kilometers (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet. It put the earthquake’s depth at 18 kilometers (11 miles).
Nagqu is more than 300 kilometers (186 miles) north of Tibet’s capital, Lhasa.

title: Man rescued after getting stuck in mud by Newport’s Sebasticook Lake
text:
A duck hunter was rescued from deep mud by Sebasticook Lake in Newport on Friday afternoon.
Newport Fire Chief Jeff Chretien said the man walked out on the lake bed to retrieve a duck he had shot when he became stuck.
The fire department responded around 12:40 p.m. Friday after a member of the nearby American Legion post spotted the man and called 911. Chretien said the man was with some friends who attempted to free him but had no luck.
First responders put ladders over the mud and walked across the rungs to where the man was stranded. They tied a rope around the man, who put his weight onto a jet sled he had with him. He had to kick his waders off, which were full of heavy mud, Chretien said.
From there, Chretien said, authorities were able to drag the man out until he could stand on the ladder rungs.
“It was great teamwork by all the rescuers,” he said.
The man was stuck for about an hour, Chretien estimated. There were no injuries — “just pride,” he said.

title: A Sneak Peek Inside the Renovated Maine State Museum
text:
A Sneak Peek Inside the Renovated Maine State Museum
It is hard to believe that it has been over six years since the Maine State Museum closed its doors.
Fortunately, the wait is almost over! The museum will reopen to the public on Saturday, October 24th!
When and Why Did The Museum Close?
Initially, the museum closed because of the COVID-19 pandemic. Like nearly all non-essential public facing spaces, the museum closed its doors in order to "flatten the curve".
However, the museum remained closed.
Why?
Well, it was decided that the closure was the perfect time to start some much needed updates to the museum. In addition to a series of needed structural repairs being made to the building and an asbestos removal project, the museum exhibits went through a significant overhaul.
About the Maine State Museum Renovations
When the museum reopens the public will have a chance to experience the history of Maine through "Beyond the Postcard". Basically, the story of Maine life will be told through the stories of people who lived here. For example, Cornelia "Fly Rod" Crosby, an outdoors influencer 120 years before we had influencers. Also, Alvin O. Lombard, who invented a motorized log hauler.
Then, of course, there is Vector the humpback whale. We have heard so much about the museum's new acquisition: a whale skeleton. She is even more impressive in person than you think! Next to Vector is the skeleton of a juvenile whale.
The new children's area has a lot of interactive experiences and contains the last operating Maine switchboard, which operated in Bryant Pond until the early 1980s.
The museum's upper-level is dominated by a massive display of Maine quilts. Some of them date back to the early 1800s.
Only about half the museum will open on Saturday. Just the top floors. The lower levels, which include the 12,000 Years In Maine & Made in Maine exhibits, will open at a later date. Probably sometime in the next year.
According to Maine State Museum Director Bernard Fishman, the lengthy renovation project cost about $3 million and much of the money came from donations by organizations and companies. These include the Lunder Foundation, the Alfond Foundation, the Betterment Fund, Avangrid, Kennebec Savings Bank, Hammond Lumber, and Bangor Savings Bank.
The Maine State Museum Will Be Free Through 2026
Thanks to a grant from Avangrid, the museum will be free through December 31st. And, also thanks to Avangrid, the museum will be free one Saturday a month through 2027.
