title: Bodycam video shows moments leading up to officer shooting HeeHaw, a beloved pet donkey
text:
CEDARTOWN, Ga. (Gray News) — Body camera video has been released of a police shooting in August that killed a beloved pet donkey.
Video from Cedartown police shows a 1-year-old donkey named HeeHaw trotting toward officers. According to an incident report, an officer tried to scare HeeHaw away with a Taser, but police said he kept coming back.
One officer then fired one shot that killed the animal.
HeeHaw was shot in his own pasture. Officers were on the property searching for a local missing child. Police said the child was later found at a church near the pasture where HeeHaw was killed.
HeeHaw’s owner, Hannah Israel, said her farm is “definitely not the same” without her beloved pet.
Israel told ANF that HeeHaw was simply saying “hello” to the officers because he loved people. The body camera video shows him running toward the officers while braying.
“That would be normal for him because he’s saying hi. That’s what donkeys do. That’s just being a donkey,” Israel told ANF.
Israel said she had bottle-raised HeeHaw from birth inside her home. The baby donkey participated in petting zoos at their farm and mobile petting zoos around the community.
Israel said HeeHaw loved all animals and people, and that he never knew a stranger.
Israel is now suing the officer who shot HeeHaw, identified as Trenton Garner. The lawsuit alleges that officers entered Israel’s pasture without permission and shot HeeHaw without justification.
Garner is fighting the lawsuit. His lawyers said he reasonably believed that HeeHaw posed an immediate threat to another officer. They also said they did not need a warrant to search the pasture.
The shooting has sparked outrage online. The family has started a GoFundMe to help pay for legal fees.

title: 9 injured after distracted driver crashes into pedal tavern, police say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) — A distracted driver rear-ended a pedal tavern, injuring multiple people Thursday night in Nashville, Tennessee.
Ten of the 13 passengers were injured after the distracted driver hit the pedal tavern, according to the Metro Nashville Police Department.
The crash happened when a westbound Toyota RAV4 rear-ended the pedal tavern around 8:30 p.m. on Demonbreun Street in downtown Nashville, police said.
The driver of the RAV4 and the operator of the pedal tavern were not hurt. However, six people remained in the hospital as of Friday morning, with one in critical condition.
Nashville Pedal Tavern owners Pete Kootsikas, Angie Gleason and Brian Gleason released a joint statement Friday morning addressing the Thursday night crash involving one of their vehicles.
“Safety has been at the center of how we operate for 16 years, and we have proudly served hundreds of thousands of guests in Nashville. We are deeply saddened by what happened last night.”
Driver reported being distracted
The Metro Nashville Police Department said the RAV4 driver reported that he was distracted at the time of the crash. Police said they are not sure what distracted the driver.
Police spokesperson Kris Mumford said the injured passengers were an “older crowd,” but she was unsure where the victims are from.
Mumford said crashes involving pedal taverns are not common, adding that this is the first one she knew of.
“Of course it’s something you do worry about, but we’ll be investigating it, talking to the driver, and all of the patients have been transported to area hospitals. We hope they all recover well,” Mumford said.
“Pending review of the video footage on the pedal tavern and further investigation, the DA will be consulted for appropriate charges,” police said Friday morning.

title: Woman charged after Facebook threat at Trump during planned trip to Alabama-Georgia game
text:
LAUDERDALE COUNTY, Ala. (WAFF/Gray News) — An Alabama woman faces federal charges after investigators said she posted a threat against President Donald Trump on Facebook ahead of his planned trip to the Alabama-Georgia college football game.
The charges against Megan Lorraine Utz, of Florence, were filed Oct. 8 in federal court in Alabama.
Threat posted after game announcement
According to investigators, around Oct. 5, a social media account under the name “Kase Utz” made a threatening comment in response to a Facebook post about Trump’s plan to attend the game that said, “He’s not allowed in my stadium! I’ll put a bullet through him if he dares.”
Investigators said the account was linked to Utz by matching the profile photo to her driver’s license photo, including a distinctive neck tattoo. Records from the social media company also matched her birthday and pointed to Florence.
Arrest followed foot chase
On Oct. 6, FBI and Secret Service agents with police went to the Salvation Army in Florence, where Utz was last known to be staying. Workers said she left in a light-blue pickup and might be at a nearby house.
Agents said they found the truck on Midway Street. Utz briefly opened the front door, then shut and locked it, and later ran on foot. Officers caught her about two blocks away.
Utz was arrested on a separate local warrant for harassing messages. Officers took an iPhone from her.
Investigators say she agreed to talk
Investigators said they read Utz her rights and she agreed to talk. She told them she suffered 18 concussions and had taken several prescription medications.
When asked about the post, Utz said she wanted her phone checked for hacking and blamed malware for the message. Utz asked officers, “How am I going to shoot him?”
Officers sent the phone to an FBI forensics lab for examination.
Prior police encounters noted in court file
The court file also mentions earlier run-ins with police, including a 2024 local warrant over harassing messages, a recent theft report where she was listed as a suspect and being removed from a rehab facility and the Salvation Army.
Utz will be arraigned in Birmingham on Nov. 4.

title: Hospice doesn’t have to happen at home
text:
(Aging Untold) — Hospice care is often misunderstood as “giving up,” but it’s really about comfort, dignity and quality of life.
For some families, that care doesn’t have to happen inside the family home — and knowing the alternatives can take the pressure off an already difficult decision.
“There’s no right or wrong”
“I like to take all judgment out of it. There’s no right or wrong. There’s no one way,” Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “People have very strong feelings about dying and how it should look.”
O’Rourke shared the story of a young client who wanted to die in a facility rather than at home, despite his sister’s wishes.
“What it was is he felt safe in a facility, community where there were nurses around, machines around,” O’Rourke said. “He felt less anxiety in that setting, and that was really what drove that.”
She said families should weigh care, safety and cost, but also check their own assumptions.
“Really take the heat out of the conversation by knowing what are your values and are you imposing that on your loved one?” O’Rourke said.
Hospice can follow you anywhere
“I’ve seen a lot of cultural issues where having someone pass in your home isn’t what the family wants,” “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “Going through that final sunset doesn’t have to be in your house. It can be in a community. It can be in independent living.”
She said she’s even seen families rent apartments in independent living communities specifically to set up hospice care outside the home.
“For me, it’s whatever brings comfort to the family,” Cradduck said. “At this point, we’ve got to make sure that the person’s comfortable, that they’re being provided the care and the dignity they deserve.”
She said the decision often comes down to whether a family can live in a space afterward.
“It really comes down to, am I going to be able to walk into my living room if that’s where I lost my spouse?” Cradduck said. “Or is it easier for me to remove that setting from the place I’m going to continue? And what if I have small children in the home or my grandkids are there frequently?”
Hospice means support, not a location
“One of the biggest things is people have to define and make sure that they understand what hospice is, and it doesn’t mean the end, doesn’t mean you’re giving up,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. “It’s just to provide additional services when people need it. And it’s the philosophy of comfort.”
Hospice can be delivered in a hospital, in independent or assisted living, or in a private home — it isn’t tied to one setting, the Aging Untold experts said.
“It doesn’t define the location,” Rogers said. “We all make these choices about what we want, what we’re living. We should be given the same choice about how we want to die.”
Katherine Ambrose, an aging-well coach, also addressed concerns about a death affecting a home’s value.
“I’m very used to people calling and asking if anyone’s ever died in that home. I wouldn’t want people to worry that it would affect your real estate value,” Ambrose said. “The only time I feel like it really makes a difference is if there was a traumatic death where the home is psychologically impacted or stigmatized.”
Plans can change — and that’s OK
“Many people want to die peacefully at home. That’s their wish, but sometimes there has to be a change of course,” Ambrose said. “Just like a childbirth plan — you might have a plan, but then you might have to change your plan. Because if you can’t control the pain or something changes, then you might make another decision.”
Morphine eases breathing
Cradduck said medications commonly used in hospice are frequently misunderstood.
“Morphine is used for many good reasons,” Cradduck said. “One, to open up airways, to help you breathe easier. So when you’re passing, the struggle to breathe as your body is shutting down — a lot of people don’t realize that the medications that are used are to prevent those struggles.”
“Morphine is not just a pain medication,” Cradduck said. “Oftentimes it is used to allow you to breathe easier because it relaxes and dilates.”
She added that other medications serve specific comfort purposes as well.
Key takeaways
- Deciding on end-of-life care is a deeply personal decision — there’s no single right answer.
- It’s OK if home does not feel like the right setting for hospice care.
- Hospice can be delivered in clinics, specialized communities, independent or assisted living, hospitals or inpatient units — it is not limited to one location.
- Focus on comfort and where you and your loved one feel safest.

title: Chilly Tonight, Stellar Fall Weekend Ahead!

title: Ask 8 Investigates: Why your recycling is going in the same truck as your trash
text:
Ask 8 Investigates: Why your recycling is going in the same truck as your trash
An Auburn resident contacted 8 Investigates after seeing a trash truck empty recycling and trash bins into what appeared to be the same part of the truck
Ask 8 Investigates: Why your recycling is going in the same truck as your trash
An Auburn resident contacted 8 Investigates after seeing a trash truck empty recycling and trash bins into what appeared to be the same part of the truck
An Auburn resident contacted 8 Investigates after seeing a trash truck empty recycling and trash bins into what appeared to be the same part of the truck.
Casella Waste Systems began using new trucks in Auburn a few months ago. From the street, it can look as if both bins are dumped together. But the truck has a divider in the middle, and the driver flips it so recycling and trash go into separate sides. It's called a split system.
Casella Waste Systems said the trucks make collection more efficient because the company doesn’t need to send two trucks along the same route.
So keep sorting your recycling.
If you have the same concern about your trash provider, ask the company whether it uses trucks with split system technology.

title: Friday’s high school football: Fryeburg Academy overtakes Skowhegan
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Marcus Sutton ran 56 yards for a touchdown 19 seconds into the third quarter to give Fryeburg the lead for good, and the Raiders pulled away for a 48-32 win over Skowhegan in a Class B North regular-season football finale Friday night in Fryeburg.
Fryeburg (4-4) earned its second straight win and will be the No. 4 seed in the upcoming playoffs. Skowhegan (5-3), which had a four-game winning streak snapped, is the No. 3 seed. Both teams will be at home in the quarterfinals next week.
Sutton threw a 22-yard pass to his brother, Darryl, with 25.2 seconds left in the second quarter to pull the Raiders within 24-20.
In the third quarter, Lars Bruhn returned an interception 45 yards for a score and Buk Awe ran 21 yards for a touchdown. Bruhn scored on a 33-yard run after an interception by Riley Hodges in the fourth quarter.
Austin Lancaster threw touchdown passes to Blake Kenyon (61 yards) and Matthew Keister (15 yards) and scored on a 14-yard run in the first half as Skowhegan built a 24-14 lead. Mike Stantze scored twice for Fryeburg in the first half on runs on 1 and 3 yards.
Lancaster threw a 20-yard touchdown pass to Kaden Pelletier in the fourth quarter.
WINTHROP 14, JOHN BAPST 6: Carter Rand and Tristyan Ortiz ran for touchdowns to boost the Ramblers (7-1) past the Crusaders (4-4) in a Class D regular-season finale in Bangor.
Winthrop/Monmouth/Hall-Dale, the reigning state champion, is the second seed D South and earns a bye into the semifinals. John Bapst will be D North’s third seed and will host a quarterfinal against Mattanawcook (2-5).
The Crusaders opened the game with an 8-minute, 8-second drive that ended with a 1-yard touchdown run by quarterback Thomas Curtis.
Rand scored Winthrop’s first touchdown on an 8-yard run with 4:27 left in the second quarter, giving the Ramblers a 7-6 lead that they took into halftime.
On the first offensive play of the second half, Ortiz took a pitch, evaded or ran through a few would-be tacklers, then sprinted down the sideline for a 69-yard TD run.
The Ramblers defense held the Crusaders scoreless over the final three quarters, securing the victory when Maksim Praschak pressured Curtis and forced an incomplete pass on fourth down near midfield with 31 seconds left.

title: Obituary: Cleora Mae “Perk” (Perkins) Vaillancourt Ramsay
text:
BRUNSWICK – Cleora Mae “Perk” (Perkins) Vaillancourt Ramsay, 92, of Bath, died Oct. 14, 2026, at HillHouse. Born March 4, 1934, in Dresden, daughter of George Winship Perkins and Alice O. (Lilly) Perkins, she was raised by her aunt and uncle, Mary and Milton Carlton.
A 1953 Morse High graduate, she married James J. “Chick” Vaillancourt in 1954; they had three children, Jim, Leon, and Ann. After Chick’s death in 1974 she married Robert W. “Bob” Ramsay in 1982.
For many years she ran “Perk’s Place” at C.W. Rogers, selling crafts and donated items to benefit Big Brothers Big Sisters of Bath/Brunswick. In recognition of her service the organization named its Perk Ramsay Acts of Service Award after her.
She was predeceased by her parents; her aunt and uncle, Mary and Milton Carlton; her sister, Marjorie Label; her brother, Robert Perkins; and her husbands, Chick Vaillancourt and Bob Ramsay.
She is survived by children, James J. Vaillancourt Jr. (Patricia), Leon J. Vaillancourt (Kelly), Ann Marie London (Eric); stepchildren, Robert T. Ramsay (Cheryl), Randy E. Ramsay, and Lori E. Rines (Mark); and several grandchildren and great-grandchildren.
Visiting hours are 9–10:30 a.m., Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026, at Desmond Funeral Home, Bath, followed by a celebration of life at 10:30 a.m. and burial at Oak Grove Cemetery at 11:30 a.m. Family and friends are invited to gather afterward at the Londons’ home, 250 Centre Street, Bath, at 12:30 p.m. for a light lunch.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to Big Brothers Big Sisters of Bath/Brunswick,
85 Maine Street,
Brunswick, ME 04011,
in honor of Perk’s long support of their youth mentoring programs.

title: ‘Neighborhood Nursing’: This program aims to be a national model for reinventing primary care
text:
BALTIMORE, Md. (InvestigateTV) — A pilot program called Neighborhood Nursing is providing basic primary care outside the traditional clinic setting in East Baltimore, setting up in a church and visiting apartment complexes and homes to reach residents.
The program’s services are open to anyone who lives in the area. Those services are free and funded for now largely through philanthropic donations.
How the program works
Stacye Cooper, a registered nurse with the program, said the goal is to be available in spaces where residents feel comfortable.
Cooper focuses on each patient’s physical condition, including blood pressure checks and diabetes management.
Terry Lindsay, a community health worker with the program, works to identify and address patients’ social needs, including help with rent, utilities and food.
“You might think, well, is that health? But that is health! And the trust comes from showing up over and over and from being in trusted spaces,” said Sarah Szanton.
Szanton is dean of the Johns Hopkins School of Nursing and leads the Neighborhood Nursing effort in partnership with three other universities in Maryland.
She would like to see the program expand beyond Maryland.
“The end goal is really to be in every state and for this to be how we do health care,” Szanton said. “Why are we here? We’re here to change the health of the nation.”
National primary care shortfalls
Nearly a third of Americans do not have a primary care provider, according to the National Association of Community Health Centers. That works out to more than 100 million people who are missing out on routine visits and screenings.
A 2026 “Health of U.S. Primary Care” report found that regular access to primary care is associated with lower hospitalizations and health costs, yet fewer than 5% of U.S. health care dollars are spent on primary care.
“We’ve really got it backwards,” Szanton said.
A model from Costa Rica
Szanton said Neighborhood Nursing was inspired by a public health care program in Costa Rica.
“It started in the mid-90s, and it’s based on having zones where everyone in a zone has the same nurse,” Szanton said. “Everyone in Costa Rica gets one visit a year and if you have higher risk for some reason you get two or three.”
Dr. Madeline Pesec, a physician and researcher at Harvard University’s School of Public Health, has studied the Costa Rican model with colleagues for years.
“It’s really impressive,” Pesec said. “To me, that is the secret sauce of Costa Rica, that they know exactly who their patients are.”
Pesec said Costa Rica has made progress in tackling infectious and chronic disease, which she said led to fewer deaths.
“We saw a 13% all-age, all-cause reduction in mortality. And we saw a 19% reduction in cardiovascular mortality, meaning diseases that come from heart attack or stroke,” Pesec said. “And the way you get those numbers down is by 10 years earlier, really working to control their blood sugar, working to control their blood pressure.”
Patients describe their experience
Edward Murray, 73, is one of the patients Neighborhood Nursing sees on a weekly basis.
“They make you feel comfortable. They talk to you. They don’t talk at you,” Murray said.
Cooper said she follows up when patients miss appointments.
“I’m looking around like, where is Mr. Murray? I’ll end up calling him. If he doesn’t answer his phone, I knock on his door. I know his apartment number,” Cooper said.
“It’s the love that they show,” Murray said.
Another couple, Maria and Brian, came in for a checkup a few weeks ago. In talking with Lindsay, it was revealed they had only recently secured housing after years living on the streets and had no furniture.
“We were basically sleeping on a rug in the living room in the apartment. So on the floor. And Terry ended up finding this Baltimore furniture bank, made an appointment for us. We got all three rooms of furniture for $350,” they said.
Asked what it means to help patients with needs beyond medical care, Lindsay said: “They look at us for all different types of advice. Sometimes it’s just being there for a person.”
Szanton said the program has served thousands of patients in the roughly three years since the pilot began.
“Oh it’s the reason to do it, right? It’s the feeling that we’re changing lives,” Szanton said.
Funding and expansion
Ann Greiner, who heads the Primary Care Collaborative, which advocates for primary care policy reform, said funding is one of the biggest challenges facing the system.
Greiner said expanding the program nationwide would require buy-in from federal and state lawmakers, health care providers and insurance companies.
“It’s not that there’s not enough money in our system. There is so much money in our system,” Greiner said. “It’s just, in my view, being spent on the wrong things. So we really need to have a reset.”
Szanton said the program is already in funding talks with policymakers.
“We see it kind of as a partnership between government and insurers,” Szanton said. “We’re not just offering it in Baltimore. We’re also at the same time working with policymakers.”
Cooper and Lindsay said they believe the program is reaching people who otherwise would not receive care.
“There’s so many people, if we weren’t here, they wouldn’t go to the doctor, they would not have these services. It’s our mission,” Lindsay said.
The Association of American Medical Colleges said primary care provider shortages are expected to worsen. By 2033, the AAMC projects a shortfall of more than 21,000 primary care physicians in the United States.

title: Somerset County, Jackman officials look at establishing search and rescue team
text:
SKOWHEGAN — If you get lost or injured in the remote woods of northern Somerset County, help is likely hours away.
And if help comes, getting out of the woods can take hours, even from established motorized trails. The nearest organized rope rescue team is based in Skowhegan, nearly two hours away. And the availability of helicopters from the Maine Forest Service or Maine Army National Guard that can expedite a rescue may be limited by weather, darkness and needs from other parts of the state.
Along with the Maine Warden Service, most of the manpower in such a scenario would come from volunteer fire departments, which may lack the specialized training.
Those factors, Jackman Town Manager Rick Petrie said, can turn a recoverable injury into a fatal one.
Emergency medical services officials in the Jackman area are looking to change that. They want to set up a search and rescue team — a service the area lacks.
At Petrie’s request, the Somerset County Board of Commissioners at its meeting Wednesday agreed to contribute $27,130 toward funding upcoming wilderness emergency medical technician and low-angle rescue courses, along with some equipment.
The funds come from a tax increment financing account designated for use in the unorganized territory, even though Jackman is a municipality. The Jackman-Moose River Fire-Rescue Department, along with Rockwood’s department, provide coverage for much of the county’s northern unorganized territory, where there is no municipal government.
Wilderness search and rescue calls are “extremely rare” in the Jackman area, said Petrie, who worked in emergency medical services before taking on his current role. The area, most often in the outlying unorganized territory, gets maybe one or two per year, he said, although he noted that could vary.
With current resources, those incidents — such as an injured hunter on a mountaintop last year — can trigger a “hodge podge” response, Petrie said. In that incident, the Maine Forest Service was able to respond with a helicopter, sparing responders from what would have otherwise been a 12-24 hour operation, Petrie said.
The upcoming training is aimed at getting responders in the area up to speed on wilderness rescue, Petrie said. The courses are expected to have capacity for up to 25 students.
“The existing firefighters and EMTs are being called out on these calls without having training because they are the only resource available in these areas,” he told the commissioners.
But as Petrie wrote in a detailed proposal he submitted to the board, the training is only the first step. Officials in the Jackman area are also taking initial steps toward establishing a formalized search and rescue team.
Under state law, the Maine Warden Service is responsible for coordinating searches for people lost or stranded in the woodlands or inland waters of Maine. The agency often relies on volunteer teams for assistance.
The northern Somerset County team would be a resource the warden service could call upon when needed, Petrie wrote. It would also complement the existing air resources.
The Maine Association for Search And Rescue lists 13 certified teams across the state. None are based in Somerset County.
Jackman officials began exploring ways to improving wilderness medical response about three years ago, and have since acquired about $100,000 worth of equipment, Petrie said. The latest proposal revives that effort.
In his proposal, Petrie mapped out a two-year process for establishing a northern Somerset County team, which would result in being fully operational by the end of 2028.
Most teams in Maine are independent organizations. Petrie’s report suggested several models, but he said Wednesday the best option appeared to be running the team through the Somerset County Emergency Management Agency.
Sara Bickford, the agency’s director, told the commissioners she supports the idea, especially as outdoor recreation tourism continues to grow in the region.
She said she is a member of the Franklin County search and rescue team and, in her experience, the warden service responds with limited manpower, often only one warden to coordinate the scene. Rescues then typically fall to volunteer firefighters and trained search and rescue team members, Bickford said.
Wilderness rescues require a lot of people, Bickford said. As an example, she pointed to a recent evacuation of an injured hiker off Tumbledown Mountain, which began at 4:30 p.m. and ended at 1:30 a.m. It involved three wardens and about two dozen firefighters and search and rescue personnel, Bickford said.
“They take a lot of time,” Bickford said. “They take a lot of labor and expertise.”

title: How AI technology is giving ALS patients their voice back
text:
LEICESTER, Vt. (InvestigateTV) - ALS, often called Lou Gehrig’s disease, is a cruel illness. There is no cure, it’s always fatal, and Vermont has the highest rate per capita in the country with around 27 people living with it now in the state.
To help those losing independence and their, a nonprofit is working to restore the ability to communicate with loved ones and doctors.
Paul Francoeur’s days didn’t always start like this, but when they did, it was difficult. The cough-assist machine helped the 67-year-old clear his lungs when he couldn’t do it himself. His ALS weakened his muscles and motor skills too much.
“I think soon after diagnosis you realize how this road ends,” said Kris Francoeur, Paul’s wife.
That diagnosis came in 2019.
Kris turned into a caregiver, allowing her husband to remain at home. They get help from their son Ben. But it’s getting more challenging, especially as Francoeur loses his ability to communicate.
During a tele-medicine appointment with his doctor, the couple learned that with no better medicine or treatments, he would have to stay the course.
“Hardest part...” Francoeur said. “...Is worrying about other people,” Kris said, finishing his thought.
She helped him communicate. He was also good at eye-gaze technology, where eye movements control mouse clicks to spell out words. The software then generates synthesized speech.
“It is very flat and robotic,” Kris said.
But new technology by the company ElevenLabs uses AI to clone voices, replacing the robot sound. It even creates emotion in each word. The trouble is that Francoeur needed enough clear audio from before he started losing his voice, and they couldn’t find any old recordings.
But WCAX did.
The Channel 3 News featured the couple in a “Made in Vermont” story 14 years ago. At the time, Francoeur made spinning wheels, seven years before ALS stole his voice.
The footage takes the couple back to another time. “I think more than anything, it’s just to see Paul walking and talking... using tools. It’s amazing to see. I miss all that. He misses all that,” Kris said.
For Paul, it was hard to remember that level of physical freedom.
But in a couple of months, that WCAX story would give Francoeur back the voice he thought he’d lost.
Richard Cave with ElevenLabs said they were able to use 16 seconds of sound from Paul in that 2012 story to mirror his voice.
“What we’ve done here is use AI for good, to enable people to recreate their natural voice,” Cave said.
“The voice that will come out of the computer will sound like him,” Kris said.
“Like me,” added Francoeur.
“This disease robs people of so much of their lives,” said Dr. Mark Garret, who runs the ALS clinic at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center and is also Francoeur’s doctor. “When speech really becomes affected by ALS, it’s one of the things that most profoundly impacts quality of life.”
Garret calls the couple inspirational for making the most of the time Francoeur has left, and is touched by their advocacy for others living with ALS.
“I think Paul, the way he confronted a terrible prognosis and a terrible disease and made the best of life throughout all of that has been extraordinary,” Garret said. And, he said, it may be part of the reason that he has survived so long after the diagnosis. Typically, ALS patients live two to five years.
Francoeur made it to year eight.
His first words through the new technology were a thank you message and raising awareness about ALS.
“Vermont has the highest rate per capita than any state in the country,” he said, the cloned voice a perfect match.
“That does sound just like you,” Fuller said.
“Made me feel more human,” Francoeur said.
“It’s been a long time since I’ve heard Paul’s voice,” Kris said.
His next big speech was for his grandkids, who’ve never heard his real voice. “The next time I see the grandkids, I can tell them I love them with actual emotion.”
ElevenLabs offers the voice cloning technology to ALS patients for free. The organization Bridging Voices helps families connect with the company.
Seven months after reporter Darren Perron talked to the couple, Paul would pass away. He is remembered by his wife and family.

title: Duck hunter rescued after getting stuck in Sebasticook Lake mud
text:
NEWPORT, Maine (WABI) - A man became stuck up to his chest in lakebed mud in Sebasticook Lake Thursday afternoon.
According to the Newport Fire Chief, the lake is drained every fall to help manage legacy pollution.
The chief said a duck hunter had gone to retrieve a bird he shot and found himself stuck in the mud.
Eyewitnesses we spoke with said they saw others trying to get him something to hold onto to no avail.
He told WABI the man is lucky they were able to get him out.
“The guys were getting sticks and tires, trying to throw stuff over to him and they couldn’t do it. So, we decided we were going to leave, and that’s when fire trucks and ambulances and police showed up,” said Jason Perkins.
One witness called 911.
While crews arrived within a few minutes, the man had already sunk a foot deeper.
They saw rescuers use a series of ladders to walk closer to the man without endangering themselves.
Video shows the fire department pulling the man ashore with a sled tied to ropes.
The Newport fire chief said the only way to safely retrieve game from the lake this time of year is by canoe or kayak.

title: Bystander jumps onto moving bus to help students during driver’s medical emergency
text:
ST. PAUL, Minn. (WCCO) — A bystander helped stop a bus carrying 19 middle schoolers Monday after the driver had a medical emergency, according to school officials in Minnesota.
Ebro Ahmed, 27, was taking a break outside his family business, Ya Bricks Snacks & Tobacco, in St. Paul’s Dayton’s Bluff neighborhood when he saw the bus moving through the streets with no hands on the wheel.
“I started yelling. I didn’t know what to do. The reason I started yelling was to get somebody’s attention,” Ahmed said.
Bystander describes boarding the bus
Ahmed said he ran toward the bus after noticing the door was open.
“It caught me by surprise because I was kind of confused about the door being open. So then I ran toward the bus and noticed he was having an emergency, so I just hopped on there,” Ahmed said.
“I wasn’t able to stop it at first, so I threw it in park, and it went in reverse by accident,” Ahmed said.
Ahmed assisted the driver while instructing students to call 911.
“It’s something you would never think would happen in real life,” Ahmed said.
Asked how he knew what to do, Ahmed said he drew on things he had seen before.
“TV shows, stuff like that. ‘Grey’s Anatomy,’ and TikTok,” Ahmed said.
School district response
In a statement, St. Paul Public Schools said there was a medical emergency on a contracted bus route from Battle Creek Middle School that likely made students late arriving home and that some children may have been upset by the situation. The district said its mental health team checked in with students afterward.
Ahmed said he and the students were alone when the incident happened.
“We were right here. No cars around, no adults around, just me alone with the kids,” Ahmed said.
Ahmed said the situation made him think of his own family.
“It’s scary. That could’ve been my sister, my brother, my daughter, my son. It could be my little cousin,” Ahmed said.
Ahmed said he wants to reunite with the driver and his family.
“It’s part of being human. We have feelings and emotions we’re supposed to feel. If I were to let him drive away, I would not be human anymore,” Ahmed said.
St. Paul Public Schools said the driver has been released from the hospital and is resting at home.

title: A Toast to the Y’s Business Partners
text:
The Y was closed last Sunday afternoon, but you wouldn’t have known it inside the Fieldhouse. Pickleballs were flying, the Patriots were dominating the Jets on a TV screen in the corner, and friends and neighbors were enjoying time together. There were snacks, specialty cocktails, cold beer, and some seriously good door prizes.
The occasion? “Pickleball and Pints,” the first event dedicated to thanking the Boothbay Region YMCA’s Business Partners and their employees. “Those are two of my favorite things,” stated Andy Hollon, when asked if he would help organize the event. “Having beer and pickleball at the same time is almost a dream come true!” Andy, recovering from a second knee replacement surgery, is also a Y trustee as well as an official USA Pickleball Ambassador.
At the event, some came to learn pickleball while others were eager to play. There were opportunities to tour the Y, meet new people, and catch up with familiar faces. And apparently, a few particularly enthusiastic players kept the pickleballs bouncing on the court until 7 p.m.
Behind every Business Partner are the people who care about the peninsula and the neighbors who call it home. Their annual sponsorships help keep the Y welcoming and accessible, and this special event was the Y’s chance to greet them, spend some time together, and say thank you.
Dogfish Head co-founders Sam and Mariah Calagione joined us for the afternoon, generously bringing beer, specialty cocktails, and plenty of fun swag. They named their brewery for Dogfish Head in Southport, where they have a seasonal home and deep family roots. We were delighted to have time with them and grateful they could meet so many people.
Mariah shared, “The Boothbay YMCA is a community hub and our company’s benevolence and philanthropy program is focused on supporting organizations like the Y that impact the community in such a broad way. Plus, we have so many connections here and love being back to spend time with our family and friends.”
That sense of community is something our Business Partners help sustain. Their generosity helps children learn to swim, gives working parents dependable child care, welcomes teens looking for a place to belong, and helps adults build strength and friendships. We love the chance to show our sponsors the Y so they can see what their generosity makes possible.
“We are so grateful to our Business Partners who support our mission through their annual sponsorships and want to show our appreciation through events like these,” said Meg Benvenuto, the Y’s CEO. “We’ll have other opportunities to thank our Business Partners and will invite them and their employees to enjoy the Y and all it has to offer later this year.”
Special thanks to Brooke and Andy Hollon, Eventide, and Dogfish Head Brewery for offering amazing door prizes. We are very grateful to our wonderful volunteers who offered a variety of skills, including set-up on Saturday, welcoming guests, playing and teaching pickleball, helping to clean up, and giving tours. We are so thankful for their time, good humor, and willingness to pitch in.
So much about what makes our Y unique is all of the different ways people can connect. Last Sunday, those connections happened over a pickleball net, during a tour, and in conversations with people who share a commitment to this special community.
So, "Cheers" to our Business Partners and everyone who helped make the afternoon possible!

title: Obituary: Richard Cloutier
text:
WINSLOW – Richard Cloutier, 83, of Winslow, Maine, passed away peacefully on Oct. 19, 2026. He was born on Jan. 26, 1943, in St. Zacharie, PQ Canada to Romeo and Julia Cloutier.
Richard was educated in schools in St. Zacharie. He was married Jan. 14, 1972, in St. Joseph, Quebec to Gertrude Cloutier.
He was a resident of the Waterville/Winslow area for 54 years and previously lived in St. Zacharie where he grew up. He started drywalling at the age of 14 in Connecticut. He then moved to Maine to continue his drywalling career, along with building homes. Then, became a long-time business owner of a construction company and apartment rentals.
He enjoyed seeing his grandchildren. He also enjoyed working on his equipment and around the home.
He was predeceased by his wife, Gertrude Cloutier; sister, Suzanne Roy, sister, Lize Lachance, and brother, Renald Cloutier.
He is survived by his longtime companion, Evelyn Willett; a son, Rodney Cloutier and his wife Jackie of Winslow, a daughter, Lynn Andrews and her husband Travis, of Madison; grandchildren, Aimee and Nicole Cloutier, Brandon Davis, and Jaynna Andrews; great-grandchildren, Aubree Cloutier, Emilee Cooper, Jordan Weatherspoon, Johnathan Owens, Connor Green, Madyson Whitlock; brothers Paul and Michael Cloutier, sisters Claudette Cyr and Francois Dulac; many nieces and nephews.
Visiting hours will be held on Nov. 5 from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. at Gallant Funeral Home, 10 Elm St., Waterville. A Mass of Christian Burial will be celebrated on Nov. 6 at 10 a.m. at Notre Dame Catholic Church, 116 Silver St., Waterville. Committal prayers and burial will follow in St. Francis Catholic Cemetery, 78 Grove St., Waterville.
An online guestbook may be signed; condolences and memories shared at http://www.gallantfh.com.

title: Farmington Grange aids Care and Share Food Closet with handmade quilt raffle
Farmington hears solar savings pitch, weighs other options
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FARMINGTON — The Select Board took no action Oct. 13 on a proposal by a community solar company, renewing concerns about municipal involvement in promoting a private company’s services.
Solar Simplified, of Chicago, Illinois, presented a potential partnership offering eligible Central Maine Power customers a 15% discount on applied solar credits without installing solar panels or changing electricity providers. The company would also contribute $100 to the town for each enrolled household or business.
Town Manager Erica LaCroix emphasized in a follow-up response that the presentation was informational and the town has not committed to pursuing a partnership.
“This was just a presentation and not something the town actively sought out,” LaCroix said.
Sasha Lukovenko, the company’s vice president of sales and marketing, estimated that at least 100 Farmington accounts could enroll, potentially generating $10,000 for the town. The figure is a projection, not guaranteed revenue.
Selectman Randall Gauvin questioned whether participating in the company’s outreach campaign would amount to a municipal endorsement of a private business.
“I’m not comfortable with being partnered with a private company to push their product,” Gauvin said.
The concern was not new. During a June 9 discussion about inviting Solar Simplified to make a presentation, Gauvin questioned the company’s sales approach, while Selectman Richard Morton called for independent information about community solar and potential consumer savings.
At that meeting, Morton expressed concern that information from a company selling subscriptions might not provide an unbiased explanation of the program. The board discussed seeking additional guidance, potentially from the state, before deciding how the town should participate in public outreach.
During the October presentation, Lukovenko maintained that the proposed arrangement would focus on consumer education rather than municipal endorsement. Solar Simplified would prepare informational materials for town review and approval, with possible outreach through public information sessions, municipal communications and community events.
The company would cover campaign expenses, while town staff would help review materials and coordinate activities.
Community solar allows customers to subscribe to electricity generated at off-site solar farms and receive credits on their utility bills. Under Solar Simplified’s proposal, participants would pay for those credits at a discounted rate, with savings depending on the credits applied to their electricity bills.
The advertised 15% discount applies to solar credits, not necessarily to a customer’s entire electricity bill.
LaCroix confirmed that participating households and businesses would not receive separate bills from Solar Simplified. Charges and credits would instead be handled through Central Maine Power.
Lukovenko said the company adjusts solar allocations monthly based on customers’ electricity use. Participants would not face enrollment or cancellation fees and could leave the month-to-month program at any time, he said.
The company’s solar projects in Standish, Freeport and Dover-Foxcroft are expected to begin operating in the first quarter of 2027. Participating customers would begin receiving credits about two to three billing cycles after the projects become operational, according to Lukovenko.
Farmington participates in community solar through Ampion for municipal electricity accounts, although the arrangement has presented challenges.
LaCroix said the town initially received insufficient solar allocations to realize its expected savings, requiring adjustments. The arrangement has since improved, but delayed billing continues to complicate municipal budget tracking.
Farmington’s Ampion agreement carries a five-year commitment, compared with the month-to-month participation proposed by Solar Simplified.
The town has also researched competing community solar providers. In June correspondence, Executive Assistant Leah Giusti identified Nexamp, RooflessSolar, Common Energy and PowerMarket as alternatives offering varying discounts and enrollment arrangements.
LaCroix said Farmington plans to examine other programs and remains open to informational presentations from companies offering services that could benefit residents.
She said programs that could help the community or respond to requests from residents may be brought before the board for discussion.
“To say we are considering this would be a bit premature,” LaCroix said.

title: $4 million fraud scheme: Influencer had hundreds of fake SNAP accounts, prosecutors say
text:
ATLANTA (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — An Atlanta social media influencer is accused of stealing millions of dollars in SNAP benefits, prosecutors said Wednesday.
Mercedes Reshard New, who goes by “Shawty Dred,” was indicted on federal charges for fraudulently obtaining more than $4 million in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia.
Fake accounts and fraudulent cards
Between January 2020 and July 2026, New allegedly controlled more than 350 fake SNAP accounts, which were created using stolen identities.
Prosecutors said New, 39, allegedly had SNAP EBT cards mailed to various metro Atlanta addresses and applied for his limited liability company, Shawty Dred LLC, to become an authorized SNAP retailer.
Between April 2024 and November 2025, New allegedly used fraudulently obtained EBT cards and a point-of-sale device associated with Shawty Dred LLC to steal more than $660,000 in SNAP benefits.
Store authorization revoked, arrest followed
In November 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture revoked New’s store authorization. About two weeks later, local police officers arrested New for allegedly selling SNAP benefits at a metro Atlanta store, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said.
Officers seized 14 EBT cards from New that had been issued to other people. New then allegedly had replacement cards mailed to his store address and other addresses in the Atlanta area.
Investigators said the scheme diverted $4.6 million in SNAP funds. The EBT debit cards were used to siphon around $4 million from the accounts.
Indictment and arrest
New has flaunted private jets, fancy cars and stacks of cash to his millions of followers on TikTok and Instagram, as he denounced others as “broke motherf****s,” prosecutors said.
On Oct. 7, a federal grand jury indicted New on 46 counts of mail fraud, 15 counts of aggravated identity theft and one count each of SNAP fraud and illegal transactions with access devices.
New was arrested on Oct. 13 and remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service pending further proceedings.
“New allegedly stole over $4 million meant for poor families who need help putting food on the table,” U.S. Attorney Theodore Hertzberg said in a statement. “My office is fully committed to rooting out abuses of the SNAP program and holding accountable criminal con artists and scammers who appallingly seek to profit by stealing taxpayer money meant to feed vulnerable Americans.”
New was previously arrested in 2022 after he allegedly exposed himself in public.

title: Fans camp out for first foldable iPhone
text:
(WSVN) - Customers waited outside the Apple store in Miami Beach as a line formed Wednesday morning for Apple’s new iPhone Duo, released Friday.
The iPhone Duo is the first foldable iPhone. The new design folds down to approximately the size of a passport.
When unfolded, the Duo becomes the largest iPhone display Apple has ever made.
The larger inner screen lets users run two apps side by side.
The departure from the iPhone’s standard design is what has so many eager to pick up the Duo.
Apple said it will have limited numbers for walk-in customers when it launches.
It also said online orders sold out in minutes, even pushing delivery times for some customers until January.
However, that did not stop anyone from camping out to get an early grab on the new phone.
The iPhone Duo costs $1,999, and it was released at 7 a.m. Friday.

title: Energy experts predict high gas prices will stick around
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Energy experts predict high gas prices will stick around
Oil prices surged to a five-month high following attacks on Saudi Arabian oil refineries and continued bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz this week.
Experts warned that this could mean higher prices at the pump.
Trump said relief is on the way
But on Friday, President Donald Trump downplayed concerns. He suggested the global energy market will soon see relief thanks to more oil shipping out of the Strait of Hormuz.
“Everybody is taking oil out," Trump told reporters before boarding Marine One. "In fact, last week we took more oil out than we have ever taken it out even before the war."
In a response to a Hearst Television inquiry, the White House clarified the president's claim came from ship-tracking company Kpler, which showed increased oil shipments from the Persian Gulf region through alternate routes.
"The increased flow is what happens when a dam or block is relieved," Ed Hirs, an energy fellow at the University of Houston, said. "What has piled up behind the blockage flows out, but it is no guarantee that these 'pre-war flows' can be maintained once the dam is broken. This increase flow for a week does not signal a return to normal at all."
Additional data from the World Trade Organization shows oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz remain far below pre-war levels.
Middle East conflict, instability could push prices higher
Hirs also said more fighting in the Strait of Hormuz, attacks on Middle Eastern energy facilities, and reported plans for the U.S. to resume strikes on Iran after the midterm elections will only add to already high energy prices.
“We’re not out of the woods even if peace breaks out today," Hirs said. "It’s going to be many, many months before the production facilities in the Middle East can be restored."
The Russia diesel deal will do little to help, experts said
Meanwhile, Russia has confirmed its first diesel tanker is enroute to the U.S., as part of a deal brokered by Trump to export diesel to help lower prices.
Still, experts argued that the expected diesel shipments will have little impact on global supply.
U.S. drivers are paying more across the board
A Get the Facts Data Team analysis found that drivers across the U.S. have seen gas prices increase since the start of the war.
According to the findings, drivers in more than 20 states are now paying at least 50% more at the pump. Utah has experienced the largest spike, with prices up by 70%, Oklahoma at more than 60%, and California at around 30%.
The Strategic Petroleum Reserve is no longer a reliable buffer
Hirs said tapping into the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve to ease prices is no longer a viable option for the country, as the reserve has been depleted to a record low.
The reserve is considered an emergency supply used to help stabilize global oil prices.
Hirs argued the U.S. government should stop intervening in the free market and allow high prices to incentivize U.S. oil companies to increase drilling and possibly bring energy prices back down again.

title: Aiden Gagnon, Ellie Cyr Win Week Seven Athlete of the Week
text:
Madawaska’s Gagnon and Wisdom’s Cyr Win Fall Week Seven Athletes of the Week
The votes are in, and Aiden Gagnon of Madawaska and Ellie Cyr of Wisdom are your Fall Week Seven Athletes of the Week.
Gagnon takes the boys honor after putting together a big offensive week for the Madawaska Owls, while Cyr earns the girls award following another high-scoring stretch for the Wisdom Pioneers.
The two emerged from a Week Seven ballot featuring 14 Aroostook County athletes, with seven boys and seven girls receiving recognition for their performances.

title: Beverley A. (Bryant) Hurst
text:
Beverley A. (Bryant) Hurst, 91, passed away peacefully on Oct. 21, 2026 at The Current in Beverly, Mass., where she lived for her final two years. She was a longtime, cherished resident of Delaware, Ohio, and later Pemaquid.
Born on Nov. 23, 1934 in Bedford County, Pa., Beverley was the daughter of the late Bertrand E. and Mary C. (MacKinnon) Bryant. She grew up in Colebrook, N.H., graduating from Colebrook Academy in 1952, and later earned her degree from Plymouth Teachers College in 1956. Shortly after graduation, on July 22, 1956, she married her beloved husband, Bernard B. Hurst.
Beverley was a dedicated educator who spent 30 years teaching elementary school in Delaware, Ohio, shaping the minds and hearts of generations of children with patience and care. Following her teaching career, she and Bernard enjoyed their retirement together in Delaware. In 2014, following Bernard’s passing, Beverley moved to Pemaquid — returning to the beautiful coastal area where her father grew up. She was a longtime member of the Order of Eastern Star, Chapters in both Colebrook, N.H. and Delaware, Ohio.
Her love, warmth, and legacy live on through her large and adoring family. She is survived by her daughter, Janet B. Hurst and her husband, Tom Goodnight, of Columbia Station, Ohio; her son, Jon B. Hurst and his wife, Jan Hurst, of Beverly, Mass.; her brother, Bruce Bryant and his wife, Dianne, of Citra, Fla.; her eight cherished grandchildren; her nine great-grandchildren; nieces, nephews, and cousins. She was predeceased by her husband, Bernard in 2009; by her parents; and a brother, Bertrand E. Bryant in 2020.
Visitation will be held Nov. 7, 2026 from 10-11 a.m. at the Bryant Funeral Home, at 180 Hillside Ave. in Berlin, N.H. A funeral service will follow the visitation at 11 a.m. in the funeral home. Interment will be in the Lary Cemetery in Gorham, N.H.
In lieu of flowers, memorial contributions may be made in Beverley’s honor to any of the following organizations that held meaning in her life journey: William Street United Methodist Church in Delaware, Ohio; The New Harbor United Methodist Church in New Harbor; or to Care Dimensions in Danvers, Mass.
Online guestbook at bryantfuneralhome.net.

title: Midcoast high school cancels classes after teacher dies
text:
Classes were canceled at Oceanside High School on Friday after a teacher’s death.

title: The Israeli army says 2 soldiers were killed in West Bank attack
text:
JERUSALEM (AP) — The Israeli army says two soldiers were killed in an attack in the occupied West Bank on Friday morning that also left two suspected gunmen dead in violence that is likely to heighten political tensions and security concerns ahead of Israel’s parliamentary election next week.
The army said two soldiers, Staff Sgt. Ron Yonatan Roytman and Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem, were killed and three others were lightly wounded during an attack by Palestinian gunmen. The attack took place near the Yehuda Junction outside the West Bank city of Hebron.
The army said it had prevented a “terror attack against Israeli civilians” and that the two suspects, both Palestinians from Hebron, were armed with an M16 rifle and a handgun.
It said the men arrived at an Israeli military position in the morning, triggering an exchange of fire lasting approximately 20 minutes, after which the gunmen were killed by Israeli troops. The army said its forces prevented the men from advancing further where the attack could have resulted in civilian casualties.
The military set up roadblocks and closures in Palestinian towns in the area.
Israeli voters will decide next Tuesday whether to grant Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu yet another term as prime minister — or usher in a new era of Israeli politics. The election comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza.
Israel’s government has warned of potential attacks by the country’s “enemies” in the lead-up to the election.
Netanyahu holds an emergency meeting
Netanyahu’s office said it had instructed security forces to immediately cordon off Hebron and prepare for a full closure of the West Bank, starting Friday.
The prime minister also held an emergency meeting of his Security Cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies, blaming Hamas for Friday’s attack.
“Our brave soldiers thwarted this attack with courage and determination,” he said, without elaborating on what the planned attack entailed.
“I commend them for their actions and wish our wounded a speedy recovery,” he added.
Earlier Friday, Israel’s far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for extremist views, said that the attack shows that Israel needs to restrict the Palestinians’ freedom of movement in the West Bank.
“The lives of the residents of Judea and Samaria, of the settlers, the lives of the soldiers, the lives of the police officers, the lives of our fighters are a million times more important than freedom of movement,” he said, using an Israeli reference to the West Bank.
Dozens are arrested in West Bank security operations
Following the shooting on Friday, the army said soldiers and Israeli security and intelligence agencies conducted dozens of operations in the West Bank and apprehended dozens of people, including those affiliated with Hamas and Islamic Jihad militant groups.
It also said it had located weapons, including M16 rifles and submachine guns.
Eyal Zamir, the Israeli army’s chief of staff, said a “large quantity of ammunition was found” in a vehicle used by the gunmen.
“This ammunition was intended to be used in a larger-scale attack,” he added.
Palestinian life is ‘impossible,’ says US congressional candidate
Closures of the West Bank are becoming more common. It was the fourth time in the past month that Israel had imposed restrictions across the territory, shutting gates and checkpoints connecting Palestinian villages to major roads.
Roads in the territory remain open to Israeli drivers, including settlers, who can still travel through the area but may face delays.
U.S Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander, who was in the West Bank on Friday, said the Israeli army’s closure following the attack was an example of Israel enforcing an apartheid system on Palestinians.
“It’s part of the effort to take more control, to make Palestinian life impossible,” Lander, who was detained by Israeli forces on Wednesday, said in an interview.
Yishai Fleisher, an international spokesperson for Hebron’s Jewish community and a political candidate for the far-right Otzma Yehudit, or Jewish Power, party, said Israel had the right to defend itself from a “hostile majority.”
“We are tired of the weapons and the brainwashing and incitement that is next door,” he said.

title: Vance intensifies rapidly and could become a major Category 3 hurricane
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Hurricane Vance rapidly strengthened into a Category 2 storm Friday as it neared Mexico’s Pacific Coast, the National Hurricane Center said.
Vance had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (170 kph) as it churned about 425 miles (685 kilometers) south-southwest of Acapulco, according to an advisory from the Miami-based hurricane center.
It could become a major Category 3 hurricane before the end of Friday, the center said.
It was moving northwest at about 5 mph (8 kph), and this motion is expected to continue through the weekend, approaching the Puerto Vallarta area by Monday. The hurricane’s outer bands were already funneling gale-force winds and rough seas into Mexico’s Gulf of Tehuantepec, the center said.
It’s been an intense hurricane season in the Pacific Ocean, with storms spawning in assembly-line fashion near Hawaii and Mexico as El Niño conditions worsened by global warming create unusual weather, like this week’s severe flooding and tornadoes hitting the southwestern United States and the prolonged drought in Central America’s Dry Corridor.
Vance would be the seventh major hurricane in a row this year in the Pacific, following Nolo, Odalys, Polo, Rachel, Simon and Trudy. The World Meteorological Organization’s Hurricane Committee doesn’t use less common names beginning with Q and U.

title: Fox shot near Bath Iron Works tests positive for rabies
text:

Fox shot near Bath Iron Works gate tests positive for rabies
Bath officials warn residents to avoid contact with wild animals and ensure their pets are vaccinated
A fox that was shot near Bath Iron Works has tested positive for rabies, according to city officials.
The City of Bath said Thursday that the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention notified officials that a fox recently shot by a game warden near the shipyard's south gate tested positive for the virus.
Officials urge residents to take precautions to protect themselves, their families and their pets.
Residents are encouraged to avoid contact with wild or stray animals, secure garbage and pet food.
Pet owners are urged to make sure their animals are up to date on rabies vaccinations.
Anyone bitten or scratched by an animal should immediately wash the affected area with soap and water and seek medical attention.
Anyone who sees an animal behaving strangely is encouraged to contact the Bath Police Department at 207-443-5563 or dispatch at 207-443-9711.

title: Bangor police use drone to help find missing woman
text:
The Bangor Police Department used an aerial drone to help find a missing woman on Thursday.
Police were called to City Forest shortly before 3 p.m. after relatives reported the woman missing. There were concerns for her wellbeing if she wasn’t found before dark because temperatures were expected to fall overnight, the department said.
The search included K9 teams from the Maine Warden Service, the Bangor Police Department’s Unmanned Aircraft System Team, and the Bangor Fire Department.
When a warden was able to hear the missing woman but not find her, the drone operator was able to pinpoint her location, according to Bangor police.
The woman was taken to an area hospital for evaluation and treatment, police said.

title: State plans public hearing on Central Maine Healthcare in Lewiston as concerns over Prime’s ownership deepen
text:
The state will hold a public hearing to determine whether Prime Healthcare Foundation is meeting staffing and care standards in operating Central Maine Healthcare, which includes Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston and several other facilities.
State Rep. Julie McCabe, D-Lewiston, requested the hearing in a letter Monday to the Maine Department of Health and Human Services. Over the past year, the state health department required Prime Healthcare Foundation, a nonprofit based in California, to make several commitments to maintain essential health services, safe patient volumes and trauma center status at Central Maine Healthcare before it could acquire the health system.
Compliance with those agreements is being called into question.
“The people of Lewiston deserve a hospital system that is safely managed and adequately staffed, that upholds the agreements entered into with the state of Maine, and that follows the laws of the state,” McCabe wrote. “Based on the many conversations I have had with healthcare providers and patients, it is my belief that Prime Healthcare is not currently abiding by their (agreement).”
A public hearing is “an appropriate step,” said Lindsay Hammes, Maine DHHS spokesperson, in an email Thursday. She said it will be scheduled in the next several weeks.
Central Maine Healthcare includes hospitals in Bridgton and Rumford and a number of physician practices. McCabe said changes at the health system, including workforce attrition, sterilization equipment issues and the premature termination of a contract with an emergency department physician group, which staffed 35 providers across the three hospitals, pose a “clear and present danger” to patients.
State officials have acknowledged the Lewiston hospital did not meet a requirement earlier this month intended to verify progress toward reestablishing trauma center status, a designation that lapsed before Prime took over — leaving just two destinations in Maine for around-the-clock emergency surgery.
EARLY TERMINATION
Central Maine Healthcare notified BlueWater Health last month that it was terminating early its three-year contract to staff three emergency departments in the Lewiston, Bridgton and Rumford hospitals, effective Jan. 12.
The departments were short 17 physicians and relying heavily on locum tenens, or temporary providers, when the Brunswick-based physician group signed the three-year contract in early 2025, said Dr. Jay Mullen, CEO of BlueWater Health. The group has since filled those vacancies and recruited 18 more physicians, nurses and physician assistants to Central Maine Healthcare.
Mullen said it’s difficult to retain board-certified emergency physicians because they can get jobs anywhere in the country, “so rural areas are always struggling.” Most of their recruits to Maine came from out of state.
With the termination, Mullen said 80% of the 35 providers will leave Central Maine Healthcare when their contract ends in January. Two-thirds will take roles elsewhere with BlueWater Health, which he said staffs emergency departments across New England and which recently signed a contract with St. Mary’s Regional Medical Center in Lewiston. Others are moving out of state.
One emergency department physician leaving the health system for another role with BlueWater Health, who asked to remain unnamed, said instability is driving her away.
“There is some fatigue of the chaos that seems to kind of be currently encircling Central Maine,” she said, “a lot of loss of the medical staff and nursing changes. I think a lot of members of my group would agree with me that people feel that they need to step away from Central Maine.”
A Central Maine Healthcare spokesperson said the health system is in ongoing discussions with BlueWater Health and Vituity, a California-based emergency physician group. “Regardless of the outcome of these negotiations,” the spokesperson said, “most physicians that have provided ED services at Central Maine Healthcare will have the opportunity to continue to do so with the firm that is selected.”
McCabe, the Lewiston lawmaker, said it was negligent for Central Maine Healthcare to terminate the BlueWater Health contract with only a few months notice and no arrangement to “fill the void.”
Hospitals are required by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to report the rate of emergency department visitors who leave without being seen by a physician. More than a year into the BlueWater contract, Central Maine Healthcare’s rate dropped from 7.2% to 3.5%. In the past three months, it’s climbed back up to 5.7%, according to data shared by McCabe and verified by Mullen.
The national benchmark is 2%.
“When you have increased wait times, people leave without being seen, and that doesn’t mean that they’re not sick. It just means that they gave up,” McCabe said. “And when you have those kinds of repeated interactions at the ED, you’re going to lose faith in your healthcare system.”
TRAUMA CENTER IN LIMBO
Maine’s health department regulates how ownership acquisitions, mergers and other major healthcare changes can happen in Maine, and by who.
To acquire Central Maine Healthcare, Prime Healthcare Foundation needed the state’s approval. One challenge: CMMC let its level three trauma center designation lapse in December 2025, a month after the state made it a mandatory condition of the acquisition.
The loss of a trauma center in Lewiston has impacted patients — sometimes with life-threatening conditions — who had to travel farther to reach the other trauma centers in Portland and Bangor. It’s also uprooted dozens of EMS agencies and increased trauma patient volumes at the other hospitals.
The state approved Prime Healthcare Foundation’s acquisition of the Maine health system earlier this year, but with the condition that CMMC must regain full trauma status by 2028. The hospital was also required to obtain a trauma manager — the person who leads the center and communicates with other hospitals ― by Oct. 2.
Hammes said on Oct. 6 that CMMC had made an offer to a candidate for the trauma manager position but that “hiring has not yet been completed.” The department, she said, “will be closely monitoring the outcome of the offer to assess compliance with the condition.”
On Thursday, she said the state had not received an update about the status of the offer and could not verify compliance.
A CMMC spokesperson has not responded to questions about the trauma manager requirement.
“We should be one of three trauma hospitals in the state, and from every indication, Prime doesn’t seem like they want that responsibility,” McCabe said. “I think our community is going to be, frankly, in danger if they are not able to adequately staff the emergency department, which provides life or death care.”
“We have many ER physicians who are very knowledgeable and interested in the care of trauma patients,” the BlueWater physician said. “I hope that there isn’t decreased momentum to gaining the level three trauma designation due to the departure of ER physicians who were ready and willing to be participatory in that process.”
Oct. 25 will mark the anniversary of the Lewiston mass shootings, which left 18 dead and more than a dozen wounded on a Wednesday night three years ago.
“On that night and in the days that followed, our teams demonstrated the critical role our hospitals and emergency services play in this community,” a CMMC spokesperson said. “We remain deeply proud of the extraordinary care they provided and mindful of our responsibility to be here for our communities every day.”
That night, it was trauma manager Tammy Lachance who made the call to secure blood from nearby hospitals, which “contributed in great measure to the survival of our operative patients,” said Dr. Richard King, a former CMMC trauma surgeon who responded to the emergency department within minutes of the shooting along with 30 other surgeons.
Lachance died after a battle with cancer last year. King hopes she is honored at CMMC this week.
It pains him to see the degradation of the trauma program they built, he said.
“Tammy was more than that one night,” King said. “She was the heart and soul of that trauma program for many years.”

title: Consolidation is worsening Maine’s rural Healthcare crisis
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Jabbar Fazeli is an independent medical provider and president of Maine Geriatrics LLC.
Maine is steadily losing its independent primary care and rural healthcare infrastructure. Small hospitals, nursing homes, and rehabilitation facilities have closed or are struggling to survive. Independent primary care practices — the backbone of community medicine — are disappearing as well.
Although inadequate Medicare and MaineCare reimbursement contribute to these losses, another cause receives far less attention: a healthcare system increasingly structured to favor large healthcare organizations over smaller independent providers.
The consequences extend beyond economics. They affect access to care, whether older adults can remain near their families, and whether patients retain meaningful freedom to choose their providers.
In 2013, Pittsfield Rehab & Nursing provided long-term care while maintaining a limited number of skilled rehabilitation beds. Rehabilitation revenue helped offset inadequate MaineCare reimbursement. The facility needed just one skilled rehabilitation referral per month to remain financially viable.
Yet local residents discharged from hospitals were frequently referred to hospital-affiliated rehabilitation facilities instead.
During Maine’s 126th Legislature, I advocated for LD 447, An Act To Increase Patient Choice in Health Care Facilities and Health Care Settings, which became law in 2013 despite opposition from major organizations.
The legislation sought to strengthen patient choice in post-hospital care, require disclosure of certain financial interests, and give nursing facility medical directors a voice in the care policies of corporate-owned facilities.
Despite these protections, Pittsfield Rehab & Nursing closed in 2014, citing financial pressures. Residents were displaced, and families faced longer drives to visit their loved ones.
Its closure illustrates how inadequate reimbursement, combined with structural disadvantages facing independent providers, can devastate rural healthcare. In my view, the promise of LD 447 remains largely unrealized. Legislation is only as effective as its implementation.
Large healthcare systems increasingly own or affiliate with hospitals, physician practices, rehabilitation facilities, home health agencies, hospice services, and specialty practices.
Although vertical integration can improve coordination, it also creates potential financial conflicts. When an organization recommends a service from which it profits, patients may not receive a complete picture of their options.
Patients deserve information about appropriate alternatives, including independent local providers, as well as disclosure of relevant financial relationships. Independent providers cannot compete fairly when referrals are steered toward affiliated entities.
I believe Maine must examine whether patient-choice protections are being followed and adequately enforced. Choice must be genuine, not merely a procedural exercise to satisfy legal requirements.
Independent primary care physicians coordinate treatment, manage multiple conditions, and help patients avoid unnecessary testing, procedures, and specialist visits. Their independence helps keep clinical decisions focused on patients’ needs rather than institutional financial interests.
Yet independent practices face mounting administrative costs, complex reporting requirements, and reimbursement systems that favor organizations with dedicated billing and compliance departments.
The elimination of Medicare’s 10% primary care incentive removed an important source of support. Meanwhile, the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) added administrative burdens, turning reimbursement into an annual exercise in metrics reporting and penalty avoidance.
Large healthcare organizations can distribute these costs across departments. Small practices cannot.
As independent practices disappear, communities lose local providers, competition, and independent voices in healthcare policy. Two decades of healthcare reforms have contributed to this imbalance without delivering the promised cost savings.
Independent physicians are the canary in the coal mine: their disappearance signals a healthcare system becoming less accessible, less competitive, and less patient-centered.
Maine’s rural healthcare debate must extend beyond reimbursement rates. I urge policymakers to examine referral patterns, enforce patient-choice and financial-disclosure protections, and ensure that independent providers can compete fairly on a level playing field. They must also recognize that current regulatory and payment requirements disproportionately burden smaller practices.
Large healthcare systems remain essential, but when a handful of organizations dominate regional markets, competition weakens, patient choice narrows, and costs may rise. Regional monopolies should be no less concerning in healthcare than in other industries.
Consolidation is often presented as synonymous with efficiency. But efficient for whom? Organizational savings do not necessarily translate into lower overall costs, better access, or improved outcomes.
Once a rural facility closes or an independent practice disappears, rebuilding that capacity can be difficult, if not impossible.
Maine’s challenge is not simply how much we are willing to spend. It is whether we will preserve a healthcare system in which patients have meaningful choices, communities retain local access to care, and independent physicians and small facilities can survive — and perhaps even thrive.
By the time Mainers fully recognize what has been lost, it may be too late.
